MZ-008 · R02.03

The Sink and Dishwashing Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Empty sink, dry basin”

The Empty Sink Standard: 6S for the Sink and Dishwashing Zone

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Close on one pan sitting in the basin under grey water, then a second dish joining it, then a third. Name the problem: soaking is the word a kitchen uses for postponing, and one soaking pan gives every other dish permission to join it. The call this zone turns on is not what to keep, it is whether the basin is allowed to be a staging area, and what deadline a pan actually gets.

Sort Everything comes out from under the sink, because that cabinet has been collecting what does not belong in a damp space.
Beats
  • Pull every bottle and box out from under the sink and line them up on the floor where they can be counted.
  • Combine the three half empty bottles of the same spray into one, and bin what has separated or lost its label.
  • Move out anything that is not dish, sink, or plumbing related, the spare bulbs, the paper goods, the vase, on the grounds that a damp cabinet under a working trap is the wrong home for them.
  • End on one tray holding dish soap, dishwasher tablets, and one all-purpose cleaner, with the pipes visible around it.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, cabinet doors open on the full contents
  • Overhead, everything lined up on the floor on a towel
  • Close, two matching sprays combined into one bottle
  • Three-quarter, the single tray going back with the pipes visible behind it
On-screen text
  • Everything out, onto the floor
  • Dish, sink, or plumbing only
Short cut · 45–60s The cabinet under a kitchen sink is emptied onto the floor, and three half empty bottles of the same spray line up next to each other.
Stands alone: Say this is the under sink cabinet and that damp storage next to the pipes is why the category rule is this narrow.
Straighten Everything at this basin has to work for one wet hand.
Beats
  • Put the soap and the brush in a caddy that lifts with one wet hand, and wipe the counter underneath in the same motion.
  • Move the dishwasher tablets into a container beside the machine rather than across the room in a cupboard.
  • Fit a towel bar within reach of somebody already standing at the basin with wet hands, showing the reach from that standing position.
Shots
  • Close, caddy lifted with one wet hand and the surface wiped beneath
  • Three-quarter, tablet container placed beside the dishwasher
  • Close, hand reaching the towel without stepping away from the basin
On-screen text
  • Liftable with one wet hand
  • Tablets beside the machine
Short cut · 30–45s A soap caddy at a kitchen sink lifts with one wet hand and the counter under it gets wiped in the same motion.
Stands alone: Establish the sink zone and the one wet hand test, which is the only rule this Short needs.
Shine The sponge and the dishwasher filter, which is why the glasses come out gritty.
Beats
  • Wring the sponge out and stand it on edge, noting that it only dries on edge and that it retires the day it smells while dry.
  • Scrub the drain flange and wipe the rubber seal all the way around the dishwasher door, into the folds.
  • Twist the dishwasher filter out of the machine floor and rinse it, showing what comes off a filter that has never been removed since fitting.
  • Wipe the basin dry at the end so the finished state is visible, not merely clean.
Shots
  • Macro, sponge wrung and stood on edge in a drainer
  • Close, brush working the drain flange
  • Close, filter twisted out of the dishwasher floor and rinsed under the tap
  • Overhead, basin wiped dry and holding nothing
On-screen text
  • Stand it on edge
  • Pull the filter, it comes out
Short cut · 45–60s A cylinder twists out of the floor of a dishwasher, and what rinses off it explains why the glasses have been coming out gritty.
Stands alone: Show where the filter sits and how it releases, since many viewers do not know their machine has one.
Safety Bleach and ammonia never share this cabinet or this basin, and this is the kitchen cabinet that earns a latch. This is the 4th S.
Beats
  • Separate the bleach from any ammonia or toilet cleaner, capping both and turning the labels out, and name the gas that will drive you out of the room if they meet in the basin.
  • Give each a fixed position at opposite ends of the tray so the separation is visible rather than remembered.
  • Move the kettle, the socket adapter, and any charging phone back out of splash distance of the basin, as this zone's water and electricity question.
  • Fit a latch if small children live here or visit, and make the point that this is the one kitchen cabinet that genuinely earns one. Cross-reference Chapter 21, the hazard hunt.
Shots
  • Close, two bottles moved apart on the tray with labels turned out
  • Macro, capped lids and the gap between them
  • Three-quarter, charging phone and kettle moved back from the basin edge
  • Close, latch fitted and tested on the cabinet door
On-screen text
  • Safety is the 4th S
  • Never in the same basin
Short cut · 30–45s Two cleaning bottles are walked to opposite ends of a tray under a sink, and the reason is a gas, not tidiness.
Stands alone: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and name the two product types, bleach and ammonia, plainly at the start.
Standardize The empty sink standard gets written down where the zone can see it.
Beats
  • Write the standard on a card by hand: dishes in the machine or washed, basin wiped, brush standing, towel hung.
  • Tape the card inside the cabinet door and check the zone against it line by line on camera.
  • Land the frozen line as the card goes up, that a standard is the best way you know today, written down. Cross-reference Chapter 23.
Shots
  • Macro, the card being written by hand
  • Close, card taped inside the cabinet door
  • Overhead, zone matching the card line by line
On-screen text
  • Written down, not remembered
  • A standard is the best way you know today
Short cut · 30–45s Four lines get written on a card and taped inside the cabinet door under a sink: dishes done, basin wiped, brush standing, towel hung.
Stands alone: Read the four items of the standard on screen, since the Short cannot rely on anything shown earlier.
Sustain Two moments hold this zone: the last light off at night, and the coffee brewing in the morning.
Beats
  • At the end of the night, empty the basin and wipe it dry before the kitchen light goes off, shot as one linked sequence ending on the switch.
  • In the morning, while the coffee brews, check and clear the sink, using time that is already being spent waiting.
  • Show why the soaking deadline works: it names a moment, the end of the current wash cycle or the next time you leave the room, and moments arrive on their own.
Shots
  • Close, basin wiped dry, then the light switch
  • Close, coffee brewing with the sink in the same frame
  • Overhead, an empty dry basin in morning light
On-screen text
  • Light off, basin dry
  • Coffee brews, sink gets cleared
Short cut · 30–45s The last two actions before a kitchen light goes off at night: the basin emptied, then wiped dry.
Stands alone: Name both triggers up front, the light going off and the coffee brewing, since the pairing is the whole idea.
Close

Hold the finished zone: empty sink, dry basin, one brush and one sponge standing, cleaners on a single tray with the plumbing visible behind them, bleach and ammonia at opposite ends. Then the trigger, coffee brewing while the sink is checked and cleared, so the standard is shown being kept rather than achieved once.

Next: Look up from the drying rack to the cabinets above it, and to the mug count nobody in the house wants to do.

Shot list
  • Overhead locked off on the basin, for before and after
  • Three-quarter at sink height for caddy, towel, and reach moves
  • Wide three-quarter on the open under-sink cabinet, bounce card lit
  • Overhead on the floor lay-out of everything from under the sink
  • Macro on sponge, drain flange, and door gasket folds
  • Close on the dishwasher filter twisting out and rinsing
  • Macro on the standard card being written and taped
  • Close on the coffee brewing with the sink in frame
Description hook

A sink you can see the bottom of makes every other kitchen decision obvious. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, plus an honest deadline for how long a pan is allowed to soak.

6Skitchen sink organisationdishwasher filterunder sink storagekitchen cleaninghome organisationcleaning safety6S Success
MZ-009 · R02.04

The Upper Cabinets

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Count the mugs honestly”

6S for Upper Kitchen Cabinets: Mugs, Plates, and the Second Set of Dishes

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Overhead on two sets of dishes sharing the same eye level shelf, the everyday one and the good one, or the one from before you moved. Name the problem: both sets are being stored at the height you reach into daily, and then the cabinet gets blamed for being full. The call this zone turns on is the second set, and it is decided by whether anyone has actually eaten off it.

Sort Count the mugs, then count the people who drink from them.
Beats
  • Take every mug in the house out and line them up in a grid, then line up one mug per person who actually drinks from them in a second row beneath.
  • Pull the conference giveaway, the chipped one, and the one nobody ever chooses, using the chips and crazed glaze as the easy calls that shorten the argument about the rest.
  • Move to the second set of dishes and size one everyday set to the people who eat here plus two.
  • Make the second set call on camera. Not on a table in two years and nobody has asked to inherit it, it goes now, whole, somewhere it will be used. Genuinely inherited, then sentiment keeps the objects but not the daily shelf: boxed, labelled, stored outside the kitchen.
Shots
  • Overhead, every mug lined up in a grid on the counter
  • Overhead, second row showing one mug per drinker
  • Macro, a chip and a crazed glaze line under raking light
  • Three-quarter, the second set boxed and labelled
On-screen text
  • Mugs out, all of them
  • Everyday set, people here plus two
Short cut · 45–60s Every mug in a house comes out onto the counter in a grid, then a second row underneath shows one mug per person who drinks from them.
Stands alone: Set up the two row comparison in the first seconds, since the grid means nothing without the row underneath.
Straighten Daily dishes live between shoulder and eye height, and height is decided by frequency.
Beats
  • Put the dinner plates and everyday bowls at eye level on the side nearest the dishwasher or the table, with the glasses beside them.
  • Cap plate stacks at about six high and check that every mug lifts without moving another mug, demonstrating both.
  • Send the serving platters and the punch bowl to the top shelf, treating a step stool once a year as an honest cost.
  • Keep one category per stack, which is what makes the shelf readable from the doorway.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, plates going to eye level on the dishwasher side
  • Close, a mug lifted cleanly without disturbing its neighbour
  • High three-quarter from a raised tripod, platters going onto the top shelf
  • Close, a plate stack counted to its cap
On-screen text
  • Daily between shoulder and eye
  • One category per stack
Short cut · 30–45s A mug is lifted out of a packed cabinet row without touching a single one beside it, which is the whole test for the shelf.
Stands alone: Explain the shoulder to eye height rule and the one mug lift test before the lift, or it looks arbitrary.
Shine Take the shelf completely empty first, because the dust band behind the plates is the finding.
Beats
  • Empty a shelf entirely rather than sliding the stacks aside, then show the band of dust at the back in raking light and what it says about the last time it was cleared.
  • Wipe the shelf front to back and lift the liner, then clean the ring where a mug has been standing in one spot and the sticky patch on the shelf edge.
  • Wipe the underside of the cabinet nearest the hob, showing the greasy film that only appears when you look up at it from an angle.
Shots
  • Close, shelf emptied and the dust band revealed at the back
  • Macro, cloth pass across the dust band and a mug ring on the liner
  • Low angle from below, greasy film on the cabinet underside in raking light
On-screen text
  • Empty the shelf, do not slide
  • Look at it from an angle
Short cut · 30–45s A cabinet shelf is emptied instead of shuffled, and a clean line of dust at the back shows exactly where the plates have been sitting.
Stands alone: Say which cabinet this is and that emptying completely is the pass itself, not a preference.
Safety Heavy and breakable do not belong above head height, and the step stool is not optional. This is the 4th S.
Beats
  • Bring the casserole stack or the cast iron lid down from overhead with two hands, naming it as the fall, cut, or crush question, and rehome it low.
  • Move the glassware out of any position at or above head height, since it fails onto a hard floor and onto whoever opened the door.
  • Show the three improvised standing surfaces this cabinet invites, a chair edge, the counter lip, and an open drawer front, filmed on feet and edges only, then replace all three with a real step stool.
  • Store the step stool where it can be reached in one move, because a stool that is awkward to get out is a stool nobody uses.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, heavy dish lowered from overhead with two hands, wrists down only
  • Close, glassware relocated from head height to a low shelf
  • Close on a chair edge and an open drawer front, framed below the ankles, then a proper stool in their place
  • Three-quarter, step stool in its storage position
On-screen text
  • Safety is the 4th S
  • Never a chair, never a drawer front
Short cut · 30–45s A cast iron lid comes down from a shelf above head height with two hands, and the weight of it tells the story on its own.
Stands alone: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and give the height rule, nothing heavy above head, before the lift.
Standardize Label the shelf edge, not the contents, so anyone can put away correctly without asking.
Beats
  • Write four shelf edge labels, plates, bowls, glasses, mugs, and fix them to the edge rather than to any item.
  • Have a household member's hands unload a clean dishwasher against those labels, filmed wrists down in a locked off frame, with nothing asked.
  • Draw the difference: labelling contents describes what happens to be there, labelling the edge decides what belongs there. Cross-reference Chapter 14, visual controls.
Shots
  • Macro, label being written and pressed onto the shelf edge
  • Three-quarter, cabinet open with all four edges labelled
  • Close, a second pair of hands putting a plate away without hesitation, wrists down only
On-screen text
  • Label the edge, not the item
  • See Chapter 14, visual controls
Short cut · 30–45s Four labels go onto four shelf edges in one cabinet: plates, bowls, glasses, mugs.
Stands alone: Show all four categories on screen, since the labels are the entire content of this Short.
Sustain Emptying the dishwasher is the check, and a homeless clean plate is the signal.
Beats
  • Empty a clean dishwasher and put everything away against the labelled edges as the routine check.
  • Hold a clean plate that has nowhere obvious to go, and read it as the shelf being over its limit rather than as a storage problem.
  • Make the point that this adds no step, because the dishwasher already gets emptied every day.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, dishwasher opened and unloading begins
  • Close, a plate hovering with no space to go into
  • Overhead, the shelf at its limit
On-screen text
  • Nowhere to put it means over the limit
  • Every time the dishwasher gets emptied
Short cut · 30–45s A clean plate hovers in front of a full cabinet shelf with nowhere to go, and that pause is the whole check.
Stands alone: Name the trigger, unloading the dishwasher, and the limit rule immediately, or the hovering plate reads as ordinary.
Close

Hold the finished cabinet: daily dishes between shoulder and eye height, one category per stack, no plate stack more than about six, every mug liftable without moving another, top shelf holding only what you use less than monthly. Then the trigger, the dishwasher opened and emptied against the labelled edges.

Next: Now go down, to the cabinet where the pans live three deep and you lift two to reach the third.

Shot list
  • Overhead locked off on the counter grid for the mug count
  • Three-quarter at cabinet height for placement and lifting moves
  • Close inside the cabinet, bounce card lit, for the dust band and shelf edges
  • Low angle from below the cabinet for the greasy underside
  • Macro on chips, crazed glaze, and shelf edge labels
  • Three-quarter on the step stool in use, framed below the ankles
  • Close on a second pair of hands unloading the dishwasher, wrists down
  • High three-quarter from a raised tripod onto the top shelf
Description hook

Most kitchens keep two sets of dishes at the height they reach into every day, then blame the cabinet for being full. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, including how to decide the second set honestly.

6Skitchen cabinet organisationupper cabinetsmug declutterdish storagehome organisationkitchen safety6S Success
MZ-010 · R02.05

The Lower Cabinets and Cookware

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Stacks capped at three”

6S for Pots and Pans: Resetting the Lower Cookware Cabinet

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Three frying pans pulled out of a low cabinet and set side by side on the floor, one of them the expensive one nobody ever liked cooking on. Name the problem: the money is already spent and keeping the pan does not bring any of it back, it only costs you the easiest shelf in the kitchen. The call this zone turns on is the cap, the most pans you had going at once in a normal week, plus one.

Sort Everything comes out onto the floor, which is the only way the third saucepan is ever found.
Beats
  • Empty the entire cabinet onto the floor and lay it out so every piece is visible at once, including the wok bought for one weekend.
  • Keep only what actually cooked something in the past year, handling each piece while the decision is made.
  • Show the nonstick pan worn through to the metal in the middle and call it finished rather than a spare, headed for metal recycling instead of the back of the shelf.
  • Do the cap count out loud, the most pans going at once in a normal week plus one, then release the guest pieces that a roasting tray you already own would cover.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, cabinet doors open on the full contents
  • Overhead, everything laid out on the floor in one frame
  • Macro, nonstick worn through to bare metal
  • Close, hands setting the keep pile out against the cap count
On-screen text
  • All of it, onto the floor
  • Most at once in a week, plus one
Short cut · 45–60s A low kitchen cabinet empties onto the floor and a third saucepan appears that nobody knew was still in there.
Stands alone: State the cap rule, most pans going at once in a week plus one, up front, since the floor lay-out only means something against a number.
Straighten Every pan comes out and goes back in one motion, with nothing lifted to reach anything else.
Beats
  • Nest by size but cap any stack at three, with a cloth or a sheet of paper between coated faces.
  • Stand the lids in a rack or on a rail inside the door, cut against loose lids sliding out over the threshold.
  • Put the baking sheets on edge in a divider so you stop lifting three to reach the fourth.
  • Place the two pans you cook with nightly at the front of the cabinet nearest the hob, and run the one motion test on each.
Shots
  • Close, three pans nested with paper between coated faces
  • Three-quarter, lids going into a door rail
  • Overhead, baking sheets standing on edge in a divider
  • Close, a nightly pan out and back in a single unbroken motion
On-screen text
  • Cap the stack at three
  • Out and back in one motion
Short cut · 30–45s The same frying pan is fetched from a low cabinet twice: once by lifting two pans out of the way, once in a single motion.
Stands alone: Establish that this is the low cookware cabinet and that out and back in one motion is the standard being tested.
Shine Clean to inspect: the shelf floor holds oil, and the handles get checked while everything is out.
Beats
  • Wipe the shelf floor itself, showing the tacky film where oil has crept down the outsides of pan bases and held dust, and why a dry cloth will not shift it.
  • Twist every pan handle in turn and tighten any rivet or screw that moves, which is only possible while the cabinet is empty.
  • Return the pieces only once the shelf is dry, so the film does not start again the same day.
Shots
  • Macro, raking light on the tacky film on the shelf floor
  • Close, damp cloth pass showing the difference
  • Macro, a handle twisted loose and a screw driven tight
On-screen text
  • Oil creeps down and holds dust
  • Twist every handle while it is out
Short cut · 30–45s A saucepan handle twists loose in the hand, and a screwdriver fixes in seconds what would otherwise have failed while carrying something hot.
Stands alone: Note that this check only happens while the cookware cabinet is emptied, which is why it belongs to this pass.
Safety Weight goes low, stacks survive a slammed door, and blades never sit loose in a bowl. This is the 4th S.
Beats
  • Move the cast iron and the full stockpot to the cabinet floor, never above waist height, and lift from a squat rather than a bend over the open door.
  • Close the door hard on purpose and watch the stack. If it slides, rebuild it until it survives a slam, since one day it will land on a foot.
  • Find the food processor and blender blades stored loose inside a bowl in the dark, and give them a closed container or a high shelf away from reaching fingers.
  • Restate the finished rule on camera: heaviest pieces on the cabinet floor, nothing sharp loose in the dark.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, stockpot lowered to the cabinet floor, lift from a squat, wrists and below only
  • Close, door closed hard and the stack holding still
  • Macro, a loose blade found inside a bowl in a dark cabinet
  • Close, blades going into a closed container
On-screen text
  • Safety is the 4th S
  • Build the stack to survive a slam
Short cut · 30–45s A cabinet door is slammed on purpose to see whether the stack of pans behind it moves, because one day it will get slammed anyway.
Stands alone: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and make clear the slam is a deliberate test of the stack, not carelessness.
Standardize Slots get sized to the pans you kept and named, so a slot cannot quietly change job.
Beats
  • Size the divider slots to the pans you kept, fitting the skillet, the two saucepans, and the baking sheets as the dividers go in rather than after.
  • Write the pan on the front edge of each slot so the wide skillet slot cannot become the place lids get dropped.
  • Offer a lid to the named skillet slot on camera and have the name turn it away to the door rail.
Shots
  • Overhead, dividers set against the actual pans
  • Macro, pan names written on slot front edges
  • Close, a lid offered to the skillet slot and redirected to the rail
On-screen text
  • Size the slot to the pan
  • Name it on the front edge
Short cut · 30–45s A divider slot in a pan cabinet gets the word skillet written on its front edge, and the lid that tries to move in gets turned away.
Stands alone: Show the named slots first so the redirect at the end reads as a rule and not as a preference.
Sustain The trigger is the drying rack: pans go back to named slots when they come off it.
Beats
  • Take the pans off the drying rack and return each to its named slot as one continuous action rather than a later job.
  • Show the pan that has lived on the hob overnight and read it as evidence that its slot is too hard to reach, then fix the slot.
  • Make the general point that a standard failing in the same place every time is a design problem in the zone, not a discipline problem in the house.
Shots
  • Close, dry pans lifted off the rack
  • Three-quarter, each pan going into its named slot
  • Overhead, a lone pan left on the hob in morning light
On-screen text
  • Off the rack, into its slot
  • A pan left out means fix the slot
Short cut · 30–45s A frying pan has slept on the hob again, and the fix is not a reminder, it is the slot it was supposed to go back into.
Stands alone: Name the trigger, pans coming off the drying rack, and the named slot standard, since the diagnosis needs both.
Close

Hold the finished cabinet: stacks capped at three, lids racked or railed, baking sheets on edge, heaviest pieces on the cabinet floor, and the two nightly pans at the front nearest the hob. Then the one motion test run on three different pieces in a row, and the trigger, pans coming off the drying rack straight into named slots.

Next: Straight above the pans, the shallow drawers, where two can openers and a loose paring knife are sharing a space.

Shot list
  • Wide overhead on the floor lay-out of the whole cabinet
  • Three-quarter at floor level for lifting and stacking moves
  • Close inside the cabinet, bounce card lit, for slot fitting and the shelf film
  • Macro on worn nonstick, loose rivets, and loose blades
  • Close on the one motion retrieval test, repeatable on several pans
  • Locked off on the closed door for the slam test
  • Macro on slot names written on front edges
  • Close on the drying rack handoff into named slots
Description hook

If you lift two pans to reach the third, the cabinet is not full, it is stacked wrong. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, including an honest cap on how many frying pans a kitchen needs.

6Spots and pans storagekitchen cabinet organisationcookware declutterpan storagehome organisationkitchen safety6S Success
MZ-011 · R02.06

The Utensil and Utility Drawers

5–7 min · thumbnail: “One job per drawer”

6S for Kitchen Drawers: Flatware, Wraps, and the Drawer Everyone Calls Junk

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

A drawer that no longer opens fully, jammed on an envelope of screws and the manual for a dead printer. Name the problem: a kitchen is allowed one drawer of small useful things, but the call this zone turns on is whether that drawer gets a name and a divider or stays an amnesty. Everything in it has to be something you would come to the kitchen looking for.

Sort One drawer at a time onto a towel, and only what you have used since the season changed goes back.
Beats
  • Tip a single drawer onto a tea towel with the others kept shut, so the job stays finishable in one sitting.
  • Put back only what has been used since the season changed, handling each item once.
  • Run the duplicates rule on camera: two can openers on the towel means one leaves.
  • Set aside the takeaway chopsticks, the rubber bands, the unlabelled key, and the loose batteries, none of which are cooking tools, and date the box for anything you cannot name a use for while holding it.
Shots
  • Overhead, one drawer tipped onto a tea towel
  • Macro, two identical can openers side by side
  • Close, non-kitchen items being separated out
  • Close, the box being dated on its lid
On-screen text
  • One drawer at a time
  • Two of a thing means one leaves
Short cut · 30–45s One kitchen drawer tips onto a tea towel and two identical can openers land next to each other.
Stands alone: Establish the one drawer at a time rule and the used since the season changed test, both of which the Short depends on.
Straighten Dividers go in before anything else, and the drawer gets named before it gets filled.
Beats
  • Fit the dividers into the empty drawer first, then name the drawer, then fill it, in that order.
  • Place the flatware nearest the dishwasher and the cooking tools nearest the hob, showing the walk each placement removes.
  • Put the measuring spoons and the scale beside the baking cupboard.
  • Stand the foil, the cling film, and the baking paper on end so the boxes read from above, in the drawer you can pull open with one hand while the other holds a dish.
Shots
  • Overhead, dividers going into an empty drawer
  • Close, the drawer named before a single item enters
  • Overhead, wrap boxes standing on end and readable from above
  • Three-quarter, a drawer pulled open one handed while the other hand holds a dish
On-screen text
  • Divider first, name second, fill third
  • Boxes on end, read from above
Short cut · 30–45s A kitchen drawer gets its dividers fitted and its name written before a single object is allowed back in.
Stands alone: Say the order out loud, divider, name, fill, since doing it in reverse is the common mistake.
Shine Lift the insert out, because the grit that jams the drawer is underneath it.
Beats
  • Show the drawer failing to close flush, then lift the divider insert right out and tip the crumbs and grit that were sitting under it onto paper.
  • Wipe both runners and the drawer box itself, including the track the grit has been packing into.
  • Push the drawer once and check it closes flush before refilling it, which is the actual test of this pass.
Shots
  • Close, insert lifted out and grit tipped onto paper
  • Macro, runner track before and after wiping
  • Close, drawer pushed once and closing flush
On-screen text
  • The grit lives under the insert
  • Closes flush with one push
Short cut · 30–45s A kitchen drawer will not close flush, and the divider insert lifts out to show the crumbs that have been jamming it.
Stands alone: Show the drawer failing to close first, so what comes out from under the insert answers a question.
Safety Every blade gets a sheath, a sleeve, or its own tray at the front. This is the 4th S.
Beats
  • Show what a hand meets rummaging in this drawer without looking: the peeler, the loose mandoline blade, and the paring knife lying among the spatulas.
  • Give each blade a sheath, a sleeve, or its own shallow tray at the front of the drawer, where it is seen before anything is reached past it.
  • Collect the loose button batteries out of the utility drawer, framed as the poison, choke, or strangle question, since at this height they are swallowed easily and do serious internal damage fast.
  • Move the batteries into a closed container out of a child's reach, and make that placement part of the drawer's written name.
Shots
  • Close, a hand entering a drawer without looking, wrists and below only
  • Macro, mandoline blade and paring knife loose among spatulas
  • Close, each blade sheathed and set into a front tray
  • Macro, button batteries collected into a closed container
On-screen text
  • Safety is the 4th S
  • Button batteries do not live loose
Short cut · 30–45s A hand goes into a kitchen drawer without looking, and the camera holds on the loose paring knife and mandoline blade waiting in there.
Stands alone: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and name both hazards plainly, loose blades and button batteries.
Standardize The name is the rule, written inside the drawer front.
Beats
  • Write the name inside each drawer front: flatware, cooking tools, wraps and bags, utility.
  • Offer an item that does not match the name at the drawer and have it turned away, which is the whole function of a name.
  • Write the utility drawer's list on the same label, tape, string, a torch, batteries, a working pen, the menus you actually order from, so it stays a category rather than an amnesty.
Shots
  • Macro, name written inside a drawer front
  • Overhead, four drawers open with four names visible
  • Close, an unmatched item refused at the drawer and carried away
On-screen text
  • The name is the rule
  • Write the utility list too
Short cut · 30–45s Four kitchen drawers open in sequence, each with its job written inside the front edge: flatware, cooking tools, wraps and bags, utility.
Stands alone: Read the four names on screen so the closing refusal has something to be refused against.
Sustain The trigger is the shopping being put away.
Beats
  • Put the shopping away and stand the new roll of foil in on end as part of the same trip.
  • Walk back whatever has migrated during the week, the whisk that landed in the flatware insert and the scissors in the wraps drawer, in the same pass.
  • Return to the dated box and hold its deadline: nothing pulled out of it by the end of the season and it leaves unopened.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, shopping bag unpacked with foil going in on end
  • Close, a whisk lifted out of the flatware insert and placed in the cooking tools drawer
  • Close, the dated box on its shelf, then leaving unopened
On-screen text
  • Shopping goes away, drawers reset
  • Nothing used by season end, it leaves
Short cut · 30–45s A new roll of foil goes into a drawer standing on end, and a whisk that has been living in the flatware insert gets walked back to its own drawer.
Stands alone: Name the trigger, putting the shopping away, and the drawer naming standard it enforces.
Close

Open all four drawers in sequence on the finished state: one category per drawer, named inside the front edge, flatware in a divided insert with nothing loose beside it, wraps standing on end and readable, blades sheathed at the front, every drawer closing flush with one push. Then the trigger, the shopping put away and one migrated item walked home.

Next: One appliance left in this kitchen, the refrigerator, and it wants a morning with real time in it.

Shot list
  • Overhead locked off on the counter for the tipped drawer contents
  • Overhead directly down into each open drawer, for before and after
  • Macro on blades, button batteries, and runner grit
  • Close on the divider insert lifting out
  • Close on the drawer closing flush with one push
  • Macro on names being written inside drawer fronts
  • Three-quarter on shopping being unpacked into named drawers
  • Close on the dated box, written and shelved
Description hook

A kitchen gets one drawer of small useful things, but it needs a category and a divider, not an amnesty. Six passes, Sort through Sustain, on the shallow drawers that jam.

MZ-012 · R02.07

The Refrigerator and Freezer

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Name it and date it”

6S Refrigerator and Freezer Reset: Label, Date, and the Eat-First Bin

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Close on a container of perfectly good leftovers being moved to the front of a shelf, again. Name the problem: this is the container you have now shifted forward three times, and the call this zone turns on is a three part question asked at the door, which meal, which day, who eats it. Without an answer, what is being stored is not food, it is the guilt of having cooked too much.

Sort One shelf at a time, judged by the date on the lid rather than by smell.
Beats
  • Work a single shelf at a time with the rest of the door shut, so nothing sits out warming while decisions are being made.
  • Clear anything frozen past recognition and unlabelled, on the grounds that an unidentifiable block is not an ingredient.
  • Judge every opened jar, sauce, and dressing against the date on its lid, since these keep smelling fine long after they should have gone.
  • Make the leftover call on camera, naming the meal, the day, and the person, or it goes today, then fix the cause by portioning into a lunch container the same evening you cook.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, one shelf cleared while the rest stay untouched
  • Macro, an unlabelled frozen block held up
  • Close, the date on a dressing lid read under a bounce card
  • Close, leftovers portioned into a lunch container and dated
On-screen text
  • One shelf at a time
  • Read the lid, not the smell
Short cut · 45–60s A container of good leftovers gets moved to the front of a fridge shelf for the third time, and the camera just holds on the move.
Stands alone: Ask the three part question, which meal, which day, who eats it, in the opening seconds, since that is the whole Short.
Straighten Position inside the fridge is decided by food safety and by what has to be seen first.
Beats
  • Put the raw proteins on the lowest shelf, where a leaking package cannot drip onto anything below it.
  • Move the dairy out of the door and into the body of the fridge, since the door temperature swings every time somebody opens it.
  • Put the produce in the drawers and actually set the humidity slider, which on most fridges has never been moved.
  • Set the eat-first bin at the front at eye level, where the door opens straight onto it.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, raw meat sealed and placed on the lowest shelf
  • Close, dairy moving from the door shelf into the body
  • Macro, humidity slider being set on a crisper drawer
  • Overhead through the open door onto the eat-first bin at eye level
On-screen text
  • Raw meat low and sealed
  • Eat-first bin at the front
Short cut · 30–45s The humidity slider on a fridge crisper drawer gets moved for the first time since the fridge was delivered.
Stands alone: Explain what the slider does and where on the drawer it sits, since the detail is invisible otherwise.
Shine Clean to inspect: drawers out, coils vacuumed, gasket folds wiped.
Beats
  • Pull the crisper drawers right out and carry them two handed to the sink, showing the sticky ring underneath where a forgotten cucumber ended.
  • Vacuum the condenser coils at the back or underneath, and show what a blanket of dust there means for the machine.
  • Wipe the door gasket inside its folds, making the point that a gasket usually fails from grime long before it fails from age.
  • Dry everything before it goes back, so the reset is finished rather than merely wet.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, crisper drawer carried two handed to the sink
  • Macro, the sticky ring under the drawer in raking light
  • Close, vacuum nozzle on the condenser coils
  • Macro, cloth worked into the gasket folds
On-screen text
  • The drawers come all the way out
  • Wipe inside the gasket folds
Short cut · 30–45s A fridge crisper drawer comes all the way out and reveals the sticky ring underneath it that no amount of wiping inside would have reached.
Stands alone: Show that the drawer lifts free and how it releases, since most people only ever slide it in and out.
Safety Raw below ready-to-eat, vents clear, and a thermometer so you know instead of assume. This is the 4th S.
Beats
  • Place the sealed raw meat below the ready-to-eat food and hold the vertical order in frame, the single move that carries most of cross contamination prevention.
  • Show what that order prevents, juices reaching the bagged salad on the shelf beneath, which nobody is going to cook again.
  • Clear the rear vents of anything pressed up against them so the compartment holds its temperature.
  • Put a cheap thermometer on the middle shelf and read it on camera, so the running temperature is known rather than assumed.
  • Move the heavy glass jars off the top door shelf and the top shelf, since they fall onto tile at foot level.
Shots
  • Three-quarter, sealed raw package placed on the lowest shelf below a bowl of salad
  • Macro, rear vents cleared of a pressed-in package
  • Close, thermometer set on the middle shelf and read
  • Close, heavy glass jars moved down from the top door shelf
  • Overhead, the finished vertical order read top to bottom
On-screen text
  • Safety is the 4th S
  • Raw goes below ready-to-eat
Short cut · 30–45s A sealed package of raw meat is placed on the shelf below a bowl of salad, and the camera holds on the order of the two.
Stands alone: State that Safety is the fourth of six passes and explain why below, and not merely apart, is the whole point.
Standardize Nothing goes in without a name and a date, and the tools to do that live on the fridge.
Beats
  • Put a roll of tape and a marker on top of the fridge so labelling never requires a search through a drawer.
  • Label and date a container before it goes in, filmed as one unbroken action from lid to shelf.
  • Land the rule that a container without a name and a date is not stored, it is abandoned. Cross-reference Chapter 24, the checklist.
Shots
  • Close, tape and marker in their spot on top of the fridge
  • Macro, name and date written on a lid
  • Overhead, a shelf of clear containers all named and dated
On-screen text
  • Name it and date it
  • Not labelled means abandoned
Short cut · 30–45s Tape and a marker live on top of the fridge, and a container gets named and dated on the counter before the door is even opened.
Stands alone: Show where the tape and marker live, since the standard fails the moment they are not within reach.
Sustain The trigger is the shopping list, written from the gaps.
Beats
  • Before the shopping list gets written, empty the eat-first bin of anything past.
  • Write the list from the gaps that leaves, with the open fridge and the list in the same frame so the link is obvious.
  • Make the case for the order: the list already gets written every week, and doing it this way round stops you buying what you already own.
Shots
  • Close, eat-first bin pulled forward and cleared
  • Overhead, list written beside the open fridge
  • Macro, a gap on the shelf and the matching line on the list
On-screen text
  • Clear the bin, then write the list
  • Write from the gaps
Short cut · 30–45s A shopping list gets written standing at an open fridge, with the eat-first bin emptied first and the list built from the gaps.
Stands alone: Name the trigger and the eat-first bin at the top, since the order of the two actions is the entire idea.
Close

Hold the finished state with the door open: raw meat sealed on the lowest shelf, leftovers in clear containers at eye level each named and dated, one eat-first bin at the front where the door opens onto it, rear vents clear, the door holding condiments only, nothing in the freezer without a label. Then the trigger, the bin cleared and the list written from the gaps.

Next: That is the kitchen. The series steps through the door into the pantry next, where the same dating rule meets a much longer shelf.

Shot list
  • Three-quarter locked off on the open fridge, bounce card lit, for before and after
  • Overhead on the counter staging area for one shelf at a time
  • Macro on lids, dates, gaskets, and the sticky ring under a drawer
  • Close on the crisper drawers coming out and being washed
  • Close on the condenser coils and the vacuum nozzle
  • Close on the thermometer being set and read on the middle shelf
  • Macro on tape and marker on top of the fridge, and the label being written
  • Overhead on the shopping list beside the open door
Description hook

A leftover that goes into the fridge already assigned to a meal gets eaten. One that goes in undecided is just a decision you postponed. Six passes, Sort through Sustain.

6Srefrigerator organisationfridge resetfood safety at homefreezer organisationleftovershome organisation6S Success

Room 03 of 20

Pantry

5 videos · 30 Shorts
Production noteA pantry is a small, dim, deep box, and that is the shooting problem. Work the contents out onto a kitchen counter or a folding table just outside the door so the sorting happens in daylight, and reserve the in-pantry camera position for matched before and after states only. Window light is the only source, with a white bounce card on the shadow side because pantry interiors go black two shelves in. One tripod covers everything: a clamp head on the door frame for the three-quarter angle, and the centre column reversed over the counter for overheads. No second operator, no lights, no moving camera, so every shot is either a lock-off or a hand-led reveal inside a static frame. Shoot each shelf fully empty once so Straighten and Shine both have a clean plate to cut to. On set: the two-step stool stays in shot and in use for any top shelf reach, glass is handled at chest height or lower with dry hands, any bulging or leaking can is bagged sealed and binned on camera rather than opened for a better shot, and every shelf is wiped and dried fully before anything goes back.
MZ-013 · R03.01

The Dry Goods Shelves

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Open bag, no date”

Pantry Dry Goods Shelves: The Full 6S Reset, Sort to Sustain

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Hands set four part-used bags from the back of the shelf down on the counter in daylight: buckwheat, coarse polenta, rice flour, and one with the date rubbed off. The decision this zone turns on is named plainly, the bag opened for a single recipe and kept ever since because binning food feels wrong and you do still intend to use it. The gap between intending and cooking is stated, and the fourteen day rule is set up as the thing that settles it.

Sort Every bag comes down off this shelf, the already-opened ones get opened and smelled, and the fourteen day rule decides what leaves today.
Beats
  • Strip the shelf bare onto the counter and show why it has to come off in one go, since the buckwheat only surfaces when the cereal boxes in front of it move.
  • Roll open the part-used bags and smell the flour and the oats, cutting to what stale grain and fine webbing look like beside clean grain.
  • Apply the fourteen day rule to each opened bag, opened stock with no named meal inside two weeks leaves now.
  • Split the leavers two ways, unopened and in date into a give-away box while it is still worth having, opened and over a year old straight into the bin.
Shots
  • Overhead of the counter filling with bags, the shelf emptying behind it in the same frame
  • Close on hands rolling a bag open, macro push on grain texture and webbing
  • Macro on a date stamp read under window light, a thumb rubbing the faded one
  • Overhead of two labelled piles building side by side, give away and bin
On-screen text
  • Name the meal, or it goes
  • Fourteen days
  • Opened and over a year: bin
Short cut · 45–60s A bag of buckwheat opened for one recipe two summers ago, and the fourteen day question that empties it.
Stands alone: Establish in the opening shot that these are opened dry goods bags off a pantry shelf, since the rule only applies to stock already opened.
Straighten Height on this shelf is assigned by how often you actually cook the grain, so the reach itself becomes the signal.
Beats
  • Return rice, pasta and oats to chest height, framed inside the arc a hand makes when the other hand is already holding a pan.
  • Send the specialty flours and the once a month lentils up to the shelf above, and show the stretch that reaching them costs.
  • Build the two blocks this shelf needs, pasta rice and oats as one, breakfast cereal as the other, so it reads as groups rather than one long row.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a container landing at chest height, a pan occupying the other hand at the edge of frame
  • Close on fingertips at full stretch on the upper shelf, the two-step stool low in frame
  • Overhead of the two blocks forming, the gap between them closing
On-screen text
  • Weekly at chest height
  • Monthly needs a stretch
  • Two blocks, not one row
Short cut · 30–45s Rice at chest height, the lentils you cook once a month on the shelf above, and the stretch is deliberate.
Stands alone: Establish that these are sealed dry staple containers already sorted, so the only open question inside the Short is what goes at which height.
Shine The empty dry goods shelf gets cleaned dry first and dried fully after, because grain dust plus damp is how a pantry starts to smell.
Beats
  • With the shelf bare, vacuum the back corners and the front lip where flour and oat dust settle, before any cloth touches it.
  • Wipe with mild soap, then dry the shelf fully, with a container held back at the edge of frame until the surface is dry.
  • Clean to inspect: rake window light across the corners of the flour, oat and rice containers looking for fine webbing or a moth.
Shots
  • Close on a vacuum nozzle running the front lip, then the back corner
  • Macro on flour dust lifting off the shelf edge
  • Overhead of a cloth drying the shelf, no streak left behind
  • Macro inside a clear container corner, light raking across the seam
On-screen text
  • Vacuum before you wipe
  • Dry fully, then load
  • Look for webbing
Short cut · 30–45s A damp cloth on a floury pantry shelf makes paste, and that paste is what you can smell a month later.
Stands alone: Open on the bare shelf and state it has just been emptied of grain containers, so the dry-first order makes sense on its own.
Safety Weight and glass come off the high shelf, because on a grain shelf the crush risk sits at head height.
Beats
  • Show the hazard honestly, cereal boxes and full grain containers stacked above shoulder height, and what the stack does when the bottom one is tugged.
  • Rebuild to the rule on camera, heavy containers low, light boxes high, nothing stacked more than two deep.
  • Bring glass grain jars down to chest height or lower and send lidded plastic up top, with wet hands on a full jar shown as the reason.
  • Stand a two-step stool inside the pantry and give the test, if the stool is not there, that shelf is too high for anything you need weekly.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a hand tugging the bottom box of a stack, the stack shifting above it
  • Close on a full glass grain jar coming down from above eye level to chest height
  • Overhead of the finished shelf, weight low, two deep at most
  • Wide lock-off of the two-step stool standing inside the pantry door
On-screen text
  • Heavy low, light high
  • Glass at chest height
  • Two deep, no more
Short cut · 30–45s A column of cereal boxes and grain jars above head height holds fine, right up until somebody pulls the bottom one.
Stands alone: Show the loaded stack on a pantry shelf above shoulder height first, since the weight and the height are the whole point.
Standardize One container style and one label per container, so a low rice level and an old opening date both read from the doorway.
Beats
  • Swap the mixed jars and boxes for one container style, with the point made that this is not about matching, it is that a half-empty oats container reads the same as a half-empty rice one.
  • Write a label carrying the item and the date the bag was opened, and fix it facing the doorway.
  • Quote the rule line, "A standard is the best way you know today, written down," over the finished shelf.
  • Run the readability test from the doorway, levels and dates read without a single container being lifted. See Chapter 14, visual controls.
Shots
  • Overhead of one container style filling the shelf, the odd old containers leaving frame
  • Macro on a marker writing item and opening date on a label
  • Three-quarter from the pantry doorway, levels legible across the whole shelf
On-screen text
  • One style, one label
  • Item plus date opened
  • Read it from the door
Short cut · 45–60s Stand in the pantry doorway and try to tell which of these staple containers is nearly empty.
Stands alone: Show the mixed original packaging first inside the Short, so both the swap and the readability change land without the parent video.
Sustain Loading order is the habit that keeps this shelf honest, and it rides on putting the shopping away.
Beats
  • Show the failure first, a new bag of rice going in front of the open one, named as the single move that undoes everything else done to this shelf.
  • Show the correct move, new stock sliding in behind the open bag as the shopping is unpacked.
  • Attach the habit to the unpacking rather than to a reminder, because the bags landing on the counter already happen.
  • Land the finished state, every opened bag sealed and dated or gone, two clear blocks, every level readable from the doorway.
Shots
  • Overhead of a new rice bag going in front, then corrected to behind the open one
  • Close on hands lifting stock out of a shopping bag beside the open shelf
  • Static three-quarter hold on the finished shelf from the doorway position
On-screen text
  • New stock goes behind
  • Oldest at the front
  • Habit rides the shopping
Short cut · 30–45s New bag of rice loaded in front of the open one, and that single move is why the back of the shelf goes stale.
Stands alone: Establish that the shelf behind the hands is already sorted, sealed and dated, so loading order reads as the last thing holding it.
Close

Hold on the finished shelf while the standard is given once, staples in one container style, labelled with item and opening date, filled front to back with the oldest bag at the front. Then show the trigger happening for real, shopping bags landing on the counter and new stock loading in behind the open bag, so the standard is seen being kept rather than described.

Next: Next along the same wall, the cans and jars, where the argument is with a best-before date you keep overruling.

Shot list
  • Wide lock-off of the full dry goods shelf, before and after, identical framing
  • Overhead tripod setup over the counter for the strip-out and the two sorting piles
  • Close on hands opening and smelling part-used bags
  • Macro on grain texture, webbing and date stamps
  • Three-quarter door frame clamp angle for reach height and the step stool
  • Close on the vacuum nozzle at the front lip and back corners
  • Overhead of the shelf being wiped and dried fully
  • Macro on a marker writing item and opening date
  • Three-quarter doorway lock-off for the readability test
  • Close on hands loading new stock behind the open bag
Description hook

The pantry shelf that fails first is the one holding bags you opened for one recipe and never cooked again. This is the full six step reset, Sort through Sustain, on real dry goods shelves.

MZ-014 · R03.02

The Canned and Jarred Goods

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Turn every can”

Pantry Cans and Jars: Reading Every Date and Rebuilding the Rows

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Hands turn three cans one after another hunting for the stamp: soup two years past, chickpeas with the date rubbed clean off, a gift jar being saved for an occasion that has not arrived. The argument this zone runs on is named, the best-before you keep overruling on a technicality while never actually eating the thing. The difference is set out plainly, best-before is about quality and use-by is about safety, and the seven day test is put on the table.

Sort Every can and jar comes off this shelf, gets turned until the date shows, and the duplicates get counted into rows.
Beats
  • Empty the shelf onto the counter and turn each can until the stamp comes into view, showing how much of this pass is simply rotation.
  • Send dented seams, rust and domed lids straight into the bin rather than back on the shelf, and make clear they do not go to a food bank either.
  • Count the duplicates into a visible row, four jars of the same pasta sauce, read as a record of what you keep buying blind.
  • Run the seven day test on anything past best-before, into a meal this week or out this week, and put anything past a use-by date out now.
Shots
  • Overhead of the shelf emptying onto the counter, cans landing in loose ranks
  • Macro on a thumb rotating a can until the stamped date enters frame
  • Close on a dented seam and a domed lid laid beside a sound can
  • Overhead of four identical sauce jars lined up as a duplicate count
On-screen text
  • Turn it to find the date
  • Dented, rusted, domed: out
  • Seven days or out
Short cut · 45–60s Four identical jars of the same pasta sauce off one pantry shelf, which means you have bought it blind four times.
Stands alone: Open on the emptied shelf with the cans already out on the counter, or the duplicate row reads as staging rather than as a count.
Straighten Rows are built by the meal they belong to rather than by can size, and nothing is allowed to hide behind anything.
Beats
  • Group by how they cook, tomatoes coconut milk and stock in one row because they end up in the same pan, beans and tuna in another because they are lunch.
  • Show the size-sorted version failing, a short can of tomatoes vanishing behind a tall passata jar, then rebuild tall behind short.
  • Spin every label to face the front and set the oldest date at the front of its row.
Shots
  • Overhead of rows rebuilding, meal groups forming out of a mixed field of cans
  • Camera at shelf level, a short can disappearing behind a tall jar, then the corrected order
  • Close on hands spinning labels forward along a finished row
On-screen text
  • Group by meal
  • Tall behind short
  • Oldest at the front
Short cut · 30–45s Sort your cans by height and the tomatoes disappear behind the passata, which is how you end up buying them again.
Stands alone: Name the shelf as pantry cans and jars and show dates already checked, so the row logic reads as visibility only.
Shine The sticky rings under the honey and the sauce jars come off, because a sticky shelf edge is how ants find the pantry.
Beats
  • Lift the honey jar to reveal the ring it has been sitting in, then find the same under the sauce lids.
  • Wash the threads of the jars you open most, showing the residue that collects under the rim.
  • Wipe the shelf edge as well as the surface, since the edge is where a running drip ends up and where ants travel.
Shots
  • Macro on a sticky ring revealed as the honey jar lifts
  • Close on a jar thread being washed at the sink, frame cut at the wrists
  • Overhead of the shelf edge being wiped end to end
On-screen text
  • Lift it, check the ring
  • Wash the threads
  • Ants follow sticky
Short cut · 30–45s Lift the honey jar off a pantry shelf and look at the ring it has been sitting in.
Stands alone: Keep the surrounding rows of cans and jars in frame so the sticky ring is not read as a fridge or countertop problem.
Safety Spoilage signs are treated as a hard stop, and the dense can rows come down off the high shelf.
Beats
  • Show the three signs against a sound can, a domed lid, a weeping seam, a hiss on opening, separating spoiled from merely old.
  • Bag the spoiled can sealed, bin it, and wash the shelf beneath where it stood, with the rule held absolute, no tasting, no decanting, nothing to the dog.
  • Quote the rule line, "Find it, and fix it now," as the bin lid closes.
  • Bring the dense can row and the glass sauce jars down below shoulder height, with the two outcomes named, a tin on a bare foot and glass on tile.
Shots
  • Macro on a domed lid catching window light beside a flat one
  • Close on a can going into a sealed bag, then the shelf beneath it being washed
  • Three-quarter of a dense can row coming down from the high shelf
  • Overhead of the finished shelf, cans and glass below shoulder height
On-screen text
  • Domed, weeping, hissing
  • Do not taste it
  • Cans and glass below the shoulder
Short cut · 30–45s A domed lid on a tin of soup is not an old can, it is a spoiled one, and it is not a taste test.
Stands alone: Show the can coming off a pantry shelf with a sound flat-lidded can beside it for comparison inside the Short.
Standardize Row labels and a riser turn this can shelf into a shopping list that writes itself.
Beats
  • Fix a category label to each row's shelf edge, positioned so it reads from standing height.
  • Put the back row up on a riser so its labels clear the front row, and compare what can be read without moving a can.
  • Show the payoff, the gap where the chopped tomatoes stood reading as the list, on the shelf rather than in your memory at the table. See Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, for the spoilage checks that ride along with each pass.
Shots
  • Close on a category label being fixed to the shelf edge
  • Matched three-quarter before and after the riser, back labels rising into view
  • Overhead of a deliberate gap in the tomato row reading as a signal
On-screen text
  • One row, one category
  • Riser lifts the back row
  • The gap is the list
Short cut · 30–45s Put the back row of cans up on a riser and the shelf starts writing your shopping list for you.
Stands alone: Show the rows already grouped by category, since the riser only pays off once the grouping exists.
Sustain Facing up the can rows rides on a trip past the pantry you already make with the recycling.
Beats
  • Attach the habit to an existing movement, recycling going out past the pantry, hands turning can labels forward on the way through.
  • Show the second habit, walking the rows and reading the gaps before sitting down to write the list.
  • Land the finished state, every label facing out, one category per row, oldest date at the front, no jar hidden behind another jar.
Shots
  • Close on hands turning labels forward as a recycling box is set down at the pantry door
  • Static three-quarter hold on the finished rows at shelf height
  • Overhead final frame of the completed shelf
On-screen text
  • Face up on the way past
  • Read the gaps first
  • Oldest at the front
Short cut · 30–45s Carrying the recycling out past the pantry takes long enough to turn every can label back to the front.
Stands alone: Show the rows already labelled and grouped, so the pass reads as upkeep rather than as setup.
Close

Rest on the finished rows while the standard is stated once, every label faces out, every row holds one category, and the oldest date sits at the front of its row. Then show the trigger in motion, the recycling going out past the pantry and hands facing up the rows on the way, so the standard is shown being held.

Next: Next, the baking shelf, where the hardest thing to let go of is a version of yourself you meant to become.

Shot list
  • Wide lock-off of the can and jar shelf, before and after, matched framing
  • Overhead tripod setup over the counter for the emptied shelf and the duplicate count
  • Macro on date stamps, domed lids, weeping seams and dented rims
  • Close on hands turning labels to face out
  • Shelf-level lock-off for the tall behind short comparison
  • Macro on a sticky ring and on jar threads being washed
  • Close on a riser going in and the back row rising
  • Close on hands facing up rows as a recycling box lands at the door
Description hook

Every can turned, every date read, and the best-before argument settled in one pass. The full six step 6S reset for a pantry can and jar shelf.

MZ-015 · R03.03

The Baking Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Baked twice, keep it”

Pantry Baking Shelf: Testing Leaveners and Settling the Kit

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Hands lift a piping set, a block of fondant, a third tart tin and a bag of specialty bread flour out onto the counter. Why this is the hardest shelf in the pantry gets named, letting the kit go feels like a statement about who you are rather than about what you bake. The test is set out before any of it moves, keep the tools for what you have baked twice and let go of the tools for what you have baked once, with both numbers explained.

Sort The leaveners get tested rather than guessed at, and the twice-not-once test decides the decorating kit and the tins.
Beats
  • Test on camera in two clear glasses, a spoon of baking powder into hot water should fizz hard and yeast in warm sugared water should foam, and the flat ones go.
  • Show the other obvious leavers off this shelf, the brick of hardened brown sugar and the cocoa gone grey.
  • Run the twice-not-once test across the piping set, the fondant and the third tart tin, with twice read as a thing you do and once read as an afternoon that has already happened.
  • Route what leaves to somebody who bakes this month rather than into a box in the garage.
Shots
  • Macro on baking powder hitting hot water, fizz climbing a clear glass
  • Macro on yeast foaming beside a flat control glass
  • Close on a brown sugar brick being tapped on the counter
  • Overhead of the kit split into keep and pass-on piles
On-screen text
  • Test, do not guess
  • Baked twice: keep
  • Baked once: pass it on
Short cut · 45–60s Two glasses of water on the counter settle whether the baking powder in your pantry is still alive.
Stands alone: Show the tin coming off a pantry baking shelf and keep a live control glass in frame for comparison.
Straighten One lift-out bin turns starting a bake into a single trip to this shelf instead of six.
Beats
  • Build the bin on camera, flour, sugar, bicarbonate of soda, vanilla and a scoop, because that is the start of every bake.
  • Show the six-trip version failing first, then the single two-handed lift that replaces it.
  • Put cutters, cases and piping tips into a second bin behind the first, because they are the end of a bake and never the beginning.
  • Move flour, sugar and brown sugar into sealed containers that open one-handed, shown being opened with the other hand full.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bin filling item by item on the counter
  • Three-quarter of the bin lifting off the shelf, both hands on it
  • Close on a one-handed lid release, the other hand holding a bowl
  • Overhead of bin two sitting behind bin one on the shelf
On-screen text
  • One trip, not six
  • Start of the bake, front
  • End of the bake, behind
Short cut · 30–45s Flour, sugar, bicarb, vanilla and a scoop in one bin, so a bake starts with one trip to the pantry.
Stands alone: Name the shelf and list the bin contents on screen, since the bin itself is the whole idea.
Shine Flour comes off this shelf dry first, because a damp cloth turns it to paste.
Beats
  • Show the mistake, a damp cloth smearing spilled flour into paste along the shelf.
  • Brush or vacuum the shelf dry, then wipe, and cut between the two finished surfaces.
  • Wash the scoop rather than burying it back in the flour, and show it returning dry to the bin.
Shots
  • Macro of a damp cloth smearing flour into paste
  • Close on a brush and vacuum nozzle clearing dry flour from the shelf lip
  • Close on the scoop washed, dried and set back into the bin
On-screen text
  • Dry first, wipe after
  • Flour plus damp is paste
  • Wash the scoop
Short cut · 30–45s Wipe a floury baking shelf with a damp cloth and watch the mess get worse instead of better.
Stands alone: Establish flour as the specific dirt on a baking shelf, since the dry-first rule is flour specific rather than general cleaning advice.
Safety Allergen separation on a shared home shelf, because one scoop moving between containers carries traces into a birthday cake.
Beats
  • Name the hazard plainly, almond meal, nut flours and sesame sharing this shelf and sharing a scoop.
  • Set up a sealed container and a dedicated scoop for each allergen on camera rather than describing it.
  • Stand the allergen containers at the end of the row where nothing gets grabbed by mistake, with position doing the work.
  • Move silver balls and mini cutters up off the low shelf and out of a toddler's reach.
  • Sweep a flour spill on the hard floor as it happens, since a hot tray is about to cross it.
Shots
  • Close on one scoop moving between two containers, then the corrected two-scoop setup
  • Macro on an allergen label and a dedicated scoop inside a sealed container
  • Three-quarter of the allergen containers in their end-of-row position
  • Overhead of a flour spill on hard floor being swept immediately
On-screen text
  • One scoop per allergen
  • End of the row
  • Sweep the spill now
Short cut · 45–60s The scoop that goes into the almond flour never goes into anything else on the shelf.
Stands alone: Establish this as a shared home baking shelf rather than a commercial kitchen, so the risk reads as cross contact between household containers.
Standardize Opening dates on leavener lids, and a bin whose contents are fixed enough that a gap shows.
Beats
  • Write the opening date across the lid on the day the tin is opened, with the point made that the printed date stops meaning much once air is in.
  • Show the bin returning to the same marked spot with the same contents, and a missing scoop or absent vanilla showing before the butter is out.
  • Point to Chapter 22, prevent and prepare, for the allergen and readiness thinking this shelf is carrying.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing the opening date across a baking powder lid
  • Overhead of the bin with one item deliberately absent, the gap obvious
  • Three-quarter of the bin landing back inside its marked spot
On-screen text
  • Date the lid, not the tin
  • Same spot, same contents
  • A gap you can see
Short cut · 30–45s Once air is in the tin, the date printed on your baking powder stops being the useful one.
Stands alone: Run a quick fizz test in the same clip so the dating reads as prevention rather than as paperwork.
Sustain The baking bin resets when the bake comes out, and the leavener check rides the preheat.
Beats
  • Attach the reset to the timer, bake out to cool, bin back on the shelf, scoop washed, flour topped up.
  • Attach the check to the preheat, lid dates read while the oven comes up to temperature.
  • Land the finished state, sealed one-handed containers, leaveners together with dates showing, cutters and tips in one lift-out bin, no loose sprinkles on the shelf.
Shots
  • Close on a timer sounding and the bin being carried back to the shelf
  • Macro on hands reading lid dates, oven light warm behind them
  • Overhead final frame of the finished baking shelf
On-screen text
  • Timer goes, bin goes back
  • Check dates during preheat
  • Scoop washed, flour topped
Short cut · 30–45s An oven preheat is dead time, and it is exactly long enough to read the dates on your leavener lids.
Stands alone: Show the dated lids in the opening shot, since the check needs something written on them to read.
Close

Hold on the shelf while the standard is given once, one lift-out baking bin with a washed scoop, leaveners dated on the lid the day they are opened, and allergen flours sealed with a scoop of their own. Then show the trigger, the oven set to preheat and hands reading lid dates while it comes up to temperature.

Next: Next, the snack and lunch shelf, where the real work is deciding once instead of several times a day.

Shot list
  • Wide lock-off of the baking shelf, before and after, matched framing
  • Overhead tripod setup over the counter for leavener tests and the keep versus pass-on split
  • Macro on fizz and foam in clear glasses beside flat controls
  • Close on the lift-out bin being built and lifted
  • Macro of a damp cloth against a dry brush on spilled flour
  • Close on the two-scoop allergen setup and its end-of-row position
  • Macro on a marker dating a leavener lid
  • Overhead of the bin with a deliberate gap in it
Description hook

Test your leaveners instead of guessing, and settle the baking kit with one rule: baked twice, keep it. The full six step 6S reset for a pantry baking shelf.

MZ-016 · R03.04

The Snack and Lunch Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Let the bin answer”

Pantry Snack and Lunch Shelf: A Yes Bin at Child Height

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Overhead on an open snack bin at child height, a small hand reaching into it, then an adult hand reaching past to the shelf above. The real load in this zone gets named, snacks negotiated several times a day while you are busy and being asked twice. The shift is set out, choose once in daylight what a child may take without asking, put exactly that in the bin, and let the shelf answer instead of you.

Sort Lids get matched to containers, orphans leave in both directions, and the rattling snack boxes get combined.
Beats
  • Pair every lid to a tub across the counter, letting the unpaired pile build in shot.
  • Bin the orphans in both directions, lidless tubs and lids for tubs that died, treated as one decision rather than two.
  • Tip out the snack boxes with two bars rattling in the bottom, combine them, and flatten the empty cartons.
  • Set the surviving container count against the number of lunches you genuinely pack in a week, not the number you might.
Shots
  • Overhead of containers and lids spread across the counter, pairing in progress
  • Close on the orphan pile growing beside the matched stack
  • Macro on two bars tipped from a nearly empty box into one
  • Overhead of flattened cartons stacked for recycling
On-screen text
  • Every lid finds a tub
  • Orphans go, both kinds
  • Count the real lunches
Short cut · 30–45s Every lunchbox lid out on the counter, and the pile of them that never finds a tub.
Stands alone: Establish that these came off a pantry snack and lunch shelf, since the pairing exercise needs the shelf as context.
Straighten Height carries the permission here, the yes bin low and the ask shelf above their eye line.
Beats
  • Load the pre-approved snacks into an open bin the child reaches without a stool.
  • Put the ones that start an argument on the shelf above their eye line, with the height doing the deciding.
  • Stand lunch bags and ice packs beside the containers so packing happens in one place instead of two rooms.
Shots
  • Camera at child height, frame cut at the wrist, a small hand reaching easily into the open bin
  • Matched frame on the higher shelf, well above that same eye line
  • Overhead of lunch bags and ice packs landing beside the containers
On-screen text
  • Yes lives low
  • Ask lives high
  • Packing in one place
Short cut · 30–45s One open bin a child can reach and one shelf they cannot, and the height answers the snack question for you.
Stands alone: State on screen that the low bin holds only pre-approved snacks, or the height split reads as ordinary storage.
Shine The bin gets tipped and wiped, and every lunch bag gets opened for what nobody mentioned.
Beats
  • Tip the bin out and wipe the bottom corners where crushed crackers and dried fruit pouch drips collect.
  • Open every lunch bag and check for the sandwich nobody mentioned, played as routine rather than as a discovery.
  • Wash the bag liners and show them going back dry.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bin tipped out, crumbs banked in the bottom corners
  • Macro on a dried pouch drip being lifted out of a bin corner
  • Close on a lunch bag being opened and emptied over a bin
  • Close on liners washed and laid out to dry
On-screen text
  • Corners hold the crumbs
  • Check every bag
  • Liners washed and dry
Short cut · 30–45s Tip out the child height snack bin from a pantry and look at what has been living in the corners.
Stands alone: Show the bin on its shelf before it is tipped, so the contents explain the mess without the parent video.
Safety The bin's contents are set by the youngest person in the house who can reach it, not the oldest.
Beats
  • Name the hazard plainly, whole nuts, hard sweets and grapes going straight from an open bin into a small mouth.
  • Set the rule on camera, contents chosen for the youngest child who can reach the bin.
  • Lift the choke risks to the shelf above eye line and show the bin reset without them.
  • Set a nut bar aside from the lunch pile, thinking about a classmate's allergy in a shared lunch hall.
  • Address the climbing risk with the two honest options, move it out of the pantry entirely or fix the shelving unit to the wall.
Shots
  • Macro on whole nuts and hard sweets sitting in an open bin at low height
  • Close on those items being lifted to the higher shelf
  • Three-quarter of a nut bar set aside from the lunch pile
  • Close on a bracket going into the wall behind the shelving unit
On-screen text
  • Set by the youngest
  • Choke risks go high
  • Fix the unit to the wall
Short cut · 45–60s An open snack bin at toddler height is set by the youngest child in the house, not the oldest.
Stands alone: Open on the bin at child height with nothing over it, since the low reach and the open top are what make the contents a hazard question.
Standardize The bin is the rule made visible, with a photo on the door showing what stocked looks like.
Beats
  • State the rule the bin carries, what is in it is allowed and what is not in it needs asking.
  • Tape a photo of a properly stocked bin inside the pantry door, then match the real shelf against it.
  • Mark the fill line inside the bin so topped up has one meaning. See Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, for why the picture beats a written list here.
Shots
  • Close on a photo being taped inside the pantry door
  • Three-quarter comparing the photo against the actual bin
  • Macro on the marked fill line inside the bin
On-screen text
  • In the bin: allowed
  • Not in it: ask
  • Fill to the line
Short cut · 30–45s A photo taped inside the pantry door settles what a properly stocked snack bin actually looks like.
Stands alone: Show that the bin holds only pre-approved snacks, so the photo reads as a standard rather than as decoration.
Sustain The refill rides the after-school unpack, and the standard becomes real only when an empty bin is allowed to be the answer.
Beats
  • Show the trigger, lunchboxes emptied at the sink, lids going back onto tubs, bin topped to its line before the bags go on their hook.
  • Return to the hard part, an empty bin at four o'clock, and hold the position that empty is the answer rather than the start of a search.
  • Make the point that this single refusal is what makes the bin real, and that until it is held the bin is decoration.
Shots
  • Overhead of lunchboxes emptied at the sink, lids going back on
  • Close on the bin being refilled to its marked line
  • Three-quarter of bags going onto their hook, the finished bin behind them
On-screen text
  • Lids on before they go back
  • Fill before the bags hang
  • Empty bin, empty answer
Short cut · 45–60s When the snack bin is empty at four o'clock, empty is the answer, not the start of a search.
Stands alone: Show the bin, its fill line and its pre-approved contents first, since the refusal only works with a stocked standard behind it.
Close

Hold on the finished shelf while the standard is stated, the open bin at child height holds only pre-approved snacks and is refilled to one marked level, and no container returns to the shelf without its lid on it. Then show the trigger running, lunchboxes emptied at the sink and the bin filled back to its line before the bags go on their hook.

Next: Last in the pantry, the backstock, where the bulk pack you bought for the unit price gets an honest number put on it.

  • Wide lock-off of the snack and lunch shelf, before and after, matched framing
  • Overhead tripod setup over the counter for the lid and container pairing
  • Child height lock-off for the reach and eye line comparisons, frame cut at the wrist
  • Macro on choke risk items sitting in an open low bin
  • Close on the bin tipped out and its corners wiped
  • Close on a photo taped inside the pantry door
  • Macro on the marked fill line inside the bin
  • Overhead of the after-school unpack at the sink
