MZ-028 · R05.06

The Floor and Circulation Path

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Full Width, Always”

Living Room Floor Reset: Clear the Route Door to Door

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a tape measure being pulled across the narrowest gap between the sofa and the coffee table, then on a full laundry basket carried through that same gap, framed on the basket and forearms as it clips the table corner. Name the pattern this exposes, that this floor keeps getting tidied and keeps failing, and that the cause may not be the clutter. State the avoided decision plainly, that the room may hold more furniture than floor and one piece has to leave.

Sort Walk the route with a basket, and nothing belonging to another room is allowed to stay.
Beats
  • Hands walk the route with a laundry basket and every floor item goes into it: shoes, toys, yesterday's bag, the pile of post, the box that has sat beside the sofa for a month.
  • Cover the honest look this gives, that much of this room's mess is items from other rooms just visiting, which means the room is not failing on its own.
  • The rule gets applied in frame: anything belonging to another room gets carried there before anyone lets themselves sit down.
  • The floor is shown emptied down to furniture legs and the rug, so the route can actually be judged.
Shots
  • Locked high wide from the doorway looking down the route, the basket passing through frame as items go in
  • Close on a hand lifting a bag and a pile of post off the floor
  • Three-quarter of the basket being carried toward the doorway, hands and forearms only
  • Locked high wide of the emptied floor, furniture legs and rug only
On-screen text
  • Walk it with a basket
  • Other rooms go home first
Short cut · 30–45s A laundry basket filling as it crosses a living room floor in one pass, shoes, a bag and a pile of post going in
Stands alone: Name the route from doorway to doorway in the first line and state the rule that other rooms' items get carried back before anyone sits down, so the basket walk reads as a method rather than a tidy-up.
Straighten Baskets go to the wall line with named categories, and the route is permanently off limits.
Beats
  • Floor baskets get pushed against a wall or under the side table, never into the route itself.
  • Each basket gets a named category. Cover why the name matters, that an unnamed basket turns into a bin nobody empties.
  • The route is declared permanently off limits for storage, including just for tonight, with that exact phrase named as the way this rule fails.
  • The full clear route from the doorway past the sofa to the other exit gets covered in one continuous forward walk.
Shots
  • Locked high wide of baskets moving out of the route to the wall line
  • Macro on a category label going onto a basket
  • Handheld forward-facing walk at chest height along the full route, basket and forearms only in frame
  • Close on the space under the side table receiving a basket
On-screen text
  • Baskets to the wall
  • Name the category
  • No storage, not even tonight
Short cut · 30–45s A basket sitting square in a walkway, then pushed to the wall, and the route opening up behind it
Stands alone: Say in the first line that the route is the line from doorway past the sofa to the other exit, and that it is permanently off limits for storage, including just for tonight.
Shine Vacuum the route, then move the furniture legs and do what was underneath.
Beats
  • The route gets vacuumed end to end first, so the floor already looks done before anything gets moved.
  • Sofa and chair legs get lifted and the floor underneath gets done. Cover that this is where pet hair and dust build up out of sight, which is why this room never quite feels clean underfoot.
  • The rug gets shaken or vacuumed on both sides and the gripper pad gets pressed to check it is still tacky, which makes this a cleaning pass that inspects a fall hazard.
Shots
  • Locked high wide of the vacuum running the full route in one pass
  • Close on a sofa leg being lifted and the dust line underneath revealed
  • Macro on fingers pressing the gripper pad to test the tack
  • Three-quarter of the rug lifted and being done on the underside
On-screen text
  • Move the legs
  • Both sides of the rug
  • Press the pad
Short cut · 30–45s A sofa leg lifted to reveal a sharp line of dust exactly where the furniture had been standing
Stands alone: Establish in the first seconds that this floor had already been vacuumed before the leg moved, because the reveal only means anything against a floor that looked finished.
Safety Three falls come out of this floor, and all three happen in the dark to the first person up.
Beats
  • A curled rug corner is shown, then fixed onto a grippy pad so the edge lies flat. Frame this as fall, the first of the three this room produces.
  • The lamp cord crossing the route gets rerouted out of the path, with the link back to the side table clip made explicit.
  • A toy left in the route is shown in low light, and the shared pattern gets named, that all three of these falls happen at night to whoever is up first.
  • The route to the door gets checked at its full width, with the reason stated plainly, in case anyone ever has to leave the house in a hurry. Quote the frozen line, find it, and fix it now. See Chapter 21, the hazard hunt.
Shots
  • Macro on a curled rug corner, then the same corner lying flat on a gripper pad
  • Close on the lamp cord being lifted out of the route
  • Low-light three-quarter of a toy sitting in the walkway
  • Locked high wide of the full-width route to the door, clear end to end
On-screen text
  • Three falls, all in the dark
  • Cord out of the route
  • Find it, and fix it now
Short cut · 45–60s Low light across a living room floor with a curled rug corner, a lamp cord and a toy all sitting in the same walking line
Stands alone: Name all three falls and say they happen at night to the first person up, then show each fix inside the Short so it resolves rather than only warning.
Standardize The standard is full width, always, and it gets checked by walking it loaded rather than by looking at it.
Beats
  • The route gets walked with a full basket carried in both hands. Cover why this is the check and standing in the doorway looking is not, because a route can look clear and still fail a load.
  • The tape comes back out at the narrowest gap. Cover the test from the call: if two adults cannot pass, or a full basket cannot go through without turning sideways, the room holds more furniture than floor.
  • The furniture decision gets made on camera and chosen by use rather than by cost. Whichever piece was sat on or set down on least this month is the one that goes, usually the spare armchair nobody chooses or the second side table that came with a set.
  • The route gets walked again with that piece gone, basket in both hands, nothing clipped.
Shots
  • Handheld forward-facing walk at chest height, full basket and forearms filling the lower frame
  • Macro on the tape measure at the narrowest gap
  • Three-quarter of the spare armchair being moved out of the room, hands only
  • Repeat forward walk with the route now clear at full width
On-screen text
  • Walk it, do not look at it
  • Full basket, no turning
  • Choose by use, not by cost
Short cut · 45–60s A full laundry basket travelling straight down a living room route between a sofa and a coffee table, clipping nothing
Stands alone: State the test before the walk, that the route has to take two people passing and a full basket carried in both hands, so the walk reads as a pass or a fail rather than a stroll.
Sustain The vacuum coming out is the trigger, and the basket goes back before the vacuum does.
Beats
  • The vacuum comes out and the route gets done, then anything still on the floor at the end goes into the basket.
  • Cover the ordering that makes it hold: the basket gets returned before the vacuum is put away, so the two actions cannot be separated.
  • The finished floor is shown from the doorway, since a room that looks reset from the doorway is a room people keep resetting.
  • Close the loop back to Sort, noting the same basket does both jobs in this zone.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the vacuum coming out and running the route
  • Locked high wide of the last floor items going into the basket
  • Close on the basket being carried out while the vacuum still stands in the room
  • Wide locked frame from the doorway of the finished floor
On-screen text
  • Vacuum out, basket out
  • Basket back before the vacuum
Short cut · 30–45s A vacuum left standing alone in the middle of a living room while the basket gets carried out first
Stands alone: Name the trigger as the vacuum coming out and make the ordering explicit, that the basket goes back before the vacuum does, because the standing vacuum is the whole visual argument.
Close

Walk the finished route one more time from the doorway past the sofa to the other exit, wide enough for two people to pass and for the vacuum to run through without being lifted, rug edges flat on a grippy pad, no cord crossing the route, and nothing on the floor but furniture legs, the rug, and baskets pushed back against the wall. State the standard, the route from door to door stays clear at its full width and the floor is for furniture legs and the rug, then show the trigger, the vacuum coming out and everything still on the floor riding the basket back.

Next: End on the locked doorway frame with the whole reset room behind it, and point back at the sofa, coffee table, media unit, bookshelves and side table as the five zones that feed this floor, because the route only stays clear while those five hold.

Shot list
  • Locked high wide from the doorway looking down the full route, used for the basket walk and the closing pass
  • Handheld forward-facing chest-height walk for the full-basket test
  • Macro on the tape measure at the narrowest gap
  • Close on the sofa leg lift revealing the dust line
  • Macro on the rug corner and the gripper pad tack test
  • Low-light three-quarter for the three night-time falls
  • Close on the lamp cord being lifted clear of the route
  • Three-quarter of a furniture piece leaving the room, hands only
  • Wide locked frame from the doorway of the finished floor
  • Close on the vacuum standing while the basket leaves
Description hook

Measure the narrowest gap on your living room route. If you cannot carry a full basket through without turning sideways, the problem is not the clutter. Full 6S reset, hands only.

6Sliving room floortrip hazardsrug safetyhome organizationcirculation pathheadless how-toMicro Zone Manual

Room 06 of 20

Family Room

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteShoot the whole room in one day, in this order: Primary Media Zone first, because its cables cross the floor into every other zone and clearing them opens the floor for the tripod everywhere else. Natural light only, so schedule the two floor-level zones (Toy and Play, Blanket and Comfort) for the brightest part of the day, and the two cabinet-interior zones (Media, Charging) for when a clamped white card can bounce window light into the dark cabinet rather than adding a lamp. Access is the constraint behind the television unit, so pull the unit forward yourself before setting up and mark its original floor position with low-tack tape so it goes back square. Tripod placement, single operator throughout: one tripod with a counterweighted horizontal arm parked over the play mat and the craft surface, one tripod at about seat height for the sofa, basket, and shelf work, and a handheld macro setup for cable ends, vent slots, thumbstick collars, and box corners. Nothing above the wrists is ever in frame, so run each reach once and check the framing on the camera screen before rolling, since there is nobody watching a monitor for you. On-set safety: the anti-tip check happens on camera with a real strap, so have a spare strap and the correct bolts on hand before the shoot rather than discovering the mount is loose mid-take. Unplug the glue gun between takes and keep its cooling tile in shot so the cooling spot is established visually. Never film a real swollen battery pack, use a clearly labeled stand-in pack and say on screen that it is a stand-in.
MZ-029 · R06.01

The Primary Media Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Label Both Cable Ends”

Media Cabinet Reset: Label Every Cable and Settle the Old Console

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the dark space behind the television unit, then a hand sliding the older console out from behind the newer one, dust line still on the shelf where it has not moved in two years. Set out the decision this cabinet has been avoiding: that machine is kept because someone's save file lives on it, which is a genuine reason and also exactly why it has sat unplugged. Show the two honest endings being set up at the start, moving the save data or handing over a controller for one real session, and make clear the console is settled inside this session rather than the next one.

Sort The cabinet is emptied to the floor, and anything pairing with a console or television no longer in the house leaves today, spare remotes included.
Beats
  • Pull every disc case, spare remote, headset, and loose cable out onto the floor in front of the cabinet, working shelf by shelf so the empty cabinet is visible before anything goes back.
  • Split the pile into what pairs with a device still in this house and what pairs with something already gone, and let the pile of dead remotes build on camera, because that is usually two or three.
  • Work the call: plug the old console into the television, and show both honest outcomes, the save data moving to a card or the current console, or a controller being handed off for one real session.
  • Photograph the save screen, then route console, controllers, and cables out together in one trip, since splitting them is how half of it returns to the cabinet.
Shots
  • Tripod at seat height on the open cabinet, hands drawing items out and building the pile on the floor
  • Overhead on the sorted piles, one hand pushing a stack of dead remotes across into the outgoing box
  • Close on the console rear ports as a hand seats the power cable and the screen wakes
  • Macro on a phone photographing the save screen
  • Wide from the doorway of one trip carrying console, controllers, and cables out together
On-screen text
  • Empty it first
  • Pairs with a device you own?
  • One trip, all of it
Short cut · 45–60s Hands hold up three remotes and press each one at a television that does not respond, then drop all three into a box.
Stands alone: Re-establish that this is a family room television cabinet and state the rule in the first line, if it pairs with a console or a television you no longer own it leaves today. Name the save-file console briefly so the ending lands.
Straighten One console per shelf with its own controllers and headset, disc cases upright in a single row, and a dock that is the resting place rather than an occasional one.
Beats
  • Assign each console its own shelf, and place its matched controllers and headset down beside it rather than into a shared heap at the bottom of the cabinet.
  • Tip the flat stack of disc cases upright into one spine-out row, and show what the flat stack was costing, the bottom four cases nobody could reach and nobody played.
  • Set each dock where the controller lands naturally from the sofa, so docked is where a controller rests rather than somewhere it occasionally gets put.
Shots
  • Overhead on a shelf as hands place a console, then its two controllers, then its headset
  • Close on hands tipping a flat stack of disc cases upright into a single row
  • Tripod at seat height on the finished cabinet, each shelf reading as one console and its own kit
On-screen text
  • One console, one shelf
  • Spine out, single row
Short cut · 30–45s A hand pulls the bottom disc case out of a flat stack and the whole stack slides sideways off the shelf.
Stands alone: Say in the first beat that this is a television cabinet and that a flat stack means the bottom four discs never get played. End on the upright spine-out row.
Shine Clean the parts that get handled and the parts that breathe, with the right cloth for each, and let everything dry before it goes back.
Beats
  • Brush the vent slots on each console and the back panel of the television with a vacuum brush head, and read the dust load as the finding, because it tells you how hard that machine has been breathing inside a closed cabinet.
  • Wipe controller grips and thumbstick collars with a barely damp cloth, working into the collar and the button seams, the most-handled objects in this room and almost never cleaned.
  • Finish the screen with a dry microfiber cloth in one direction only, and show the spray bottle being set aside rather than used.
  • Lay everything out to dry fully before any of it returns to a shelf.
Shots
  • Macro on a vacuum brush head drawing dust out of a console vent slot
  • Macro on a cloth working around a thumbstick collar and into the button seams
  • Close on a dry microfiber cloth crossing the screen in one direction
  • Overhead on controllers laid out to dry on a towel
On-screen text
  • Barely damp, never sprayed
  • Dry fully before it goes back
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on the grey ring of grime around a thumbstick collar, then the same collar clean.
Stands alone: Establish that a game controller is the most-handled object in the house and almost never cleaned. Cover the barely damp cloth and the full dry, so the viewer has the whole method without the parent video.
Safety The television tip check done by hand, vent slots kept clear, and the power strip off the carpet and out of the walking line.
Beats
  • Press the top edge of the television with a hand and let it rock on camera, then treat that as the finding that stops everything else in the room until the anti-tip strap or the mount bolts are dealt with.
  • Frame it as the fall, cut, or crush question using this specific setup, a flat screen on a low unit with a shelf underneath that a child climbs.
  • Take the burn or fire question to the vents: a throw from the blanket basket laid over a console, disc cases stacked on the top, or the cabinet door kept shut during a long play session.
  • Lift the power strip off the carpet onto a hard surface and out of the line people walk between the sofa and the door, named as the fall question in a room crossed in the dark.
Shots
  • Tripod at seat height on a hand pressing the top edge of the television, the frame visibly rocking, then held still
  • Close on hands seating the anti-tip strap and tightening the mount bolt
  • Macro on a vent slot with a disc case sitting over it, then the slot clear
  • Low overhead along the walking line between sofa and door as hands lift the power strip off the carpet
On-screen text
  • Check with your hand, not your eye
  • Vents need air
  • Off the carpet, out of the walkway
Short cut · 45–60s A hand pushes the top corner of a flat screen on a low unit and it rocks forward, caught before it goes.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that this is a television on a low family room unit and that the scenario is a child pulling on the frame. Show the strap and bolt fix on camera so the Short ends resolved rather than alarmed.
Standardize Both ends of every cable labeled, and a card inside the cabinet door naming which controller and headset belong to which console.
Beats
  • Label both ends of every cable while the cabinet is still open and the unit is still pulled forward, and show why one end labeled fails, by following a tagged cable to an untagged end behind the unit.
  • Write and tape a small card inside the cabinet door listing which controller and which headset belong to which console.
  • Show both working together: a blind reach behind the unit lands on a tagged end, and the door card answers the headset question without anything being pulled out. Point to Chapter 14, visual controls.
Shots
  • Macro on a hand wrapping a labeled flag tag onto a cable end, then the matching tag at the far end
  • Close on a marker writing the console-to-controller list on a card
  • Tripod at seat height on the card being taped inside the open cabinet door
On-screen text
  • Both ends, every cable
  • The card lives on the door
  • Ch 14, visual controls
Short cut · 30–45s Hands trace a cable behind a television unit end over end until it disappears into a knot, then the same reach lands straight on a tagged end.
Stands alone: Establish the cabinet in the first beat and give the rule, both ends or it does not count. Add the door card as the second half so the Short carries the whole standard.
Sustain The kit goes back while the credits roll, before the television goes off, because that is the last moment hands are free and the controllers are still out.
Beats
  • Show credits arriving on the screen this family already watches, and hang the habit there, since it is the one moment in an evening when the controllers are still out and nobody's hands are busy.
  • Controllers go back on their dock and remotes into the tray before the television goes off, and show the ordering being obeyed, because once the screen is dark nobody stands up for it.
  • Close the loop against the standard: each console alone on its shelf with its matched kit, card on the door, no vent covered.
Shots
  • Tripod at seat height with screen and hands in one frame as credits roll and a controller enters
  • Close on a controller seating into its dock and remotes dropping into the tray
  • Wide from the doorway of the finished cabinet, lamp on, then the screen going dark
On-screen text
  • Credits roll, kit goes back
  • Before the television goes off
Short cut · 30–45s Credits roll on a television and a hand is already moving a controller toward its dock before the music ends.
Stands alone: Name the room and the trigger in the opening beat, since the trigger is the whole Short. Show the docked controller and the tray of remotes so the end state reads without the parent video.
Close

Hold the finished cabinet from the doorway and read the standard against what is in frame: each console alone on its shelf with its matched controllers and headset, the cable card taped inside the door, no vent slot covered, the power strip off the carpet. Then show the trigger once in real use, credits rolling and the kit going back before the television goes off, so the standard and the thing that starts it are seen together.

Next: The floor in front of this cabinet is the next zone, and it belongs to whoever is four years old.

Shot list
  • Fixed tripod at seat height on the open cabinet, used for all pull-out and put-back work
  • Overhead arm on the floor in front of the unit for the sorted piles
  • Macro handheld for cable ends, vent slots, thumbstick collars, and label tags
  • Behind-the-unit setup with the television pulled forward and a white card clamped to bounce window light into the gap

  • Close on the anti-tip strap and mount bolts, framed so only hands and hardware are in shot
  • Doorway wide of the finished cabinet, held long enough to read the standard against
  • Screen and hands in one frame at seat height for the credits trigger, shot at dusk with the lamp on
Description hook

The family room media cabinet, reset one shelf at a time: every cable labeled at both ends, one console per shelf with its own controllers, and the television tip-checked by hand rather than by eye. Hands only, no presenter.

MZ-030 · R06.02

The Toy and Play Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “No Lids, Photo Labels”

Five Open Bins, No Lids: A Toy Shelf a Four-Year-Old Can Reset Alone

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on a hand moving one large, loud, expensive toy two feet along the lowest shelf and setting it back down in the same kind of gap. Set out the decision this shelf keeps postponing: a relative gave that toy, no child has chosen it unprompted in months, and every reset moves it rather than settles it. Establish the rule the video runs on, that the shelf belongs to the child and not to the giver, and set up the honest week as the test that decides it.

Sort Every bin is tipped onto the mat and split four ways, and broken toys are repaired today or leave today.
Beats
  • Tip every bin out onto the play mat and keep tipping until the shelf is bare, because a bin sorted in place only ever loses its top layer.
  • Build the four piles on the mat: played with this month, broken, missing its other half, and outgrown, so the categories are visible rather than described.
  • Hold up a cracked seam, a corroded battery compartment, and a wheel that will not stay on, and apply the today rule, repaired today or gone today, because later is not a real time.
  • Start the honest week on the gift toy: tape a square on the mat, set it in the square, touch nothing, then show the square still marked and the toy still square-on at the end of it.
Shots
  • Overhead arm on the mat as bins are tipped and the four piles build
  • Macro on a cracked seam, then a corroded battery compartment
  • Close on hands testing a wheel that will not stay on
  • Overhead on the gift toy sitting inside its taped square on the mat
  • Close on hands holding a phone, the photo of the toy already sent to the giver on screen
On-screen text
  • Tip it all out
  • Repaired today or gone today
  • The shelf belongs to the child
Short cut · 45–60s Overhead: one toy bin upends onto a play mat and keeps pouring for longer than anyone expects.
Stands alone: Establish this is a family room toy shelf and name the four piles fast, since the pile-building is the whole Short. End on the broken pile and the repaired today or gone today rule.
Straighten One category per open bin, no lids, all on the lowest shelf, with the overflow living in a closet rather than creeping back here.
Beats
  • Fill one category per bin and let each fill on camera: blocks, vehicles, dolls and figures, pretend food, art toys.
  • Take the lids off and stack them out of the room, because a lid is one more step than a four-year-old will take at the end of a play session.
  • Move every bin to the lowest shelf and check the reach from the height a child actually looks down from, camera dropped to that height rather than described.
  • Send the overflow to labeled bins in a closet, and show the swap, one bin out and one in, that happens when a child asks for something by name.
Shots
  • Overhead on five open bins filling one category at a time
  • Close on a lid being lifted off and set onto a separate stack
  • Low camera at child eye level looking along the lowest shelf
  • Tripod at seat height on labeled overflow bins going into a closet
On-screen text
  • One category per bin
  • No lids
  • Overflow lives in the closet
Short cut · 30–45s A lid goes onto a toy bin, then comes straight back off and onto a discard stack.
Stands alone: Say this is a toy shelf for a young child and give the reason in the opening line, a lid is one more step than a four-year-old will take. Show the five open bins on the lowest shelf as the payoff.
Shine Hard toys washed and dried fully, soft toys through the machine in a bag, and the mat lifted so what is under it can be read.
Beats
  • Wash hard plastic toys in mild soapy water and lay them out in a single layer, because a damp block goes back into a bin and stays damp.
  • Load fabric dolls and soft blocks into a wash bag and show the bag zipped, so nothing loses an eye in the drum.
  • Lift the play mat and vacuum underneath, and read what comes out as the finding, dice and pawns off the game shelf, seed beads off the craft table, and single puzzle pieces that were never lost at all.
Shots
  • Overhead on hands washing blocks in a basin of soapy water
  • Overhead on washed toys laid out in a single layer on a towel
  • Close on soft toys going into a wash bag and the bag zipping
  • Tripod at seat height on the mat rolled back and the vacuum head going over what was underneath
On-screen text
  • Dry fully, or it stays damp
  • Wash bag for the soft ones
  • Lift the mat
Short cut · 30–45s A play mat rolls back and the floor underneath is a different colour, with dice and a puzzle piece sitting in the dust.
Stands alone: Establish the family room play mat in one line. The mat lift and what it turns up is the Short, so end on the recovered pieces going back to the game shelf.
Safety The toilet paper tube test for any house with a child under three, cracked plastic out, and nothing loaded heavy above shoulder height.
Beats
  • Drop small parts through the middle of a toilet paper tube one at a time, framed as the poison, choke, or strangle question on a floor a crawling child also uses.
  • Give the routing answer, that anything passing through belongs in the older child's room rather than in a floor-height bin in the shared room.
  • Take the fall, cut, or crush question to cracked hard plastic, running a thumb along an edge sharp enough to cut a knee, then reload the low shelf heavy at the bottom.
  • Check the tallest bin against the child's shoulder height marked on the wall, so nothing on this shelf can be pulled down onto a face.
Shots
  • Macro on a marble, a small figure accessory, and a snapped-off toy wheel dropping through a tube
  • Close on hands running a thumb along a cracked plastic edge, then dropping it in the outgoing box
  • Tripod at seat height on a low shelf unloaded from the top and reloaded heavy at the bottom
  • Low camera measuring the tallest bin against a shoulder-height tape mark on the wall
On-screen text
  • Fits through the tube, out of this room
  • Heavy at the bottom
  • Nothing above shoulder height
Short cut · 45–60s Macro: a marble drops clean through a toilet paper tube and lands on a play mat.
Stands alone: State up front that this test is for houses with a child under three and that this floor is shared. Give the routing answer, older child's room, so the Short ends with an action rather than a warning.
Standardize Photo labels on the bin front faces, and one printed picture of the finished shelf at child eye height.
Beats
  • Photograph each bin's contents and tape the picture to the front face, at the height a child looking down sees, not on the rim where only an adult reads it.
  • Print one picture of the finished shelf and tape it on the wall beside it at child eye height.
  • Show match the picture being used as the instruction, a child-height view of the wall photo and the real shelf with one bin out of place. Point to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo.
Shots
  • Overhead on a bin's contents laid out and photographed
  • Macro on the printed photo being taped to the front face of a bin
  • Low camera at child eye height on the shelf photo taped to the wall
  • Tripod at seat height comparing the wall photo and the real shelf in one frame
On-screen text
  • Photo on the front face
  • Match the picture
  • Ch 25, ideal-state photo
Short cut · 30–45s A printed photo of a finished toy shelf goes up on the wall, and the real shelf beside it has one bin visibly wrong.
Stands alone: Say this is a young child's toy shelf and that the photo is the instruction, since match the picture only reads if the viewer knows who is following it. The compare shot carries the rest.
Sustain The floor gets cleared when the bedtime story is announced, and the story starts when the mat is empty.
Beats
  • Show the bedtime story being announced, hands holding the book at the doorway, and hang the habit there, because it is the one moment in the evening when a child wants something and the mat is the price.
  • Clear the floor first and start the story only once the mat is empty, and show that the ordering is what does the work, not the instruction.
  • Roll the mat against the wall and hold on enough clear floor that two children could build tomorrow without moving anything first.
Shots
  • Overhead arm on the mat covered in toys, hands entering and the five bins filling
  • Close on the last item going into a bin and the mat clear
  • Tripod at seat height on the mat being rolled and stood against the wall
  • Wide of the finished floor from the doorway
On-screen text
  • Story starts when the mat is empty
  • Mat rolled to the wall
Short cut · 45–60s A hand sets a picture book down at the edge of a toy-covered play mat and does not open it.
Stands alone: Name the trigger in the opening beat, the story starts when the mat is empty, since the whole Short is that exchange. Run the clear-up in one honest take and close on the rolled mat.
Close

Hold the finished shelf and floor from a low camera at child height and read the standard against it: five or six open bins on the lowest shelf, one category each, picture labels on the front face, nothing above shoulder height, and the overflow waiting in labeled closet bins rather than on this shelf. Then run the trigger once in real use, the story announced and the mat cleared before it starts.

Next: The shelf above this one holds the games, and at least one of those boxes cannot be finished.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm fixed over the play mat for tipping, sorting, the washing layout, and the nightly reset
  • Low camera on a short tripod at child eye height for shelf reach, the wall photo, and the finished state
  • Macro handheld for the toilet paper tube test, cracked plastic, and bin labels
  • Tripod at seat height on the shelf face for bin loading and lid removal
  • Basin and towel setup for the wash and dry sequence, shot from directly above
  • Closet setup for the labeled overflow bins and the one-in-one-out swap
  • Tape marks on the wall at shoulder height and child eye height, placed before the shoot
Description hook

A family room toy shelf rebuilt so a four-year-old can reset it alone: five open bins with no lids on the lowest shelf, photo labels on the front face, and the toilet paper tube test run on every small part. Hands only, no presenter.

MZ-031 · R06.03

The Board Game and Puzzle Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Missing Piece: Two Answers”

Count It Back In: A Game Shelf Where Every Box Is Playable Tonight

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open close on a hand lifting a game lid, then overhead as the pieces go out in counted rows with one obvious gap. Set out the decision this shelf has been avoiding for years, the box with one piece missing, and make clear the answer is not the same for every box. Establish the split the video runs on, substitutable against structural, and show the sticky note that turns a vague guilt into a date the box either meets or fails.

Sort Every box is opened and counted against its rules sheet, and any box that cannot be counted comes off the shelf until it is settled.
Beats
  • Open every box and count the pieces against the list printed on the rules sheet, showing the count being done in rows rather than eyeballed.
  • Bag cards, tokens, and dice separately inside their own box, since loose pieces rolling under the board are how the next count fails.
  • Take any box that cannot be finished counting off the shelf entirely, because a game you cannot finish counting is one you cannot finish playing.
  • Work the call on camera by sorting the gaps into substitutable, a meeple, a token, a die, a bill of play money, and structural, a rules booklet, a board section, a card from a deck that must be complete, a puzzle piece. Show a coin and a printed sheet standing in for the first kind.
Shots
  • Overhead on a game box opened and its contents laid out in counted rows
  • Macro on the piece list printed on a rules sheet with a finger tracking down it
  • Close on cards, tokens, and dice going into separate bags inside the box
  • Overhead on two boxes side by side, one marked substitutable and one structural
On-screen text
  • Count against the rules sheet
  • Substitutable or structural
  • Cannot count it, cannot play it
Short cut · 45–60s Hands count game pieces into rows, stop one short, and hold up the rules sheet showing the number they should have reached.
Stands alone: Establish this is a family game shelf and give the substitutable against structural split with one example each, since that split is the entire value of the Short.
Straighten Boxes flat and stacked by height with the heaviest at the bottom, capped at five high, and puzzles kept in their own stack.
Beats
  • Take down a leaning stack and rebuild it flat, heaviest at the bottom, with the tallest boxes on the lower shelf.
  • Cap stacks at five high and show what a taller stack costs here, a reach you cannot make one-handed and a crushed box at the bottom of it.
  • Give puzzles their own short stack, because they come down most often and go back least carefully, and a puzzle box that gets crushed loses pieces into the shelf.
Shots
  • Tripod at shelf height on a leaning stack being taken down and rebuilt heaviest first
  • Close on a hand counting a stack off against five boxes
  • Overhead on the puzzle stack set apart from the game stacks
On-screen text
  • Heaviest at the bottom
  • Five high, no more
  • Puzzles get their own stack
Short cut · 30–45s A hand pulls the bottom box from a stack of seven games and the rest of the stack sags forward.
Stands alone: Say this is a game shelf and give both rules fast, flat with the heaviest at the bottom, and five high. The rebuild is the payoff, so hold on the finished stacks.
Shine Wipe lids and edges, and read the bottom boxes for the damage the stack above has been doing.
Beats
  • Wipe the box lids and edges and name where the film comes from, a room where people eat while they play.
  • Press the bottom corners of the lowest boxes and treat a soft or bowed corner as the finding, because it tells you the stack is too heavy before the box actually fails.
  • Split any stack that is crushing the box beneath it, on camera, as the fix that follows the finding.
Shots
  • Macro on a cloth crossing a game lid, dirty and clean halves in the same frame
  • Macro on a bowed bottom corner with a finger pressing it in
  • Tripod at shelf height on a stack being split into two shorter stacks
On-screen text
  • Clean to inspect
  • Soft corner means too much weight
Short cut · 30–45s Macro: a finger presses the bottom corner of a game box and it gives like cardboard that has been holding weight for years.
Stands alone: Establish the game shelf and the stack sitting on top of that box. Give the fix, split the stack, so the Short resolves rather than just diagnoses.
Safety Small game pieces kept above the youngest child's reach, and no heavy stack parked on the highest shelf.
Beats
  • Take the poison, choke, or strangle question to what scatters out of an open box during play, dice, pawns, and the small metal pieces from older games, on a floor shared with the play mat below.
  • Move the game boxes above the youngest child's reach and check the height against a tape mark rather than assuming it.
  • Take the fall, cut, or crush question to the top shelf, where five or six boxes come down as one weight onto whoever reached for the bottom one.
  • Unload the heavy stack off the highest shelf one box at a time, then show a bottom box drawing out cleanly from a properly loaded shelf.
Shots
  • Macro on dice and pawns scattering off a game box and rolling toward the play mat
  • Low camera checking the lowest game shelf against a taped reach mark
  • Tripod at shelf height on a heavy stack coming down off the top shelf, one box at a time
  • Close on a hand drawing the bottom box out of a five-high stack cleanly
On-screen text
  • Dice are mouth sized
  • Above the youngest reach
  • Nothing heavy on the top shelf
Short cut · 30–45s Overhead on dice bouncing off a game box and rolling off the shelf onto a child's play mat below.
Stands alone: Establish in the first line that this game shelf sits over a shared play floor. State the action, boxes above the youngest child's reach, so the Short is usable on its own.
Standardize The name on the short edge, the date of the last passed count on the lid, and a sticky note with a deadline on anything unsettled.
Beats
  • Tape the short edge of each box and write the game name on it, then check the read from the doorway rather than from arm's length.
  • Write today's date on the lid of every box that has just passed its count, so the shelf shows at a glance which boxes are verified and which are due.
  • Set the mechanism for the unsettled boxes: the missing item and today's date on a sticky note pressed to the lid, and the rule that any box still wearing that note at the next reset leaves the house.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing a game name on tape along a short edge
  • Wide from the doorway reading the short edges of the whole shelf
  • Close on a date being written on a lid
  • Macro on a sticky note naming the missing piece and the date, pressed onto a lid
On-screen text
  • Name on the short edge
  • Date the last passed count
  • Note still there next time, it goes
Short cut · 30–45s A sticky note goes onto a game lid reading one missing piece and today's date, and the box goes back on the shelf with the note showing.
Stands alone: Set up in the opening beat that this box has been on the shelf incomplete for years. The note is the whole mechanism, so state the leaving rule plainly at the end.
Sustain The count happens as the box is packed at the end of game night, not when the next person opens it.
Beats
  • Show the last turn finishing with the lid still off and the pieces still on the table, and start the count there while everything is out.
  • Count back into the bags rather than counting on the way out, so the next person is never the one who discovers the loss.
  • Update the date on the lid in the same motion as closing the box, so the standard maintains itself as part of packing up.
Shots
  • Overhead on a finished game being counted back into its bags at the end of the evening
  • Close on the old date on the lid being crossed out and rewritten
  • Tripod at shelf height on the box going back flat into its stack, name edge out
On-screen text
  • Count it back in, not out
  • Update the date as you close it
Short cut · 30–45s The last token drops into its bag on a table still scattered with a finished game, and a hand writes tonight's date on the lid before the box closes.
Stands alone: Name game night as the trigger in the opening beat and give the reason, so the next person is never the one who finds the loss. The date on the lid is the payoff.
Close

Hold the shelf from the doorway and read the standard against what is visible: every box has passed a piece count with the date on its lid, loose pieces are bagged inside their own box, and the name is readable on the short edge from across the room. Then show the trigger, game night, with the count happening as the box goes back and the date being rewritten in the same motion.

Next: The basket beside the sofa is next, and it is holding more throws than anybody in this house reaches for.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm on a table for opening, counting, and bagging box contents
  • Doorway wide of the whole shelf for the short-edge name read
  • Macro handheld for rules sheets, dates, sticky notes, and bowed corners
  • Tripod at shelf height for stacking, restacking, and the top shelf unload
  • Low camera at child reach height with a tape mark for the safety check
  • Evening setup on the table for the game night count-back sequence
Description hook

A family room game shelf where every box you pull down is complete and playable tonight: counted against the rules sheet, dated on the lid, and named on the short edge so you can read it from the doorway. Hands only, no presenter.

MZ-032 · R06.04

The Blanket and Comfort Zone

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Reaches, Not Looks”

One Basket, One Rule: Sorting Throw Blankets by Use Instead of Looks

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on two throws in one frame, a pilled grey fleece pulled half off the sofa and a handsome wool throw folded untouched on the arm of a chair. Set out the decision this basket keeps getting backwards, the instinct to keep the wool one because it looks like the room you want and quietly retire the fleece because it looks tired. Establish the test the video runs on, that this basket stores comfort and not decoration, so the measure is reaches rather than looks.

Sort Every throw is held to the window light, and the three failures leave this room today rather than getting washed again.
Beats
  • Hold each throw up against the window and let the light do the judging, pilled through and thinned along the fold lines where nobody can see it folded.
  • Add the third failure, a smell that survives washing, and rule out washing it again as the next step.
  • Route the failures honestly on camera, into car blankets, pet bedding, or rags, and out of this room today.
  • Work the call by reaches rather than looks: the fleece everyone fights over stays, and the untouched wool throw goes to the guest bed where beautiful and unused is actually the job, or it goes out. Apply the same test to the knitted heirloom, into the linen closet or to the relative who will wrap up in it.
Shots
  • Tripod at seat height against the window as a throw is held up and the light comes through the thin fold lines
  • Macro on a pilled surface raked with a fingertip
  • Overhead on the sorted piles, keep against car, pet, and rags
  • Close on the wool throw being folded and set aside for the guest bed
On-screen text
  • Hold it to the light
  • Reaches, not looks
  • Out of this room today
Short cut · 30–45s A throw goes up against a bright window and the fold lines glow straight through it.
Stands alone: Establish this is a family room throw basket and name all three failures, pilled, thinned, and a smell that survives washing, since the window test is the whole Short.
Straighten One basket, the rim is the limit, every throw folded to the same rectangle, and nothing draped anywhere else in the room.
Beats
  • Make one basket the only home and show the rim doing the deciding, with a throw that will not fit going straight back to the sort pile.
  • Fold to the same rectangle and run the fold sequence once, slowly, from overhead, so it can be copied.
  • Stack two more the same way and show what matching folds buy, a squared stack where one missing throw or one extra is visible without counting.
  • Strip the sofa back, the radiator, and the chair arm, so the basket is telling the truth about how many there are.
Shots
  • Overhead on one throw being folded to a rectangle in a repeated sequence
  • Close on fold edges lining up as the second and third throws stack
  • Tripod at seat height on the basket filling to the rim and stopping
  • Wide of the sofa back and chair arm going bare
On-screen text
  • The rim is the limit
  • Same rectangle every time
  • Nothing on the sofa back
Short cut · 30–45s Overhead: four throws folded one after another, every fold edge landing on the one below it.
Stands alone: Say this is one basket in a family room and give the reason in the first line, matching folds are what make a missing throw visible. The stack forming carries the rest.
Shine Everything in the basket gets washed including what looks clean, and the basket corners get vacuumed before anything goes back.
Beats
  • Empty the whole basket into the wash including the throws that look clean, because this is where pet hair and popcorn oil concentrate.
  • Work a crevice tool into the basket's inside corners and show what comes out, which is the argument for doing it before the clean throws go back.
  • Return the clean throws folded to the same rectangle, so Shine ends in the state Straighten set rather than undoing it.
Shots
  • Overhead on the whole basket tipped into a laundry basket
  • Macro on a crevice tool working the inside corner of the basket
  • Close on the corner debris in the vacuum head
  • Overhead on folded clean throws going back to the rim line
On-screen text
  • Wash the clean-looking ones too
  • Corners first, then the throws
Short cut · 30–45s A crevice tool goes into the corner of an empty blanket basket and pulls out a surprising amount.
Stands alone: Establish the blanket basket and the rule in one line, wash everything including what looks clean. The corner shot is both the hook and the payoff.
Safety Throws kept off radiators, floor heaters, and lamp shades, which is half the reason the basket rule exists.
Beats
  • Walk the room and find where throws end up when nobody is folding, over the radiator, across the floor heater, hung on the lamp shade.
  • Name it as the burn or fire question and be specific, synthetic fabric against a hot surface as a slow fire that starts once the room is empty.
  • Tie it back to the basket rule so it does not read as a separate chore, since the basket is what keeps the throws off those surfaces.
  • Take the fall question to the throw slumped beside the sofa in low light, exactly where the next person puts a foot standing up in the dark, then put it in the basket instead.
Shots
  • Tripod at seat height on a fleece draped over a radiator, then the same radiator bare
  • Close on a throw hung over a lamp shade being lifted away
  • Low camera on a throw slumped on the floor beside the sofa in low light
  • Close on the same throw going into the basket
On-screen text
  • Off the radiator, off the heater
  • Never on a lamp shade
  • It starts once the room is empty
Short cut · 30–45s A fleece throw lies draped across a radiator and the camera holds on it without cutting away.
Stands alone: Name the room and the hazard plainly in the first beat, a synthetic throw on a hot surface. End with the throw folded into the basket so the Short leaves an action.
Standardize One throw per regular seat plus one spare, with that number written on a label inside the basket rim.
Beats
  • Count the regular seats in this room on camera, a hand landing on each one, and derive the number from the count rather than announcing it.
  • Write that number on a small label and fix it inside the basket rim, where whoever is folding sees the rule without being told it.
  • Show the rule doing work, a fifth throw arriving at a basket labeled for four, and the label deciding what happens next.
Shots
  • Wide of the room with hands touching each regular seat as the count runs
  • Macro on the number being written on a small label
  • Close on the label being pressed inside the basket rim
  • Overhead on four folded throws against the label
On-screen text
  • One per seat, plus one spare
  • The label lives in the rim
Short cut · 30–45s A hand counts the seats around a family room and then writes a single number on a label.
Stands alone: Establish the throw basket and derive the number on camera, since the arithmetic is the idea. Hold on the label going inside the rim as the payoff.
Sustain Whatever is on the sofa gets folded into the basket on the walk to the last lamp.
Beats
  • Show a hand reaching for the last lamp switch and stopping, since that walk past the sofa already happens every night and the throw is on the way.
  • Fold whatever is on the sofa and drop it in the basket on the way past, shown once in real time so the size of the task is honest.
  • End on the basket at the rim line with the fold edges square, which is the state tomorrow evening starts from.
Shots
  • Tripod at seat height at dusk on a hand reaching for the lamp switch
  • Overhead on a throw being folded on the sofa in a few motions
  • Close on it dropping into the basket, fold edges lining up
  • Wide of the dark room with the basket squared away
On-screen text
  • Last lamp, fold on the way past
  • One pass, not a chore
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches for a lamp switch in a dim room, stops, and picks up the throw off the sofa first.
Stands alone: Name the trigger immediately since it is the whole Short. Shoot the fold and the drop in one continuous take so the cost of the habit reads as small.
Close

Hold the finished corner and read the standard against it: one basket, one throw per regular seat plus one spare, every throw folded to the same rectangle, and no blanket left over a radiator or a heater. Then run the trigger once, the last lamp going off and the sofa throw folded into the basket on the way past.

Next: The side table beside this sofa is next, and every phone in the house ends up on it.

Shot list
  • Window-backed tripod setup at seat height for the hold-to-the-light sort
  • Overhead arm over a low table or the sofa seat for all folding sequences
  • Macro handheld for pilling, the rim label, and basket corners
  • Tripod at seat height on the basket for filling and the rim line
  • Radiator, heater, and lamp shade setups for the hazard sequence, appliances cold and switched off
  • Dusk setup on the lamp switch and the sofa for the trigger
Description hook

A family room blanket basket that tells the truth about how many throws you own: one per seat plus one spare, folded to the same rectangle, and nothing left over a radiator. Hands only, no presenter.

MZ-033 · R06.05

The Charging and Device Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “One Named Slot Each”

One Strip, Named Slots: Setting Up a Family Charging Station

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a drawer being pulled open and a hand lifting a retired phone, screen dark, out of a nest of cables. Set out the contradiction that has kept it there: it is being held as a backup in case something breaks and as an archive because there are photos on it never transferred, and it cannot be both. Make clear it is serving neither right now, and that it gets settled in this session while the device is in hand and the charger is on the table.

Sort Every cable and plug is matched to a device in this house that currently works, and the unmatched go to recycling rather than back in the drawer.
Beats
  • Lay every cable and plug out in one straight line, because a drawer cannot be sorted while it is still a tangle.
  • Bring the actual devices to the line and set each one at the end of the cable that fits it, rather than working from memory.
  • Sweep what is left into a recycling bag, since unmatched is not spare, and keep one spare of each connector type in a labeled bag.
  • Settle the retired phone: a backup is one you have charged and switched on within the last year, so run the photo transfer now on camera, or say plainly it will never happen, then send the handset with its battery to a proper collection point.
Shots
  • Overhead on cables laid out in a straight line across a table
  • Close on a device being set at the end of the cable that matches it
  • Overhead on the unmatched cables swept into a recycling bag
  • Macro on the labeled spare connector bag being written and sealed
  • Close on the retired phone plugged in and the photo transfer running on screen
On-screen text
  • Match it to a living device
  • Unmatched is not spare
  • Backup or archive, not both
Short cut · 45–60s Overhead: a drawer of tangled cables becomes one straight line, and half of it has nothing left in the house to plug into.
Stands alone: Establish this is a household cable drawer and give the matching rule in the opening beat. End on the recycling bag beside the one labeled bag of spares, so the viewer has both halves.
Straighten One strip on a hard surface, one named slot per device, cables shortened to just reach, and no charger left anywhere else in the room.
Beats
  • Set one power strip on a hard surface and assign one slot per device, with the owner's name going on the slot.
  • Coil each cable to the length that just reaches its slot and clip the excess, so the ends stay up on the surface instead of hanging toward the floor.
  • Walk the room and unplug every other charger, bringing them all in, so this station is genuinely the only charging point.
  • Leave the empty slots visible during the day, which is what lets anyone read the station in one glance from the doorway.
Shots
  • Tripod at table height on the strip being placed on a hard surface and squared up
  • Macro on a cable being coiled to length and clipped
  • Close on cable ends resting up on the surface rather than hanging over the edge
  • Wide of the room as hands collect chargers from two other sockets
On-screen text
  • One strip, one slot each
  • Shorten to just reach
  • No chargers anywhere else
Short cut · 30–45s A charging cable hangs off a side table almost to the floor, then a clip takes up the slack in one motion.
Stands alone: Say this is a family charging station and that cables are cut to just-reach length. Name the hanging loop as the reason in one beat so the clip reads as a fix rather than tidiness.
Shine Inspect the cable ends where the sheath cracks first, and clear the lint out of the charging ports.
Beats
  • Wipe each cable end and inspect the last few centimetres near the plug, where the sheath splits first, and treat a crack there as the finding.
  • Brush the lint out of the charging ports, since packed lint is why a plug stops seating long before the cable is actually broken.
  • Show a port before and after and the plug seating fully with no gap, which is the test that says the port was the problem.
Shots
  • Macro on the last few centimetres of a cable near the plug, sheath cracked
  • Macro into a charging port packed with grey lint
  • Macro on a soft brush drawing the lint out
  • Close on the plug seating fully with no gap
On-screen text
  • The sheath cracks nearest the plug
  • Lint, not a broken cable
Short cut · 30–45s Macro straight into a phone charging port that is completely packed with grey lint.
Stands alone: Establish it is a charging port and state the misdiagnosis in the first line, that people buy a new cable when the port is the problem. The brush-out and the fully seated plug close it.
Safety Nothing charges on soft material, swollen or hot packs come off immediately, cables stay short, and drinks stay off this surface.
Beats
  • State the rule first and clear each thing it names, a tablet off a cushion, a pack out from under a blanket, a phone off a stack of paper, framed as the burn or fire question.
  • Lay a hand flat on every device on the station once during this pass, since lithium batteries need air and heat is the thing a hand finds first.
  • Use a clearly labeled stand-in pack to show what stop now looks like, bulging at the seam, and take it off the strip so it does not go back on.
  • Take the poison, choke, or strangle question to the cable long enough to hang to the floor and loop at a toddler's neck height, then clip it flat, and move the glasses off a surface that holds a live strip.
Shots
  • Overhead on a tablet charging on a cushion, then the same tablet on a hard surface
  • Close on a hand laid flat across each device on the station in turn
  • Macro on the labeled stand-in pack with a bulged seam, on-screen note that it is a stand-in
  • Low camera on a hanging cable loop at toddler height, then the same cable clipped flat
  • Close on a glass being lifted off the charging table
On-screen text
  • Never on soft material
  • Swollen, hot, bulging: off now
  • No glasses on this surface
Short cut · 45–60s A tablet lies face down charging on a sofa cushion, and a hand lifts it to show the warm hollow underneath.
Stands alone: Name the burn or fire question and the rule immediately, nothing charges on soft material. Include the swollen and too hot to hold signs, since a viewer may only ever see this Short.
Standardize Names on the slots rather than only on the cables, and the strip left in open view.
Beats
  • Write name labels for the slots themselves rather than for the cables, so an empty slot reads as a missing device rather than as free space.
  • Show that reading happening, a mid-morning station with two named slots empty and the names answering whose phones are out of the house.
  • Keep the strip in open view instead of pushed behind furniture, because a scorched socket or a chewed cable behind a sofa goes unnoticed. Point to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, and to the line, find it, and fix it now.
Shots
  • Macro on name labels being written and placed at each slot on the surface
  • Overhead on the station mid-morning with two named slots empty
  • Tripod at table height showing the strip in open view rather than tucked behind furniture
On-screen text
  • Name the slot, not just the cable
  • Empty slot means missing device
  • Ch 21, the hazard hunt
Short cut · 30–45s Two slots on a charging station sit empty, and the labels underneath say exactly whose phones are not home.
Stands alone: Establish the station and the naming rule in one beat. The insight, that an empty slot reads as a missing device, is the whole Short, so land it on the labels.
Sustain Devices come to the station when the dishwasher is started for the night and stay until morning.
Beats
  • Show the dishwasher door closing and the cycle starting, and hang the habit there, because it is the last thing anyone does in this house before phones would otherwise walk to bedrooms.
  • Bring every device to the station in one trip rather than announcing a rule, and show them staying there until morning.
  • End on every named slot filled, the strip in view on a hard surface, and nothing charging anywhere else in the room.
Shots
  • Close on a dishwasher door closing and the cycle button being pressed
  • Tripod at table height on hands carrying phones and a tablet to the station in one trip
  • Overhead on every named slot filled
  • Wide of the room at night with the station lit and in view
On-screen text
  • Dishwasher on, devices in
  • They stay until morning
Short cut · 30–45s A dishwasher cycle button is pressed, and the next shot is three phones landing on their named slots.
Stands alone: Name the room and the trigger in the first beat. The one-trip carry is the demonstration and the full station is the payoff, so both must be in the Short.
Close

Hold the station and read the standard against what is visible: one strip on a hard surface, one named slot per device, one labeled bag of spare connectors, no charger plugged in anywhere else in the room, and nothing charging on soft material. Then show the trigger once, the dishwasher started and the devices coming to the station for the night.

Next: The table where the glass could not go is next, and something on it has been half finished for months.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm on a table for the cable line-up, the device matching, and the recycling sweep
  • Macro handheld for plug sheaths, ports, lint, and slot labels
  • Tripod at table height on the strip for placement and the nightly fill
  • Low camera at toddler height for the hanging cable loop and the clipped fix
  • Cushion and hard surface pair setup for the charging comparison, with the labeled stand-in pack
  • Kitchen setup on the dishwasher for the trigger, cut to the station in the same evening light
  • Night wide of the room with the station in open view
Description hook

One charging station for the whole house, on a surface that can take the heat: named slots so an empty one means a missing phone, cables shortened to just reach, and nothing charging on a cushion. Hands only, no presenter.

MZ-034 · R06.06

The Craft and Activity Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Name The Next Action”

Bins Named for What They Make: Resetting a Family Craft Corner

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a bag holding something started with real enthusiasm and abandoned in the middle, sitting on the good end of the work surface with dust along its top edge. Set out why it stays: clearing it feels like quitting, so nothing else gets started on that surface. Establish the test the video runs on, naming the very next physical action and the day you will do it, and make clear that failing to produce both halves is itself the answer.

Sort Every marker is tested on a scrap, dried and separated supplies go, and the abandoned project either gets a next action and a date or gets broken down.
Beats
  • Draw every marker across one scrap sheet, because the cap tells you nothing and the sheet tells you everything, and let the gaps build in the row.
  • Bin the dried glue sticks and the paint that has separated, showing the stir attempt failing so the judgement is visible rather than asserted.
  • Search once for the missing instruction sheet on camera, and discard the kit only after the search fails.
  • Work the call on the abandoned project: name the very next physical action and the day, not the goal, and when it stalls, break the project down, good materials back into the paper, drawing, and glue bins, the partly worked piece to somebody who will finish it or out.
Shots
  • Overhead on a row of markers drawn one after another across a single scrap sheet
  • Close on a stir stick lifting separated paint that will not recombine
  • Overhead on a kit box with no instruction sheet, phone beside it mid-search
  • Overhead on the abandoned project being unpacked and its materials sorted back into the bins
On-screen text
  • The scrap tells you everything
  • Next action, and the day
  • Materials go back to the bins
Short cut · 30–45s Overhead: a row of markers drawn one after another across a single scrap sheet, and several leave nothing behind at all.
Stands alone: Establish this is a family craft supply sort and give the rule in the first line, a cap tells you nothing. Hold on the finished scrap sheet with its gaps as the payoff.
Straighten Four lidded bins packed by what gets made, each one liftable to the table and back in one hand.
Beats
  • Pack each bin by what gets made rather than by material, with the drawing bin taking paper, pencils, and the sharpener together.
  • Show what that avoids by walking the shelves the old way first, three stops to start one drawing.
  • Set the four bins, paper and card, drawing, glue and tape, kits in progress, and lift each one out to the table one-handed.
  • Carry the same bin back to its slot the same way, so the trip works in both directions and a child can make it too.
Shots
  • Overhead on the drawing bin being packed with paper, pencils, and the sharpener together
  • Close on the four labeled bins in a row on the shelf
  • Tripod at table height on one bin lifted one-handed and carried to the table
  • Tripod at table height on the same bin going back into its shelf slot
On-screen text
  • Packed by what it makes
  • One hand, one trip
  • Four bins, lidded
Short cut · 30–45s A hand takes paper off one shelf, pencils off another, and the sharpener off a third, then cuts to all three sitting in one bin.
Stands alone: Say this is a family craft shelf and give the principle in one line, pack by what gets made rather than by material. The one-handed carry closes it.
Shine Scrape the surface before wiping, clear the glitter out of the seams, and dry brushes bristle up.
Beats
  • Scrape dried glue and paint off the work surface with a plastic scraper before any cloth touches it, and show what wiping first would have smeared.
  • Get into the table seams where glitter sits, showing the tool that actually reaches into them.
  • Stand the brushes bristle up to dry and put a bent head next to a straight one, so the cost of drying them the other way is visible.
Shots
  • Macro on a plastic scraper lifting dried glue off the work surface in one pass
  • Macro along a table seam packed with glitter, before and after
  • Close on brushes standing bristle up in a jar
  • Macro comparing a bent bristle head against a straight one
On-screen text
  • Scrape first, then wipe
  • Glitter lives in the seams
  • Bristle up to dry
Short cut · 30–45s Macro: a plastic scraper takes a long ribbon of dried glue off a craft table in one unbroken pass.
Stands alone: Establish the craft work surface and the order in the first line, scrape before you wipe. Use the brush drying comparison as a fast second half.
Safety The glue gun is the real hazard here, and knives, beads, and solvents go up high rather than into a floor-level bin.
Beats
  • Name the glue gun as the hazard and show why, framed as the burn or fire question: no obvious off signal, a tip that stays hot long after the last bead, and a plug left in on a surface a child reaches.
  • Give it a fixed cooling spot on a hard tile and pull the plug before the clean-up starts, demonstrated in that order rather than described.
  • Take the fall, cut, or crush question to craft knives and sharp-point scissors, and turn the scissors point down in the cup instead of blade up.
  • Take the poison, choke, or strangle question to seed beads, googly eyes, and pompoms in a room a crawling child shares, and move them with the glue and the solvent based markers to a high shelf.
Shots
  • Close on a glue gun tip with a bead still forming, then the plug being pulled at the wall
  • Tripod at table height on the gun placed on its hard tile in a marked spot
  • Macro on scissors turned point down into a cup
  • Overhead on seed beads, googly eyes, and pompoms being lidded and moved to a high shelf
  • Low camera confirming that shelf is above the youngest child's reach mark
On-screen text
  • Unplug before you clean up
  • The tip stays hot
  • Point down, and up high
Short cut · 45–60s A glue gun sits on a tile with a bead still hanging from the tip, and a hand pulls its plug at the wall without touching the gun.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a craft table children use and name the specific danger, no off signal and a tip that stays hot. Give the fixed cooling tile as the fix so the Short ends with a setup, not a scare.
Standardize One project out at a time, and each lidded bin labeled with what it makes rather than what it holds.
Beats
  • Set the rule, one project bin out at a time, and show what it protects, a work surface that otherwise fills from both ends.
  • Write two candidate labels for the same bin, one naming the material and one naming what it makes, and choose on camera.
  • Hold the state the rule produces, one clear work surface with exactly one bin on it and the other three lidded and named on the shelf.
Shots
  • Macro on two candidate labels side by side, one naming a material and one naming what it makes
  • Close on the chosen label going onto the bin front
  • Overhead on the clear work surface with exactly one bin on it
  • Tripod at table height on the shelf with the other three bins lidded and named
On-screen text
  • One project out at a time
  • Name what it makes
  • Clear surface, one bin
Short cut · 30–45s Two labels for the same craft bin sit side by side, one naming the contents and one naming what it makes, and a hand picks up the second.
Stands alone: Establish this is a craft bin and let the two labels carry the idea without needing the parent video. Close on the clear surface with one bin out so the rule has a visible result.
Sustain When the table is being set for dinner, the open project bin closes and goes back whatever state the project is in.
Beats
  • Show placemats and cutlery landing on the far end of the same surface the project bin is on, since dinner and craft compete for this one table every evening.
  • Press the lid onto a genuinely mid-project bin and put it back on the shelf, because that resistance is the whole habit.
  • End on the clear surface with the table set beside it, which is what makes tomorrow's restart one motion instead of an excavation.
Shots
  • Close on placemats and cutlery entering frame at the edge of the work surface
  • Overhead on a half-worked project having its lid pressed on
  • Tripod at table height on the bin going back to its named shelf slot
  • Overhead on the clear surface with the table set beside it
On-screen text
  • Table gets set, bin gets closed
  • Whatever state it is in
Short cut · 30–45s A lid presses down on a craft project that is visibly half finished, and it goes back on the shelf anyway.
Stands alone: Name the trigger in the opening beat, the table being set for dinner in a room where craft and dinner share one surface. The resistance is the lesson, so the lid closing on unfinished work is the hook.
Close

Hold the finished corner and read the standard against it: four lidded bins labeled by what they make, one project bin out on a clear surface, the glue gun unplugged on its tile, and knives, beads, and solvents above the youngest child's reach. Then run the trigger once in real use, the table being set and the open bin closing and going back whatever state the project is in.

Next: That is all six zones in this room, and the next room starts at the door everybody comes in through.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm fixed above the craft work surface for marker testing, bin packing, and the dinner trigger

Description hook

A family room craft corner where a project starts in one motion and the surface clears just as fast: four lidded bins named for what they make, scissors point down, and the glue gun on a fixed cooling tile. Hands only, no presenter.
