Room 07 of 20

Primary Bedroom

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteOne person, one tripod, window light. Shoot on a clear morning with the curtains fully open and the overhead light off, because the bedroom ceiling fitting sits directly above the bed and throws a hard shadow of the camera into every overhead frame. Bounce a white board off the wall opposite the window to lift the shadow side of the bed. Two positions carry the whole room: a low three-quarter at the foot of the bed for wide work, and an overhead arm clamped to a stand for drawer, nightstand and dresser tops, set up on the side of the bed away from the door so the walking strip stays clear for the Safety frames. Everything is locked off. There are no tracking, following or handheld travel shots in this room, so movement is carried by hands entering and leaving a static frame. Strip and remake the bed yourself before you start rolling so the linen reads clean. Take the closet door off its hinges rather than squeezing a tripod into the opening. Save the two darkened passes, the bedside floor strip and the closet floor, for last: close the curtains, shoot both, then stop for the day rather than trying to get daylight back. On-set safety: the dresser anti-tip strap and the closet rod brackets are filmed as real fixes, so have a stud finder, the correct fixings and a driver on hand. Never stage a loaded chest with two drawers open as an unanchored tip demonstration; the strap goes in first and the shot shows it taking the load. Extinguish the candle before filming the sleeve pass. Keep your own lamp and camera cables out of the same floor strip the video tells viewers to keep bare.
MZ-035 · R07.01

The Bed and Bedding Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Two Sheet Sets, Not Five”

Bed and Bedding: Two Sheet Sets and a Clear Floor

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a linen shelf with four or five sets stacked on it, hands lifting each one out in turn: the wedding gift, the new set that turns out to be scratchy, the good set still in its wrapper. Name the honest number the manual gives, two per bed, one on and one clean, and name the one condition that earns a third, which is a child or a pet who actually sleeps here and a bed you have stripped in the middle of the night within the last year. Land the specific discomfort that the good set has never been slept on, and promise the video ends with it on the bed.

Sort Stripping the bed and pulling out everything underneath it, and knowing which linen is genuinely finished rather than demoted to a spare.
Beats
  • Strip the bed completely and pull out what is actually under it: the wrapping paper, the shoe boxes, the box of paperwork nobody filed, none of which belongs to sleep and all of which is here because the door usually stays shut.
  • Show the three retirement tests on real items: a sheet worn thin at the hip held up to the window, a blanket gone pilled and scratchy under the hand, a pillow bent in half that stays folded.
  • Explain that these leave as rags or textile recycling and not as spares for a guest who never comes, and bag them on camera.
  • Count the surviving sets against the two per bed standard and set the good one aside for tonight.
Shots
  • Three-quarter wide from the foot of the bed, hands pulling the fitted sheet off the corners.
  • Overhead of the floor filling with bins, shoe boxes and wrapping paper coming out from under the bed.
  • Backlit close on a sheet held to the window so the thin patch at the hip reads on camera.
  • Macro on a pillow folded in half by two hands and staying folded when released.
On-screen text
  • Strip it, then look under it
  • Thin at the hip
  • Rags, not spares
Short cut · 30–45s A pillow bent in half by two hands that just stays folded, with the retirement test named in the first seconds.
Stands alone: Re-establish that this is a bed and bedding reset and that the pillow is being tested, not played with, because the folded-pillow shot is meaningless without the test being named up front.
Straighten Storing each set folded inside one of its own pillowcases, keeping this bed's linen off the guest and kid shelves, and putting the good set on tonight.
Beats
  • Fold a full set flat on the bare mattress and slide the whole bundle into one of its own pillowcases.
  • Explain that this stops the flat sheet and the fitted sheet travelling separately, which is the actual failure it fixes.
  • Show the linen shelf reorganised so this bed's two sets sit on one shelf rather than stacked in with guest doubles and kid singles.
  • Make the bed with the good set, the one that has never been slept on, because a sheet saved for an occasion is a sheet nobody ever uses.
Shots
  • Overhead of the fold sequence on the bare mattress, hands only, single continuous framing.
  • Close on the bundle sliding into the pillowcase and the case being squared off.
  • Three-quarter of the linen shelf before and after, matched framing on a locked tripod.
  • Close on the good set coming out of its wrapper and the fitted sheet going onto the first corner.
On-screen text
  • One set, one pillowcase
  • This bed gets its own shelf
  • The good set goes on tonight
Short cut · 30–45s A whole sheet set disappearing into its own pillowcase in one motion, overhead.
Stands alone: Say what the bundle contains and which bed it belongs to, since the fold shot alone reads as a folding tip rather than a storage rule.
Shine Cleaning the mattress and behind the headboard while the bed is bare, which is the only moment either is reachable.
Beats
  • With the mattress bare, vacuum the whole surface and then work the seam where the protector tucks under.
  • Feed the vacuum head down behind the headboard and show the dust and hair packed against the wall there, which is cleaning to inspect rather than to impress.
  • Note that the cases get washed constantly and the pillows inside them almost never do, and put the pillows themselves through the machine as the seasons turn.
Shots
  • Overhead of the vacuum head crossing the bare mattress in overlapping passes.
  • Macro on the protector seam being lifted and the nozzle going into it.
  • Low three-quarter from beside the bed, hands feeding the vacuum head down the gap behind the headboard.
  • Close on the pillows going into the machine drum.
On-screen text
  • Bare mattress, both seams
  • Behind the headboard
  • Wash the pillows, not just the cases
Short cut · 30–45s The vacuum head going down the gap behind the headboard, into a space the viewer has never cleaned.
Stands alone: Establish that the bed is stripped and that this gap is only reachable now, or the shot reads as ordinary vacuuming.
Safety The floor strip you cross in the dark, and the weight sitting above a sleeping head.
Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as fall: hold a locked low frame on the strip of floor between the bed and the door with a storage bin corner, a shoe and a charging cable sitting in it.
  • Clear the strip on camera and set the rule that nothing goes under the bed that sticks out into it, so the under-bed bins sit flat and fully back.
  • Frame the second hazard as fall, cut or crush: framed pictures, a speaker and a stack of books on a headboard ledge sitting directly over a sleeping head.
  • Show the two acceptable outcomes, moving them off entirely or fixing them into the wall properly, and drive a fixing into the wall on camera.
Shots
  • Locked low frame along the bare floor strip from bedside to door, curtains closed to read as night.
  • Close on a bin corner and a coiled cable being lifted out of the strip.
  • Three-quarter from the side of the bed looking up at the headboard ledge with the pillow in frame beneath it.
  • Close on hands driving a fixing into the wall behind a frame.
On-screen text
  • Keep this strip bare
  • Nothing heavy above the pillow
  • Move it or fix it
Short cut · 30–45s A darkened floor between a bed and a bedroom door with a bin corner and a cable lying in it, framed as what your foot finds at three in the morning.
Stands alone: Name the room and the moment in the first line, because the darkened floor strip is unreadable without knowing it is a bedside walking route at night.
Standardize Writing down what a made bed means in this house, precisely enough that it looks the same whoever does it.
Beats
  • Make the bed to the agreed state and hold the wide as the reference frame.
  • Show the standard being written down to the pillow count and whether the duvet is folded back or pulled flat, because those two details are what drift between people.
  • Leave the written standard where the linen lives, and quote the frozen rule line that a standard is the best way you know today, written down.
  • Photograph the finished bed and point to Chapter 25 and the ideal-state photo as why the photo goes on the linen shelf.
Shots
  • Locked three-quarter wide of the finished made bed, held long enough to work as a reference frame.
  • Overhead close on the standard being written out by hand.
  • Close on a phone photographing the made bed and the photo being tucked onto the linen shelf.
On-screen text
  • Pillow count, in writing
  • Folded back or pulled flat
  • Ch 25: the ideal-state photo
Short cut · 30–45s Two beds cut back to back that differ only in pillow count and duvet fold, showing what an unwritten standard costs a household.
Stands alone: State in the opening seconds that both beds were made by different people in the same house on different mornings, which is the entire point of the comparison.
Sustain Making the bed before you leave the room, and using the sheet wash as the trigger to look underneath.
Beats
  • Show the one-pull version, duvet still thrown back, done in the moment before leaving the room.
  • Contrast with the ten o'clock version where yesterday's clothes have to come off the bed first, which is why the habit is placed where it is and not later.
  • Attach the under-bed check to stripping the sheets for the wash, so the space under the bed gets seen every time the linen cycles.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of hands pulling the duvet up in a single motion beside a still-warm bed.
  • Matched shot later in the day with clothing piled on the cover, hands clearing it first.
  • Overhead of a stripped bed with hands sweeping under it before the clean set goes on.
On-screen text
  • Before you leave the room
  • One pull, not ten minutes
Short cut · 30–45s The same bed made twice in one clip, once in a single pull and once after a pile of clothes has to come off it first.
Stands alone: Establish that the only difference between the two is the time of day, not the person and not the bed.
Close

Return to the finished wide: two sets for this bed each folded inside its own pillowcase, the agreed pillow count on the cover and nothing else, the good set actually on the bed, and a bare floor strip on both sides. Show the trigger as a physical sequence, sheets coming off for the wash and hands going under the bed before the clean set goes back on.

Next: Next, the smallest zone in this room and the one you look at last thing and first thing, your own nightstand.

Shot list
  • Locked three-quarter wide from the foot of the bed, used for the made-bed reference and every before and after pair.
  • Overhead arm over the mattress for the strip, the vacuum passes and the fold sequence.
  • Locked low frame along the bedside floor strip, curtains closed, shot last with the closet floor pass.
  • Close on hands at the mattress protector seam and behind the headboard.
  • Backlit close at the window for the worn sheet and the folded pillow tests.
  • Three-quarter on the linen shelf, matched before and after.
  • Close on hands writing the made-bed standard and photographing the finished bed.
  • Close on hands fixing a frame into the wall above the headboard.
Description hook

Two sheet sets per bed, one on and one clean, and a floor strip you can cross barefoot in the dark. This is the bed and bedding zone from the Micro Zone Manual, worked start to finish through all six S's.

MZ-036 · R07.02

Your Own Nightstand

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Five Things. Count Them.”

Your Nightstand: Five Things or Fewer, and the Phone Charger Decision

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on a nightstand top with the phone charging on it, and name the trade the manual names: you know the phone should not sleep here and you have kept it because it is your alarm. Show that as one job a small clock already does. Set up the two honest routes the video makes you pick between, moving the charger across the room to the dresser or keeping it face down and taking something else off the top so you are still at five, and say plainly that the option gone is calling the current arrangement temporary.

Sort Emptying the drawer onto the bed, clearing the four books you started, and settling the phone charger one way or the other.
Beats
  • Tip the whole drawer out onto the bed in one movement and let the volume land before sorting starts.
  • Work the four named categories on camera: dead pens tested on paper, chargers for phones nobody owns any more, hotel earplugs still in their wrappers, and the started-and-abandoned books.
  • Apply the book rule as the manual states it, that a book you are not reading this week belongs on the shelf and not beside your head, and carry three of the four out.
  • Settle the charger on camera rather than deferring it: the clock goes onto the top and the charger is carried to the dresser across the room, with the honest alternative shown as a second option, charger stays, phone face down, and something else leaves the top.
  • Count the remaining items on the top with a finger to land on five or fewer.
Shots
  • Overhead of the drawer inverting onto the bedspread, single take.
  • Close on hands scribbling each pen on a pad and dropping the dead ones into a pot.
  • Close on a stack of four part-read books, hands lifting all but one out of frame.
  • Close on the charger being unplugged from the nightstand and set down on the dresser across the room, with the clock going into its place.
  • Overhead of the cleared top with the remaining items counted by a finger.
On-screen text
  • Empty it onto the bed
  • Reading it this week?
  • Count to five
Short cut · 30–45s A whole nightstand drawer tipped onto a bed in one motion, with the five things or fewer target named before the pile lands.
Stands alone: Name the zone and the target number immediately, so the pile has a destination and the Short is not just a shot of mess.
Straighten Dividing the drawer into named sections and getting every cord off the surface.
Beats
  • Fit dividers so glasses, lip balm and earplugs each get their own section instead of sliding into one heap.
  • Apply the test from the manual, naming what is in each section with the drawer still shut and then opening it to check.
  • Clip the lamp and clock cords down the back leg so nothing loops across the top, and hold a surface-level frame with no cable crossing it.
Shots
  • Overhead of dividers going into the empty drawer and each section being filled.
  • Overhead of the drawer shut, then opening to confirm the three named sections.
  • Low three-quarter behind the nightstand, hands running clips down the back leg.
  • Close along the bare top at surface level, no cable in the frame.
On-screen text
  • Three sections, three names
  • Cords down the back leg
Short cut · 30–45s Three drawer sections named on screen while the drawer is still shut, then the drawer opens to prove the names right.
Stands alone: Set the naming up as a test of the storage before performing it, or it reads as somebody listing objects.
Shine The water ring on the top, and the lampshade and bulb that have been quietly dimming your reading light.
Beats
  • Lift everything off and wipe the top, working at the ring the water glass has been leaving.
  • Wash the lampshade and the bulb, which is what gets your reading light back to the brightness you paid for.
  • Cut a before and after of the lamp switched on in identical conditions, showing the difference without claiming a number.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bare top with hands working the water ring in one continuous pass.
  • Close on the shade being lifted off and washed, and the cooled bulb being wiped.
  • Locked three-quarter of the lamp lit before and after, identical framing and exposure.
On-screen text
  • The ring under the glass
  • Wash the shade and the bulb
Short cut · 30–45s A bedside lamp switched on before and after its shade and bulb are washed, in one locked frame.
Stands alone: State that framing and exposure are unchanged between the two, because a brightness comparison is worthless if the viewer suspects the camera did it.
Safety Water and electricity sharing one small surface, and open flame at bedding height.
Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as water and electricity: an open glass beside the lamp base, a charger and a power strip all crowded onto one small top, one knocked elbow from a problem.
  • Perform both fixes on camera, the power strip moving down to the floor behind the nightstand and the open glass being swapped for a bottle with a lid.
  • Frame the second as burn or fire: a candle sitting level with the bedding and directly in the path your sleeve takes reaching for the lamp.
  • Move the candle to the dresser and set the rule that if you want one burning at night it burns there.
Shots
  • Low surface-level three-quarter showing glass, lamp base, charger and strip crowded in one plane.
  • Close on hands lifting the power strip down behind the nightstand and dressing the cable.
  • Close on the open glass being replaced by a lidded bottle on the same coaster.
  • Side-on close of a sleeve passing directly over a candle at bedding height, flame extinguished before the pass is filmed.
On-screen text
  • Water and electricity, one surface
  • Power goes on the floor
  • Candles burn on the dresser
Short cut · 30–45s A sleeve passing straight over a bedside candle at bedding height on the reach to the lamp, shot side on.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a nightstand and a nightly reaching motion, and say plainly that the flame is out for the filmed pass.
Standardize Five things or fewer, countable from the doorway, and knowing what the sixth item usually is.
Beats
  • Put the camera at the doorway and count the top from there, showing the standard is checkable without walking over.
  • Name the manual's observation that the sixth item is almost always a finished book or an empty glass, and show the sixth appearing.
  • Route both on camera, the finished book going to the shelf and the empty glass going to the kitchen that night.
Shots
  • Doorway-height three-quarter of the nightstand across the room, items countable in frame.
  • Overhead close as a sixth item lands on the top and is picked up.
  • Locked close on a shelf as the book arrives, and on the bedroom door as the glass leaves frame.
On-screen text
  • Countable from the doorway
  • The sixth is a book or a glass
Short cut · 30–45s Counting a nightstand top from the bedroom doorway without walking over or touching anything.
Stands alone: Give the number and the reason for counting from a distance, so the shot reads as a daily check and not as a camera position.
Sustain Using the reach for the lamp switch as the moment the top goes back to five.
Beats
  • Show the habit exactly where the manual puts it, in the reach across to switch off the lamp, with the hand putting the sixth thing back before it returns.
  • Show that the reset finishes inside the reach itself, with the lamp off and no second trip made and nothing to remember tomorrow.
  • Cut to the same top the next morning to show what waking to a clear surface actually looks like.
Shots
  • Low three-quarter from pillow height, a hand reaching across, resetting an item and returning.
  • Close on the lamp switch under the same hand in the same motion.
  • Overhead of the top in morning light, unchanged from the night before.
On-screen text
  • Reset on the way to the switch
  • Wake up to five
Short cut · 30–45s One hand reaching for a bedside lamp switch, putting the nightstand top back to five things on the way, and never making a second trip.
Stands alone: Name the trigger as the lamp reach and the target as five in the opening line, since the motion is small and easily missed.
Close

Finish on the overhead: lamp, lidded bottle on its coaster, one book, a small dish with your glasses, five or fewer and no cable crossing the surface. Open the drawer to show three named sections with room left in each. Show the trigger as the physical reach for the lamp switch, with the top going back to five inside that movement.

Next: Next, the other side of the bed, and the one zone in this room that is not yours to decide about.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm locked over the nightstand top, the spine of the whole video.
  • Overhead of the drawer inverted onto the bed and of the dividers going in.
  • Low surface-level three-quarter for the crowded-top hazard and the candle pass.
  • Doorway-height three-quarter across the room for the countable-from-the-doorway check.
  • Locked three-quarter of the lit lamp, matched before and after the shade wash.
  • Behind-the-nightstand close for cord clipping and the power strip relocation.
  • Close on the charger leaving the nightstand and landing on the dresser.
  • Pillow-height low three-quarter of the hand reaching for the lamp switch.
  • Morning overhead of the untouched top.
Description hook

Five things or fewer on the top, countable from the doorway, and a drawer where every section has a name. The nightstand zone from the Micro Zone Manual, including the phone charger decision made on camera.

MZ-037 · R07.03

The Other Sleeper's Nightstand

5–7 min · thumbnail: “You Clean, They Cull”

The Shared Bedroom Nightstand: You Clean, They Cull

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on two nightstands in one frame, one finished and one untouched, and name the fight the manual names: you want to fix that side because you can see it from yours, and every argument about tidiness in a shared bedroom starts right here. State the rule that settles it, that you may wipe, vacuum and straighten anything on that side and may not remove a single object from it, and flag the one exception the video ends up handling out loud, which is out of date medication, because that is a safety question and not a taste question.

Sort The sort you do not do, and how the offer gets made instead.
Beats
  • Carry a bin liner and a box in and set them down beside the other nightstand, unopened, so the offer has something to point at.
  • Show your own side already finished to standard, because finishing first is the only argument you are allowed to make.
  • Show only what gets handed over going into the liner, one item at a time, with the drawer never being tipped out and no pile ever being made.
  • Hold on the closed drawer and the untouched top to land the discipline, that what they keep stays and you say nothing about it.
Shots
  • Wide three-quarter holding both nightstands, one finished and one untouched.
  • Close on a bin liner and box set down on the floor beside the untouched side, lids closed.
  • Close on a single item entering frame from the far side of the bed and going into the liner.
  • Overhead of the closed drawer with hands resting on the top and not opening it.
On-screen text
  • Finish your side first
  • Ask, do not empty
  • What stays, stays
Short cut · 30–45s A hand resting on a closed bedside drawer in a shared bedroom and deliberately not opening it, with the rule that stops it stated out loud.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a shared bedroom and the other sleeper's side within the first line, or the restraint has no meaning at all.
Straighten Agreeing only on the shared edge, the floor and the cord, and leaving the drawer entirely alone.
Beats
  • Define the shared edge on camera, the floor beside this nightstand that you both walk past.
  • Clear that floor and run the lamp cord down the leg, and explain that both qualify because they affect the person who does not sleep on this side.
  • Open the drawer once, show that its contents are entirely their business, and close it again without a hand going in.
Shots
  • Low overhead of the shared floor beside the nightstand, before and after clearing.
  • Close on hands dressing the lamp cord down the back leg to the skirting.
  • Close on the drawer opened briefly and closed, no hand entering it.
On-screen text
  • The shared edge only
  • Cord down the leg
  • The drawer is theirs
Short cut · 30–45s Drawing the line in a shared bedroom between the floor beside the bed, which you may fix, and the bedside drawer, which you may not.
Stands alone: State the shared bedroom setup and that there are two owners, because the whole distinction collapses without it.
Shine Cleaning is the part you are fully allowed to do, including the slot neither of you looks into.
Beats
  • Dust the top and wipe the lamp base and the switch, working around objects rather than clearing them off their spots.
  • Vacuum the slot between the nightstand and the bed frame where tissues, hairbands and dust collect, and tip out what comes back.
  • Land that this is the clean half of you clean, they cull, and that it happens without a word about what is on the top.
Shots
  • Overhead of a cloth working around objects rather than clearing them off.
  • Macro on the lamp switch and base being wiped.
  • Low three-quarter with a crevice tool going into the slot between nightstand and bed frame.
  • Close on what the vacuum brings out, tipped onto a sheet of paper.
On-screen text
  • Clean around, not through
  • The slot nobody looks into
Short cut · 30–45s A crevice tool going into the gap between a bed frame and a nightstand, and the tissues and hairbands that come back out.
Stands alone: Name the gap and why nobody ever cleans it, since the shot is visually narrow and hard to place without context.
Safety Medication, the one exception where you are allowed to raise the subject out loud.
Beats
  • Frame this as poison, choke or strangle and show why: sleep aids and prescription bottles loose in an open bedside drawer sit at the height a toddler or a dog reaches from the mattress.
  • Show the check as a joint job rather than a raid, dates read off the bottles and caps screwed down properly.
  • Move tablets from the open drawer into a closed box, under the manual's condition that this applies where a child or a dog gets up onto this bed.
  • Handle the fall question on this side too, taking the lamp cord out of the walking strip and running it down the leg and along the wall.
Shots
  • Bed-height close from the mattress looking into an open drawer, showing the reach line.
  • Close on bottles turned to the light and dates read off the caps.
  • Close on caps screwed down and bottles going into a closed box.
  • Low overhead of the walking strip with the cord relocated to the skirting.
On-screen text
  • Dates, caps, closed box
  • Reachable from the mattress
  • Ch 21: find it, and fix it now
Short cut · 30–45s The view from mattress height into an open bedside drawer full of loose pill bottles, at exactly the reach of a small child or a dog climbing onto the bed.
Stands alone: Establish the camera height as mattress level and the room as a bedroom, because the framing is carrying the entire point.
Standardize Matching the standard rather than the contents, so two different drawers can both be correct.
Beats
  • Put both tops in one frame and show the same item count and the same lidded drink rule holding on each.
  • Show both drawers open with contents that match at nothing, and land why that is completely fine under this standard.
  • Write the shared standard down and leave it where both sleepers see it, and quote the frozen line from Chapter 27, that an audit checks the home, not the household, and what it finds is always a system to fix, never a person to blame.
Shots
  • Wide locked frame holding both nightstand tops, counts matching.
  • Two matched overheads of each drawer open, paired in the edit to sit side by side.
  • Close on the shared standard written down and left where both can see it.
On-screen text
  • Same count, different contents
  • Match the standard, not the drawer
  • Ch 27: the friendly audit
Short cut · 30–45s Two bedside drawers in the same room, obviously nothing alike inside, both passing the same written standard.
Stands alone: State the standard being matched before the reveal, or the clip reads as two untidy drawers and nothing else.
Sustain Tying both tops to the sheet wash so one side cannot quietly drift while the other holds.
Beats
  • Show the sheets coming off and both tops being cleared and wiped inside that same job.
  • Land why pairing them works, that the wash happens to the whole bed and not to one person, so neither side gets a turn skipped.
  • Finish the pass with both tops wiped, both lamps back, and the same count standing on each.
Shots
  • Wide three-quarter of the bed being stripped with both nightstands in frame.
  • Matched close on each top being cleared and wiped in turn.
  • Final wide with both tops reset and the clean set going on.
On-screen text
  • Sheets off, both tops cleared
  • One job, both sides
Short cut · 30–45s Sheets coming off a bed triggering both bedside tops getting cleared, not just the tidy one.
Stands alone: Say this is a shared bedroom and that pairing the two sides to one job is the whole reason the trigger works.
Close

Finish on the pair: matching item counts on both tops, the same lidded drink rule, a lamp cord running down the leg instead of across the floor, medication in date and closed away, and drawer contents belonging to whoever sleeps on that side. Show the trigger physically, sheets going into the wash and both tops cleared and wiped in the same pass.

Next: Next, the surface where your pockets land at the end of the day, and the perfume you were given and never wear.

Shot list
  • Wide locked three-quarter holding both nightstands, the reference frame for every comparison.
  • Overhead over the second nightstand top and drawer.
  • Bed-height close from the mattress into the open drawer for the reach line.
  • Low overhead of the shared floor strip beside the nightstand.
  • Macro on lamp base, switch and cord clips.
  • Crevice-tool close in the slot between nightstand and bed frame.
  • Matched overhead of each drawer open, shot separately and paired in the edit.
  • Wide of the bed being stripped with both nightstands in shot.
Description hook

You clean, they cull. The one nightstand in the house you are not allowed to empty, and the single exception where you get to raise it out loud.

MZ-038 · R07.04

The Dresser Top

5–7 min · thumbnail: “One Tray Is The Edge”

Dresser Top: One Tray, an Anti-Tip Strap, and the Perfume You Never Wear

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on three or four fragrance bottles standing on a dresser top, hands lifting each in turn. Name the honest count from the manual, that you wear one of them, and name why the others are still standing there: they were gifts, or they were expensive, or they were who you were five years ago. Set up the test the video applies, that fragrance turns, and a bottle that has stood open for years smells sharper and flatter than the one you were handed.

Sort Working through pocket sediment, applying the fragrance test, and moving the jewellery that never gets put on.
Beats
  • Show what has actually accumulated here, the loose change, the receipts, the single earrings and snapped chains, swept into one working pile.
  • Route each category on camera, coins into a jar that lives in another room, receipts binned or photographed, broken jewellery into one small bag.
  • Set the condition on that bag out loud, that it goes to a repair counter this month or it goes, so it does not quietly become permanent storage.
  • Apply the fragrance test to the bottles from the cold open: the one you wear stays, the one you honestly alternate to stays, and the rest leave, because whoever gave it to you wanted you to smell good and not to store glass.
  • Move jewellery you love but never put on to a box in the closet rather than back onto this top.
Shots
  • Overhead of the loaded dresser top before anything is touched.
  • Close on coins going into a jar and the jar leaving frame toward another room.
  • Macro on single earrings and a snapped chain going into one small bag.
  • Close on the fragrance bottles worked one by one, two set back on the dish and the rest lifted out of frame.
  • Close on the closet jewellery box receiving the loved but unworn pieces.
On-screen text
  • Pocket sediment
  • One bag, one deadline
  • Worn, or it goes
Short cut · 30–45s Four perfume bottles on a dresser worked down to the one you actually wear, with the reason each of the others is still standing there named as it goes.
Stands alone: Say up front that fragrance turns over years, since without that the clip reads as somebody throwing away expensive gifts for no reason.
Straighten One tray for daily carry, a dish for fragrance, and nothing else living on the wood.
Beats
  • Place one valet tray and show keys, wallet, watch and rings all landing inside it.
  • Group the surviving fragrance on its own small dish so the bottles stop wandering across the top.
  • Set the rule that folded clothes never rest here on the way to the drawer, and carry a stack straight past the dresser into the drawer instead.
Shots
  • Overhead of the tray being set down and filled item by item.
  • Close on bottles gathered onto the dish and set back from the edge.
  • Locked close on the dresser top as a stack of folded laundry passes over it without landing, then a matched frame of it going into the open drawer.
On-screen text
  • One tray, everything in it
  • Fragrance gets a dish
  • Laundry does not stop here
Short cut · 30–45s A stack of folded laundry travelling over a dresser top without ever touching it and going straight into the drawer below.
Stands alone: Name the rule being demonstrated in the first line, because a clip of laundry being put away is otherwise completely unremarkable.
Shine The sticky ring under the fragrance, and the handles that get touched every day.
Beats
  • Take the tray and the bottles off completely and wipe the bare top.
  • Work at the sticky ring where the sprayer has been misting the wood for years, showing it takes a second pass and does not lift with the first wipe.
  • Wipe the drawer fronts and the handles while the top is bare, which is the only easy moment to reach them.
Shots
  • Overhead of the fully bare dresser top before the first wipe.
  • Macro across the sticky ring with the window light coming in low and grazing, so the residue reads on camera.
  • Close on the second pass working the ring, with the finish coming back.
  • Close on drawer handles and fronts being wiped.
On-screen text
  • Take everything off
  • Two passes on the ring
  • Fronts and handles too
Short cut · 30–45s Low grazing light across a dresser top revealing the sticky halo a perfume sprayer has misted into the finish over years.
Stands alone: Explain what caused the ring within the first seconds, or the macro shot is an unidentifiable smear on some wood.
Safety Anchoring the chest so it cannot tip, and getting glass back from the edge.
Beats
  • Frame this as fall, cut or crush and show the mechanism: a loaded drawer open puts the weight forward, and a child leaning on it does the rest, on a chest heavy enough to pin someone underneath.
  • Fit an anti-tip strap into a stud on camera, finding the stud first rather than driving into plasterboard alone.
  • Reload the drawers with the heaviest clothes at the bottom so the weight sits low, and say why that order is part of the same fix.
  • Set the glass bottles back from the front edge onto the dish, above a floor you walk to the bed on barefoot.
Shots
  • Low three-quarter of the chest with a loaded drawer open, weight visibly forward of the base.
  • Close on a stud finder crossing the wall and the mark being made.
  • Close on the strap being driven into the stud and tensioned at the dresser end.
  • Overhead of bottles moved from the front edge back onto the dish.
On-screen text
  • Strap it into a stud
  • Heaviest clothes lowest
  • Glass back from the edge
Short cut · 45–60s A stud finder crossing the wall behind a bedroom dresser, then the anti-tip strap going in, start to finish in one clip.
Stands alone: State what the strap prevents and why it must reach a stud rather than plasterboard, so the fix is understood and not just copied.
Standardize The tray as the physical edge, and what to do when the day's carry will not sit in it.
Beats
  • Show the tray holding keys, wallet, watch and rings flat, with the rule that anything which will not sit in it does not live on this dresser.
  • Show the failure state, the same four items stacking on top of each other rather than lying flat.

The Dresser Drawers

9–12 min · thumbnail: “One Category Per Drawer”

Dresser Drawers: One Category Each, Folded to Stand Up

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on two drawers being pulled out, part filled with clothes that do not fit today. Name the cost the manual names, that every morning starts with a small unpleasant reminder instead of a clean choice. Set up the decision the video makes on camera: one box, not two, today's date written on the lid, stored somewhere else in the house, and if it is still sealed a year from now it leaves sealed and unopened. Land the reframe, that these drawers dress the body you have this morning, and that this is not giving up on anything.

Sort One drawer at a time onto the bed, the dated box for the wrong size, and knowing what becomes a rag rather than a donation.
Beats
  • Tip one drawer onto the bed and set the rule that you work one drawer at a time, because that is what keeps a job this size finishable.
  • Work the named categories on camera: socks whose partners never turned up, waistbands that have given up, the six workout tops sitting behind the two that get worn, and the t-shirts from events nobody thinks about now.
  • Demonstrate the waistband test physically, stretched and released, rather than describing it.
  • Pack the wrong-size clothes into one box, write today's date on the lid, tape it shut and carry it out of the bedroom entirely, without a second box being started.
  • Split the disposal, anything stained or holed into textile recycling rather than a donation somebody else has to bin, with the two bags filling separately on camera.

  • One box, today's date

Primary Closet: One Hanger Style and Two Fingers of Space

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a single garment sliding out on its hanger, the one that cost real money and does not fit your life: the suit for the job you left, the coat that is beautiful and far too warm, the shoes that turn on you after twenty minutes. Name why it is still hanging there, that letting it go makes the money real, and answer it the way the manual does, that the money left the day you bought it and the garment brings back none of it while taking a hanger you need. Set the deadline the video actually carries out on camera: photograph it, list it, thirty days.

Sort Pulling the unworn and the unrepaired off the rod, listing the expensive mistake, and moving the wrong season out.
Beats
  • Work the rod end to end pulling anything not worn in a year, with the decision happening at the hanger rather than in a pile on the floor, and flag honestly that the try-on pile runs longer than anyone plans for.
  • Pull everything waiting on a repair you are never going to make, and be direct that an intention is not the same thing as a plan.
  • Carry out the cold open decision: the expensive mistake photographed against a plain wall, listed for sale, and the thirty day deadline written on the tag so it does not quietly go back on the rod.
  • Strip out every wire hanger and dry cleaner's plastic sheath, which also sets up the suffocation hazard handled in Safety.
  • Move winter coats and heavy knits into a labelled bin or the guest wardrobe so the rod carries only what this month asks for.

Finish on the wide: one hanger style throughout, grouped by type and then by shade with every hook facing the same way, shoes in pairs on the rack, bags standing upright on the shelf, belts on one hook, two fingers of space between hanging items, a bare stretch of rod at one end and floor you can stand on. Room 08 of 20

Guest Bedroom

5 videos · 30 Shorts
Production noteShoot all five zones on one daylight day, ideally under overcast sky, because this room usually has a single window and hard sun through a blind puts stripes across every overhead frame. Overhead shots are made with the tripod centre column reversed or a horizontal arm clamped over the bed, set once at the start of the day and left in place, since four of the five zones empty their contents onto the bed and that frame becomes the series signature. Keep the second tripod at three quarter height in the doorway corner for matching wide before and after plates, and tape its feet so every zone's wide lines up. The room is narrow, so plan to move the tripod between setups rather than walk backward past loaded bins. No presenter, no face, nothing above the wrists in any frame, so every beat has to be readable as hands, overhead or detail. On set safety: the anti-tip strap fixing, the closet top shelf and the folding luggage rack all put real weight over hands, so load test the rack and the top shelf bins before rolling, keep the extension lead off the walking line even in the shots where the lead is the subject, and never stage a cord loop near the bed for the camera. Voiceover is recorded separately, off set, so the room stays silent and the window can stay open for the airing shots.
MZ-041 · R08.01

The Guest Bed and Linens

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Two Good Sets, Not Six”

Guest Bed and Linens: Two Sheet Sets That Actually Fit the Mattress

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Hands pull six sheet sets out of the cupboard and stack them on the bed, and the shared history of the pile gets named: every one of them was demoted from your own bed. Thin sheets, the pilled set, the flat pillows, quietly reassigned to people who will never say anything about it. The hard decision this video settles is stated up front, that guest linen is not the linen you stopped wanting, and a shelf holding six tired sets is a backlog rather than a decision.

Sort That fit and spring, not sentiment, decide which sets stay in this room, and that two sets which pass beat six that do not.
Beats
  • Every demoted set laid out across the bed at once, with the point made that the pile gets judged as one backlog rather than one piece at a time.
  • Each fitted sheet tried on the actual mattress, with the pass and fail explained: a corner that pops off while the bed is being made makes it a rag, not a spare.
  • Each pillow folded in half and released, and the verdict shown rather than argued, since a pillow that stays folded has stopped doing its job.
  • The rule that settles the whole zone landed plainly, that anything you would not sleep on yourself for a week is cleaning cloth and not guest linen.
  • Two keepers separated from the rest, with the honest consequence named, that stopping at two may mean buying a set.

  • Sleep on it for a week?
  • Two good sets

  • The space under the bed cleared to its finished state, one empty suitcase lying flat and nothing else, since that is where a guest will slide their own case.

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

A desk in a guest room buried under gift wrap, an ironing pile, a printer nobody has switched on this year, and somebody's paperwork. The truth the video is built on gets said early, that almost every guest room is also something else, the home office, the sewing room, the place the exercise bike ended up, and that this is exactly why hosting takes an afternoon: you are not tidying, you are relocating a whole activity under time pressure. The test the video runs is set up in the same breath, whether that second job clears into one bin or one cupboard, in a single trip, without unplugging anything.

Sort That the surface goes completely clear first, and then the room's second job gets named and measured.
Beats
  • The surface cleared completely, with what was on it named as it comes off: gift wrap, an ironing pile that never made it back, a printer not switched on this year, and paperwork someone carried in here to deal with in peace.
  • Each pile routed in frame, ironing back to the wardrobe it came from, paperwork into the file it was always headed for.
  • The printer decision made live, it either earns a desk somewhere it gets used or it leaves the house.
  • The second job test run: the room's other activity named out loud, then its whole footprint gathered to see whether it clears into one bin or one cupboard in a single trip with nothing unplugged.
  • The verdict taken honestly, share the room and set the boundary in tape, or accept that the second job is too big for this room and something moves out for good.

  • Close on hands unplugging the printer, then the clean rectangle of desk it leaves behind
  • Overhead of the fully cleared desk surface
  • Floor level wide of the second job's whole footprint gathered into a single bin

  • Clear it completely
  • One bin, one trip, nothing unplugged
  • Name the second job

Stands alone: Establish that this is a guest room desk and the pile on it belongs to whatever else the room does, since that is the entire point being made.

  • The floor square taped once the clearance is proved, so the footprint survives the next time furniture moves.
  • The bin's contents laid out and counted: spare charger, wifi card, water glass, tissues, folded spare blanket.

Stands alone: Say that this is a spare room where visitors have been living out of a case on the floor, which is the problem the rack and the taped footprint solve.

Beats
  • The desk wiped, taking the clean rectangle where the printer sat with it, so the last trace of the room's second job comes off the surface.
  • Chair seat and back both wiped, with the film they collect in a room nobody sits in shown on the cloth.
  • The desk lamp switched on now rather than during a guest's first evening, and the pass named as the moment a loose chair joint or a failing bulb gets found.

Short cut · 30–45s A cloth wipes across a spare room desk and takes with it the clean rectangle where a printer sat all year.
Stands alone: Establish that the room sits unused most of the year, which is why a surface that looks clean is not, and why the outline is there at all.
Safety The extension lead crossing the carpet because the only outlet is behind the bed, and a folding luggage rack nobody has ever load tested.
Beats
  • The fall question framed on the classic setup here, an extension lead run from the desk across open floor to the only reachable outlet, laid through the strip of carpet a guest walks in the dark.
  • The fix made the right way round, the desk moved to the outlet rather than the lead run to the desk, and the finished layout shown with no cord crossing a walking line.
  • The fall, cut, or crush question run on the folding luggage rack, opened and pressed down hard through both hands to be sure it holds a packed case without folding.
  • The second version of it caught, a hard case sitting proud of the desk edge in a room where a child may be playing while cases are carried in and out, and the case moved fully onto the surface.

  • Find it, and fix it now
Short cut · 30–45s An extension lead runs straight across the carpet a guest will cross in the dark, and the fix is to move the desk rather than the cord.
Stands alone: Establish that the only outlet in the room is behind the bed, which is the reason the lead is lying there in the first place.
Standardize That a photograph of the ready state turns setting the room up into matching a picture.
Beats

  • The print taped inside the lid of the welcome bin, where it is found by whoever opens the bin.
  • What this buys explained, that setup becomes matching a picture rather than remembering a list, with a pointer to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo.

Sustain That the welcome bin rides out with the departing sheets and comes back restocked.
Beats
  • The trigger shown as something already happening, the departing guest's sheets going to the wash.
  • The welcome bin carried on the same trip and restocked on the way back, item by item against the photo in its lid.
  • The bin put back on its doorway sightline before leaving the room, and the frozen line landed, that you do not finish 6S, you keep it.

  • Three quarter on hands carrying stripped sheets with the welcome bin balanced on top, framed at forearm height and no higher

  • Bin rides with the sheets

Stands alone: Explain the bin and the photo in the lid in one opening beat, because the restock loop depends on both being understood.

Room 09 of 20

Kids Bedroom

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteShoot this room in daylight with the curtains fully open and the ceiling light off, because a child's room has low surfaces and an overhead bulb throws hand shadows straight down onto everything you are filming. Window light only, one operator, no lighting kit. Access is the real constraint: floor work, under bed work and closet floor work all need a low tripod, so plan on a tabletop tripod plus a taller one and expect to work kneeling. Set the overhead shots on a horizontal arm clamped to a heavy stand beside the bed, never over the bed frame, so nothing hangs above where a child sleeps. There is no slider and no second operator, so every floor level move is a locked off before and a locked off after rather than a tracking shot. Keep the child out of frame at all times: every keep or go call is filmed as adult hands with the child's choices already made off camera, and every child height shot means the camera is at that height, not the child. On set safety while filming: the anti tip strap, the blind cord cleat and the socket work are real fixes, so make them properly on camera and leave them made rather than staging and undoing them. Bag small parts and button batteries into a labelled tub the moment they leave a bin, and never leave a loose blind cord looped for a shot.

Bed and Sleep Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Which Animals Actually Sleep Here”

6S the Kids Bed and Sleep Zone: Thin the Stuffed Animals, Cleat the Blind Cord, Make It in One Pull

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on the bed lost under stuffed animals, hands lifting them off one at a time until the pillow finally shows. Frame the decision this room has been dodging: the two or three that genuinely get slept with are already known, and the avoided part is not thinning the rest, it is whether you are allowed to do it without the child standing there. Set up that this video answers that with a dated lidded box and a six week wait, and that nothing leaves the house the same day it leaves the bed.

Sort A child sleeps with a handful of animals, not a herd, and the rest is drift from birthdays and fair prizes that arrived without anyone choosing it.
Beats
  • Hands pull every stuffed animal out of the bed and lay them in one row across the carpet, so the actual count is visible for the first time.
  • Set out the split that makes this workable: the child picks the sleepers off camera, you handle the drift, and nothing leaves the house the day it leaves the bed.
  • Show the lidded box going onto the wardrobe shelf with a date written on the end, and give the six week rule complete: no request and the box goes quietly, one asked for by name and that one comes back while the rest still go.
  • Return three or four to the bed and set an open basket at the foot for the ones that stay visible rather than boxed.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bed as hands clear it, animals leaving frame one at a time
  • Flat overhead of the full floor row, every animal that was in the bed in one frame
  • Close on hands writing the date on the box end and sliding it onto the wardrobe shelf
  • Three quarter of the open basket at the foot of the bed, animals visible over the rim
On-screen text
  • Everything out first
  • Sleepers stay, drift boxes
  • Six weeks, then it goes
Short cut · 45–60s Every stuffed animal in one child's bed comes out onto the floor in a single row, shot flat from above, and the row keeps going.
Stands alone: Open by establishing that this is one child's bed and that only two or three are actually slept with, then give the dated box and the six week rule in full, because the box is the payoff and it means nothing without the rule attached.
Straighten Bedding a seven year old can handle alone, because making this bed has to be one pull rather than four layers nobody will ever line up.
Beats
  • Take the old set off layer by layer, top sheet then blanket then quilt, laid side by side so the layer count is undeniable.
  • Fit one duvet into a washable cover and set out why it wins here: a single pull is the only version that survives a school morning.
  • Hands make the bed the new way in one movement, then square the single pillow at the head.
  • Set the animal count that goes back: what fits in two arms in one trip, everything else in the basket.
Shots
  • Overhead of the four bedding layers laid out side by side on the floor
  • Three quarter of hands feeding the duvet into its washable cover
  • Overhead of the single pull that flattens the duvet, one unbroken take
  • Close on the pillow being squared at the head
On-screen text
  • Four layers to one
  • Made in one pull
Short cut · 30–45s Two beds, same hands, timed: four layers lined up one by one against one duvet flattened in a single pull.
Stands alone: State in the first line that the person who has to make this bed is seven, since the whole case for one duvet is that a child cannot line up a top sheet, a blanket and a quilt before school.
Shine Stripping this bed is how you finally see the mattress seams, the slats and the strip of floor nobody has looked at since the frame went in.
Beats
  • Strip to bare mattress and vacuum the seams, with the point of the pass being what a stripped bed lets you inspect rather than how it looks.
  • While the frame is bare, check the slats and the frame bolts and tighten anything that has worked loose under a child who jumps on it.
  • Pull the bed away from the wall and vacuum the floor strip and the skirting behind it, showing what comes up.
  • Wipe the headboard and the nightlight casing, the two places hands land every single night, and run the nightlight cord behind the bed leg on the way back.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bare mattress mid vacuum, nozzle tracking the seams
  • Macro on a loose slat bolt with the spanner going on
  • Low three quarter of the frame pulled out, the untouched floor strip in frame
  • Macro on the nightlight casing before and after the cloth
On-screen text
  • Strip to bare mattress
  • Check the slats while it is bare
  • Under the bed counts
Short cut · 30–45s A child's bed gets pulled away from the wall and the camera drops to carpet level on a strip of floor that has not been seen since the frame was built.
Stands alone: Establish that this bed has not moved in years, and say the point of the pass in the first line, that you strip it in order to inspect the slats and seams rather than to make it look nice.
Safety The fourth S here is the blind cord hanging at pillow height and the route from bed to door in the dark.
Beats
  • Hold on the blind cord loop beside the bed head and name it as poison, choke, or strangle: a loop at exactly the wrong height next to a sleeping child.
  • Fit a cleat high on the wall and wind the cord onto it properly, or show the cordless blind swap where that is the available fix.
  • Locked off at floor level from pillow to door, showing the bin, the bag and the book pile that turn a half asleep bathroom trip into a fall.
  • Clear that route to a width crossable in the dark without looking down, then repeat the same locked off frame, and close on the rule from Chapter 21, find it and fix it now.
Shots
  • Macro on the blind cord loop level with the pillow
  • Close on hands driving the cleat into the wall above child height and winding the cord onto it
  • Locked off floor level frame from pillow to door with the obstacles in place
  • The identical locked off frame with the route clear
On-screen text
  • Cord at pillow height
  • Cleat it high
  • Clear in the dark
Short cut · 30–45s A looped blind cord hanging exactly level with a child's pillow, held in macro before anything moves.
Stands alone: Name it as a strangle risk in the opening line and finish on the cleat fitted and the cord wound, because a Short that only points at the hazard leaves a viewer with a problem and no fix.
Standardize One photo of the made bed inside the wardrobe door, so made stops being an adult's opinion and starts being a picture.
Beats
  • Photograph the finished bed straight on: duvet flat, one pillow squared, animals at the count that stays.
  • Tape the print inside the wardrobe door at the child's eye height, and show the height difference against adult eye height plainly.
  • Set out what the photo settles, including the animal count, so a six year old can meet the standard with no adult ruling on what made means.
  • Reference Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, and land the line that a standard is the best way you know today, written down.

  • Photograph the finished state

Short cut · 30–45s A phone photo of a made bed gets taped inside a wardrobe door, then the camera drops to a six year old's eye height to show why that spot and not higher.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that made is otherwise an adult judgement a child cannot win, which is the reason the photo exists, and show the eye height drop rather than describing it.
Sustain The bed gets made while the school bag goes onto the shoulder, so the habit rides on something that already happens every school morning.
Beats
  • Show the trigger in order: hands reach for the school bag, the duvet gets pulled flat, then the bag goes onto the shoulder.
  • Set out why this beats a reminder: the bag going on already happens, and the bedroom door closing is the deadline.
  • Run the whole standard once at speed, one pull and one armful, which is what makes it survive a rushed morning.
  • Land the frozen line, you do not finish 6S, you keep it, on the door closing over the finished room.

Stands alone: Name the trigger explicitly in the first line, bed made while the bag goes on, or this reads as a tidying clip instead of a habit built onto something that already happens.
Close

Show the finished state against the print taped inside the wardrobe door: one duvet pulled flat, one pillow squared, and the animals that fit in two arms in a single trip, with the dated box up on the shelf still running. Then fire the trigger once more, duvet pulled flat while the school bag goes on, before the bedroom door closes.

Toy Storage Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Tipped Out And Abandoned”

6S the Toy Storage Zone: Six Open Bins, No Lids, and a Six Week Rotation Box Test

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on the set every kids room has, the forty small figures or the enormous block set, emptied across the carpet with nothing built and the room empty. Name why it is still here: it was expensive, or the person who gave it asks after it. Set up that this video swaps that feeling for a test, half the set into a dated rotation box on the top shelf for six weeks, and shows exactly what to watch for on the afternoon it comes back down.

Sort Every bin comes out onto the carpet and gets sorted into toy families before anything goes back, and the outs leave during the sort rather than into a pile to be decided later.
Beats
  • Tip every bin onto the carpet, all of them, so the true volume is on the floor at once before a single keep or go call is made.
  • Sort into families first, blocks with blocks, figures with figures, vehicles with vehicles, and set out why families have to come before keep or go.
  • Broken toys, orphan puzzle pieces and party bag plastic go straight into the out bag during the sort, with the reason stated plainly: a decide later pile becomes a seventh bin.
  • Introduce the rotation box on the set that always gets abandoned: half of it goes up dated for six weeks, and what happens with it on the afternoon it comes back down is the answer.
Shots
  • Overhead wide of the whole carpet as bins are tipped out
  • Overhead of hands sweeping pieces into family groups, sped up in the edit
  • Close on the out bag taking broken parts and orphan puzzle pieces
  • Close on hands dating the rotation box and sliding it onto the top shelf out of reach
On-screen text
  • Everything out, then families
  • No decide later pile
  • Half goes up for six weeks
Short cut · 45–60s Every toy bin in one bedroom gets tipped onto the same patch of carpet, filmed from directly above, until the floor disappears.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that this is a child's toy storage and that families come before keep or go, then land the single rule that carries the Short: nothing goes into a decide later pile, because that pile just becomes another bin.
Straighten One open bin per toy family and no lids anywhere, because the lid is the extra step that ends with the dinosaur on the carpet.
Beats
  • Lay out six open bins and assign one family to each, blocks, vehicles, small figures and the rest.
  • Demonstrate the lid problem hands only from one fixed angle: the lidded bin needs both hands and a pause, the open bin takes one drop.
  • Heaviest bin on the bottom, daily favourites at hand height, and a check that no bin sits higher than the child's shoulder against a mark on the wall.
  • Show the carpet left clear enough to lie down on, which is the actual result the bins exist for.
Shots
  • Overhead of six open bins laid out with one toy family beside each
  • Close on hands returning the same toy to a lidded bin, then to an open bin, identical framing both times
  • Three quarter of the bin stack against the shoulder height mark on the wall
  • Overhead wide of clear carpet with the bins ranged along one wall
On-screen text
  • One family, one bin
  • No lids
  • Nothing above the shoulder
Short cut · 30–45s The same toy put away twice from the same angle: once into a lidded bin, once into an open one, and only one of them takes two hands.
Stands alone: Establish in the first line that the person putting this toy away is five, since the whole case against lids is that one extra step is why it lands on the carpet instead of in the bin.
Shine Washing the hard plastic and checking the bins themselves, because Shine here inspects the containers you are about to trust a child to carry.
Beats
  • Run the hard plastic through a sink of warm soapy water in batches and lay it on a towel to dry.
  • Vacuum the skirting corners where small parts migrate, and show what actually comes out of them.
  • Turn every empty bin over and flex the base for splits before refilling, with the reason stated: a split bin gives way while it is being carried full.
  • Refill only once everything is dry, so nothing goes back damp into a closed corner of the room.
Shots
  • Overhead of the sink with plastic toys in soapy water
  • Overhead of the drying towel laid out with sorted pieces on it
  • Macro of the vacuum nozzle in a skirting corner, small parts visible
  • Close on hands flexing an upturned bin base, the split running along it
On-screen text
  • Wash in batches
  • Check the bin, not just the toys
Short cut · 30–45s An empty toy bin gets turned over and flexed, and a split runs the whole length of the base.
Stands alone: Frame it as cleaning in order to inspect rather than a cleaning tip, and give the consequence in the first line: this bin gives way while a child is carrying it full across the room.
Safety The fourth S here is small parts and button batteries, sized against a toilet roll tube and checked hatch by hatch.
Beats
  • Run the tube test hands only: anything that drops through a toilet roll tube is a choke risk for a younger sibling and belongs in a bin they cannot reach.
  • Move the small part families up to the high shelf and show the height gap against the low bins.
  • Work through the battery toys hatch by hatch, naming button batteries as the serious one.
  • Any toy whose battery cover has lost its screw goes out, and it leaves in the out bag on camera rather than back into a bin.
Shots
  • Macro of small figures dropped through a toilet roll tube one after another
  • Three quarter showing the high shelf against the child height bins
  • Close on a screwdriver checking a battery hatch screw
  • Macro on a button battery in its open hatch, then the toy going into the out bag
On-screen text
  • Fits the tube, goes up high
  • Check every battery hatch
  • No screw, no keep
Short cut · 45–60s Toy after toy gets dropped through a toilet roll tube, and the ones that pass straight through pile up underneath.
Stands alone: Name the risk as choking for a younger sibling in the opening line, and include the battery hatch rule before the end, because the tube test on its own misses the button battery, which is the serious one.
Standardize A photo of the contents taped to the front face of every bin, never the lid, at the height the child actually looks from.
Beats
  • Photograph the contents of each bin from above, one shot per family.
  • Tape each photo to the front face of its bin and set out why the front face is the surface a child sees on the way past.
  • Drop the camera to child eye height and check every label reads from there.
  • Reference Chapter 14, visual controls, and land the point that a picture of six blocks works long before reading does.
Shots
  • Overhead of blocks laid out being photographed for the label
  • Close on hands taping a photo to a bin front face
  • Camera at child eye height panning the labelled bin row
  • Macro on one photo label with the matching contents visible over the bin rim
On-screen text
  • Photograph the contents
  • Front face, never the lid
  • Readable from their eye level
Short cut · 30–45s A row of toy bins seen from a child's eye height, every one carrying a photograph of exactly what lives inside it.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that the child using these bins cannot read yet, which is the entire reason the labels are photographs and sit on the front face rather than on a lid.
Sustain Pickup happens while the bedtime story is being chosen, not after it, because the story is the thing worth clearing the carpet for.
Beats
  • Show the trigger in order: the book comes off the shelf, the floor gets cleared, then the story starts.
  • Set out why the story has to come after the pickup, and what happens to the habit the first time that order gets flipped.
  • Show the pickup finishing inside the time a child's attention actually lasts, which is why the bins are open and the labels are pictures.
  • Land the clear carpet as the light goes off, with the dated rotation box on the top shelf as the loop still open.
Shots
  • Close on a bedtime book being pulled off the shelf
  • Overhead of the carpet clearing into the bins, hands only, one continuous take
  • Three quarter of the last toy dropped into its labelled bin
  • Overhead wide of clear carpet from the bed side as the light goes off
On-screen text
  • Book first, then the floor
  • Story is the reason
Short cut · 30–45s The bedtime book comes off the shelf first and the carpet clears before it opens, in that order and not the other way round.
Stands alone: State the order rule explicitly at the top, pickup before the story rather than after it, because the ordering is the whole idea and without it this is an ordinary tidy up clip.
Close

Show the standard holding: every toy family in one open, photo labelled bin at child height, none above the shoulder, and carpet clear enough to lie down on when the light goes off. Fire the trigger once, floor cleared while the bedtime story is being chosen, and end on the dated rotation box up on the top shelf with the test still running.

Next: Pan off the clear carpet to the desk in the corner, where the pile that never gets decided on is paper rather than plastic.

Study Desk

7–9 min · thumbnail: “The Pile You Keep Moving”

6S the Study Desk: One Tray for Live Work, One Box per School Year, One Strip in One Socket

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the stack of finished schoolwork being lifted from one end of the desk to the other, exercise books, paintings, a folder of worksheets. Name the block honestly: binning any of it feels like saying you did not care, so the pile gets moved instead of decided on. Set up that this video takes the judgement out of the moment and hands it to a box with a fixed size, so the call is not being made at nine on a Tuesday, and rebuilds the surface so homework gets started rather than avoided.

Sort Paper first, every sheet to exactly one of three places, with a fixed size memory box making the hard call for you.
Beats
  • Clear every sheet off the desk into one stack, then set out three destinations on the floor: the live work tray, the memory box, recycling.
  • Work the stack sheet by sheet and state the rule that hurts, that a worksheet from a finished term is recycling even when the marking was good.
  • Introduce the box that makes the call: one lidded box per child per school year, fixed size, on the wardrobe top, where full means full and room is made by taking something out rather than by getting a second box.
  • Photograph the oversized art flat on the floor and let the paper go, keeping the pieces where their hand is visibly getting better.
Shots
  • Overhead of the whole desk stack lifted into one pile
  • Overhead three way layout of tray, memory box and recycling with hands feeding all three
  • Close on the memory box lid closing with the school year written on the end
  • Overhead of a large painting flat on the floor being photographed on a phone
On-screen text
  • Three places, no fourth
  • Full is full
  • Photograph the oversized art
Short cut · 45–60s One stack of a child's finished schoolwork, three destinations laid out on the floor, and every sheet lands in one of them without a pause.
Stands alone: Re-establish in the first line that this is finished schoolwork and why it never gets decided on, then give the fixed size box rule complete, because the box is what makes sorting possible at all.
Straighten The surface stays a work surface, with pens inside one reach of the writing hand and books up on the shelf above.
Beats
  • Stand pens and pencils in a cup within a hand's reach of the writing hand, and show the reach it replaces, the one that crosses the desk and takes the water bottle with it.
  • Move books and folders up onto the shelf, with the rule stated: anything stacked on the surface is the surface no longer being a work surface.
  • Set the final layout, lamp, pen cup, one tray of live work, and nothing else on the wood.
  • Show the chair pulled in and empty, because a chair holding a bag is a desk nobody sits down at.
Shots
  • Overhead of the reach arc from the writing hand to the pen cup, marked on the desk
  • Close on hands lifting a book stack from the desk up onto the shelf
  • Overhead of the finished layout: lamp, pen cup, tray
  • Three quarter of the empty chair pulled in to the clear desk
On-screen text
  • Cup within one reach
  • Books go up, surface stays clear
Short cut · 30–45s Trace the reach from the writing hand to the pen cup, then run the version where the reach crosses the desk and catches a full water bottle.
Stands alone: Say up front that this is a child's homework desk and the point is getting started rather than looking tidy, so the reach argument reads as function and not as styling.
Shine Down to bare wood, then into the drawer runners and the lamp shade, which are the two places dirt here is actually costing something.
Beats
  • Clear the desk completely to bare wood and wipe the surface in one pass.
  • Open the drawer and get the pencil sharpener dust and dried glue out of the runners, showing what has been binding it.
  • Wipe the lamp shade with the lamp lit and show the direct payoff, that a dusty shade is a dimmer desk.
  • Return only the three things that live on this surface.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bare desk mid wipe, cloth crossing the whole surface
  • Macro into the drawer runner with sharpener dust and dried glue visible
  • Close on the lamp shade being wiped, lamp lit, before and after
  • Overhead of the three items returning to the bare surface
On-screen text
  • Down to bare wood
  • Runners, not just the drawer
  • A dusty lamp is a dimmer lamp
Short cut · 30–45s Macro into a desk drawer runner packed solid with pencil sharpener dust and dried glue, then the same drawer sliding shut with one finger.
Stands alone: Establish in the first line that this drawer had been sticking, since the runner clean only lands once the viewer knows which problem it just solved.
Safety The fourth S here is what is chained together under the desk and what is standing point up in the pen cup.
Beats
  • Get the camera under the desk and count the plugs, finding the strip plugged into another strip feeding a lamp, a charger and a console.
  • Bring it back to one strip in one wall socket on camera, name the risk as water and electricity, and move the water bottle off that end of the desk.
  • Turn the pen cup out and show scissors and a craft knife standing point up where a hand goes in blind, then reset them point down.
  • Blades go into a closed drawer if a younger child comes into this room, and close on the rule, find it and fix it now.
Shots
  • Low under desk shot of the chained strips and the plug tangle
  • Close on hands unplugging the second strip and consolidating to one socket
  • Macro into the pen cup interior, the blade edge visible point up
  • Close on the craft knife going into a closed drawer
On-screen text
  • One strip, one socket
  • Water bottle off that end
  • Points down, blades away
Short cut · 30–45s The camera goes under a child's desk and finds a strip plugged into another strip, and the count of what hangs off it keeps climbing.
Stands alone: Name the hazard as water and electricity in the opening line and finish on the single consolidated strip, so the Short delivers the fix and not only the problem.
Standardize The tray is the standard: if it does not fit in the tray, it is not live work.
Beats
  • Set the tray on the desk and state what it enforces, that anything which does not fit goes to the shelf, the memory box or the recycling.
  • Show the tray turned out on the same evening the backpack gets emptied, so the emptying has a rhythm and the tray never quietly becomes a second pile.
  • Name the failure this prevents, a tray that fills up and then stops meaning anything at all.
  • Reference Chapter 24, the checklist, schedule and name: the tray is the name, and the backpack evening is the schedule.
Shots
  • Overhead of the tray with live work in it, the tray edges clearly the limit
  • Close on the tray tipped out beside the emptied backpack
  • Overhead of the sorted result feeding shelf, memory box and recycling
  • Three quarter of the tray back on the clear desk holding only live work
On-screen text
  • If it does not fit, it is not live
  • Turn it out with the backpack
Short cut · 30–45s Live work goes into a tray until the next sheet will not fit, and that sheet gets sent somewhere else on the spot instead of stacked on top.
Stands alone: Explain that the tray has a fixed size on purpose and pair it with the turn out evening, because a tray with no emptying rhythm is just a neater version of the pile.
Sustain The desk gets cleared when the laptop lid closes at the end of homework, not the next morning.
Beats
  • Show the trigger: the laptop lid closes and the clear down starts in the same movement.
  • Clear back to the photographed state, lamp, pen cup, tray, and thread the charger through the clip on the desk edge so the plug never drops behind the desk again.
  • Set out why the next morning fails as a trigger and why the lid closing does not.
  • Land on the empty chair and the bare wood, a desk ready to be started at rather than cleared first.
Shots
  • Close on the laptop lid closing
  • Overhead of the surface clearing in one continuous take
  • Macro on the charger threaded through the desk edge clip
  • Three quarter of the finished desk with the chair empty
On-screen text
  • Lid closes, desk clears
  • Charger stays clipped
Short cut · 30–45s A laptop lid shuts at the end of homework and the desk clears in the same motion, one unbroken overhead take.
Stands alone: Name the trigger as the lid closing and contrast it with leaving the desk until morning, or this reads as a satisfying clean up clip with no rule behind it.
Close

Show the finished surface holding the current task, the lamp, the pen cup and one tray, with the tray holding only work that is still live. Fire the trigger once, the desk clearing the moment the laptop lid closes, and end on the memory box on the wardrobe top with the school year written on the end.

Next: Open the closet door on the rod, where the pile nobody decides on is clothes, and a good part of it fits nobody in this house.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm on a stand centred on the desk for sorting, clear downs and the finished layout
  • Low under desk tripod for the plug count and the consolidation
  • Macro setup for drawer runners, blade edges and the charger clip
  • Three quarter tripod at seated height for chair, shelf and layout shots
  • Floor setup for photographing the oversized art
  • Wardrobe top shelf coverage for the memory box
  • Lamp shade before and after with the lamp lit
  • Three way destination overhead with tray, memory box and recycling all in frame
Description hook

One tray decides what counts as live work, one fixed size box per school year decides what you keep, and the chained extension strips under the desk come back to one socket. Zone three of six in the Kids Bedroom.
