MZ-049 · R09.04

Clothing Closet

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Kept For Nobody In Particular”

6S the Kids Clothing Closet: Lower the Rod, Run the Size Test, Reverse Every Hanger

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a rod packed so tight the hangers will not slide, and hands pulling out garment after garment that fits nobody in the house. Name why it is here: it is being kept for a younger sibling, a cousin, or a second child who is currently hypothetical. Set up the test this video applies, name the child and name the season they will fit it, and what it means when you cannot say both out loud.

Sort Children's clothes fail in one direction only, too small, so the size test is fast and physical.
Beats
  • Take everything off the rod onto the bed and run the three part size test garment by garment: sleeves above the wrist bone, waistbands that leave a mark, shoes where the toe is already touching.
  • Apply the keeping for someone test to the pile that fits nobody, name the child and name the season, and state what it means when you cannot say both: it is not being stored, it is being deferred.
  • Show one sealed labelled box per next size, with the rule that when the box is full the overflow goes now rather than after one more sort.
  • Name the cost of deferring, that clothes kept for nobody in particular arrive at the right size stained, dated and unworn anyway.
Shots
  • Overhead of the emptied rod with everything laid across the bed
  • Macro on a sleeve ending above the wrist bone, then on a waistband mark
  • Close on shoes with the toe already touching the end
  • Close on a next size box being sealed and labelled in large numbers
On-screen text
  • Fails one way only, too small
  • Name the child, name the season
  • Full box means it goes now
Short cut · 45–60s Three fast physical tests on a child's clothes, sleeve above the wrist bone, waistband mark, toe touching the shoe end, and the reject pile builds in seconds.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that children's clothes only ever fail by getting too small, which is why the test can be this quick, then finish on the name the child and name the season rule so the Short carries the hard part too.
Straighten Lowering the rod is one bracket move, and it changes who is capable of using this closet at all.
Beats
  • Measure the child's reach against the current rod and mark the new height on the closet wall.
  • Move the bracket, drop the rod, and take a hanger down from the new height with no stool anywhere in frame.
  • Group by type and then by colour inside each type, shirts together, dresses together, jackets together, with a hand's width gap between groups so a row can be read rather than dug through.
  • Set shoes in pairs on the floor rack and the backpack on its own low hook.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the reach measured and marked against the old rod height
  • Close on hands moving the bracket and seating the lowered rod
  • Hands taking a hanger down from the new height, camera at child height, no stool in frame
  • Overhead along the rod showing grouped rows and the gaps between them
On-screen text
  • One bracket, different closet
  • Gap between groups
  • Reach it without a stool
Short cut · 30–45s A child's reach gets marked on a closet wall, one bracket moves, and the rod comes down to meet the mark.
Stands alone: Establish in the opening line that nobody under adult height could reach this rod before, since the entire result of the move is a child dressing themselves from it.
Shine The closet floor and the top shelf, the two surfaces in this room nobody has looked at in a year.
Beats
  • Empty the closet floor completely and vacuum it corner to corner, showing what was living under the shoe pile.
  • Wipe the rod where hangers have left a grey line along it, and show the cloth afterwards.
  • Check the top shelf for the dust that has been settling all year, and connect it directly to the clothes boxed up there.
  • Refill the floor with shoes in pairs on the rack only, so the floor stays a surface you can see.
Shots
  • Low overhead of the empty closet floor mid vacuum
  • Macro on the grey hanger line along the rod, before and after the cloth
  • Close on a hand drawn across the top shelf, the dust line visible
  • Three quarter of shoes going back in pairs on the floor rack
On-screen text
  • Floor completely empty first
  • The grey line on the rod
  • Dust settles onto stored clothes
Short cut · 30–45s A closet floor gets emptied to bare carpet and the vacuum goes in on everything that had been living under the shoe pile.
Stands alone: Frame it as cleaning in order to inspect, and connect the top shelf dust to the next size clothes boxed up there, so it is not just a satisfying vacuum clip.
Safety The fourth S here is the rod itself and the weight stored above a child's head.
Beats
  • Hang everything back on and give the loaded rod one hard downward pull before trusting it, with the plastic end brackets carrying the load in frame.
  • Name the risk as fall, cut, or crush: an overloaded rod on plastic brackets comes down onto a child's head.
  • Move the heavy things, sports kit and boots and skates, down to the closet floor, because the top shelf is where a child pulls weight onto themselves reaching for something else.
  • Clear the closet floor, since a stool or a storage box used as a step on a cluttered floor is the second fall in this zone.
Shots
  • Macro on a plastic rod end bracket under full load
  • Close on hands giving the loaded rod one hard downward pull
  • Three quarter of boots and sports kit coming off the top shelf down to the closet floor
  • Low shot of the clear closet floor with the storage box taken out of step duty
On-screen text
  • Pull test before you trust it
  • Heavy things live low
  • Nothing stacked to climb on
Short cut · 30–45s A closet rod loaded full, then one hard downward pull on it, with the plastic end bracket held in macro throughout.
Stands alone: Name the fall, cut, or crush risk in the opening line and include the heavy things live low rule, because the pull test alone leaves the boots on the top shelf exactly where they were.
Standardize One hanger style, box numbers readable from the doorway, and every hanger turned backwards at the start of the season.
Beats
  • Swap the mixed hangers for one style throughout and show what a uniform rod does to how fast a row reads.
  • Label the next size box in numbers big enough to read from the doorway, then prove it by shooting from the doorway.
  • Turn every hanger backwards at the start of the season and set out the record it creates, that the ones still reversed at the end are the things not being worn.
  • Reference Chapter 22, prevent and prepare, because the reversed hangers do next season's sorting before you get there.
Shots
  • Overhead of mixed hangers replaced one by one with a single style
  • Doorway wide with the box label legible at that distance
  • Close on hands reversing a row of hangers along the rod
  • Macro on one reversed hook against forward facing neighbours
On-screen text
  • One hanger style
  • Readable from the doorway
  • Reversed means not worn yet
Short cut · 30–45s Every hanger on a child's rod gets turned backwards in one pass, and whatever is still facing backwards in three months is a garment nobody wore.
Stands alone: Give the full loop inside the Short, reversed at the season start and still reversed means unworn, because half the explanation makes the trick meaningless.
Sustain The hanger gets flipped forward as the garment comes off the drying rack, so the record keeps itself.
Beats
  • Show the trigger: a shirt comes off the drying rack, onto its hanger, and back onto the rod facing forward.
  • Set out why this works, that nobody has to remember anything because the record rides on laundry that already happens.
  • Show the rod part way through a season with forward and reversed hooks mixed, and read what it is telling you about what gets worn.
  • Land the finished closet, only clothes that fit today, grouped by type, one hanger style, at a height reachable without a stool.
Shots
  • Close on a shirt lifted off the drying rack
  • Macro on the hanger hook turning forward as it goes onto the rod
  • Overhead along the rod mid season with the hook directions mixed
  • Wide of the finished closet with the door open, camera at child height
On-screen text
  • Flip it as it goes back
  • The record keeps itself
Short cut · 30–45s A backwards hanger means nobody has worn that shirt yet, so watch the hook turn forward the moment the shirt comes off the drying rack.
Stands alone: State what a reversed hanger means before the flip happens, otherwise the movement is just a hanger being turned round and carries nothing.
Close

Show the finished closet against the standard: only clothes that fit today on the rod, grouped by type, one hanger style, at a height reachable without a stool, with the next size box sealed and labelled on the top shelf. Fire the trigger once, a hanger flipped forward as the shirt comes off the drying rack.

Next: Turn from the closet to the dresser, where the problem is not what fits, it is eleven shirts in a drawer that only closes if you lean on it.

Shot list
  • Three quarter tripod square to the open closet for rod work and finished states
  • Low tripod at child height for reach marks, hanger takedowns and the finished wide
  • Macro setup for brackets, hanger hooks, wrist bones and waistband marks
  • Overhead along the rod for grouping and gap coverage
  • Low overhead on the closet floor for the vacuum pass
  • Doorway wide for the label legibility test
  • Top shelf coverage for the dust check and the next size box
  • Drying rack setup for the flip trigger sequence
Description hook

Lower the rod so a child can dress themselves, run the sleeve and waistband size test, and settle the clothes you are keeping for a sibling who may never exist. Zone four of six in the Kids Bedroom.

MZ-050 · R09.05

Dresser Drawers

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Only Closes If You Lean”

6S the Kids Dresser: File Fold Upright, Set the Number by Arithmetic, Strap It to the Wall

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a drawer that only shuts when a hand presses down on it, then the same hand pulling the whole stack out to find one shirt. Name the real problem, that this is not a folding problem, it is eleven shirts in a drawer built for fewer. Set up that this video sets the number by arithmetic rather than garment by garment feeling, and ends on the mechanical test that settles it without an argument: if it does not close with one push, the sort is not finished.

Sort One drawer at a time onto the bed, with the quantity set by counting days between washes rather than by judging each garment.
Beats
  • Tip one drawer onto the bed and state the rule for the whole pass, that the next drawer stays shut until this one is back in.
  • Take out the single socks with no pair, the underwear with dead elastic, and the pyjama bottoms that now stop above the ankle.
  • Run the arithmetic on camera: days between washes, add two, and that is the number for socks, underwear and shirts.
  • Everything above the number goes, starting with whatever you would not choose on a normal morning, and the test stays mechanical enough to run without an argument.
Shots
  • Overhead of one drawer tipped onto the bed with the empty drawer in frame
  • Macro on dead elastic being stretched, then a single unmatched sock held flat
  • Close on hands counting shirts into a row up to the calculated number
  • Overhead of the surplus pile beside the counted keep pile
On-screen text
  • One drawer at a time
  • Days between washes, plus two
  • Above the number, it goes
Short cut · 30–45s Count the days between washes, add two, and lay out exactly that many shirts while everything above the number goes into a pile beside them.
Stands alone: State in the first line that this is a child's drawer that will not close, and give the arithmetic complete, since the number is the whole point and useless as a half rule.
Straighten File folding upright turns this drawer into something a child reads from above instead of excavating.
Beats
  • Demonstrate the fold hands only and slowly on a single shirt, then stand it upright in the drawer.
  • Fill a row upright so the drawer reads like a card index, cut against the flat stack it replaced.
  • Add dividers, or two shoebox lids, so the rows do not fall sideways the first time the drawer gets yanked.
  • Check the drawer closes with one push and no pressing down, which is the test that says the sort was finished.
Shots
  • Overhead close on one shirt file folded, unbroken take
  • Overhead of the drawer half flat stacked and half upright for the cut
  • Macro of socks standing in a row with every pair visible from above
  • Close on the drawer closing with one push, the hand leaving the front
On-screen text
  • Upright, not stacked
  • Two shoebox lids work
  • Closes with one push
Short cut · 30–45s Half a drawer stacked flat, half filed upright, shot from directly above so the difference needs no explaining at all.
Stands alone: Say who opens this drawer, a child getting themselves dressed alone, so the upright fold reads as findability rather than as an aesthetic choice.
Shine Pull the drawers right out, because the grit in the frame is where the sticking drawer, and then the slammed drawer, comes from.
Beats
  • Lift each drawer clear of the carcass and set it aside, leaving the empty frame open to the camera.
  • Vacuum the inside of the frame and wipe the runners, showing what comes off them.
  • Follow the chain from grit to sticking drawer to slammed drawer, and land it as a safety point rather than a cleaning one.
  • Refit the drawers and test the slide with one finger before anything goes back in.
Shots
  • Three quarter of a drawer being lifted clear of the carcass
  • Low overhead into the empty frame, vacuum nozzle working the back corners
  • Macro along a runner before and after the wipe
  • Close on the refitted drawer sliding shut with one finger
On-screen text
  • Drawers all the way out
  • Grit makes it stick
  • Sticks, then gets slammed
Short cut · 30–45s A dresser drawer comes all the way out of the carcass and the camera goes into the empty frame after what has been collecting in the back corners.
Stands alone: Connect the grit to the slammed drawer in the opening line, because the reason to pull drawers out is not tidiness, it is that a jammed drawer pulls a child off balance when it gives.
Safety The fourth S here is the anti tip strap, because a chest with two drawers open is a climbing frame.
Beats
  • Open two drawers and shoot the shape from low down, then name what it is to a small child, a ladder that tips forward onto whoever climbs it.
  • Find the wall stud, fit the anti tip bracket properly on camera, and show the strap taut rather than slack.
  • Take the tablet and the toy off the dresser top, because anything a child wants up there is an invitation to climb for it.
  • Cover the second hazard, the jammed drawer that needs a hard yank and pulls a child backwards when it gives, and tie it back to the runners you just cleaned.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the dresser with two drawers open, camera low
  • Close on a stud finder against the wall, then the bracket going in
  • Macro on the strap pulled taut between dresser and wall
  • Overhead of the dresser top going bare, tablet and toy removed
On-screen text
  • Two open drawers is a ladder
  • Strap it to a stud
  • Nothing on top worth climbing for
Short cut · 45–60s Two drawers open on an unanchored chest, filmed from the height of a small child, and the shape it makes is a ladder.
Stands alone: Name the fall, cut, or crush risk immediately and finish on the strap fitted to a stud and the top cleared, so the Short ends on a fix rather than on a warning.
Standardize A picture label on each drawer front so a child finds and returns without reading, and the same category stays in the same drawer forever.
Beats
  • Photograph the contents of each drawer and fix a picture label to each front, socks on the socks drawer.
  • Show the labelled fronts from child eye height and set out that the label serves the return trip as much as the finding trip.
  • State the rule that costs something: same category in the same drawer forever, even when that leaves one drawer half empty.
  • Reference Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, because the taut strap fitted in the last pass is part of the finished state, not a one off job.
Shots
  • Overhead of socks laid out being photographed for the label
  • Close on hands fixing a picture label to a drawer front
  • Wide of five labelled drawer fronts, camera at child eye height
  • Overhead of one deliberately half empty drawer with the category intact
On-screen text
  • A picture beats reading
  • Socks on the socks drawer
  • Half empty is allowed
Short cut · 30–45s Five drawer fronts, five photographs of what is inside them, filmed from the eye height of whoever has to put the clothes back.
Stands alone: Explain in the first line that the label exists for putting clothes away rather than only for finding them, which is what makes the same category forever rule worth a half empty drawer.
Sustain Refolding happens straight out of the laundry basket into the drawer standing up, never stacked flat on the bed for later.
Beats
  • Show the trigger: the basket lands beside the open drawer and each item is folded upright and goes straight in.
  • Show the alternative it replaces, the flat stack left on the bed to be dealt with, and name that stack as the exact point where the system fails.
  • Close each drawer with one push in sequence and confirm the quantities are still holding.
  • Land the finished dresser: one category per drawer, upright rows, strapped to the wall, bare on top.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the laundry basket set down beside the open drawer
  • Overhead of one item folded and placed upright, continuous take
  • Close on each drawer closing with one push in sequence
  • Three quarter wide of the finished dresser, top bare, strap visible behind
On-screen text
  • Basket to drawer, no stack
  • Still closes with one push
Short cut · 30–45s Laundry goes basket to drawer with nothing landing on the bed in between, filmed as one unbroken overhead take.
Stands alone: Name the failure being avoided in the opening line, the flat stack on the bed for later, since the value of the trigger is only visible against the thing it replaces.
Close

Show the standard holding: one category per drawer, file folded upright, quantities set by the wash rhythm, and every drawer closing with a single push and no leaning. Fire the trigger once, clothes folded upright straight out of the basket, and hold on the taut anti tip strap and the bare dresser top.

Next: Move to the square metre by the bedroom door, where tomorrow morning either gets assembled tonight or gets argued about at seven.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm over the bed for tip outs, folding and the flat against upright cut
  • Overhead repositioned over the open drawer for the upright fills
  • Low tripod at child height for the labelled fronts and the two open drawers
  • Macro setup for elastic, runners, strap tension and label detail
  • Behind the dresser access for stud finding and bracket fitting
  • Three quarter tripod for drawer removal and the finished dresser wide
  • Basket to drawer lane for the trigger sequence
  • Matching close of each drawer front closing with one push, shot in sequence
Description hook

Set the shirt count by arithmetic instead of argument, file fold so a child can read the drawer from above, and strap the dresser to a wall stud before it gets climbed. Zone five of six in the Kids Bedroom.

MZ-051 · R09.06

School and Activity Launch Zone

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Who Actually Packs It”

6S the School Launch Zone: A Five Line List, One Hook Each, and Handing the Packing Over

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on adult hands packing a child's backpack at speed, zipping it, hanging it on the hook. Name the decision hiding inside that competence: you pack it because they are slow and you are not, and every rushed morning proves you right again. Set up that this is the one worth reversing, and that the video gives the five line list, the handover, and the rule that holds it, that you never silently repack the bag afterwards.

Sort The backpack gets turned fully upside down every Friday, so nothing lives in it by accident for another week.
Beats
  • Invert the backpack over a bin and empty every pocket, turning out the leftover lunch, the dead permission slip and the newsletter from three weeks ago.
  • Set out why complete emptying beats a look inside, that the things which survive are the things nobody ever sees.
  • Send the sports kit to the wash basket rather than back into the bag damp, and name damp kit as what actually makes the bag smell.
  • Fix the rhythm plainly, this is a Friday job, so the weekend never starts with last week's bag.
Shots
  • Overhead of the backpack inverted over a bin, contents falling out
  • Close on each pocket held open and turned out in turn
  • Overhead of the contents laid on the floor, split into out and back in
  • Three quarter of damp sports kit dropping into the wash basket
On-screen text
  • Upside down, every pocket
  • Damp kit never goes back in
  • Friday, every Friday
Short cut · 30–45s A school backpack gets held upside down over a bin and emptied pocket by pocket, and what falls out has been in there for weeks.
Stands alone: Establish in the first line that this is a full weekly empty rather than a tidy up, and say what survives when you only look inside, since that contrast is the entire reason for inverting it.
Straighten Hook, then shoes, then bag along the wall in the order they get grabbed, with the lunchbox on its own hook doing the telling.
Beats
  • Set the hook at child height and hang the packed bag, then place the shoes side by side directly underneath it.
  • Stand the instrument case upright against the wall where it cannot be trodden on, and put the sports bag on the second hook.
  • Give the lunchbox its own small hook and set out what it reports, that an empty hook at bedtime means the box is still in the bag with yesterday's sandwich in it.
  • Show the floor completely clear, which is the state this whole zone exists to hold.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the hook rail at child height with the packed bag hung
  • Overhead down onto shoes placed directly under the bag
  • Close on the instrument case standing upright against the wall
  • Macro on the empty lunchbox hook, then the lunchbox hanging on it
On-screen text
  • In grab order
  • Shoes directly underneath
  • An empty hook is a message
Short cut · 30–45s One small empty hook by a bedroom door at bedtime means a lunchbox is still shut inside a school bag with yesterday's sandwich in it.
Stands alone: State the pairing at the top, that this hook belongs to the lunchbox and nothing else, because the hook only reads as a signal once you know what is meant to be hanging there.
Shine Seals, lids and the base of the bag, which is where the growth and the old spill actually are.
Beats
  • Wipe the lunchbox seal groove and take the water bottle lid apart, showing the inside of the lid where the mould actually grows.
  • Turn the backpack over a bin and shake it out, then wipe the base where the drink leaked back in March.
  • While the bag is empty, check the base seam and the zip pulls, since a failing zip is what strands the bag on a Monday.
  • Everything dries fully before it goes back on the hook.
Shots
  • Macro on the water bottle lid taken apart with the inner seal visible
  • Close on the lunchbox seal groove being wiped out
  • Overhead of the backpack shaken out over a bin
  • Macro on the stained bag base and the zip pulls, before and after
On-screen text
  • The lid, not the bottle
  • Check the seam and the zips
  • Dry before it hangs
Short cut · 30–45s A kid's water bottle gets washed every day and the lid almost never comes apart, so here is the macro lens on the inside of that seal.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that the bottle gets washed but the lid does not come apart, which is exactly why the seal is the thing worth showing.
Safety The fourth S here is a clear doorway at seven in the morning, and one named pocket for the thing that must never be forgotten.
Beats
  • Shoot the doorway low with the bag and the instrument case lying across it, and name the risk as a fall in the line everyone walks at seven in the morning.
  • Set the rule that fixes it, everything hangs and nothing rests on the floor, then repeat the identical low frame with the floor clear.
  • Cover the second hazard as poison, choke, or strangle: loose medication in a backpack pocket, reachable by a younger sibling and easy to forget entirely.
  • Give the inhaler, the epipen or the dose one named pocket that is checked at packing rather than remembered at the school gate.
Shots
  • Locked off low doorway frame with bags and a case across the walking line
  • The identical locked off doorway frame with everything hung and the floor clear
  • Close on hands labelling one named pocket on the backpack
  • Macro on medication going into the named pocket and the zip closing over it
On-screen text
  • Everything hangs, nothing rests
  • One named pocket
  • Checked at packing, not at the gate
Short cut · 45–60s Camera on the floor of a bedroom doorway at bag height, with a school bag and an instrument case lying exactly where feet go at seven in the morning.
Stands alone: Name the fall risk and the seven in the morning walking line at the top, and include the named medication pocket before the end, because the doorway fix alone leaves the more serious hazard standing.
Standardize Five lines taped beside the hook at the child's eye level, in pictures for a younger one and words for an older one.
Beats
  • Write the list on camera, five lines and no more: bag, shoes, lunch, form, kit.
  • Tape it beside the hook at the child's eye level, checked with the camera down at that height.
  • Set out the constraint that matters, that a longer list gets skipped, so a missing item means you swap a line rather than add a sixth.
  • Reference Chapter 27, the friendly audit, and quote it: an audit checks the home, not the household. What it finds is always a system to fix, never a person to blame.
Shots
  • Overhead of the five line list being written out
  • Close on the list taped to the wall beside the hook
  • Camera at child eye height showing the list sitting level with it
  • Macro across the five lines, each one legible in frame
On-screen text
  • Five lines, no more
  • Bag, shoes, lunch, form, kit
  • At their eye level
Short cut · 30–45s A packing list for a school bag stops dead at five lines, and the reason line six never gets added is the whole point.
Stands alone: State that the list belongs to the child and hangs beside the hook at their eye level, so the five line limit reads as a deliberate design constraint rather than laziness.
Sustain The bag gets packed while the bath is running, and the packing is genuinely handed over rather than supervised.
Beats
  • Show the trigger: the bath taps go on, and the packing starts in the bedroom while the water runs.
  • Set out why this window works, that it happens before anyone is tired enough to argue, and it ends when the bath is full.
  • Show the handover as a rule rather than a performance: the packing is done off camera, and what is filmed is a finger running down the five line list instead of going into the bag.
  • Give the rule that makes the handover real, never silently repack it, and the honest cost, a few genuinely bad weeks bought back on every school morning after.
Shots
  • Close on the bath taps opening
  • Three quarter of the packed bag on the hook, hands only, camera at child height
  • Close on a finger running down the five line list, never entering the bag
  • Wide of the finished launch zone, floor clear, bag hung and zipped
On-screen text
  • Packed while the bath runs
  • Check the list, not the bag
  • Never silently repack it
Short cut · 45–60s A finger runs down a five line packing list and stops there, without once going into the school bag underneath it.
Stands alone: Set up in the first line that the adult used to pack this bag and now only checks the list, and include the never silently repack rule, because that rule is the only thing that makes the handover real.
Close

Show the standard in place: bag on the hook, shoes directly underneath, forms in the front pocket, and the five line list taped beside the hook at the child's eye level. Fire the trigger once, the bag packed and hung while the bath is running, and hold on the completely clear doorway floor.

Next: Pull back to the whole room with all six zones standing at once, then point at the next room in the series, where the same six passes meet a much smaller occupant.

  • Floor level wide of the finished zone with everything hung
  • Wash basket setup for the damp sports kit
  • Camera at child eye height for the list height check

Empty the backpack upside down every Friday, hang everything so the doorway is clear at seven in the morning, and hand the packing over to a five line list you check instead of the bag. Zone six of six in the Kids Bedroom.

6Sschool morning routinebackpack organizationkids checklistlaunch zonedoorway safetyschool runmicro zone

Room 10 of 20

Nursery

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteShoot the whole room in daylight with the blind up and no overhead bulb, because the nursery reads warm and soft on camera and hard top light flattens the pale surfaces the room is made of. No baby, no doll and no person above the wrists appears in any frame at any point, so every demonstration is built from hands, overhead angles and detail shots, and any beat that looks like it needs a body gets solved with an empty pad or an empty crib instead. Treat every crib frame as if it will be screenshotted on its own, which means the crib is never filmed holding bedding except in the deliberate before shots at the top of that video. The tripod lives in two places: a horizontal centre column over the crib and the changing pad for the locked overhead angles, and a three quarter stand at dresser height for drawer and shelf work. Crib slats eat light, so bounce a white card from the window side rather than adding a lamp, and shoot the two low light beats at dusk using the night light already in the room. Real hazards get demonstrated at rest and never in motion: cords are shown slack and then shortened, the anchor bracket goes on the wall before the chest goes back, and any kettle or sterilizer is filmed cold and unplugged. Wipe the changing pad between takes on camera, since that is the standard the room is teaching. Keep a spare fitted sheet and a second set of clean bottle parts on hand so resets between takes do not cost a wash cycle.
MZ-052 · R10.01

Crib and Sleep Zone

5–7 min · thumbnail: “One Sheet. Nothing Else.”

Crib Reset: One Fitted Sheet and Nothing Else (6S Nursery)

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on the loaded crib: the handmade quilt folded over the rail, the plush pile, the bumper, the wedge, the muslin stack. Name the hard call this zone forces, that the bedding was made for this crib by somebody who loves you, took them weeks, and still cannot go inside the rails. Hands lift each item out and set it on the floor until the mattress is bare. Frame the problem as a decision about a gift and about who you now have to tell, not as clutter.

Sort Everything comes out of the crib in one armful, and exactly one thing goes back in.
Beats
  • Hands lift the quilt, the plush, the bumper, the wedge and the muslin stack out and lay them on the floor as a single spread, small enough to prove this is one armful of work rather than a project.
  • Each item is walked to its actual destination on camera: plush to the toy basket, muslins to the changing station, quilt to the keepsake box.
  • Explain that the crib is the one zone in this room with a number instead of a judgement call, and that the number is one.
  • One fitted sheet goes back onto the bare mattress and nothing follows it over the rail.
Shots
  • Overhead of the loaded crib before anything is touched
  • Overhead of the floor spread, every item separated and readable
  • Close on hands folding the quilt into the keepsake box and closing the lid
  • Overhead of the bare mattress with the single fitted sheet going on
On-screen text
  • Empty it first
  • One fitted sheet
  • Everything else has a home
Short cut · 30–45s Overhead of a crib packed with quilt, bumper, wedge and plush, swept out by hands in one continuous move down to a bare mattress.
Stands alone: Open by naming the nursery crib and stating the one fitted sheet standard as a flat rule, since nobody watching has seen the rest of the video.
Straighten Spares live where your hand finds them in the dark, because the sheet change happens at 3 a.m.
Beats
  • The top dresser drawer is emptied to its bare base, then two fitted sheets and one spare sleep sack go in and nothing else.
  • Explain the test being applied: one drawer, one motion, no ceiling light.
  • A hand opens the drawer in a dark room and comes out with a fitted sheet without looking down, shot at dusk on the room's own night light with no added fixture.
  • Explain what fails if the spares live in the airing cupboard down the hall, which is a walk you will not make with a wet mattress and a crying baby.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the top drawer emptied to its bare base
  • Close on hands folding two fitted sheets and a sleep sack into the drawer
  • Close on a hand opening the drawer and lifting a sheet out blind, lit by the room's night light
On-screen text
  • Top drawer, nothing else
  • One drawer, one motion
Short cut · 30–45s A hand in a dark nursery opens one drawer and comes out holding a fitted sheet without looking down.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that this is the crib zone and that the drawer holds sleep spares only, or the shot reads as a generic drawer tip.
Shine Cleaning the crib is the inspection that catches loose frame bolts.
Beats
  • Sheet comes off to a hot wash, the mattress is lifted out and stood against the wall, leaving the frame empty and reachable on all sides.
  • Hands wipe the mattress cover and every rail, holding on the top rail where hands and gums end up.
  • A palm runs down each slat, then a spanner goes onto the frame bolts. Explain that crib hardware works loose over months of being leaned on, which is why the check belongs to cleaning day rather than to a worry in the middle of the night.
  • Mattress goes back and the fresh sheet is pulled tight to all four corners.
Shots
  • Close on a cloth working along the top rail
  • Close on a palm sliding down a slat
  • Close on a spanner seating on a frame bolt and turning
  • Overhead of the sheet pulled tight, corner by corner
On-screen text
  • Clean to inspect
  • Check the bolts while it is empty
Short cut · 30–45s Close on a spanner seating on a crib frame bolt and taking up a quarter turn of slack that was already there.
Stands alone: Explain in the first line that the crib is empty because the sheet is in the wash, so the bolt check reads as routine rather than an emergency.
Safety A cord reachable through the slats and a mattress left high are the two things in this zone that hurt a baby.
Beats
  • Frame it as poison, choke, or strangle. The blind cord, the lamp flex and the monitor cable are shown in turn, then a hand comes through the slats to test which of the three can actually be reached, framed tight so nothing above the wrist enters.
  • The reachable cord is shortened and clipped high on the wall and the crib is slid clear. Explain that reachable from inside the rails means it comes down or gets shortened today.
  • Frame the second hazard as a fall. The mattress bracket is unhooked and dropped to its lowest setting.
  • Name the trigger for that drop as the day your baby can push up onto hands and knees, because pulling to stand is what they learn next.
Shots
  • Close on a hand between the slats reaching toward a hanging cord
  • Close on the cord being shortened and clipped high, well back from the rails
  • Three-quarter of the mattress bracket being unhooked and reset low
  • Overhead of the monitor mounted on the wall with its cable clipped an arm's length back
On-screen text
  • Reachable cord comes down
  • Lowest setting
  • Find it, and fix it now
Short cut · 45–60s A hand comes through the crib slats and closes on a blind cord that should never have been in reach.
Stands alone: Name Safety as the fourth S and state both hazards plainly, since a viewer arriving cold needs the rule and not just the demonstration.
Standardize A photograph of the correct crib means nobody has to ask you what goes in it.
Beats
  • Shoot the overhead frame of the finished crib, bare mattress and one sheet, as the reference image itself.
  • The printed picture is taped inside the closet door. Explain that a visiting grandparent putting your baby down can now see the right state without asking you.
  • The quilt is hung on the wall above the crib in the same frame as the taped photo, which closes the cold open decision and gives you the thing you say to the giver.
Shots
  • Overhead reference frame of the crib, held long and clean

  • Wide three-quarter showing the quilt hung on the wall above the crib

  • Tape it inside the door
Short cut · 30–45s An overhead photo of a bare crib mattress with one fitted sheet gets printed and taped inside a nursery closet door.
Stands alone: Say what the photo shows and who it is for, because the picture means nothing without its contents and its audience.
Sustain The wash is the trigger, so the crib rebuilds itself to standard every time.
Beats
  • The sheet is stripped for the wash, then the crib is remade with a sheet and nothing else.
  • Explain that the crib is already empty at this exact moment, which is why the rebuild costs nothing extra and needs no reminder attached to it.
  • Close on the live crib matching the taped photo.

  • Close on hands stripping the sheet in one motion
  • Overhead of the crib remade, sheet only
  • Match cut between the taped photo and the live crib

  • Trigger: when the sheet comes off
  • Sheet, sleep sack, baby
Short cut · 30–45s A crib sheet stripped for the wash, then the same crib remade with one sheet and nothing else.
Stands alone: State the trigger and the full standard in the first two lines, since this Short is the whole habit compressed.
Close

Hold the finished crib beside the taped photo and give the standard as the room's rule: the crib holds a fitted sheet, a sleep sack, and your baby, and nothing else crosses the rail. Show the trigger once more as the sheet comes off for the wash, and point to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo.

Next: Next, the changing station, where the whole design question is what one arm can reach with the other hand still on your baby.

The crib is the one surface in the house where your baby is left alone, which is why the standard is a fitted sheet and nothing more. This is the full 6S reset, including the hard conversation about the quilt somebody made you.

MZ-053 · R10.02

Changing Station

7–9 min · thumbnail: “One Hand Stays On Baby”

Changing Station Setup: Everything Inside One Arm's Sweep

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the half-built changing setup on the living room floor, a wipe pack and no diapers. Name the decision this zone forces: you built a second spot downstairs because carrying the baby up eight times a day is unbearable, and the half-stocked version is the one that fails you. A hand reaches for a diaper that is not there. Name the rule the video settles, that you run it as a full station or you do not run it at all.

Sort Only what your hand touches during a real change earns a place on the dresser top.
Beats
  • The entire dresser top is cleared onto a towel on the floor, and the count of what was living up there is left on screen long enough to register.
  • Explain the single test for getting back: does your hand touch this during an actual change.
  • Diapers, wipes, cream and a burp cloth go back one at a time, each named as it lands.
  • The lamp, the framed scan photo and the unopened lotion leave the surface entirely, and the shot follows each to where it now lives.
Shots
  • Overhead of the loaded dresser top before anything moves
  • Overhead of the towel spread with every item laid out separately
  • Close on hands returning the four items that stay
  • Close on the lamp and framed photo being carried off the surface
On-screen text
  • Clear it all
  • Does your hand touch it?
  • Four things go back
Short cut · 30–45s A crowded dresser top emptied onto a towel in one sweep, then only four items are allowed back onto it.
Stands alone: Name the four survivors and the test that chose them, because the sweep is only persuasive once the rule is stated.
Straighten The reach arc defines the station, and the dominant hand decides which side of it holds diapers.
Beats
  • Hands pin a length of string at the pad and swing it across the dresser top to mark the limit of a planted reach, laying tape along the arc it draws. Shot overhead and framed tight to hands and string.
  • Explain the split the tape creates: inside the arc is the station, outside the arc is storage.
  • Diapers go on the side the dominant hand lands, wipes beside them, cream where a thumb can flip the cap without looking.
  • The lined pail is set within one step and two spare outfits go into the drawer directly beneath the pad.
Shots
  • Overhead of a string and marker drawing the reach arc across the dresser top
  • Overhead of the taped arc with diapers, wipes and cream placed inside it
  • Close on a thumb flipping the cream cap one handed with no eyes on it
  • Three-quarter showing the pail one step from the pad and the drawer directly beneath
On-screen text
  • Inside the arc: station
  • Outside the arc: storage
  • Feet planted
Short cut · 45–60s A line of tape drawn across a dresser top marks exactly how far one hand can reach without leaving the changing pad.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that the other hand never leaves the baby, since that is the entire reason the arc exists.
Shine The pad is the surface bare skin touches most in this house, so it gets wiped every change.
Beats
  • The pad is wiped on camera, and the beat explains why this one alone does not wait for the weekly reset.
  • The pad cover comes off for a hot wash, noted as weekly rather than monthly.
  • The drawer under the pad is pulled right out and upended, showing the crusted cream lids and dried wipes that collect underneath the spare outfits where nothing ever disturbs them.
  • Fragrance free, infant safe cleaner goes down on camera, and the beat explains that the cleaner choice matters more at this pad than anywhere else in the room.
Shots
  • Close on a cloth crossing the pad surface, edge to edge
  • Close on the pad cover being pulled off
  • Three-quarter of the drawer pulled fully out and upended over a bin
  • Close focus on a dried cream lid and crusted wipe in the drawer corner
On-screen text
  • Wipe after every change
  • Pull the drawer right out
Short cut · 30–45s The drawer under a changing pad comes fully out and what was living underneath the spare outfits tips into a bin.
Stands alone: Name the changing station and the monthly rhythm, since a viewer needs to know this is scheduled and not a one-off discovery.
Safety A roll off a dresser is a fall from adult waist height, and loose plastic on top is inside a grabbing reach.
Beats
  • Frame it as a fall. One hand stays planted on the pad while the other reaches to the taped arc and stops rather than lifting. Explain that the fall is onto a hard floor from adult waist height, with no exception for reaching a shelf.
  • The anchor bracket goes into the wall and the dresser is fixed to it before it goes back.
  • Frame the second hazard as poison, choke, or strangle. The wipe refill bag and the pail liner roll are shown sitting on the dresser top, then both go into a shut drawer.
  • The diaper cream tube moves off the surface edge and out of a grabbing reach, and the empty edge is held on screen.
Shots

  • Close on the anchor bracket and screws going into the wall behind the dresser
  • Close on the loose wipe refill bag and liner roll lifted off the top and shut in a drawer
  • Close focus on a cream tube at the dresser edge, then the same edge empty
On-screen text
  • One hand stays on
  • Anchor the dresser
  • No loose plastic on top
Short cut · 45–60s A hand planted on a changing pad reaches sideways and stops dead at a taped line rather than lifting off.
Stands alone: Name Safety as the fourth S and state the fall height plainly, so the demonstration carries its stakes without a person on camera.
Standardize A restock card with counts tells you the station is low before a bare baby does.
Beats
  • The card is written on camera: eight diapers in the caddy, one wipe pack open, one sealed behind it.
  • It is taped to the wall beside the pad, at the height of somebody already standing at the station.
  • The caddy is counted against the card and shown matching, so the card reads as a live check rather than decoration.
  • Explain that the counts get rewritten the day the diaper size changes, so the card follows your baby instead of turning into wallpaper.

  • Close on the card being written, marker on paper
  • Close on the card taped to the wall at station eye level
  • Overhead of diapers being counted into the caddy against the card

Sustain The last change before bed is the restock, so the station is never found empty at night.
Beats
  • The caddy is shown low at end of day, then restocked to the numbers on the card.
  • Explain why this trigger and not a reminder: the last change before bed already happens, every night, without anyone deciding to do it.
  • The cold open decision is resolved on camera. The downstairs setup is rebuilt as a single carry caddy that comes down in the morning and goes back up at night, packed to the same counts as the card.
Shots
  • Overhead of a low caddy, then the same caddy full against the card
  • Close on hands packing the carry caddy to the same counts

  • Trigger: last change before bed
  • One station or one caddy
Short cut · 45–60s A near-empty diaper caddy filled back to a number written on a card taped to the wall above it.
Stands alone: Give the trigger phrase and the counts, and say that a half-stocked second spot is the failure this prevents.
Close

Show a full change performed with feet planted and one hand on the pad the whole way through, ending with the caddy counted back up to the card. Give the standard as the rule: everything you touch during a change is reachable with your feet planted and one hand on your baby. Name the trigger as the last change before bed.

Next: Next, the clothing drawers, and the outfit with the tags still on that is three sizes too small.

Description hook

A changing station works when everything you touch is inside one arm's sweep and your other hand never leaves your baby. Here is the full 6S build, including the restock card and why a half-stocked second spot downstairs is the option that fails you.

MZ-054 · R10.03

Baby Clothing Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Keep Two Per Size”

Baby Clothes: One Size Per Drawer, and Outgrown Leaves Today

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a newborn outfit with the tags still attached, held against a drawer of clothes three sizes bigger. Name the decision: it came from somebody who mattered, it was never once worn, and keeping it feels like keeping the gift while giving it away feels like a small betrayal. The outgoing bag hangs empty on the door hook behind it. Say plainly that this video settles that call with a rule rather than a mood.

Sort Read the label, compare it to today's size, and accept that there are only two destinations.
Beats
  • A drawer is emptied onto the bed and every garment laid flat in a single layer, dropped into rough size order as it goes down so the spread of sizes living in one drawer is visible at a glance.
  • A label is read between two fingers, and the beat explains why reading beats judging by eye on baby clothing, where the same garment shape runs across four sizes.
  • Each garment is checked against the size your baby is wearing today, and anything smaller leaves the drawer now.
  • The two destinations are shown physically, the outgoing bag on the hook and the keepsake box, and the beat explains that a third pile is exactly what stalls this zone.
  • The cold open rule is applied on camera: two garments per size, chosen by what your baby actually lived in, and the unworn gift goes out while it is still new enough to delight somebody.
Shots
  • Overhead of a drawer emptied and laid flat, every garment separate and in size order
  • Close focus on a size label being read between two fingers
  • Close on a garment going into the outgoing bag on the door hook
  • Close on the keepsake box taking the two chosen keepers
  • Overhead of the outgoing bag with something already in it
On-screen text
  • Read the label
  • Two destinations only
  • Keep two per size
Short cut · 45–60s A newborn outfit with the tags still on, held up against a drawer full of clothes three sizes bigger.
Stands alone: State the two-per-size rule and both destinations inside the first ten seconds, because without them the shot is just a sad object.
Straighten One size per drawer, filed upright, so a half-asleep hand cannot pick wrong.
Beats
  • One size is assigned to each drawer, with the largest size in the lowest drawer, and the beat explains why the largest goes low.
  • Sleepers and bodysuits are filed upright on their spines, shown as an overhead where every collar is readable at once and cut against the same drawer stacked flat.
  • A gift in a bigger size goes straight into the next-size bin on the closet shelf rather than into any drawer.
  • Explain the reason plainly: this drawer gets opened half asleep, so nothing that does not fit today may live in it.
Shots
  • Overhead of a drawer stacked flat, then the same drawer filed upright with the same garments
  • Close on hands folding a sleeper into a standing file
  • Three-quarter of the closet shelf with the next-size bin taking a gift
  • Wide three-quarter of the chest with the drawers stepping largest at the bottom
On-screen text
  • One size per drawer
  • File upright, read every collar
  • Bigger sizes go to the bin
Short cut · 30–45s The same baby drawer, the same clothes, shown stacked flat and then filed upright from directly overhead.
Stands alone: Name the one-size-per-drawer rule first, so the filing technique reads as part of a system rather than a folding trick.
Shine Empty to the base, and deal with set stains before they ever reach the drawer.
Beats
  • Each drawer is taken down to its bare base and wiped out, showing the sock lint and dried spit-up gathered in the corners.
  • Explain that this only shows up once the drawer is fully out and turned over, which is why the full empty belongs to reset day and not to laundry day.
  • Hand-me-downs are turned to the window and inspected for stains that have set, and washed before they go in rather than after you have pulled one out at 6 a.m.
  • The washed hand-me-downs go into the drawer, filed upright with everything else.
Shots
  • Overhead of a drawer taken down to its bare base
  • Close focus on lint and dried residue in a drawer corner
  • Close on a set stain on a hand-me-down turned to the window light
  • Close on clean hand-me-downs being filed into the drawer
On-screen text
  • Down to the base
  • Wash before it goes in
Short cut · 30–45s The corner of a baby clothes drawer taken down to bare wood, with the sock lint and dried spit-up nobody sees until it is empty.
Stands alone: Say this is the clothing drawers and that they only come fully out on reset day, so the grime reads as expected rather than shocking.
Safety An unanchored chest is a ladder and a crush risk, and old trims come off in a mouth.
Beats
  • Frame it as fall, cut, or crush. Two drawers are opened at once and the weight is shown carrying forward, turning the chest into a ladder for a climbing child.
  • The wall anchor is fitted on camera and the chest is fixed to it before it goes back against the wall.
  • The working rule is demonstrated as a repeated hand motion, each drawer closing before the next one opens.
  • Frame the second hazard as poison, choke, or strangle. Decorative buttons, ribbon ties and a hood drawstring on a hand-me-down cardigan are cut off before the garment ever enters a drawer.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a chest with two drawers open and the weight carried forward
  • Close on the anchor strap or bracket being screwed to the wall
  • Close on one drawer closing as the next opens, repeated
  • Close focus on scissors taking off a hood drawstring and a loose decorative button
On-screen text
  • Anchor it to the wall
  • One drawer at a time
  • Cut the trims off first
Short cut · 45–60s Two drawers open at once on a chest that is not fixed to anything, then the wall bracket goes in.
Stands alone: Name Safety as the fourth S and state both hazards, since the drawstring cutting will otherwise read as a styling choice.
Standardize A written size on the drawer front means nobody opens three drawers to dress your baby.
Beats
  • A size is written large on a label and fixed to the drawer front, then repeated across the chest so the sizes read as a sequence from the doorway.
  • Explain that the label changes the same day the size changes, not the same week.
  • A second person's hand goes straight to the correct drawer on the first try and pulls out a sleeper that fits, which is the whole point of the label.
Shots
  • Close on a size being written on a label
  • Wide three-quarter of the chest with every drawer front labelled in sequence
  • Close on a hand going straight to one drawer and lifting out a correct-size sleeper
On-screen text
  • Write the size on the front
  • Change it the day it changes
Short cut · 30–45s Every drawer front on a baby chest carries a size in marker, and a hand goes straight to the right one without opening the others.
Stands alone: Explain that each drawer holds one size and nothing else, or the labels look decorative.
Sustain The snap that will not close is the trigger, and it sends the garment to the bag rather than the wash.
Beats
  • A hand tries to close a snap over the diaper and cannot.
  • That garment goes into the outgoing bag while the wash basket sits visible and untouched beside it, and the beat explains that the wash basket is the route by which outgrown clothes rejoin the drawer.
  • The bag is lifted off the hook and carried out of the room, which is the standard that outgrown clothing never spends a night in here.
Shots
  • Close focus on a snap that will not close over the diaper
  • Close on the same garment dropped into the outgoing bag, with the wash basket in frame and passed over
  • Three-quarter of the bag lifted off the hook and carried out of the room
On-screen text
  • Trigger: the snap will not close
  • Bag, not basket
Short cut · 30–45s A snap that will not close over the diaper, and the sleeper goes straight past the wash basket into an outgoing bag.
Stands alone: State the trigger and the standard that outgrown clothing never spends a night in the room, since the basket refusal is the whole point.
Close

Pan the finished chest: one size per drawer, the sizes written on the fronts, sleepers filed upright, the next-size bin on the closet shelf, and the outgoing bag on the hook with something already in it. Give the standard as the rule, one size per drawer and outgrown clothing never spends a night in the room, and name the trigger as the snap that will not close.

Next: Next, the feeding station, and the three bottle brands you now own because the first one was refused.

Shot list
  • Locked overhead over the bed for the full drawer spread and the flat versus upright comparison
  • Close focus setup on the same tripod for size labels, drawer corners, snaps and trims being cut
  • Three-quarter dresser stand for the chest, the drawer sequence and the anchor install
  • Close on the outgoing bag on the door hook, empty and then filled
  • Close on the keepsake box taking the two chosen keepers
  • Three-quarter of the closet shelf and the next-size bin
  • Close on size labels being written and fixed to the drawer fronts
  • Close on the bag being carried out of the room
Description hook

Baby clothes turn over faster than any storage you own, so the drawer has to hold this month's size and nothing else. This is the full 6S reset, including the rule that settles the unworn gift with the tags still on.

6Sbaby clothes organizationnursery drawersoutgrown clotheshome organizationfurniture anchoring6S Successmicro zone
MZ-055 · R10.04

Feeding Station

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Clean Never Meets Used”

Feeding Station: A Clean Bottle in Your Hands at 2 a.m.

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on three bottle brands lined up on the surface with spare teats and mismatched collars scattered between them. Name the decision: the first bottle was refused, everybody swore the second one worked for them, and you now wash, sterilize, store and match parts for three systems in order to use one. A hand hunts through the pile for a collar that fits the teat it is holding. Point out that every one of those steps happens at 2 a.m.

Sort Lay out every part at once, then bin the failed ones and remove the brands you have stopped using.
Beats
  • Every bottle, teat, valve, membrane and pump part is laid out in a single row grouped by brand, so the true count and the number of separate systems both read at once.
  • A teat gone cloudy and one split at the slit are held to the window, and the beat explains why these go in the bin rather than back in the drawer.
  • Every part belonging to a brand or pump you have stopped using is gathered and the whole system leaves, box and spares included.
  • Explain the three-feed test from the cold open: a new teat gets three honest feeds across a week, offered when your baby is calm and hungry rather than already crying, and then it either stays or the system leaves the house.
Shots
  • Overhead of every feeding part laid out in a single row, grouped by brand
  • Close focus on a cloudy teat and a split slit held against window light
  • Close on a full brand's parts swept into a box and lidded
  • Overhead of the surviving parts, one system wide
On-screen text
  • Every part out, at once
  • Cloudy or split goes
  • One system, not three
Short cut · 45–60s Every bottle, teat, valve and collar in the house laid out in one row, then whole brands going into a box to leave.
Stands alone: State the three-feed test and that a failed brand leaves complete, since the removal is the claim people will argue with.
Straighten Two bins in obviously different colors, and bottles assembled the moment they are clean.
Beats
  • Two bins in clearly different colors are set down, one for clean and ready, one for used and waiting.
  • Bottles come out of the sterilizer and are assembled fully, teat and collar seated, before they are allowed into the clean bin.
  • Explain the payoff: the middle of the night becomes a grab rather than a hunt for a matching collar in the dark.
  • The drying rack is shown standing empty as its correct resting state, and the burp cloths are stacked where a hand finds them without looking down.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the two bins side by side, colors clearly different
  • Close on hands assembling a bottle fully, teat and collar seated
  • Overhead of four assembled bottles standing in the clean bin
  • Close on a hand grabbing a burp cloth without looking down
On-screen text
  • Clean bin. Used bin.
  • Assemble before you store
  • Grab, do not hunt
Short cut · 30–45s A bottle comes out of the sterilizer and gets fully assembled, teat and collar on, before it is allowed into the clean bin.
Stands alone: Name the two bins and the 2 a.m. reason first, or the assembly step looks like extra work for its own sake.
Shine Parts must be bone dry before they go into a closed bin, and the sterilizer needs descaling.
Beats
  • Parts go into the sterilizer fully disassembled, valve and membrane separated from the collar, on the schedule the kit itself prints, shot as a hands only sequence.
  • Parts are spread to air dry with space between them, and the beat explains that a damp valve in a closed bin is where mold starts.
  • The kettle or sterilizer is descaled, filmed cold and unplugged, and noted as monthly.
  • The drying rack is lifted and the drip ring underneath it is wiped off the surface.
Shots
  • Close on parts being spread to air dry, spaced apart
  • Close focus on a valve, dry and held to the window light
  • Close on descaling solution going into a cold, unplugged sterilizer
  • Close on the rack lifted and the drip ring wiped away
On-screen text
  • Bone dry before the bin
  • Descale monthly
  • Wipe under the rack
Short cut · 30–45s A bottle drying rack lifted off the counter to reveal the drip ring that has been sitting underneath it.
Stands alone: Say that a damp part in a closed bin is the actual risk, which is why drying is a step you do rather than a wait you allow.
Safety Hot appliances at pad height and standing water beside live sockets are the two real risks here.
Beats
  • Frame it as burn or fire. The kettle, warmer or sterilizer is filmed cold and unplugged with its cord hanging at full length off the surface edge, and the drop is shown reaching well below the counter.
  • Every cable is looped short and run behind its appliance, and the beat explains that a pulled cord brings scalding water down at child height.
  • Frame the second hazard as water and electricity. The water jug and the wet drying rack are shown standing beside the sterilizer socket and the monitor plug on one surface.
  • The jug and the rack are moved well clear so nothing wet stands next to anything live, and the finished separation is held on screen.
Shots
  • Close on a long appliance cord hanging off the surface edge at full drop, filmed cold and unplugged
  • Close on the cable looped short and tucked behind the appliance
  • Overhead of the wet rack and jug beside a socket and monitor plug, then the same surface separated
  • Close focus on the dry stretch of surface between the water side and the live side
On-screen text
  • Cords looped short
  • Scald height
  • Wet away from live
Short cut · 45–60s A kettle cord hanging at full length off a counter edge, with the drop reaching well below the worktop.
Stands alone: Name Safety as the fourth S and state both hazards, since the cord shot alone does not explain the scald path.
Standardize The mixing numbers go on a card so a night visitor gets it right the first time.
Beats
  • The scoop-to-water numbers you actually use are written on a card and taped above the station, readable from standing height.
  • Explain who the card is for: a grandparent or a night visitor mixing a feed without waking you to ask.
  • A hand follows the card once while mixing, so it reads as live rather than as decoration.
  • Give the rule as the book puts it, that a standard is the best way you know today, written down, and show the card corrected in pen when the scoop size changes.
Shots
  • Close on the numbers being written on the card
  • Close on the card taped above the station, readable from standing height
  • Overhead of a scoop being levelled against the card's numbers
On-screen text
  • Numbers on the wall
  • For whoever mixes it at 2 a.m.
Short cut · 30–45s Formula mixing numbers written on a card, taped above a feeding station, and followed by a hand in a dark kitchen.
Stands alone: Explain that the card exists for other people in the house rather than for you, which is the reason it goes on the wall at all.
Sustain The kitchen light going off is the trigger that resets both bins.
Beats
  • The used bin is carried down at the end of the night and the clean bin comes back stocked to four assembled bottles.
  • Explain why this trigger works: the kitchen light already goes off every night without anyone deciding to do it.
  • Close on the two bins in their finished state, clean and ready full, used and waiting empty, rack standing bare.
Shots
  • Close on the used bin lifted and carried out
  • Overhead of the clean bin restocked to four assembled bottles
  • Three-quarter of the finished station, both bins and an empty rack
On-screen text
  • Trigger: kitchen light goes off
  • Four assembled, ready
Short cut · 30–45s Two bins at the end of the night, one carried out full of used bottle parts, one coming back with four assembled bottles.
Stands alone: Give the trigger phrase and the count of four, since this Short is the whole habit in miniature.
Close

Hold the finished station: one bin of clean assembled bottles, one bin waiting, an empty rack, the formula scoop inside the tin with the lid shut, and burp cloths within a blind grab. Give the standard as the rule, clean and ready never shares a bin with used and waiting, and name the trigger as the kitchen light going off for the night. Point to Chapter 14, visual controls.

Next: Next, the backstock shelf, and the six half-price packs in a size your baby skipped.

Shot list
  • Locked overhead over the feeding surface for the full parts row and both bins
  • Close focus setup on the same tripod for teats, valves and the dry check against window light
  • Three-quarter stand at surface height for the bins, the rack and the appliance cords
  • Close on a bottle being fully assembled straight out of the sterilizer
  • Close on the appliance cord at full drop and then looped short behind the unit, filmed cold and unplugged
  • Overhead of the wet side and the live side, before and after separation
  • Close on the mixing card being written and taped above the station
  • Close on the used bin being carried out at night
Description hook

At 2 a.m. a feeding station either puts a clean assembled bottle in your hand or makes you hunt for a matching collar. Here is the full 6S build, including the three-feed test that decides which bottle brand stays in the house.
