MZ-056 · R10.05

Diaper and Care Backstock

7–9 min · thumbnail: “One Size Ahead. Two Packs.”

Diaper Backstock: One Size Ahead, Two Packs Deep

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on six packs of size 2 stacked on a shelf with a size 3 diaper held up beside them. Name the decision: they were half price, it felt like money in the bank, and two weeks later your baby went from size 1 straight to size 3. A hand pulls a pack down and reads the printed size on the end. Say plainly that this video sets a buying limit that a sale price does not get to argue with.

Sort Read the printed size on every pack, and accept that an opened pack in the wrong size is still the wrong size.
Beats
  • Every pack comes off the shelf and stands on the floor on its short end, printed size facing the camera, so the whole size range you have been buying reads in one frame.
  • The printed size is read rather than the picture on the front, and the beat explains why the picture on a diaper pack misleads.
  • Everything smaller than the size in use today is set aside, including packs already opened, because a half-used pack of size 1 is still size 1.
  • The outgoing route is shown on camera, unopened packs bagged for a friend or a diaper bank this week, and the opened ones going with them.
Shots
  • Overhead of every pack pulled down and standing on end, sizes facing up
  • Close focus on the printed size on the short end beside the picture on the front
  • Close on an opened pack being added to the outgoing pile
  • Three-quarter of the outgoing packs bagged and set by the door
On-screen text
  • Read the printed size
  • Opened still counts
  • Out this week
Short cut · 30–45s A half-used pack of diapers in an outgrown size goes onto the outgoing pile instead of back on the shelf.
Stands alone: State that opened packs leave too and that they are not going to fit better later, since that is the belief the clip has to break.
Straighten Sizes written large enough to read from the doorway, current at the front, next size directly behind.
Beats
  • The size is written in marker on the short end of every pack and the ends are turned out to face the room.
  • The result is tested with the camera at the doorway, showing that every size reads without stepping into the room.
  • The current size is shelved at the front with the next size directly behind it, on a low shelf.
  • Creams, teething gel and the thermometer are gathered into one lidded box rather than living loose between the cartons.
Shots
  • Close on a marker writing a size large on the short end of a pack
  • Doorway-height wide of the shelf with every size readable from the door
  • Three-quarter of the current size at the front and the next size directly behind
  • Close on creams, gel and thermometer collected into a lidded box
On-screen text
  • Size on the short end
  • Reads from the doorway
  • Current front, next behind
Short cut · 30–45s Camera standing in the doorway, and every diaper size on the shelf across the room is readable from there.
Stands alone: Say the sizes were hand written on the short ends and why that face is the one turned out, since the shot is the result of a step it does not show.
Shine An empty shelf is when you find damp cartons and expired creams.
Beats
  • The shelf is wiped down while it is completely bare.
  • Cartons are turned over and their undersides checked for damp, and the beat explains that packs stored against an outside wall wick moisture up through the cardboard.
  • The dates on every cream and infant medicine are read while the shelf is still empty, and what has passed goes in the bin.
  • The shelf is reloaded only once it is dry and the expired items are gone.
Shots
  • Close on a cloth crossing the emptied shelf
  • Close focus on the damp underside of a carton
  • Close on a date being read on a cream tube, then the tube dropped in a bin
  • Overhead of the shelf reloaded, dry and clear
On-screen text
  • Check the undersides
  • Read every date
Short cut · 30–45s A diaper carton flipped over to show the damp that wicked up through the cardboard from the outside wall behind it.
Stands alone: Explain that this only shows up with the shelf fully emptied, which is why the sorting and the cleaning happen in the same session.
Safety Nothing heavy above the crib, and every cream and medicine behind a lid a toddler cannot open.
Beats
  • Frame it as fall, cut, or crush. A heavy carton is shown on the shelf above the crib with the crib in the same frame, and the line it would fall along is traced.
  • The weight is moved low and the shelf above the crib is left bare, stated as a rule rather than a preference.
  • Frame the second hazard as poison, choke, or strangle. The outer plastic wrap and the pail liner roll are lifted away and put out of reach.
  • Creams, teething gels and infant medicine go into a closed box a standing toddler cannot open, and the box is placed accordingly.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a heavy carton on the shelf above the crib, with the crib in frame below it
  • Close on the same shelf left bare after the weight comes down
  • Close on the outer plastic wrap and liner roll being lifted away
  • Close focus on a lidded box closing over creams and infant medicine
On-screen text
  • Nothing heavy over the crib
  • Weight goes low
  • Lid on the medicines
Short cut · 45–60s A heavy carton of diapers sitting on a shelf directly above a crib, with the crib in the same frame underneath it.
Stands alone: Name Safety as the fourth S and give the rule that weight goes low and nothing at all is stored above the crib.
Standardize The minimum and maximum go on the shelf edge itself, where the decision actually gets made.
Beats
  • The limits are written along the shelf edge: never fewer than one unopened pack of the current size, never more than two packs of any one size.
  • Explain that the buying decision gets made either standing at this shelf or standing in a shop aisle, so the number lives on the thing your hand is on when you pull a pack.
  • The shelf is counted against the written limits on camera and shown holding.
  • Tie it back to the cold open: the limit is what stops the next half-price offer from becoming six cartons.
Shots
  • Close on the minimum and maximum being written along the shelf edge
  • Three-quarter of the shelf with the edge markings and the packs together in frame
  • Overhead count of packs against the written maximum
On-screen text
  • Min 1 unopened
  • Max 2 per size
  • The shelf tells you
Short cut · 30–45s A minimum and a maximum written straight onto a shelf edge, directly under the diapers those numbers govern.
Stands alone: Give both numbers and say they override any sale price, since overriding the price is the entire function of the limit.
Sustain The last diaper out of an open pack moves the reserve forward and writes the shopping list, in one motion.
Beats
  • The last diaper comes out of an open pack.
  • The reserve pack slides forward to the front and the size goes onto the shopping list in the same motion, filmed as one continuous action.
  • Explain that joining the two actions is what stops the shelf running to empty without warning.
  • Close on the finished shelf matching the numbers written on its edge.
Shots
  • Close focus on the last diaper leaving an open pack
  • Close on the reserve pack sliding forward to the shelf front
  • Close on the size being added to the shopping list
  • Three-quarter of the finished shelf against the edge markings
On-screen text
  • Trigger: last diaper out
  • Move it forward, write it down
Short cut · 30–45s The last diaper comes out of the pack and the reserve behind it slides forward in the same movement.
Stands alone: State the trigger and both halves of the action, because the shopping list half is the one people drop.
Close

Hold the finished shelf: one unopened pack of the current size at the front, no more than two of the next size behind it, sizes readable from the doorway, creams and thermometer in a lidded box, and nothing at all on the shelf above the crib. Give the standard as the rule, one size ahead, two packs deep, and nothing heavy stored above the crib. Name the trigger as the last diaper coming out of an open pack, and point to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt.

Next: Next, the books and quiet play ledge, and the beautiful paper-paged books you bought for yourself.

Shot list
  • Doorway-height wide for the readability test, shot before and after the sizes are written
  • Locked overhead over the floor for the full pack spread
  • Close focus setup on the same tripod for printed sizes, carton undersides and cream dates
  • Three-quarter of the shelf above the crib with the crib in frame, weight on and then off
  • Close on the marker writing sizes on the pack ends
  • Close on the lidded box for creams, gel and thermometer
  • Close on the shelf edge minimum and maximum being written
  • Close on the last diaper leaving an open pack
Description hook

A half-price bulk buy turns into six cartons the moment your baby skips a size, so the backstock shelf runs on a limit instead of an offer. This is the full 6S reset, sizes readable from the doorway and nothing heavy stored above the crib.

6Sdiaper storagenursery organizationbackstockhome organizationchild safety6S Successmicro zone
MZ-057 · R10.06

Books and Quiet Play Zone

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Twelve Covers. One Basket.”

Nursery Book Ledge: Twelve Covers Out, One Basket at the Rim

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a gorgeous paper-paged picture book sitting on the low ledge among the board books. Name the decision: you bought it because you wanted to read it aloud, and within a week of it being in reach your baby will chew it into pulp. A hand lifts it off the ledge. Say that the split coming in this video is not the same as giving the book up, and that refusing to make the split leaves you with neither a usable ledge nor an intact book.

Sort Get down to your baby's eye level and pick up everything in reach, then cut the number hard.
Beats
  • The camera sits on the floor at a baby's eye height, and hands pick up every book and toy that is genuinely within reach from there.
  • Board books stay. Paper-page books, torn spines and loose stitched eyes come out and are held up as they go.
  • A battery flap that will not screw shut is tested on camera, and the beat explains that the toy leaves or goes high until it can be fixed.
  • The beautiful books move to a shelf in your room, resolving the cold open call, because the low ledge holds only what your baby can handle unsupervised.
Shots
  • Floor-level wide at a baby's eye height across the ledge and basket
  • Close on hands separating board books from paper-page books
  • Close focus on a loose stitched eye and a battery flap that will not close
  • Close on the beautiful books being set on a higher shelf in another room
On-screen text
  • Sit at their eye level
  • Board books stay
  • Paper goes up
Short cut · 30–45s Camera on the floor at baby eye height along a book ledge, hands pulling out everything that will not survive a mouth.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that the ledge holds only what a baby can handle unsupervised, since that one rule explains every removal in the clip.
Straighten Covers face out because a pre-reader chooses by picture, and the basket rim is the limit.
Beats
  • Every book is turned cover out along the ledge and the count is taken to twelve on camera.
  • Explain that a pre-reader cannot read a spine, so a spine-out shelf is a shelf they cannot use.
  • The soft toy basket is filled to its rim and stopped there, with a hand levelling across the top and everything above the line lifted out.
  • The overflow goes into the rotation box in the closet.
Shots
  • Overhead of the ledge with spines out, then the same ledge with covers out
  • Close on hands counting twelve books along the ledge
  • Three-quarter of the basket filled level with its rim, a hand levelling across the top
  • Close on the overflow going into the rotation box in the closet
On-screen text
  • Covers out, not spines
  • Fill to the rim, stop
  • Overflow goes to rotation
Short cut · 30–45s A hand levels flat across the top of a nursery toy basket and everything standing above the rim comes out.
Stands alone: Name the rim as the hard limit and say the overflow goes to a rotation box, or the removal looks arbitrary.
Shine Chewed corners and drool are essentially the whole cleaning job in this zone.
Beats
  • The board book covers and the ledge itself are wiped down.
  • Explain that cleaning here is mostly saliva, which is why it is frequent and quick rather than deep.
  • Soft toys go through a monthly wash, and tags, seams and stitched eyes are checked on each one as it comes out of the machine.
  • The checked toys go back into the basket, still level with the rim.
Shots
  • Close focus on a chewed board book corner being wiped
  • Close on a cloth running the length of the ledge
  • Close on a soft toy out of the machine with seams and eyes being checked
  • Overhead of the basket refilled level to the rim
On-screen text
  • Wipe covers and ledge
  • Check seams out of the wash
Short cut · 30–45s A soft toy comes out of the wash and every seam, tag and stitched eye gets checked before it is allowed back in the basket.
Stands alone: Say this is the monthly wash for the nursery quiet play basket, so the inspection reads as a routine step and not a scare.
Safety The ledge becomes the nearest handhold the day your baby pulls to standing, and small parts sit at floor level.
Beats
  • Frame it as fall, cut, or crush. A hand pulls on the unfixed ledge and it moves visibly.
  • The ledge is bolted to the wall and the identical pull is repeated, with nothing moving this time.
  • Frame the second hazard as poison, choke, or strangle. Every light-up or musical toy is checked for a battery compartment that needs a screwdriver, one screwed shut and one loose shown side by side.
  • Anything with a loose button battery or a ribbon tag long enough to wind around a wrist is removed, shown item by item.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a hand pulling the unfixed ledge, then the same pull after bolting
  • Close on the bracket and screws going into the wall
  • Close focus on a battery flap being tested, one screwed shut and one loose
  • Close focus on a long ribbon tag being cut from a toy
On-screen text
  • Bolt it to the wall
  • Screwed flap only
  • Cut the long tags
Short cut · 45–60s A hand pulls on a low nursery book ledge and it rocks, then the same pull after a bracket goes into the wall.
Stands alone: Name Safety as the fourth S and say that this ledge is the handhold a baby pulls up on, which is why bolting it is not optional.
Standardize Twelve covers and one full basket is the whole standard, and a new arrival costs something the same day.
Beats
  • The standard is stated visually: twelve covers along the ledge, one basket level with its rim.
  • A new book arrives and, in the same shot, something goes into the rotation box.
  • Explain that same day is the part that holds, and that same month lets the number drift.
  • The clear stretch of floor big enough for an adult to lie down on is shown, and the beat explains that the floor is part of the standard rather than a bonus.
Shots
  • Overhead of the finished ledge and basket together
  • Close on a new arrival going onto the ledge as another book goes into the rotation box
  • Wide three-quarter of the clear floor stretch beside the ledge
On-screen text
  • 12 covers, 1 basket
  • One in, one out, same day
  • Keep the floor clear
Short cut · 30–45s A ledge holds twelve board books cover out, and when a new one arrives another goes into the rotation box in the same motion.
Stands alone: Give the twelve and the one basket up front, because one in one out only holds when the limit is known.
Sustain The bedtime lamp is the trigger, and it refreshes the ledge without any new spending.
Beats
  • The lamp goes off after the bedtime story, then the books are stood back cover out along the ledge.
  • Two books come off the ledge and two come out of the rotation box, filmed as one continuous trade.
  • Explain that rotation is what makes a small set feel new, which is why the number can stay at twelve.
  • Close on the finished zone at rest.
Shots
  • Close on a hand at the lamp switch, the room going warm and low
  • Close on books stood back cover out along the ledge
  • Close on two books traded with the rotation box
  • Overhead of the finished ledge, basket and clear floor
On-screen text
  • Trigger: lamp off after the story
  • Swap two, every night
Short cut · 30–45s A nursery lamp goes off after the bedtime story, and two books trade places with a box from the closet.
Stands alone: State the trigger and the swap count, and establish that a rotation box of spare books exists in the closet.
Close

Hold the finished zone: twelve board books standing cover out on the ledge, one basket of soft toys level with the rim, the rest boxed in the closet as rotation stock, and a clear stretch of floor an adult could lie down on. Give the standard as the rule, twelve covers facing out and one basket at the rim with everything else waiting in the rotation box. Name the trigger as switching the lamp off after the bedtime story, and close on the book's line: you do not finish 6S, you keep it.

Next: That closes the nursery. Next room, the kids bedroom, where the floor is the zone and the owner has opinions.

Shot list
  • Floor-level wide at baby eye height, the anchor angle for the whole video
  • Locked overhead over the ledge and basket for before and after and the covers-out comparison
  • Close focus setup on the same tripod for chewed corners, battery flaps, stitched eyes and ribbon tags
  • Three-quarter for the ledge pull test, before and after bolting
  • Close on the wall bracket install
  • Close on the rotation box in the closet, opened and used twice
  • Close on the lamp switch and the room going low and warm
  • Wide three-quarter of the clear floor stretch
Description hook

A book ledge a baby can actually use holds twelve covers facing out and nothing they cannot handle unsupervised. This is the full 6S reset, including where the beautiful paper-paged books go instead.

6Snursery bookshelftoy rotationbaby play spacehome organizationfurniture anchoring6S Successmicro zone

Room 11 of 20

Primary Bathroom

7 videos · 42 Shorts
Production noteSmallest room in the series and the hardest to shoot headless, because a mirror faces almost every angle. Scout the tripod position first with the camera running and check the mirror, the shower glass, the chrome faucet, and the tap spout for reflections of the operator, then mask or reposition before a single take. Best light is a single window mid morning with the overhead off; if the room is windowless, bounce one soft source off the ceiling so the mirror does not throw a hotspot. Overhead work needs a low tripod with a side arm over the counter, the drawer, or the open cabinet, with the camera dressed in a lens cloth so a bare hand never enters frame while adjusting. Shoot the shower and tub with the lens protected against spray and the enclosure door held open by a wedge rather than a hand. Real chemistry on set means real rules: only ever open one cleaning product per take, never film bleach and bowl cleaner within reach of each other even as a prop, keep the extractor fan on for every cleaning setup, and unplug any heat tool at the wall between takes rather than leaving it live for the shot. Medicine cabinet takes should use the household's own boxes with any patient name and prescription label covered before rolling.
MZ-058 · R11.01

Vanity Counter

5–7 min · thumbnail: “One Tray. Bare Counter.”

The Vanity Counter Reset: One Tray, Four Products

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open tight on the straightener sitting on the counter beside the basin, cord crossing the sink, because the outlet is right there. Widen to show what that one convenience has grown around it: bottles, sachets, a hair tie pile, a mirror nobody can see past. Name the decision the household keeps stepping around, that a tool used three or four times a week is being treated as a daily tool, and that this is what is costing them a clear counter.

Sort The counter earns its place only for what your hands touched today and yesterday, and everything else leaves the surface.
Beats
  • Hands lay a towel on the floor or the closed toilet lid and clear the entire counter onto it in one sweep, basin to wall, nothing left standing.
  • Explain the today-and-yesterday test as the sorting question, and show it applied object by object as items go back or go to a holding pile.
  • Show the three piles this room always produces, travel bottles, sample sachets, and the hair tie graveyard, and explain that these route to a drawer or out of the room entirely rather than back to the stone.
  • Count the survivors on camera against the ceiling of four daily products plus soap and the toothbrush holder.
Shots
  • Overhead of the loaded counter before anything moves, held long enough to read the clutter
  • Three-quarter of hands sweeping the counter onto the towel below
  • Overhead of the full towel, objects spread in one layer
  • Macro on a single sample sachet turned over in fingers, then dropped into the out pile
  • Overhead of bare stone on both sides of the basin
On-screen text
  • Touched it today?
  • Four daily products, max
  • Samples leave the room
Short cut · 45–60s Start on the sweep itself, a full bathroom counter going onto a towel in one continuous move, before any explanation lands.
Stands alone: Re-establish that this is a bathroom vanity counter and that the target state is one liftable tray, since the Short opens mid action with no room context.
Straighten The daily set gets one tray on the dominant-hand side, and the heat tool cord parks behind the basin instead of across it.
Beats
  • Hands set the tray down on the reach side and load the daily set into it, explaining that the side is chosen by which hand actually reaches, not by which side looks balanced.
  • Demonstrate the lift test, one hand under the tray, raising it clear of the counter to show the whole daily set moves as a single unit for cleaning.
  • Route the heat tool cord behind the basin on the far side from the tap and set the tool on its heat-safe rest, explaining that the cord path is a placement decision, not a tidiness one.
Shots
  • Overhead of the empty tray landing on the counter, then filling item by item
  • Three-quarter of one hand lifting the loaded tray clear of the stone
  • Close on the cord being drawn behind the basin, tap in the same frame for reference
  • Macro on the heat tool settling onto its metal rest
On-screen text
  • One tray, one hand
  • Cord behind the basin
Short cut · 30–45s Open on the one-hand lift test, the entire morning routine rising off the counter on a single tray.
Stands alone: State up front that the tray holds the daily set and that lifting it in one hand is the test the counter has to pass.
Shine Clean in order, tray, counter beneath it, faucet base, then mirror and the light switch plate.
Beats
  • Wipe the tray first with it lifted away, then the counter underneath, explaining why the order stops you cleaning around an object twice.
  • Work the base of the faucet where toothpaste dries into a crust, showing the cloth getting into the joint rather than passing over it.
  • Finish on the mirror and then the light switch plate, calling out the plate as the surface in this room nobody ever wipes and the one that shows it.
  • Explain cleaning to inspect here, that wiping the faucet base is also how you notice a drip or a loose escutcheon.
Shots
  • Overhead of the tray lifted off, counter shown mid wipe with the clean line visible
  • Macro on the faucet base, dried toothpaste before and clean joint after
  • Three-quarter of the mirror being worked, camera angled off axis so no reflection of the rig
  • Macro on the light switch plate, cloth passing over it
On-screen text
  • Tray, counter, faucet
  • Nobody wipes the switch plate
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on the crust at the base of the faucet, then the cloth going into the joint and the joint coming up clean.
Stands alone: Name the faucet base and the switch plate as the two surfaces that get skipped, so the Short teaches a rule rather than showing a wipe.
Safety Water and electricity share one small surface here, so the cord stays clear of the basin and the plug comes out at the wall the moment the tool goes down.
Beats
  • Show the hazard plainly, a plugged-in heat tool within cord reach of a full basin, then show the correction, unplugged at the wall with water standing in the bowl.
  • Explain the timing rule, that the plug comes out when you set the tool down, not once your hair is finished, because the gap between those two moments is the whole risk.
  • Cover the burn hazard, a hot iron cooling on a towel or a cosmetic bag, and give it the metal or ceramic rest it returns to in the same spot every time.
  • Move glass bottles from the counter edge to the back row against the mirror, or show decanting into something that does not shatter on tile.
Shots
  • Close on the cord lying between tap and basin, then the same frame with it rerouted
  • Macro on a hand pulling the plug at the wall socket
  • Three-quarter of the hot tool being set on its rest instead of on fabric
  • Overhead of glass bottles moving from the front edge to the back row
On-screen text
  • Water and electricity
  • Unplug when you set it down
  • Glass goes to the back row
Short cut · 30–45s Hold on a live cord draped across a full basin, then a hand pulling the plug at the wall, with no other action in the frame.
Stands alone: Say that this is a bathroom counter where a heat tool and a basin share one surface, and give the set-it-down-unplug-it rule in full.
Standardize The four-product limit gets written down and the cleared counter gets photographed, so a fifth bottle has something to argue with.
Beats
  • Hands write the four-product limit on a strip of tape and stick it to the underside of the tray, explaining that a written limit is the best way you know today, written down.
  • Take the ideal-state photo of the cleared counter, print or tape it inside the vanity door, and show it in place with the door open.
  • Demonstrate the standard working, a fifth bottle arriving at the counter and being held against the taped limit before it lands.
Shots
  • Macro on the pen writing the limit on tape
  • Close on the tape being pressed to the underside of the tray, tray then flipped upright
  • Three-quarter of the vanity door swinging open with the photo taped inside
  • Overhead of a new bottle hovering over the counter beside the photo
On-screen text
  • Write the limit down
  • Photo inside the door
Short cut · 30–45s Open on the photo of the finished counter taped inside the vanity door, then the real counter matching it exactly.
Stands alone: Explain that the photo is the standard for this counter and where it is taped, since the door interior alone reads as ambiguous.
Sustain The trigger is the nightly toothbrush rinse, and the tray goes back to match the photo before the light goes off.
Beats
  • Show the trigger as it already happens, the toothbrush going under the tap at night, then hands resetting the tray in the same standing position.
  • Explain why the trigger is attached to something the house already does rather than to a reminder, and that the photo is what tells you when the reset is finished.
  • Show the counter at the end of the reset next to the photo, matching, with the light going off.
Shots
  • Close on a toothbrush under running water
  • Overhead of two or three items returning to the tray, seconds of work
  • Three-quarter of counter and taped photo in the same frame
  • Wide low angle of the dark room with the counter bare
On-screen text
  • Same moment, every night
  • Match the photo
Short cut · 30–45s Toothbrush under the tap, then a ten second counter reset that happens without anyone deciding to do it.
Stands alone: Name the toothbrush rinse as the trigger and the taped photo as the finish line, both of which the parent video established.
Close

Hold the finished counter beside the taped photo while stating the standard in full, that the counter carries one liftable tray and nothing beside it and anything used less than daily lives behind a door, then show the trigger once more as the toothbrush is rinsed and the tray goes back.

Next: The bottles that left the counter went into a drawer, and the drawer is where the dates are hiding, so the vanity drawers are next.

Shot list
  • Overhead counter setup on a side arm, before state, after state, and every tray sequence
  • Three-quarter tripod at basin height for sweeps, cord routing, and the tray lift
  • Macro on the faucet base, the light switch plate, and the tape being written
  • Close on the wall socket for the plug pull
  • Overhead of the towel with the full counter contents spread in one layer

MZ-059 · R11.02

Vanity Drawers

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Every Jar Gets Read”

Vanity Drawers: Sorting by Routine and Reading Every Date

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on a drawer being pulled, then a hand lifting out one expensive palette or bottle that has been used twice. Hold on it. Name the avoidance directly, that keeping it is not thrift but paying storage on a decision that already went wrong, and that this is the object skipped past on every Sort pass because binning it means admitting the money is gone. Then show the rest of the drawer it has been protecting.

Sort One drawer at a time onto a towel, and every tube, jar, and bottle gets turned over to find a date or an open-jar symbol.
Beats
  • Empty a single drawer onto a towel and explain the one-drawer-at-a-time rule, that the room stays usable and the pass actually finishes.
  • Demonstrate the turn-and-read action on several items, showing where the printed date and the open-jar symbol sit on different packaging.
  • Call the usual offenders as they surface, mascara, liquid foundation, and sunscreen, and separate them from the usual volume, dead hair ties and orphan bobby pins.
  • Show the two outbound piles forming, past-date and simply not used, and the small survivor pile that will go back.
Shots
  • Overhead of the drawer being tipped onto the towel
  • Macro on a hand rotating a bottle to find the open-jar symbol
  • Macro on a printed date on a crimped tube end
  • Overhead of the three piles resolving on the towel
  • Close on a handful of orphan bobby pins going into a bin
On-screen text
  • One drawer at a time
  • Turn it over, read it
  • Open-jar symbol
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on a thumb rotating a jar until the little open-lid symbol appears, a mark most people have never noticed on something they use daily.
Stands alone: Explain what the open-jar symbol means and where it is printed, because the Short depends entirely on the viewer reading that mark.
Straighten Divide by routine, morning, evening, and weekly, rather than by product type, and stand the long-handled things upright.
Beats
  • Lay dividers into the empty drawer and assign them out loud as morning, evening, and weekly or occasional, explaining why time of day beats product category in a drawer you reach into half awake.
  • Load each compartment from the survivor pile, narrating the routine question asked of each item rather than what kind of product it is.
  • Stand combs, brushes, and dental supplies upright in their own section, showing that upright means nothing has to be dug through to reach what is underneath.
Shots
  • Overhead of empty drawer with dividers being placed
  • Overhead of the three compartments filling one at a time
  • Close on brushes being stood upright in a section
  • Three-quarter of the drawer opening to a readable layout in one look
On-screen text
  • Morning. Evening. Weekly.
  • Upright, not stacked
Short cut · 30–45s Two drawers side by side, one sorted by product type and one sorted by time of day, with a hand finding the same item in each.
Stands alone: State the sorting principle explicitly, divide by when you use it rather than what it is, since the comparison carries no meaning without it.
Shine Lift the dividers out and tip the drawer, because loose powder, hair, and grit collect underneath where nobody looks.
Beats
  • Remove the dividers and tip the empty drawer over a bin, showing the amount of loose powder, hair, and grit that comes out.
  • Wipe the drawer bottom and then the runners, explaining that the runners are what makes a drawer feel cheap when they are gritty.
  • Wipe each divider separately before it goes back, so the clean drawer does not receive dirty inserts.
Shots
  • Overhead of dividers lifting out to reveal the grit trapped beneath
  • Three-quarter of the drawer being tipped over a bin
  • Macro on a cloth running along the drawer runner
  • Close on dividers being wiped on a towel before reinstallation
On-screen text
  • It all lives under the dividers
  • Wipe the runners
Short cut · 30–45s Dividers lift out of a drawer and the camera holds on the layer of powder and hair that was underneath the whole time.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a bathroom vanity drawer and that lifting the dividers is the step people skip, since the reveal is the entire payload.
Safety Loose blades in a drawer you reach into blind will find a fingertip, and low drawers hold liquids and pills a child can pull open.
Beats
  • Show the hazard as it actually appears, bare cartridges and blade refills loose among the brushes, and explain that a hand going in for a comb without looking meets the blade first.
  • Correct it two ways, cap every blade, or give all razors one lidded box in a fixed corner you never grope past, and show the box going into that corner.
  • Address the low drawer, polish remover, small scissors, and loose vitamins within reach of a child who can pull a drawer open, and show the fix, move liquids and pills to an upper drawer or fit a catch.
Shots
  • Macro on a bare blade cartridge sitting among brush bristles
  • Close on caps going onto blades one at a time
  • Three-quarter of the lidded box being set into its fixed corner
  • Low angle at child height of a bottom drawer sliding open, hands only
  • Close on a drawer catch being fitted
On-screen text
  • Fall, cut, or crush
  • Blades get a lidded box
  • Liquids and pills go up
Short cut · 30–45s Open at child height on a bottom vanity drawer sliding open to reveal polish remover and loose vitamins at eye level.
Stands alone: Frame it as one of the five safety questions, poison, choke, or strangle, and give both fixes, move it up or fit a catch.
Standardize Each divider label carries a count, so a new item has to beat something already in the slot.
Beats
  • Write counts onto the divider labels on camera, two lipsticks in rotation, one comb, one brush, and explain that the count is what makes the right state obvious at a glance.
  • Show the rule in action, a third lipstick arriving and being held against the two already in the slot until one of them leaves.
  • Explain that a standard is the best way you know today, written down, and that the count can change later as long as it stays written.
Shots
  • Macro on a label being written with a count
  • Overhead of labeled dividers reading across the open drawer
  • Close on three lipsticks held over a two-slot compartment
  • Overhead of the loser leaving the drawer
On-screen text
  • Put a number on the label
  • Three has to beat two
Short cut · 30–45s A third lipstick hovering over a compartment labeled for two, and a hand deciding which of the existing two leaves.
Stands alone: State the counted-label standard first, because the Short is only a decision if the viewer knows the slot has a written limit.
Sustain Laundry day is the trigger, and the top drawer gets one look while the towels are already in your arms.
Beats
  • Show the trigger in its real form, towels being carried into the bathroom on laundry day, then the top drawer being pulled with the load still under one arm.
  • Do the pass on camera, lifting out anything empty or dried out, and show how short it is, one drawer, one look.
  • Explain that this catches a week of drift and that attaching it to a trip already being made is what keeps it happening.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of folded towels being carried in, arms only, no face
  • Overhead of the top drawer opening with one hand
  • Macro on an empty tube being squeezed and dropped in a bin
  • Overhead of the drawer closing, contents unchanged otherwise
On-screen text
  • Laundry day, top drawer
  • One drawer, one look
Short cut · 30–45s Towels under one arm, the other hand opening a drawer and pulling two dead tubes out of it before the towels are even put away.
Stands alone: Name laundry day as the trigger and the top drawer as the scope, so the Short reads as a habit rather than a tidy-up.
Close

Open each drawer in turn on camera to show the standard holding, divided by routine, every category carrying a written count on its label, nothing past its date, and then show the laundry day trigger once, towels in one arm, top drawer in the other hand.

Next: Everything that left these drawers in bulk went below the basin, and that cabinet is hiding something more expensive than clutter.

Shot list
  • Overhead side arm above the open drawer for every empty, divide, and reload sequence
  • Macro rig for dates, open-jar symbols, blades, and labels
  • Three-quarter tripod at drawer height for tipping and wiping
  • Low child-height angle for the bottom drawer hazard sequence
  • Overhead of the towel with one drawer's contents spread out
  • Close on the wall or drawer front for the catch fitting
  • Three-quarter of towels being carried in for the trigger beat, arms only
  • Overhead of all drawers open in sequence for the closing standard

Every jar in a vanity drawer has a date on it, and the drawer is sorted by the wrong thing. Here is the full 6S pass, including the palette you have been skipping past.

MZ-060 · R11.03

Under-Sink Cabinet

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Keep the Trap Visible”

Under the Sink: Storage That Never Hides a Leak

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the cabinet doors swinging wide to a wall of product, then push in to where the P-trap should be and find paper towels stacked in front of it. State the arithmetic being avoided, that a joint which weeps unnoticed for months turns a cheap washer into a rotted cabinet base and a floor that has to come up. This cabinet is the only storage in the room, which is exactly why it has been packed wall to wall.

Sort Everything comes out and lines up by job, and the duplicates and the unidentifiable bottle reveal themselves.
Beats
  • Empty the cabinet completely onto the floor and line the contents up by job, glass, tub and tile, toilet, drain, polish, explaining that sorting by job is what exposes duplication.
  • Show the result this room always produces, three half-full bottles of the same thing standing together in one job line.
  • Handle the bottle nobody can identify, no readable label, unclear contents, and explain plainly that it goes, because an unidentified chemical is not stock.
  • Separate paper goods and bulk toiletries from the chemistry, since they are going to be treated differently in the next pass.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the cabinet doors opening on the full state
  • Overhead of the floor with contents lining up in job columns
  • Close on three matching half-full bottles standing side by side
  • Macro on a faded or missing label being turned in the hand
  • Overhead of the empty cabinet interior, pipework finally visible
On-screen text
  • Line it up by job
  • Three of the same thing
  • Cannot identify it? It goes.
Short cut · 30–45s A cabinet emptied onto the floor and the products lining up by job, with three identical half-full bottles landing in the same column.
Stands alone: Say this is the under-sink cabinet and that the sorting rule is by job rather than by brand, which is what makes the duplicates visible.
Straighten Build the bins around the P-trap rather than fighting it, and keep the joint and both shut-off valves in the sightline.
Beats
  • Point out the P-trap and both shut-off valves in the empty cabinet, establishing them as the fixed features everything else works around.
  • Fit two pull-out bins clear of the trap, showing them sliding without touching the pipework, and explain that building around the plumbing is the whole design decision here.
  • Load paper goods and bulk toiletries on the side with headroom, and place sprays at the front where a label reads without kneeling.
  • Set the pale tray on the cabinet floor and leave it empty, explaining that a pale surface is what makes a drip visible early.
Shots
  • Three-quarter into the empty cabinet with the trap and valves in frame
  • Close on a bin sliding out past the trap without contact
  • Overhead through the open doors of both bins in position
  • Macro on the pale tray being set on the cabinet floor
  • Three-quarter of the doors open with valves and trap still clearly visible
On-screen text
  • Build around the trap
  • Valves stay in sight
  • Nothing on the tray
Short cut · 30–45s A bin sliding out from under a sink and passing clean around the P-trap, with the joint staying visible the whole time.
Stands alone: Identify the P-trap and the shut-off valves by name and say why they must stay visible, since the Short is otherwise just a bin moving.
Shine Clean to inspect, because the cabinet floor is where a slow leak shows itself before it ever looks like water.
Beats
  • Wipe the cabinet floor and then look hard at it, explaining what to look for, a dark ring or a soft patch in the board, which is what a slow leak looks like before it looks like water.
  • Press the board with fingertips to test for softness on camera, showing the difference between a stain and a spongy patch.
  • Wipe the neck of every bottle before it goes back, explaining that this is what keeps the pale tray from turning sticky and unreadable.
  • Tie the pass back to the principle, that cleaning here is an inspection with a cloth in your hand.
Shots
  • Overhead through the doors of the cabinet floor being wiped
  • Macro on a dark ring in the board under a low raking light
  • Close on fingertips pressing the board to test for softness
  • Macro on a bottle neck being wiped clean before it returns
On-screen text
  • Clean to inspect
  • Dark ring or soft patch
  • Wipe every bottle neck
Short cut · 30–45s Fingertips pressing a cabinet floor and finding a soft patch in the board, the shape a leak takes before it ever looks wet.
Stands alone: Explain that this is the base of an under-sink cabinet and that a soft board means a slow leak, since the visual alone reads as nothing.
Safety This cabinet holds the harshest chemistry in the house at toddler height, and two of these products must never meet.
Beats
  • State the two absolute rules plainly, never store bleach where it can tip into an ammonia-based cleaner, and never decant anything into a drink bottle, and show a drink bottle being removed from the cabinet as the example.
  • Show the separation being built, the two products physically placed so a tip cannot land one into the other.
  • Address the height, filming at a crawling child's eye level to show bleach, drain opener, and bowl cleaner behind one unlatched door, then fit a magnetic catch or move the chemistry above the sink line.
  • Handle the crush hazard, a heavy bulk jug stacked on a pull-out bin ready to come down on your hand, and move heavy goods to the cabinet floor beside the tray.
  • Cover the water and electricity question, a drip at the trap creeping toward a socket or a plugged-in nightlight behind the cabinet, framed as find it, and fix it now.
Shots
  • Low angle at crawling height of the cabinet door opening
  • Close on a drink bottle being lifted out and set aside
  • Three-quarter of a magnetic catch being fitted to the door
  • Close on a heavy jug moving from atop a bin down to the cabinet floor
  • Macro on the trap joint with a socket visible on the wall beyond
On-screen text
  • Poison, choke, or strangle
  • Never into a drink bottle
  • “Find it, and fix it now.”
Short cut · 45–60s Camera on the floor at crawling height as a cabinet door swings open onto drain opener and bowl cleaner at eye level.
Stands alone: Name the hazard as poison, choke, or strangle, and give both remedies, a magnetic catch or moving the chemistry above the sink line.
Standardize One open container per job, backstock capped at two, and bins labeled by job rather than by brand.
Beats
  • Write bin labels by job, glass, tub and tile, toilet, and explain why labeling by job rather than brand stops bowl cleaner quietly ending up among the glass sprays.
  • Apply the one-open-per-job rule on camera, consolidating or removing the second open bottle in a job line.
  • Set the backstock cap at two and show what exceeds it leaving the room rather than being squeezed in.
  • Restate the sightline standard as part of the written standard, that the trap joint and both valves stay visible whenever the doors are open.
Shots
  • Macro on a label being written with a job name
  • Close on the label going onto the front edge of a bin
  • Overhead of a job column reduced to one open bottle plus backstock
  • Three-quarter of the finished cabinet, doors open, trap and valves in clear view
On-screen text
  • Label the job, not the brand
  • One open per job
  • Backstock capped at two
Short cut · 30–45s Two bins side by side, one labeled with a brand name and one labeled with a job, and a hand reaching correctly first time for only one of them.
Stands alone: State the label-by-job rule outright and give the one-open-per-job cap, since the comparison is the whole lesson.
Sustain The hand soap refill is the trigger, and the entire leak check is a low look before the doors close.
Beats
  • Show the trigger as it already happens, the hand soap at the basin being refilled from the bottle stored below.
  • Drop to a low look over the cabinet floor and the trap joint, and state that this is the entire leak check, nothing more.
  • Close the doors and explain why attaching the check to a refill already being made is what stops it becoming a chore that gets skipped.
Shots
  • Close on hand soap being topped up at the basin, hands only
  • Low three-quarter from a crouch height, cabinet floor and trap joint in frame, no body shown
  • Macro on the trap joint, dry and clean
  • Three-quarter of the doors closing on the finished cabinet
On-screen text
  • Refill the soap, check the trap
  • That is the whole check
Short cut · 30–45s A hand soap bottle topped up, then a low look along the cabinet floor and the pipe joint before the doors shut.
Stands alone: Say the refill is the trigger and that the look at the trap joint and cabinet floor is the complete check, so it does not read as an incomplete inspection.
Close

Swing the doors open on the finished cabinet and state the standard against what is in frame, the P-trap and both shut-off valves in plain sight, one open bottle per job, backstock capped at two, then run the trigger, a soap refill followed by a low look along the cabinet floor.

Next: The medicines that came out of this cabinet do not belong down here at all, and the cabinet they do belong in needs a session with the small print.

  • Close on bin runners and the pale tray at cabinet floor level

  • Three-quarter of the magnetic catch being fitted to the door frame
Description hook

The cabinet under the bathroom sink is usually packed to the wall, which means the pipe joint is buried. Here is how to store everything you need and still see a leak on day one.

6Sunder sink storagebathroom organizationleak checkhome safetycleaning supplies6S Success Home Editionmicro zone
MZ-061 · R11.04

Medicine Cabinet or Wall Storage

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Take It Back Today”

The Medicine Cabinet: In Date, Labeled, Actually Needed

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a hand lifting a half-course of antibiotics or a bottle of strong painkillers from a procedure two years ago out of the cabinet. Hold on the label. Name what is being avoided, that it is kept because it might come in useful and because handing it back feels like waste, and state the reality plainly, that leftover painkillers sitting behind a mirror are the most likely thing in this room to seriously hurt a visitor.

Sort Read every label and every date, and route expired, unlabeled, and no longer needed medicine into a take-back bag.
Beats
  • Clear the cabinet shelf by shelf and read every label and every date on camera, including the small print on boxes kept because the box was still good.
  • Show the three disqualifiers being applied one item at a time, expired, unlabeled, and prescribed for a condition nobody here has now.
  • Show the take-back bag filling and state where it goes, a pharmacy take-back, and that nothing goes down the toilet.
  • Set the survivors aside as the only stock that will be reloaded.
Shots
  • Overhead of a shelf's contents laid out on a towel
  • Macro on a printed expiry date on a blister foil
  • Macro on a prescription label with the patient name masked
  • Close on boxes going into the take-back bag one by one
  • Three-quarter of the empty cabinet with shelves bare
On-screen text
  • Read every date
  • Expired. Unlabeled. Not needed.
  • Pharmacy take-back, never the toilet
Short cut · 45–60s Macro on the small print of a box someone kept because the box still looked fine, with the date landing well in the past.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a medicine cabinet Sort and name the three disqualifiers, since the Short turns on the rule rather than the single box.
Straighten Group by the reason you come to this cabinet, and put the two-in-the-morning items where you can find them without the light on.
Beats
  • Sort the survivors into groups by reason rather than by brand or by box size, headache, stomach, cut, cold, eyes.
  • Load the groups into three bins, pain relief, stomach and cold, first aid, and show the first aid bin being lifted one-handed to prove it can be carried to whoever is bleeding.
  • Place the two things you reach for at two in the morning on the shelf you can find without turning the light on, and demonstrate that reach in low light.
Shots
  • Overhead of survivors grouping into reason piles on a towel
  • Close on three bins being loaded through the open cabinet
  • Three-quarter of the first aid bin lifted out with one hand
  • Low-light close on a hand finding the front shelf item without looking
On-screen text
  • Group by the reason you came
  • First aid lifts one-handed
Short cut · 30–45s A first aid bin lifted out of a cabinet with one hand and carried away, the test that decides how big it is allowed to be.
Stands alone: Say the bin has to be carryable one-handed to whoever is bleeding, which is the reason for the size limit.
Shine Shelves come out and get washed, and they go back completely dry, because a damp shelf is what turns tablets chalky.
Beats
  • Take the shelves out and wash off the sticky rings left by cough syrup and the dust of old blister foil.
  • Dry them all the way through before they go back and explain the reason specific to this room, that a damp shelf turns tablets chalky in here.
  • Wipe the cabinet body and the mirror door hinge line while the shelves dry.
Shots
  • Macro on a sticky syrup ring on a glass shelf
  • Three-quarter of shelves being lifted out of the cabinet body
  • Close on shelves being dried on a towel, both faces
  • Macro on blister foil dust in a shelf corner being wiped out
On-screen text
  • Shelves come out
  • Dry all the way through
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on the sticky ring a cough syrup bottle has left welded to a glass shelf, then the shelf coming out of the cabinet entirely.
Stands alone: Note that the shelf has to go back fully dry because damp turns tablets chalky, which is the point the Short exists to make.
Safety Bathroom humidity breaks tablets down, this cabinet must stay above real child reach, and nothing ever goes down the toilet.
Beats
  • Explain that bathroom humidity breaks tablets and capsules down faster than a bedroom shelf does, and move anything taken daily out of this room entirely, showing it leave.
  • Measure child reach the honest way, from the height of the closed toilet lid a child can climb onto rather than from the floor, shown as a hand rising into frame to that height with the closed lid in shot below as the reference.
  • Fit a child-secure catch to whatever stays, and show it engaging.
  • Move a glass peroxide bottle or a heavy first aid tin down from the top shelf above a hard basin, since heavy and breakable belongs at eye level, not overhead.
Shots
  • Close on a hand carrying daily medication out through the bathroom doorway
  • Three-quarter of a hand and forearm rising into frame to the reach height, the closed toilet lid in shot below as the climb reference, no body shown
  • Macro on a child-secure catch engaging on the cabinet door
  • Close on a glass bottle moving from top shelf down to eye level
On-screen text
  • Measure from what they can climb
  • Daily medicine leaves the bathroom
  • Heavy and breakable at eye level
Short cut · 30–45s A hand rising to the height of a closed toilet lid and landing easily on the cabinet shelf everyone assumed was out of reach.
Stands alone: State the rule that reach is measured from what a child can climb onto, not from the floor, because the shot is meaningless without it.
Standardize Bins are labeled by symptom rather than brand, and the first aid bin holds a fixed kit that never becomes a home for spare vitamins.
Beats
  • Write bin labels by symptom and explain the test, that a guest or a sitter should find what they need without asking which box the cold tablets are in.
  • Lay out the fixed first aid contents on camera, plasters, tape, gauze, and one pair of scissors, and load them.
  • Show the drift being refused, spare vitamins being offered to the first aid bin and going elsewhere instead.
  • Restate the standard as the best way you know today, written down, and put the labels where they read from outside the closed door.
Shots
  • Macro on symptom labels being written
  • Overhead of the fixed first aid contents laid out before loading
  • Close on a vitamin bottle being turned away from the first aid bin
  • Three-quarter of the cabinet open with all three labels readable
On-screen text
  • Label by symptom
  • Plasters, tape, gauze, scissors
  • Not a vitamin drawer
Short cut · 30–45s Three labeled bins in a medicine cabinet and a hand going straight to the right one without hesitating or reading a brand name.
Stands alone: Give the sitter test in full, that someone who does not live here should find it without asking, since that is what justifies symptom labels.
Sustain The pharmacy trip is the trigger, and the new box does not go in until the dates in that bin have been read.
Beats
  • Show the trigger as it already happens, a pharmacy bag coming through the bathroom door and being set down.
  • Put the new box into its bin and read the dates of everything already in that bin before the door shuts, showing the read happen rather than describing it.
  • Show the take-back bag being placed where it will ride back on the next trip, closing the loop without a reminder or an app.
Shots
  • Close on a pharmacy bag being set on the counter, hands only
  • Overhead of one bin lifted out and its contents date-checked
  • Macro on a date being read on an item already in stock
  • Three-quarter of the take-back bag hung ready by the door
On-screen text
  • New box in, dates read
  • Take-back bag rides back
Short cut · 30–45s A pharmacy bag lands on the counter and the new box is held back while every date already in that bin gets read first.
Stands alone: Name the pharmacy trip as the trigger and the one-bin scope, so the Short does not read as a full cabinet clear-out.
Close

Open the finished cabinet and state the standard against what is visible, only in-date, correctly labeled, currently needed medicine, grouped by symptom and kept above child reach, then show the trigger, a pharmacy bag arriving, a box going in, and the dates in that bin being read before the door closes.

Next: The room's other daily surface is the one you stand in wet with your eyes half shut, so the shower and tub are next.

Shot list
  • Three-quarter tripod square to the open cabinet, framed off the mirror axis
  • Macro rig for expiry dates, prescription labels with names masked, and blister foil
  • Overhead of the towel with one shelf's contents laid out
  • Reach-height three-quarter for the climb-and-reach hazard beat, forearms only
  • Close on the child-secure catch fitting and engaging
  • Close on shelves out of the cabinet being washed and dried
  • Overhead of the fixed first aid kit contents before loading
  • Close at counter height for the pharmacy bag trigger
Description hook

Most medicine cabinets hold at least one thing that should have gone back to the pharmacy years ago. This is the full 6S pass, including the leftover prescription nobody wants to hand over.

MZ-062 · R11.05

Shower or Tub

5–7 min · thumbnail: “In Use or It Leaves”

Shower and Tub: Four Bottles, One Squeegee, Real Grip

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a hand shifting eight bottles along a shower shelf to clean the space behind them, then hold on the ring the caddy has grown and the four or five bottles nobody uses. Name the reason they stay, some cost too much to admit, some were gifts, and some hold an inch that cannot be poured away, and name what that costs, a caddy that never dries out.

Sort Every bottle comes out to the tub edge and gets shaken, and anything not used in the last two weeks of showers leaves the enclosure.
Beats
  • Line every bottle along the tub edge and shake each one, showing how much is actually left and how many are near empty.
  • Apply the in-use test on camera, touched in the last two weeks of showers or it leaves, and show the bottles that fail going into a bag.
  • Handle the hotel bottles and the conditioner that did nothing as a group, since they leave without a separate decision.
  • Show the nearly-empty ones being set aside to be finished this week or poured together.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of bottles lining up along the tub edge
  • Close on a hand shaking a bottle, weight audible in frame
  • Macro on an inch of product in a clear bottle held to the light
  • Overhead of the survivor group, four bottles and a bar
On-screen text
  • Line them up, shake them
  • Two weeks of showers
  • Gifts get no exemption
Short cut · 30–45s Every bottle out of a shower and lined along the tub edge, then each one shaken in turn to reveal how little is in most of them.
Stands alone: Give the in-use test explicitly, touched in the last two weeks of showers, since the line-up alone does not carry a decision rule.
Straighten Each person gets their own shelf or corner rather than one mixed crowd, and the squeegee hangs where a wet hand meets it.
Beats
  • Assign each person a shelf or a corner of the caddy and load them separately, explaining why one mixed crowd is what makes people shift bottles instead of reaching.
  • Hang the squeegee inside the enclosure where a wet hand meets it without leaning out over the tub wall, and demonstrate that reach.
  • Show the cap-down rule and its limit, cap-down only if the bottle truly seals, otherwise it rings the shelf, with the ring shown.
Shots
  • Overhead into the caddy showing separated per-person sections
  • Three-quarter of a hand reaching the squeegee hook from inside the enclosure
  • Macro on a ring left under a cap-down bottle
  • Close on the finished caddy, four bottles and a bar, spacing visible
On-screen text
  • One shelf each
  • Squeegee within wet reach
Short cut · 30–45s A wet hand reaching for a squeegee without leaning out over the tub wall, and the same reach failing from the hook someone would normally choose.
Stands alone: State that the hook goes inside the enclosure within reach of a wet hand, which is the placement rule the two reaches are demonstrating.
Shine Spray, leave the room to work another zone, come back and wipe, then squeegee from the top down and leave the door open.
Beats
  • Spray the walls and the tray, then step out, explaining that chemistry needs time rather than scrubbing and that this is where the counter or the toilet gets done instead of waiting.
  • Return, wipe, and rinse, then squeegee glass and tile from the top down, showing why top down means you never re-wet a finished surface.
  • Work the dark line where the wall meets the tray specifically, since that is the join this zone is judged on.
  • Leave the door standing open and the fan running as the last action of the pass.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of walls being sprayed, lens shielded
  • Macro on the wall-to-tray join, dark line before and clean after
  • Close on the squeegee working top down on glass
  • Three-quarter of the enclosure door propped open, fan audible
On-screen text
  • Spray, then leave it
  • Top down, always
  • Door open, fan on
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on the dark line where the shower wall meets the tray, then the same join clean, with the squeegee pass that got it there.
Stands alone: Explain that the cleaner was sprayed and left to work while another zone got done, otherwise the Short implies scrubbing did it.
Safety Wet glaze under soap film is the most slippery surface in the house, so grip is not optional and razors go high.
Beats
  • Show the hazard as a surface rather than a stumble, the wet glaze under a film of soap where a foot lands entering the tub, kept to the wet floor itself and a hand bracing the enclosure wall.
  • Fit grip strips or set a mat with real suction, and show the suction being tested by pulling at a corner.
  • Explain that a grab bar is a morning's work to fit and show the position it belongs in, at the point you climb in, not decoratively.
  • Move the razor from the tub edge to a high hook, naming the reason, that the tub edge is exactly the height a child grabs to steady themselves.
Shots
  • Close on a hand bracing the enclosure wall at the point you climb in
  • Macro on soap film on wet glaze under a low raking light
  • Close on a mat corner being pulled to test suction
  • Three-quarter of a razor moving from tub edge to a high hook
  • Close on a grab bar position being marked where you enter the tub
On-screen text
  • Fall
  • Grip is not optional
  • Razors go high, every time
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on soap film sitting on wet glaze under a low raking light, the most slippery surface in the house shown as a surface rather than a warning.
Stands alone: Name it as the fall question and give both fixes, grip strips or a mat that truly grips, plus the grab bar where you climb in.
Standardize The caddy holds a bottle limit, and a new bottle comes in only on the day an empty goes out.
Beats
  • State and mark the caddy limit, one shampoo, one conditioner, one wash, and one bar per person, and show it written where it is visible.
  • Demonstrate the one-in-one-out rule as a physical exchange, an empty leaving the enclosure and a new bottle entering in the same motion.
  • Fix the squeegee to one hook and show it hanging wet, explaining that a standard that only works when things are dry is not a standard for a shower.
Shots
  • Overhead into the caddy at its limit
  • Close on an empty bottle out and a new bottle in, one exchange
  • Macro on the squeegee hanging wet on its single hook
  • Three-quarter of the enclosure at its finished state
On-screen text
  • One in, one out
  • Same day, same hook
Short cut · 30–45s An empty bottle leaving a shower caddy and a new one taking its exact slot in the same movement, nothing added.
Stands alone: State the caddy limit per person and the one-in-one-out day rule, so the exchange reads as a standard rather than a restock.
Sustain The last person out squeegees, props the door, and leaves the fan running, all while already wet and standing there.
Beats
  • Show the trigger at its natural moment, the last shower finishing, and the squeegee coming off its hook before anyone dries off.
  • Run the full routine on camera, glass and walls squeegeed, door propped, fan left running, and show how short it is.
  • Explain why it works, that it costs nothing extra because the person is already wet and standing in the enclosure.
Shots
  • Close on a wet hand lifting the squeegee off its hook
  • Three-quarter of glass being squeegeed from inside
  • Close on the door being propped open
  • Macro on the fan switch being left on, then a wide of the dry enclosure later
On-screen text
  • Last one out
  • Before you dry off
Short cut · 30–45s A wet hand lifting a squeegee off its hook before it reaches for a towel, and the whole routine finishing in seconds.
Stands alone: Name the trigger as whoever showers last and include the door prop and the fan, since the squeegee alone is only half the habit.
Close

Hold on the finished enclosure while stating the standard against it, one of each product in use per person, no empties in the caddy, squeegee on its hook, floor grip intact, then run the trigger, the last person out squeegeeing and propping the door before drying off.

Next: The smallest and dirtiest patch in the room is the one with a shelf on top of it, and that shelf is inside splash range.

Shot list
  • Three-quarter tripod outside the enclosure with the door wedged open, lens shielded from spray
  • Overhead into the caddy for all bottle count and layout beats
  • Macro rig on the wall-to-tray join and on soap film under a low raking light
  • Three-quarter along the tub edge for the bottle line-up and shake
  • Close on the squeegee hook for reach tests and the wet hang
  • Close on mat suction test and grab bar position marking
  • Three-quarter of the razor moving from tub edge to high hook
  • Wide of the enclosure door propped and fan running for the closing state
Description hook

A shower caddy fills with bottles nobody uses, and the shelf never dries out because of it. Here is the full 6S pass, grip strips included.
