MZ-063 · R11.06

Toilet Area

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Nothing Within Splash Range”

The Toilet Area: A Bare Cistern Lid and One Colored Cloth

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on a loaded cistern lid, a candle, a hand cream, a phone charger, a stack of reading, then hold as a flush runs beneath it. Name the decision being avoided, that the question is not whether a flush throws a fine mist across that shelf but which of your things you are willing to keep there anyway.

Sort Clear the cistern top down to the porcelain, because everything stored there has been sitting inside a flush's spray.
Beats
  • Sweep the cistern lid completely clear onto a tray or towel, down to bare porcelain, in one pass.
  • Go item by item through what came off, the candle, the spare hand cream, the charger, the reading stack, and explain that most of it does not belong in this room at all rather than merely belonging elsewhere in it.
  • Show the small survivor group forming, which is almost nothing, and set expectations that a bare lid is the correct outcome.
Shots
  • Overhead of the loaded cistern lid before anything moves
  • Three-quarter of the sweep clearing the lid to porcelain
  • Overhead of the removed items spread on a towel
  • Close on the bare cistern lid, nothing on it
On-screen text
  • Clear to the porcelain
  • Most of it leaves the room
Short cut · 30–45s A cistern lid cleared to bare porcelain in one sweep, then the pile of things that had been living inside splash range laid out on a towel.
Stands alone: Say that a flush throws a fine mist across the lid, which is the reason the sweep happens and the reason the lid stays bare.
Straighten Two reserve rolls within seated reach, the rest of the pack in the cupboard, and marked floor spots for the brush and the bin.
Beats
  • Place a holder with two reserve rolls where it is reachable from a seated position, and demonstrate that reach with a hand from seat height.
  • Carry the rest of the pack out to the linen cupboard, explaining that bulk in this zone is what makes the floor impossible to mop.
  • Mark a spot on the floor for the brush and the bin so a mop has a clean run around the pedestal, and show the mop run working.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a hand reaching a roll holder from seat height
  • Close on two rolls loading into the holder
  • Overhead of marked floor spots beside the pedestal
  • Three-quarter of a mop passing around the pedestal without obstruction
On-screen text
  • Two rolls within reach
  • The pack lives in the cupboard
  • Give the mop a clean run
Short cut · 30–45s A mop running a clean circle around a toilet pedestal because the brush and the bin have marked spots instead of floating positions.
Stands alone: Establish that outlined floor spots are a visual control and that the test is whether a mop can pass without anything being moved.
Shine Treat the bowl and leave it, then work the outside in a fixed order with one cloth in one color used for this job only.
Beats
  • Apply bowl cleaner and leave it, explaining that this is when the rest of the room gets done and that the sit time does the work.
  • Work the outside in the fixed order on camera, handle, lid, seat top, seat underside, rim, pedestal, and the floor around the base where drips land.
  • Show the cloth throughout, one cloth, one color, this job only, and show it going to its own hanging spot rather than into the general wash pile.
Shots
  • Close on cleaner going into the bowl, then the room being left
  • Three-quarter sequence following the fixed order surface by surface
  • Macro on the floor at the base of the pedestal where drips land
  • Close on the colored cloth hanging apart from all other cloths
On-screen text
  • Let the cleaner sit
  • Handle, lid, seat, rim, base
  • One cloth, one color
Short cut · 45–60s The full cleaning order run as one continuous sequence, handle through to the floor at the base, with a cloth nobody else in the house will ever pick up.
Stands alone: Say the bowl was treated first and left to sit, and that the cloth color is reserved for this job alone, both of which the order depends on.
Safety Bowl cleaner is the harshest chemistry in the house, it must never meet bleach in the same bowl, and it must not stand at floor level.
Beats
  • State the rule plainly, one product per bowl, never bowl cleaner and bleach together, and show the two products being physically stored apart rather than only being warned about.
  • Move the bowl cleaner off the floor beside the pedestal, naming why, that this is where a child stands to reach the flush, and store it high or in the under-sink cabinet behind a catch.
  • Address the water and electricity question, a phone charger run up to the cistern top, and end it, showing the cord pulled and the charger leaving the room, with a cord, a water tank, and a hard tile floor named as the combination.
Shots
  • Close on two products being separated to different storage
  • Low angle at child height beside the pedestal showing the cleaner at eye level
  • Three-quarter of the cleaner being placed high behind a catch
  • Close on a charger cord being unplugged and coiled out of the room
On-screen text
  • One product per bowl
  • Never with bleach
  • Water and electricity
Short cut · 30–45s A phone charger cord running up the wall to a cistern lid, then the plug coming out and the cord leaving the room for good.
Stands alone: Name the combination, a cord, a water tank, and a hard tile floor, and frame it as the water and electricity question.
Standardize The toilet cloth and gloves are a color no other job uses, hung apart, and two reserve rolls is the floor.
Beats
  • Show the color choice being made and applied, cloth and gloves in a color no other job in the house uses, and hang them apart from every other cloth.
  • Explain that the color is the visual control, so the right cloth is obvious at a glance and cross use becomes an active mistake rather than an accident.
  • Set two reserve rolls as the floor and show the signal, that dropping to one is the restock trigger, marked on the holder.
Shots
  • Close on colored cloth and gloves together, distinct from a neutral pile
  • Three-quarter of them hanging on their own hook, separated
  • Macro on the roll holder at two, then at one
  • Overhead of the finished zone, bare lid, marked spots, holder loaded
On-screen text
  • A color used for nothing else
  • Two rolls is the floor
Short cut · 30–45s One cloth in a color that appears nowhere else in the house, hung on its own hook away from every other cloth in the cupboard.
Stands alone: Explain that color coding here is what stops the toilet cloth being used anywhere else, since the visual alone is just a cloth.
Sustain The empty holder does the remembering, and whoever hangs the last roll carries two more in on the next trip through.
Beats
  • Show the trigger firing, the last roll going onto the holder and the pack in the cupboard being noted in the same moment.
  • Show the follow-through, two rolls carried in on the next trip through the room, not as a special journey.
  • Explain the principle, that the empty holder is doing the remembering rather than a person, which is why it keeps working.
Shots
  • Close on the last roll being hung on the holder
  • Three-quarter of two rolls being carried in under one arm on a pass-through
  • Close on the holder returning to two
  • Overhead of the finished zone at rest
On-screen text
  • Last roll on, two come in
  • The holder remembers
Short cut · 30–45s The last roll going onto the holder, then two more arriving on the next walk through the room without anyone making a trip for them.
Stands alone: State that two reserve rolls is the standard and that hanging the last one is the trigger, so the Short reads as a rule and not a coincidence.
Close

Hold on the bare cistern lid and the marked floor spots while stating the standard, the lid stays bare, the toilet cloth is a color used for nothing else, and two reserve rolls is the minimum on hand, then show the trigger, the last roll hung and two carried in on the next trip past.

Next: One thing left this room to live in a cupboard, and that cupboard has a count problem of its own.

Shot list
  • Overhead on a side arm above the cistern lid for the before, the sweep, and the bare state
  • Three-quarter tripod at seat height for the roll holder reach test
  • Low child-height angle beside the pedestal for the chemical storage hazard
  • Continuous three-quarter following the fixed cleaning order around the pedestal
  • Macro on the floor at the base of the pedestal where drips land
  • Close on the colored cloth and gloves in isolation and on their own hook
  • Overhead of marked floor spots with a mop passing through
  • Close on the roll holder at two and at one for the restock signal
Description hook

The cistern lid is the most tempting shelf in the bathroom and it sits inside the spray of every flush. This is the full 6S pass for the smallest zone in the room.

6Stoilet cleaningbathroom hygienecolor coded clothscleaning routine6S Success Home Editionmicro zone
MZ-064 · R11.07

Linen and Towel Storage

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Stop Saving the Good Ones”

Bathroom Linen: Three Towels Per Person, Ranked Honestly

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a guest set lifted out of a cupboard, still crisp, kept back for visitors who come twice a year, then cut to the three thin gray towels being pulled off the rail because they are the ones actually used every day. Name it as a shelf running backwards, and note that it has been running backwards for years.

Sort Every towel comes out and gets ranked by which one your hand actually goes to after a shower.
Beats
  • Empty the shelf completely and rank every towel by hand, explaining that ranking beats sorting into keep and toss because it forces a comparison.
  • Show the four categories that always fail, the thin, the stiff, the shedders, and the odd single from a lost set.
  • Split the rejects on camera, the best of them becoming cleaning rags and the rest going to a shelter that takes textiles.
  • Count the survivors against three bath towels per person, one in use, one in the wash, one folded on the shelf.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the shelf emptying, stacks lifted out by hand, no body in frame
  • Overhead of towels laid out in a ranked row on the floor
  • Macro on a shedding edge and a stiff worn nap side by side
  • Close on the rag pile and the donation bag forming separately
On-screen text
  • Rank them, do not sort them
  • Thin. Stiff. Shedders.
  • Three per person
Short cut · 45–60s Every towel in the house laid out in a single ranked row on the floor, best to worst, before a single one goes back.
Stands alone: State that ranking rather than keep-or-toss is the method, and give the three-per-person count as the target the ranking is measured against.
Straighten Fold to one width so the stack squares up, keep columns by type, and nest each guest set in its own pillowcase.
Beats
  • Fold to one consistent width on camera and show the stack squaring up as a result, explaining that a matched fold is what makes a column readable.
  • Build separate columns for bath towels, hand towels, and washcloths rather than one mixed pile, and show a hand pulling from a column without disturbing it.
  • Nest a guest set inside its own pillowcase and lift the whole set off the shelf in one grab to demonstrate why.
Shots
  • Overhead of a towel being folded to a marked width
  • Three-quarter of three columns squaring up on the shelf
  • Close on a hand pulling one towel from a column cleanly
  • Close on a guest set sliding into a pillowcase and lifting out as one unit
On-screen text
  • One width, every towel
  • Columns, not piles
  • Guest set in a pillowcase
Short cut · 30–45s A guest set sliding into a pillowcase and then the whole thing lifting off the shelf in one grab, sheet, towels and all.
Stands alone: Say the pillowcase is the container for a complete guest set so it travels in one movement, which is the entire reason for the trick.
Shine Wipe the shelves and press the back wall for damp, because one towel put away not quite dry will scent the whole cupboard.
Beats
  • Wipe the shelves with everything out, then press the back wall with a flat hand to test for damp, showing where the cold spot usually sits.
  • Explain the specific failure, that a towel put away not quite dry will scent the whole cupboard within days, and demonstrate a sniff test being applied to a stack.
  • Route anything sour back through a hot wash with no softener before it returns, and explain why softener is left out of that wash.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of empty shelves being wiped end to end
  • Close on a flat palm pressed against the back wall of the cupboard
  • Macro on a damp mark or discoloration at the back corner
  • Close on a towel going into a wash basket rather than back on the shelf
On-screen text
  • Press the back wall
  • Hot wash, no softener
Short cut · 30–45s A flat hand pressed against the back wall of a linen cupboard, checking for the damp that quietly scents everything on the shelf.
Stands alone: Explain that one not-quite-dry towel scents the whole cupboard, since the wall press means nothing without the consequence attached.
Safety A deep stack of linen sits on a load nobody ever weighed, and reaching the top shelf on a wet floor is its own hazard.
Beats
  • Show the brackets and wall fixings being checked by hand, explaining that a full linen shelf is a load nobody ever weighed.
  • Move heavy bath towels to the lower shelves so nothing tall comes down on your head, and show the redistribution happening.
  • Show the toppling failure and its cause, a stack tall enough to fall when a towel is pulled from the middle, and correct the stack height.
  • Address the fall question, a step stool on a wet bathroom floor to reach the top shelf, and move the everyday linens down to shelves reachable flat-footed.
Shots
  • Close on fingers testing a bracket and a wall fixing
  • Three-quarter of heavy bath towels moving from a high shelf to a low one
  • Close on a towel pulled from mid stack and the stack shifting
  • Low three-quarter of a step stool on a wet tile floor, then removed
On-screen text
  • Fall, cut, or crush
  • Heavy goes low
  • No stool on a wet floor
Short cut · 30–45s A towel pulled from the middle of a tall stack and the whole column shifting toward the edge of the shelf.
Stands alone: Name it as the fall, cut, or crush question and give the fix, shorter stacks with the heavy bath towels kept on the lower shelves.
Standardize The count is the standard, three bath towels per person, one width, one label per column, and a full column retires its worst towel.
Beats
  • Write and apply one label per column and explain that the count on the label is what makes the right state obvious at a glance.
  • Show the retirement rule working, a full column receiving clean laundry, and the most worn towel in that column becoming a rag that day.
  • Show a fold guide, a marked width used so every towel matches, and explain that this is the standard being made repeatable rather than remembered.
Shots
  • Macro on a column label being written with a count
  • Overhead of three labeled columns reading across the shelf
  • Close on the worst towel being pulled and cut or bagged as a rag
  • Close on a fold guide being used to set the width
On-screen text
  • Three per person
  • Full column retires one
  • One label per column
Short cut · 30–45s A clean towel arriving at a full column, and the most worn towel in that same column leaving as a rag in the same movement.
Stands alone: Give the column count standard first, since the swap only makes sense once the viewer knows the column has a written limit.
Sustain The laundry fold is the trigger, clean towels go to the bottom of the column, and nothing goes onto the shelf damp.
Beats
  • Show the trigger as it already happens, towels being folded from a laundry load, and each clean one being slid to the bottom of its column.
  • Explain the reason, that bottom loading keeps the oldest towel coming to your hand so wear spreads evenly across the set.
  • Show the count being checked in the same motion, one glance at the column while the hands are already there.
  • End on the absolute rule, nothing goes onto the shelf damp, ever, with a towel being sent back rather than shelved.
Shots
  • Overhead of folded towels stacking beside a laundry basket
  • Three-quarter of a clean towel sliding under a column rather than on top
  • Close on a hand counting the column at a glance
  • Close on a towel being felt for damp and set aside
On-screen text
  • Clean towels go underneath
  • Nothing damp, ever
Short cut · 30–45s A clean towel sliding under the column instead of onto the top of it, so the oldest one keeps coming to your hand.
Stands alone: Say the trigger is the laundry fold and explain that bottom loading rotates the set, which is the whole point of the movement.
Close

Open the finished cupboard and state the standard against the shelf, three bath towels per person, folded to one width, columns labeled by type, and nothing put away damp, then show the trigger, laundry being folded, clean towels going to the bottom of the column, and the most worn one in a full column becoming a rag.

Next: That is the seventh and last zone in this bathroom, and the series moves next to the one room a visitor uses alone with the door shut, the guest bathroom.

Shot list
  • Three-quarter tripod square to the open linen cupboard for before and after states
  • Overhead on a side arm over a bed or floor for the ranked towel row and all folding
  • Macro on shedding edges, worn nap, and column labels
  • Close on brackets, wall fixings, and the back wall damp press
  • Close on a guest set entering a pillowcase and lifting out as one unit
  • Low three-quarter of a step stool on wet tile for the fall hazard beat
  • Close on a towel being pulled from mid stack to show the topple
  • Overhead of laundry folding for the sustain trigger
  • Wide of the finished shelf with three labeled columns
Description hook

Most households dry themselves on their worst towels and save the good ones for visitors twice a year. Here is the full 6S pass that puts the shelf back the right way round.

6Slinen cupboardtowel storagetowel foldingbathroom organizationshelf safety6S Success Home Editionmicro zone

Room 12 of 20

Guest Bathroom

5 videos · 30 Shorts
Production noteSmall, hard surfaced and reflective, which makes it the trickiest headless room in the series. The mirror and any glass screen will show the camera and the tripod, so set the tripod off the mirror axis, shoot the mirror from a low three quarter angle, and check every frame for a reflected camera before rolling. This is a one person shoot: tripod, window light or the open door, a white bounce card on the floor to lift shadows inside the vanity cabinet and behind the pedestal, and one small battery light panel gelled to daylight for interiors and for raking light on the tile. Tape or clamp the panel, never rest it on a wet surface. The overhead needs a horizontal arm because the counter sits tight to the wall and a standard tripod cannot centre over it. Floor is tile, so pad the tripod feet and lay a towel for kneeling shots. Shoot the whole room in one day and follow the manual's own start order: put the stored guest towels in the wash before the first frame, shoot the vanity counter first, and shoot the linen shelf last when the wash is done. On set safety: shoot the chemical handling beats with capped bottles only, and open the door and window for any sequence involving bowl cleaner. Never film bleach and an acid cleaner open in the same frame, even as a demonstration.
MZ-065 · R12.01

Guest Vanity Counter

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Guest Or Used Bathroom”

Guest Bathroom Vanity Counter: The Three Item Reset

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead on a vanity holding two lives at once: a soap pump and a tissue box on one side, a family toothbrush cup, hair clips behind the tap and a razor on the other. Pose the fork this household has been dodging, whether this is a guest bathroom or a bathroom somebody actually lives in, and set up that the video settles that question out loud instead of resetting the same counter twice a week forever.

Sort The counter is cleared, the guest or resident question is settled out loud, and only the answer goes back on the stone.
Beats
  • Clear the counter onto a folded towel on the floor, naming each stray as it comes off: the family toothbrush cup, the hair clips from behind the tap, the travel conditioner, the spare contact lens case, the razor that landed here when the main bathroom ran out of room.
  • Settle the fork before anything goes back. If nobody actually brushes their teeth at this basin, the toothbrush cup leaves today and nothing personal returns. If a child or a housemate genuinely uses it, that one named person gets a labeled caddy or drawer holding their two items, alongside the guest three.
  • Make the reasoning visible: a hotel counter standard aimed at a room somebody lives in fails twice a week, which is a standard pointed at the wrong room rather than anybody being careless.
  • Put back only the answer you picked, soap, tissues and hand towel, plus the named caddy if that was the call.
  • Cover the demotion trap for this counter, that half used products on their way out of the house do not get parked here, they leave.
Shots
  • Overhead, locked off, of the loaded counter before anything is touched.
  • Three quarter at counter height on hands lifting each item onto the towel on the floor.
  • Overhead of the towel with two groups set well apart, the guest keep list and the household strays.
  • Macro on the family toothbrush cup being lifted away, then on a labeled caddy being set into the drawer.
  • Overhead of the bare counter, then the keep list landing back on it.
On-screen text
  • Empty it first
  • Guest bathroom or used bathroom
  • Three things, plus one named caddy
Short cut · 30–45s Time compressed overhead of a crowded vanity clearing to bare stone in one sweep of hands, then a family toothbrush cup lifted out of frame and exactly three items landing back down.
Stands alone: Open by naming the room and the fork, guest bathroom or bathroom somebody lives in, and state the keep list as soap, tissues and hand towel so the number three is earned rather than asserted.
Straighten Each item on this counter is positioned by how a stranger will actually use the basin.
Beats
  • Place the soap on the side a hand reaches without crossing over the basin, demonstrating the difference by tracking a hand to the pump in the wrong position and then the right one.
  • Set the tissues at the back corner and test the splash arc with the tap running so the viewer sees why that corner and not another.
  • Hang the hand towel on a ring or hook visible from the doorway, on the rule that a visitor should never open a cabinet to find a towel.
  • If the named caddy exists, give it a home inside the drawer rather than on the stone, so the counter still reads bare from the door.
Shots
  • Three quarter of a hand reaching for the pump, first crossing the basin, then not.
  • Overhead of the tap running and the tissue box moved out of the splash arc.
  • Wide from the doorway at standing height, tripod only, hand towel clearly visible on the ring.
  • Macro on the towel being squared on the ring, and on the caddy sliding shut in the drawer.
On-screen text
  • Reach without crossing the basin
  • Towel visible from the door
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches for soap and has to pass right over a full basin to get it, then the same reach after the pump changes sides.
Stands alone: Say in the first beat that this is a guest vanity and that the test is a stranger finding and using things without opening anything.
Shine An order of work for this counter that stops you cleaning the same surface twice, and the one spot where scale hides.
Beats
  • Wipe the counter surface first, then the tap and the drain lip, showing the toothpaste film and hard water scale that collect there and read as neglect to a visitor.
  • Go in close on the collar at the base of the tap and show that the chalky ring living there is the spot most people wipe around rather than through.
  • Do the mirror last, top to bottom, and show why: drips land on surfaces you have not finished yet if you take it first.
Shots
  • Overhead of a cloth crossing the counter in a single pass.
  • Macro with the small panel set low for raking light on the chalky tap collar, matched framing before and after.
  • Close on the drain lip being wiped.
  • Three quarter on the mirror worked top to bottom, tripod off the mirror axis, frame checked for a reflected camera before the take.
On-screen text
  • Counter, tap, drain, mirror
  • Clean the collar, not around it
  • Mirror last, top to bottom
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on a cloth wiping straight past the base of a tap, then a turn to the chalky ring hiding in the collar that was never actually touched.
Stands alone: State the full order, counter then tap then drain then mirror, so the single detail lands inside a sequence rather than floating alone.
Safety Water and electricity, and fall, cut or crush, on a wet counter a stranger will use.
Beats
  • Water and electricity: show a shaver or hair dryer left plugged in beside the basin a guest is about to fill, unplug it and put it away, and be clear that coiling the cord neatly on the counter is not the fix, the cord comes off the counter entirely.
  • Fall, cut or crush: put a glass tumbler and a glass trinket dish on the wet stone and demonstrate the slide with a controlled tilt, naming the consequence in this room, a small tiled floor and a barefoot visitor.
  • Swap both for ceramic on camera and reset the counter.
Shots
  • Three quarter of a cord running from the socket to the counter beside a filled basin.
  • Close on a hand pulling the plug and coiling the cord away into a drawer.
  • Macro, low across the wet counter, of a glass tumbler sliding clear of its position under a light hand.
  • Close on the ceramic replacement being set down.
On-screen text
  • Cord off the counter, not coiled
  • Glass slides on wet stone
  • Bare feet, tile floor
Short cut · 30–45s Low macro across a wet stone counter as a glass tumbler slides clear of where it was standing under barely any pressure.
Stands alone: Name the room and the floor material inside the Short, since the whole point is glass meeting tile with a barefoot visitor standing over it.
Standardize The answer you picked becomes a picture anyone in the house can reset the counter against.
Beats
  • Read the standard against the finished counter: three things live here permanently, soap, tissues and hand towel, plus the named caddy if that was the call.
  • Photograph that exact arrangement from the doorway angle, pointing to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, and make the case that a picture of the right answer beats a description of it.
  • Tape the print inside the vanity door and show it being found by someone opening the cabinet.
  • Make the placement point: the picture lives where the person resetting the counter is already standing.
Shots
  • Overhead of the finished counter, held clean and still.
  • Close on a printed photo being taped to the inside of the vanity door.
  • Three quarter of the cabinet door swinging open to reveal the photo.
  • Split framing of the printed photo held against the real counter behind it.
On-screen text
  • Photograph the right answer
  • Tape it inside the door
Short cut · 30–45s A printed photo of a finished vanity is held up in front of the real vanity, and the two frames line up item for item.
Stands alone: Say inside the Short that the photo is the standard for this counter and that it lives taped inside the cabinet door where the next person will already be standing.
Sustain Both triggers hang off trips that already happen, so the counter never waits on somebody remembering.
Beats
  • Give the guest arrival trigger: the moment someone confirms they are coming, walk in, top up the soap and hang a fresh hand towel, since soap level and towel are the two things a visitor registers.
  • Give the standing household trigger from the standard: when fresh towels go away after laundry, the guest hand towel gets swapped in the same motion.
  • Shoot both as single unbroken trips, hands only, so it is visible that the soap top up happens on a walk through you were making anyway and the towel swap happens with the laundry already in your arms.
Shots
  • Close on a soap bottle being topped up beside a phone lying face down, no screen content in frame.
  • Three quarter of a folded stack of laundered towels being carried in and one peeled off for the ring.
  • Overhead of the fresh towel squared on the ring, the rest of the counter unchanged.
On-screen text
  • Attach it to a trip you already make
  • Soap level and towel
Short cut · 30–45s A stack of clean laundry comes through the door and one towel peels off the top straight onto the guest ring without a second trip being made.
Stands alone: Name the trigger plainly inside the Short, that putting laundry away is when the guest hand towel gets swapped, and say which room the ring is in.
Close

Land on the finished counter from the doorway and read the standard off what is in frame: soap, tissues and hand towel, plus the one named caddy if that was the answer, and anything a visitor brings leaves with them. Then run the trigger once more, the laundry stack coming in and one towel going onto the ring in the same motion, so the standard and the thing that holds it are seen back to back.

Next: The counter is clear because everything that did not belong went somewhere. Next we open the door underneath it, where the hotel miniatures have been collecting for years.

Shot list
  • Overhead arm rig locked over the counter for the before, the clearing, the sorted groups and the finished state.
  • Three quarter tripod at counter height for hand work at the basin, tap and soap pump.
  • Doorway wide at standing height for the visitor's view, used for before, after and the ideal-state photo match.
  • Macro on a tabletop tripod, repositioned between takes, for the tap collar, drain lip and the label of a discarded travel bottle.
  • Low macro across the wet counter for the glass slide hazard beat.
  • Floor level three quarter on the towel with the sorted groups laid out.
  • Cabinet door interior close for taping and revealing the standard photo, small panel taped under the counter.
  • Mirror pass from an off axis three quarter position, frame checked for a reflected camera before every take.
Description hook

A guest vanity counter holds three things: soap, tissues and a hand towel. The harder question is whether this is really a guest bathroom at all.

MZ-066 · R12.02

Guest Vanity Storage

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Keep Four, Bin The Rest”

Under the Guest Sink: Two Bins and a Toilet Paper Line

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a hand pulling a bag of hotel miniatures out from under the guest sink and tipping it onto a towel: shampoos from three different trips, a lotion nobody opened, conditioner samples with battered labels. Name the deadlock exactly, that throwing out free soap feels like waste and keeping it feels like hospitality, so the bag has sat under this sink for years doing neither, and set up that the video settles it with arithmetic rather than feeling.

Sort The cabinet comes out entirely and the miniature question gets settled with a number.
Beats
  • Pull everything out onto a towel on the floor and show the true volume, which is always more than the cabinet suggested.
  • Work the miniatures honestly: keep the unopened ones a guest would actually use, throw out the started ones, and make the point that a half used bottle is not an offering.
  • Do the arithmetic on camera. A guest staying two nights uses one shampoo, one conditioner, one soap and one lotion, so four unopened bottles with the least battered labels stay and the rest go today.
  • Separate the household backstock that drifted in here and show it going back to the bathroom it came from.
  • Close the escape route: if binning them is genuinely beyond you, they go into a shelter donation box this week and into the car, not back onto the shelf.
Shots
  • Three quarter, low, of the cabinet door opening on the loaded state.
  • Overhead of everything spread across a towel on the tile floor.
  • Macro on hands turning bottles to check seals, one clearly opened and one clearly sealed.
  • Overhead of the four chosen bottles set well apart from a much larger discard pile.
  • Close on the discard pile going into a bag and the bag being carried out of frame.
On-screen text
  • Two nights, four bottles
  • Started bottles are not an offering
  • In the car this week
Short cut · 45–60s A bag of hotel miniatures tips out onto the floor, four bottles get picked out of the spread, and everything else goes into a bin bag.
Stands alone: Give the arithmetic before the picking starts, one guest, two nights, one of each, so the number four is earned and the viewer can run it on their own cabinet.
Straighten Two lift out bins and a toilet paper stack a guest sees without asking.
Beats
  • Set the rule at two bins rather than five, and show that more containers in a cabinet this size only hide things at a higher resolution.
  • Load one bin with guest supplies, a new toothbrush, a wrapped bar of soap and the four travel bottles in a small dish. Load the other with the cleaning kit standing upright on a shallow tray.
  • Test both by lifting each with one hand, and make the reason explicit, that the cabinet base has to stay visible.
  • Stack the toilet paper on its own where it is seen the second the door opens, on the plain fact that a guest hunting for a roll will not come and ask you.
Shots
  • Overhead of two empty bins side by side before loading.
  • Close on the four travel bottles being arranged in a small dish so they read as an offering.
  • Three quarter of one hand lifting a loaded bin clear of the cabinet.
  • Low three quarter from seated height showing what is visible the instant the cabinet door opens.
On-screen text
  • Two bins, not five
  • Lift out with one hand
  • They will not ask
Short cut · 30–45s A cabinet door swings open and the toilet paper stack is the first thing in frame, before anything else in there registers.
Stands alone: Say inside the Short that this is the guest bathroom cabinet and that a visitor hunting for a roll will not knock on your door to ask.
Shine The cabinet base gets cleaned to inspect it, because it is the only place a slow leak can announce itself.
Beats
  • Empty the cabinet completely and wipe the base, describing what you are looking for rather than only cleaning: dark rings, staining, or softened board that mean the trap has been weeping.
  • Get a light in and inspect the trap and the joint above the base.
  • Wipe the neck and cap of every bottle before it goes back, showing the cause and effect, that dried cleaner running down the outside of a bottle is what makes a whole cabinet sticky.
Shots
  • Close, small panel taped under the counter, on the bare cabinet base being wiped.
  • Macro on a dark ring in the board with the panel set low for raking light.
  • Macro up at the trap joint from floor level.
  • Close on a cloth wiping the neck and cap of a cleaner bottle.
On-screen text
  • Clean to inspect
  • Dark ring means weeping trap
  • Wipe the neck and cap
Short cut · 30–45s A cloth wipes a cabinet base clean and a dark ring stays behind in the board, unmoved by any amount of scrubbing.
Stands alone: Explain inside the Short that this is the base under a bathroom sink and that the ring is not dirt, it is the trap above it telling you something.
Safety Poison, choke or strangle in the one bathroom a visiting child gets sent into alone.
Beats
  • Show the height problem directly: bowl cleaner and bleach under this sink sit at exactly the height of a visiting toddler who has been sent in to wash their hands without an adult.
  • Give the two acceptable fixes and no third one, lift the cleaning bin to a high shelf elsewhere or fit the cabinet with a latch, and fit the latch on camera.
  • State the storage rule hard, that bleach never shares a bin with an acid limescale or bowl cleaner, because a loose cap on both is all it takes for them to meet. Handle only capped bottles in frame.
  • Cover the second hazard, fall: a slow weep from a trap nobody sees, because nobody opens this cabinet, reaches the tile as a thin invisible film long before it shows as a puddle, which is why the base stays bare.
Shots
  • Low three quarter with the camera set at a small child's eye height, on the open cabinet full of chemicals.
  • Close on hands fitting a cabinet latch, screwdriver in frame.
  • Close on the cleaning bin being lifted out of the room entirely.
  • Macro on two capped bottles being separated into different containers.
  • Close on a flat hand sweeping the tile in front of the cabinet, checking for film.
On-screen text
  • Child height, closed door
  • Latch it or move it
  • Never bleach beside bowl cleaner
Short cut · 45–60s The camera drops to a small child's eye height in front of an open cabinet under a sink, and the whole shelf of chemicals sits level with the lens.
Stands alone: Establish that this is the bathroom visiting children get sent to on their own, which is what makes this cabinet different from the one in your own bathroom, and end on the latch going on.
Standardize Labels a guest can read, and a line on the shelf that counts the toilet paper for you.
Beats
  • Write the two bin labels by hand in plain words, Guest Supplies and Cleaning, and make the point that these are written to be read by a visitor rather than by you.
  • Draw a line on the shelf at the toilet paper minimum, then show the stack sitting above it and below it.
  • Explain the mechanism, pointing to Chapter 14, visual controls: when the stack falls below the line it goes on the shopping list and nobody counts anything.
  • Point out that the bare cabinet base is itself a visual control, since a leak now has somewhere obvious to show.
Shots
  • Close on a marker writing a bin label by hand.
  • Close on a line being drawn along the shelf edge at the minimum height.
  • Overhead of the stack above the line, then a matched frame with it below.
  • Wide of the finished cabinet from the doorway with both labels legible.
On-screen text
  • Plain words a guest can read
  • Below the line, on the list
Short cut · 30–45s A line gets drawn along a shelf edge behind a stack of toilet paper, then rolls come off one at a time until the line is showing.
Stands alone: Say what the line means and where this shelf is before the stack starts dropping, otherwise the reveal has nothing to land on.
Sustain Restocking hangs off a shop you already do, inspection hangs off a chore you already do.
Beats
  • Give the restock trigger: when you restock your own bathroom after a shop, open this cabinet on the same trip and build the toilet paper stack back up to the line.
  • Give the inspection trigger from the standard: you already open this cabinet for the brush before the weekly bowl clean, so a hand runs across the base while you are down there.
  • Make the point that neither one is a reminder or an app, both hang off something that already happens in the house.
Shots
  • Three quarter of shopping bags set down and rolls carried straight through to the guest cabinet.
  • Overhead of the stack being rebuilt up to the line.
  • Close on a hand reaching in for the brush and sweeping flat across the base on the way out.
On-screen text
  • Same trip, not a new one
  • Hand across the base
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches into a cabinet for the toilet brush and, on the way back out, sweeps flat across the bare cabinet base without breaking rhythm.
Stands alone: Name the weekly bowl clean as the thing that already happens and say what the hand is feeling for, damp on a base that should be dry.
Close

Open the cabinet door on the finished state and read the standard against what is in frame: two labeled lift out bins, a visible toilet paper stack sitting above its line, and nothing loose on the base so a leak has somewhere obvious to show. Then run the trigger once, a hand going in for the brush and coming back out across the bare base.

Next: The cleaning kit now lifts out with one hand. Next we carry it to the tub and deal with the grout line you have scrubbed three times and quietly started calling clean.

Shot list
  • Low three quarter tripod at open cabinet height, the primary setup for before, loading and the finished reveal.
  • Camera resting on the tile at a small child's eye height for the chemical height hazard beat.
  • Overhead arm rig over a towel on the bathroom floor for the full unload and the sorting of miniatures.
  • Macro on a tabletop tripod for bottle seals, labels, the cabinet base ring and the trap joint.
  • Small battery panel taped under the counter for all interior cabinet work.
  • Close setup on the shelf edge for drawing the minimum line and for writing the labels.
  • Doorway wide for the visitor's eye view of the open cabinet.
  • Hallway pickup of shopping bags coming in for the restock trigger.
Description hook

The bag of hotel miniatures under the guest sink is not hospitality and it is not thrift. Here is the arithmetic that finally settles it.

MZ-067 · R12.03

Shower or Tub

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Not Dirt, A Repair”

Guest Shower Reset: Three Bottles and the Grout You Cannot Clean

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open macro on one grout line being scrubbed hard, rinsed, and still coming up gray. Name the thing this household has quietly agreed to accept, that the line has been scrubbed three times and started getting called clean anyway. Set out what it actually is, mold grown into porous grout or a silicone bead that has failed underneath, and that part of every week's clean is being spent on a job that cannot succeed.

Sort Every bottle in this caddy comes out and gets turned over, because this is where the household's rejected products retire.
Beats
  • Take every bottle out of the caddy, line them up along the tub rim, and turn each one over, reading weight and label as the two tests.
  • Name what this particular zone collects: the shampoo nobody liked, the body wash that smells wrong, the conditioner welded to the shelf by its own dried drip.
  • Set the keep rule and apply it in frame, one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, all readable and all more than a third full.
  • Bin the old razor and the disintegrating loofah without ceremony, and make the point that a guest reading a stranger's rejected products is the impression actually being left.
Shots
  • Three quarter into the tub, tripod outside on the tile, of the loaded caddy before anything moves.
  • Overhead of every bottle lined up on a towel laid across the tub rim.
  • Macro of a hand lifting a conditioner bottle and the ring of dried product welding it to the shelf.
  • Macro on a faded, unreadable label.
  • Overhead of the three survivors beside a full discard pile.
On-screen text
  • Turn every bottle over
  • One shampoo, one conditioner, one wash
  • Readable and a third full
Short cut · 30–45s A hand lifts a conditioner bottle out of a shower caddy and the shelf lifts with it, welded on by its own dried drip.
Stands alone: State the keep rule in the same breath, one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, readable and above a third full, and say this is a guest shower nobody has used since spring.
Straighten Nothing stands on the tub floor, and a wet guest without glasses can reach everything.
Beats
  • Hang the caddy or fit a corner shelf, on the single reason that anything standing on the tub floor collects water underneath itself.
  • Move a bar of soap into a draining dish and show the puddle ring it had been sitting in.
  • Fit a hook inside the door at a height reachable with wet hands and no glasses on, and demonstrate that reach from inside the tub with hands only.
  • Make the placement principle explicit for this zone, that a guest is operating this room half blind and half wet, and every decision here answers to that.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the caddy being hung, water clearly not pooling beneath it.
  • Macro of the puddle ring under a soap bar, then the same soap in a draining dish.
  • Close on the hook being set at reach height inside the door.
  • Tripod low inside the tub, framed so only a forearm and hand enter the shot as it reaches for the hook.
On-screen text
  • Nothing stands on the tub floor
  • Wet hands, no glasses
Short cut · 30–45s A bar of soap lifts off a tub ledge and leaves a grey puddle ring in exactly its own shape.
Stands alone: Name the fix inside the Short, that soap in a shower gets a draining dish and never a flat ledge, and show the dish going in.
Shine Mold gets treated first so its dwell time runs while you work elsewhere.
Beats
  • Spray the grout lines and the bottom band of the curtain liner first, on the reasoning that this needs time and time is not something to spend standing there watching.
  • Show the dwell as an actual absence: hands leave frame, the locked shot holds on the empty tub, the work moves to the rest of the room, then the same locked frame comes back for the rinse.
  • Take a fabric liner off the rings and put it into the washing machine instead of scrubbing it by hand.
  • Rinse and show the result on the grout lines that do respond, which sets up the harder question about the ones that do not.
Shots
  • Macro on grout lines being sprayed along their length.
  • Close on the pink film band at the bottom of a liner being treated.
  • Locked wide of the empty tub held through the dwell, hands out of frame.
  • Three quarter of hands unhooking a fabric liner and carrying it out of the room.
  • Macro on a rinsed grout line in matched framing with the earlier shot.
On-screen text
  • Treat first, leave it
  • Liner goes in the machine
  • Come back and rinse
Short cut · 30–45s Grout in a shower gets sprayed, the hands leave the frame completely, and the shot just holds on an empty tub while the cleaner does the work.
Stands alone: Explain inside the Short that dwell time is the active ingredient and that standing there scrubbing it early is the wasted part.
Safety Fall, and fall, cut or crush, for someone stepping into a tub they have never used before.
Beats
  • Set the scene precisely, that the person using this tub is stepping into an unfamiliar one, probably at night, onto a surface they cannot judge the grip of.
  • Fit a non slip mat or adhesive strips on the tub floor, testing the grip on the bare glaze first and on the fitted strips after.
  • Fall, cut or crush: show what a towel bar screwed into drywall actually is, and that it tears straight out the moment it takes a person's weight, with the tub rim in the way on the fall.
  • Show what a real grab point looks like, one thing solidly anchored, and be plain that a suction rail is not it.
  • Land the principle behind both, pointing to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt: a non slip surface is a fix, and a warning is not.
Shots
  • Low three quarter into the tub showing the bare glazed floor with the panel set low for raking light.
  • Macro of a flat hand pressing and sliding on the wet glaze, then the same press on the fitted strips.
  • Close on adhesive strips being laid and pressed down.
  • Macro on a towel bar mount and the drywall behind it, then on a suction rail cup lifting at one edge.
  • Close on a hand gripping a properly anchored rail and pulling against it.
On-screen text
  • Unfamiliar tub, at night
  • Towel bars are not grab handles
  • A fix, not a warning
Short cut · 45–60s A flat wet hand presses down onto the glazed floor of a tub and slides away under barely any pressure at all.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a guest tub and the person standing in it has never used it before and cannot judge the grip, which is the entire hazard.
Standardize A short checkable list for a shower that stands unused for months, and the point where cleaning becomes repair.
Beats
  • Read the standard against the finished tub: three bottles, one soap, one mat, one anchored grab point, and no personal items.
  • Add the unused shower clause and explain why it exists in this zone and nowhere else in the house, that a shower standing a month gets run hot for a minute before a guest arrives.
  • Show that run and say what it proves, that it clears the stale water sitting in the line and confirms the drain is still moving freely.
  • Settle the call as the hardest clause in this standard: one proper treatment with full dwell time and a stiff brush, and if the line darkens again inside two weeks it stops being a cleaning job and moves to the repair list, meaning raking out and regrouting or cutting the old silicone and running a fresh bead. Make clear that naming it a repair is the decision, and that it buys one Saturday instead of a chore with no end.
Shots
  • Wide of the finished tub from outside with everything in the standard visible in one frame.
  • Close on the tap running hot, steam rising, water going down freely.
  • Macro on a treated grout line, then a matched frame of the same line darkened again.
  • Close on that line being marked and written onto a repair list on paper.
On-screen text
  • Run it hot before they arrive
  • Two weeks, then it is a repair
  • One Saturday, not forever
Short cut · 45–60s A grout line gets one proper treatment and comes up clean, then a matched shot of the same line two weeks later shows it dark again.
Stands alone: Deliver the whole rule inside the Short, one treatment with full dwell time and a stiff brush, and if it comes back within two weeks it goes on the repair list instead of the cleaning list.
Sustain Whoever used this tub last leaves it in a state that stops the film coming back.
Beats
  • Set the rule for the last person out, squeegee the glass or shake out the liner, and drape the bath mat over the tub rim rather than leaving it flat on the floor.
  • Show the failure mode specifically, a liner left bunched against the tile, and that this fold is exactly where the pink film starts again.
  • Give the standing trigger from the standard: when you strip the guest bed after a visit, whatever the guest left in the shower goes out on the same trip to the laundry.
Shots
  • Close on a squeegee crossing a glass screen in one pass.
  • Three quarter of a liner being shaken out and spread flat rather than bunched.
  • Macro on a bunched liner pressed to tile, then on the pink film sitting only in that fold.
  • Overhead of a bath mat being folded over the tub rim.
  • Three quarter of hands carrying stripped bedding through with the shower items balanced on top.
On-screen text
  • Last one out
  • Bunched liner, pink film
  • Strip the bed, clear the shower
Short cut · 30–45s A curtain liner is pulled away from the tile where it had been bunched, and the pink film is sitting only inside the fold.
Stands alone: Say who the rule belongs to, whoever used the shower last, and give the three actions, squeegee or shake out, spread the liner flat, mat over the rim.
Close

Hold on the finished tub and read the standard as the frame shows it: one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, all readable and above a third full, over a non slip tub floor with one anchored grab point. Then run the trigger, stripped bedding going out with the guest's leftovers carried on the same trip, and point at which grout line now sits on the repair list rather than the cleaning list.

Next: One thing in this room belongs on a list too, and it is not grout. Next we deal with the object this household has silently agreed not to look at.

Shot list
  • Three quarter tripod set outside the tub at rim height, the primary setup for caddy work, hanging and the finished wide.
  • Low in tub angle with the small panel set low for raking light across the glaze, for the bare floor and the non slip fitting.
  • Macro on a tabletop tripod for grout lines, liner film, bottle labels and the puddle ring under the soap.
  • Overhead arm rig over a towel laid across the tub rim for the bottle lineup and sort.
  • Low in tub position framed to hold everything above the wrist out of shot, for the wet hand reach demonstrations.
  • Matched framing pairs, locked and marked with tape, for every before and after on grout and glaze.
  • Hallway pickup for carrying the liner and the bedding out to the laundry.
  • Flat surface setup with paper and pen for writing the repair list.
Description hook

You have scrubbed that grout line three times and quietly started calling it clean. It is not dirt, and no product is going to fix it.

MZ-068 · R12.04

Toilet Area

5–7 min · thumbnail: “The Brush Is Consumable”

The Guest Toilet Area: The Brush Is a Consumable

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open close on a toilet brush being lifted out of its holder: splayed bristles, and an inch of gray water in the bottom of the holder coming up with it. Name what this object is, the thing the household has silently agreed not to look at, and that it has stood there for years spreading more than it removes. Put the avoided decision on the table, that a brush is a consumable and not a fixture.

Sort The tank top and the floor behind the bowl get cleared down to one reserve roll.
Beats
  • Clear everything off the top of the tank and out from behind the bowl, naming the usual population as it comes off: the collection of air fresheners, the second brush, the magazines, the box of something nobody has identified in years.
  • Give the reason this particular zone accumulates, that these surfaces are flat, hidden from the doorway, and never inspected because nobody in the house uses this room.
  • Set the keep rule and apply it, one reserve roll stays in the open and nothing else.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the loaded tank top and the gap behind the pedestal before anything moves.
  • Overhead of everything cleared onto a towel on the floor.
  • Macro on the dust outline left behind an object that had not been lifted in years.
  • Close on the single reserve roll being set back.
On-screen text
  • Tank top and behind the bowl
  • One roll stays, nothing else
Short cut · 30–45s Objects come off a toilet tank one at a time and each one leaves a clean rectangle behind it in the dust.
Stands alone: Name the zone as the guest toilet area and give the keep rule, one visible reserve roll on the tank and nothing else, so the clearing has a destination.
Straighten Placement here is decided by a seated guest and by the door swing.
Beats
  • Put the reserve roll where a seated person reaches it without standing, and demonstrate that reach from seated height, since a roll a seated person cannot reach is not a reserve roll.
  • Set the brush and the trash can on the side away from the door swing, and show the door opening into where they used to stand.
  • Give the standard behind both placements, that a guest should never have to stand, reach across, or move something to use this room.
Shots
  • Camera at seated height beside the bowl, a hand reaching to the roll in its old position and then its new one.
  • Three quarter of the door swinging open and just clearing the relocated can and brush.
  • Overhead of the finished floor layout around the pedestal.
On-screen text
  • Reachable while seated
  • Clear of the door swing
Short cut · 30–45s Camera sits at seated height beside a toilet and a hand reaches for the spare roll, comes up short, then the roll moves and the same reach lands.
Stands alone: State the rule inside the Short, that a reserve roll a seated person cannot reach without standing is not doing its job.
Shine Treat the bowl first and work outward, because the smell is not coming from where people scrub.
Beats
  • Treat the bowl first, under the rim and at the water line, then leave it, so dwell time runs while the rest of the work happens.
  • Work outward in order while it dwells: seat hinges, then the base of the pedestal, then the floor behind it.
  • Show the finding plainly, that the floor behind the pedestal is where splash and dust collect and where the smell in a guest bathroom actually comes from.
  • Introduce the color coded cloth, a color used nowhere else in the house, so it cannot travel to a kitchen surface by accident.
Shots
  • Macro under the rim as cleaner is run along it.
  • Close on the water line ring before treatment, matched framing for after.
  • Macro on seat hinges opened and cleaned.
  • Low close on the floor behind the pedestal with the panel set low for raking light across the dust and splash line.
  • Close on a distinctly colored cloth being taken from the bin and held clear of everything else.
On-screen text
  • Under the rim first, then leave it
  • The smell is behind the pedestal
  • One color, this room only
Short cut · 30–45s A low camera slides in behind a toilet pedestal under raking light, into the strip of floor that has never once been cleaned.
Stands alone: Say up front that this strip is where a guest bathroom smell actually comes from, otherwise the shot is just a dirty floor with no argument attached.
Safety Poison, choke or strangle, twice over: what gets stored in this corner and what gets mixed in it.
Beats
  • Show the bowl cleaner parked behind the pedestal and give the geometry, that it stands at a crawling child's eye level and usually with the cap loose.
  • Fix it on camera, cap tight and back into the cleaning bin every time, and make clear this is a placement rule rather than an intention.
  • State the mixing hazard without softening it: bleach and an acid bowl cleaner used one after the other in a small room with the door shut and no fan running produce a gas that will drop a healthy adult.
  • Give the rule as three plain instructions, use one product, ventilate, never store the two together, shown with capped bottles only and the door and window open in frame.
Shots
  • Camera resting flat on the tile behind the pedestal, on a cleaner bottle with a loose cap.
  • Macro on the cap being tightened fully.
  • Close on the bottle going back into the labeled cleaning bin.
  • Three quarter of the door and window being opened, air visibly moving a light curtain.
  • Overhead of two capped bottles being placed into separate containers, well apart.
On-screen text
  • Floor level, cap loose
  • One product, door open
  • Never store them together
Short cut · 45–60s The camera lies flat on the tile behind a toilet pedestal, at a crawling child's eye height, staring straight at a bowl cleaner bottle with the cap sitting loose on it.
Stands alone: Name the room and finish on the fix, cap tight and straight back into the cleaning bin every time, so the Short ends on an action rather than a warning.
Standardize Five checkable lines, put where the person holding the brush will read them.
Beats
  • Read the five lines against the finished zone: one visible reserve roll, backstock in the cabinet, brush dry in its holder, liner in the can, and no ring at the water line.
  • Write those five lines by hand on a card and stand the card upright in the cleaning bin.
  • Make the placement argument, that the person holding the brush reads the standard at the exact moment they can meet it, rather than on a fridge or in a folder.
  • Settle the call as part of the standard: splayed bristles or liquid in the holder means both go out today and a fresh set comes in, and from then on the brush gets rinsed in the flush and propped under the closed seat to drip before it goes back. Offer the honest alternative, that a disposable head version ends the argument for anyone who will not realistically do that handling.
Shots
  • Close on a hand writing five short lines on a card.
  • Three quarter of the card standing upright in the cleaning bin.
  • Close on a splayed brush and its holder of gray water going into a bag together.
  • Macro on a fresh brush propped under a closed seat, dripping.
  • Wide of the finished zone with all five standard items visible in one frame.
On-screen text
  • Five lines, one card
  • Read it while holding the brush
  • Splayed means out today
Short cut · 30–45s A splayed toilet brush and its holder of gray water both go into a bin bag in a single movement.
Stands alone: Give the two part test before the disposal, splayed bristles or liquid standing in the holder, so a viewer can walk off and check their own.
Sustain The trigger is a trip already being made on a fixed night, plus the monthly habit a room nobody uses still needs.
Beats
  • Give the trigger from the standard: carrying the trash out on collection night already puts you standing here, so a new liner drops in and the reserve roll gets checked while the bag is in your hand.
  • Shoot it as one continuous motion, bag out, liner in, roll straightened, so it is visible that nothing was added to the evening.
  • Close the loop on the monthly habit for a room nobody uses, a mug of water down the traps and a bowl treatment with full dwell time whether or not anybody has been in here.
Shots
  • Three quarter of a bag being lifted out of the can.
  • Close on a fresh liner being snapped into the empty can.
  • Close on a hand straightening the reserve roll upright.
  • Overhead of a mug of water going down the sink and then the floor drain.
On-screen text
  • Collection night is liner night
  • Bag out, liner in, roll upright
Short cut · 30–45s One unbroken take from beside the bin: bag out, fresh liner snapped in, a hand straightens the spare roll, done.
Stands alone: Name the trigger, trash collection night, and say which room this is, since the whole idea is attaching the task to a trip already being made.
Close

Hold the finished zone wide and read the standard off what is in frame: one reserve roll visible from the seat, a dry brush in a dry holder, a lined can, and no ring at the water line. Then show the card standing in the cleaning bin and run the trigger, bag out and liner in on collection night.

Next: The room is clean and stocked. The last thing a guest touches is a towel, so next we deal with the good ones you have never let anybody use.

Shot list
  • Three quarter tripod at bowl height for the clearing, the placement work and the finished frames.
  • Seated height camera position beside the bowl for the reserve roll reach test.
  • Camera resting on the tile behind the pedestal, used for both the dust and splash reveal and the child eye height chemical beat.
  • Macro on a tabletop tripod for the rim, the water line ring, the seat hinges and the cap threads.
  • Small battery panel set low on the tile for raking light behind the pedestal.
  • Overhead arm rig over a towel on the floor for the cleared tank top contents.
  • Flat surface setup for writing the five line standard card.
  • Bin side setup for the single take liner change, door open for ambient light.
Description hook

The brush in your guest bathroom is a consumable, not a fixture. Splayed bristles or liquid in the holder and both go out today.

MZ-069 · R12.05

Guest Linen Zone

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Good Towels, In Service Today”

Guest Towels: One Bundle Per Guest, Built From Your Best

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on two towel stacks side by side, one plush and untouched, one thin and gray, and a hand reaching past the good one for the worn one. Name the arrangement nobody in this house says out loud, that guests are not quite allowed to use the nice towels. Then set out the fact that breaks it, that towels thin whether they are used or not, so the good set is aging untouched on a shelf while visitors dry off on something gray.

Sort Every towel is unfolded and judged in daylight, not in closet light.
Beats
  • Carry the stack out to daylight and unfold every towel fully, on the point that closet light hides exactly the things you are looking for.
  • Name the four disqualifiers and show each one in frame: thin along the fold line, permanently gray, stiff from too much softener, or carrying a hair dye or nosebleed stain.
  • Anything disqualified leaves the guest stack and becomes a rag or a car towel today, shown being cut or bagged so it cannot come back.
  • Close the loophole out loud, that a disqualified towel does not go back on the shelf just in case.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the stack being carried out of the closet into window light.
  • Overhead of a towel unfolded flat and backlit, light coming through along the fold line.
  • Macro on a stain, then on a stiff, matted pile surface.
  • Close on a rejected towel being cut into rags on a hard surface.
  • Overhead of the survivors set against the discard pile.
On-screen text
  • Daylight, not closet light
  • Thin, gray, stiff, stained
  • Rag today, not just in case
Short cut · 30–45s A towel is held flat against a window and the light comes straight through along the fold line.
Stands alone: List all four disqualifiers inside the Short, since the backlight only demonstrates one of them, and say these are guest towels being judged.
Straighten Towels are stored as complete sets, so hosting is one lift instead of three searches.
Beats
  • Reject the usual method on camera, stacking like with like, and show its cost, that setting up for a visitor becomes three separate searches.
  • Build a bundle instead, bath towel, hand towel and washcloth folded together into one unit, with the fold sequence shown in full so it is repeatable.
  • Set the quantity honestly, two bundles ready covers most households, matched to the number of guests actually expected.
  • Give the bath mat its place flat underneath the bundles, and finish with a hand's width of air above the stack.
  • Name the shelf disqualifier, that no thin gray towel kept for the dog shares this shelf.
Shots
  • Overhead of three separate like with like stacks, then hands breaking them apart.
  • Overhead, locked and continuous, of the full bundle fold sequence.
  • Three quarter of one finished bundle lifted off the shelf in a single hand.
  • Close on the bath mat sliding in flat beneath the bundles.
  • Wide of the finished shelf with clear air above the stack.
On-screen text
  • One lift, not three searches
  • Bath towel, hand towel, washcloth
  • Air above the stack
Short cut · 45–60s Overhead and unbroken, three towels fold down into one bundle that then lifts off the shelf in a single hand.
Stands alone: Say what goes into the bundle before the fold starts and why it exists, so that setting up for a visitor is one lift rather than three searches.
Shine The stored set gets washed although nobody used it, and the closet gets checked for what it has been doing to them.
Beats
  • Give the reason the stored set goes in hot even though it looks clean, that a towel folded in a closed closet all season carries a musty note that appears the instant it gets wet.
  • Connect it to the shoot order and the working order, that the wash goes in before anything else in the room is touched and this shelf finishes last because the cycle sets the pace.
  • Wipe the empty shelf, then run a flat hand along the back wall of the closet, saying what the hand is checking for, damp, which is what the towels have been drinking.
  • Show what that damp looks like on the back wall, so a viewer can recognise it in their own closet.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the stored set going into the machine untouched and unused.
  • Close on the empty shelf being wiped end to end.
  • Macro of a flat hand moving along the closet back wall under the small panel.
  • Macro on a damp patch or bloom on that back wall, panel set low for raking light.
On-screen text
  • Wash it even though it is clean
  • Check the back wall
  • Damp is what they drink
Short cut · 30–45s A stack of clean looking guest towels goes straight into a hot wash without anybody having used them, then a flat hand runs along the closet back wall behind where they were sitting.
Stands alone: Explain that this is stored guest linen nobody has touched, and that the wash and the wall check are one job, since the closet is why the towels smell of the closet.
Safety Burn or fire, and fall, both specific to a linen shelf in a shared closet.
Beats
  • Burn or fire: if this closet also holds the water heater, show towels pressed against the tank, a hot pipe, or the heater's cable, and be plain that no amount of neat folding fixes a scorch and fire risk.
  • Set the clearance rule and measure it on camera, a hand's width of clear air around anything that gets hot, with no stack leaning on the unit and no cable trapped behind one.
  • Free the cable from behind the stack and route it clear.
  • Fall: bring the bath mat back in for the second hazard, a curled or hardened rubber backing. Flex it so the cracks open on camera, and give the failure, that it stops gripping tile and slides out from under someone stepping off wet.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the shared closet showing textiles pressed against a water heater or hot pipe.
  • Close on a flat hand held against the tank to measure clearance, then the stack pulled back to that line.
  • Macro on a cable trapped behind a stack, then freed and routed clear.
  • Macro on a bath mat backing being flexed, cracks opening across the rubber.
  • Low close of that mat sliding on tile under a light push.
On-screen text
  • A hand's width of clear air
  • Folding does not fix heat
  • Cracked backing stops gripping
Short cut · 30–45s A bath mat is turned over and the rubber backing gets flexed until cracks open right across it.
Stands alone: Say what the backing is for and what the cracks mean, that it stops gripping tile and slides out from under a wet foot stepping off a tub.
Standardize The shelf is marked so a missing bundle reads as a gap without anyone counting, and the good towels go into service.
Beats
  • State the shelf standard, two complete bundles on the marked shelf with the bath mat flat beneath them.
  • Mark the shelf edge where the second bundle ends, and give what the mark does, it turns a count into a look.
  • Demonstrate it by lifting one bundle away so the exposed mark reads as an obvious gap, then putting it back.
  • Name the standard as Chapter 24 teaches, so the shelf, the mark and the name all agree and the household calls it the same thing every time.
  • Settle the call as the hardest clause here: the guest bundle is built from the best towels in the house, put into service today, and the ones they replace get demoted to rags on the same trip so they cannot creep back. Handle the exception too, that a towel genuinely too good for a guest is not linen at all, it is a keepsake, and it belongs anywhere except this shelf.
Shots
  • Close on a mark being made along the shelf edge.
  • Overhead of two bundles sitting flush to the mark.
  • Matched overhead with one bundle lifted away and the mark exposed.
  • Close on the old set going into the rag bag on the same trip.
  • Close on a keepsake towel being carried out of the linen closet entirely.
On-screen text
  • Mark where the second bundle ends
  • A gap you see, not count
  • Best towels, in service today
Short cut · 30–45s One towel bundle lifts off a shelf and the mark drawn underneath it suddenly reads as an obvious gap.
Stands alone: Explain the mark and the shelf standard, two bundles with the mark at the end of the second, before the bundle is lifted, or the reveal has nothing to land on.
Sustain The guest leaving is the trigger, and the whole loop closes before you sit down.
Beats
  • Give the trigger exactly as the standard states it: the guest's departure starts it, bed and bathroom get stripped together, washed together, and the shelf restocked before you sit down.
  • Show the used bathroom set going into the same load as the bed linen, one wash and one trip.
  • Show the shelf restocked before the sheets are dry, on the point that this shelf is never left part stocked waiting on somebody's memory.
  • Close the room out by noting that a full marked shelf is what makes the next arrival a single walk through rather than a search.
Shots
  • Three quarter of bedding gathered and carried through with the bathroom set balanced on top.
  • Close on both going into the machine together.
  • Overhead of fresh bundles going back onto the marked shelf.
  • Wide of the finished closet, a hand's width of air above a full stack.
On-screen text
  • Bed and bathroom, one wash
  • Restock before you sit down
Short cut · 30–45s Stripped bed linen and used bathroom towels get carried through in one armful and go into the same machine together.
Stands alone: Name the trigger, a guest leaving, and finish on the shelf restocked before the sheets are dry so the loop closes inside the Short.
Close

Hold the finished shelf and read the standard against it: two complete bundles, a bath towel plus a hand towel plus a washcloth in each, the bath mat folded flat beneath, and the mark showing where the second bundle ends. Then run the trigger in full, the guest leaves, bed and bathroom get stripped and washed together, and the bundles go back before the sheets are dry.

Next: That wash is running now, and it has to come out right. Next we follow it into the room where every standard in this house either holds or quietly falls apart, the laundry room.

Shot list
  • Three quarter tripod at shelf height in the linen closet, the primary setup for storage, marking and the finished reveal.
  • Overhead arm rig on a table near a window for the full unfold, the inspection and the bundle fold sequence.
  • Backlit window position for the towel thinning test, with a dark card opposite to control flare.
  • Macro on a tabletop tripod for stains, pile texture, mat backing cracks and the closet back wall.
  • Small battery panel for the closet interior and the back wall damp check.
  • Low close on tile for the bath mat slide hazard.
  • Water heater or hot pipe setup in the shared closet for the clearance beat, with a flat hand for scale.
  • Machine side setup for the wash going in at the start of the room and the combined load at the end.
  • Hallway carry through position for the departure trigger sequence.
Description hook

Your guests dry off on the worn towels while the good ones age untouched on a shelf. Towels thin whether anyone uses them or not.

6Sguest bathroomlinen closettowel organizationguest towelshome standardslaundry routine6S Success

Room 13 of 20

Laundry Room

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteMost laundry rooms are interior and narrow, lit by one overhead bulb, so the working light is that fixture plus whatever spills through the open door from the nearest window. Lift the shadow under the machine lids with a white bounce card or a folded sheet angled off the ceiling rather than adding a second source, and shoot the machines with the tripod set low and tight against the opposite wall for three-quarter angles, since there is rarely room to stand back. For tops of machines and the folding counter, reverse the centre column or stand the tripod on the counter itself and angle down; there is no space for an overhead rig and no second pair of hands on this shoot. Record all voiceover separately, because a running drum, a spin cycle and an extractor fan will bury a live track. On set safety, and this is not optional because the camera does not care: unplug the dryer at the wall and shut off both taps before any shot that involves pulling a machine out, tilting it back, or disconnecting a duct or a fill hose. Sheet metal under a tilted machine is sharp, so gloves on the hands in frame for those setups. Bleach and any ammonia based cleaner stay capped in every shot and are never opened in the same take, even for illustration. Keep the walking line between door and machines clear of cable at all times, and tape down anything crossing the floor near the drying rack, since that floor gets wet on purpose in one of these shoots.
MZ-070 · R13.01

Washer and Dryer

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Behind the dryer”

Washer and Dryer Reset: Lint Screen, Door Gasket, and the Dryer Duct

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on towels going round for a second tumble while a hand rests on a warm dryer casing, the household's standing excuse in one image, that the machine just runs a bit slow these days. Then narrow the whole video to the single question this zone turns on, the month the dryer was last pulled out and the duct cleared, and frame what follows as what happens when nobody in the house can name it.

Sort Both machine tops and both drums come clear in one pass, and what comes off leaves the room instead of moving sideways.
Beats
  • Both machine tops shown as found, then hands sweeping the whole surface into one holding basket, so nothing gets sorted while it is still standing on a lid.
  • A hand reaching into the washer drum and behind the agitator for the single sock, which goes to the folding zone basket rather than back onto a machine.
  • The three usual survivors handled one at a time, a hardened box of dryer sheets, a bottle of softener that stopped being used, a cap with no bottle, each routed out of the room rather than shelved.
  • The rule that governs this pass made visible: nothing coming off one machine is allowed to land on the other.
Shots
  • Overhead of both machine tops as found, one continuous take of hands clearing them into a basket
  • Three-quarter of a hand reaching behind the agitator and coming out with a sock

  • The burn or fire question opened on the lint screen, pulled and cleared, including the lint that collects on the heating element side of the screen housing.

Detergent and Treatment Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “One product per job”

Laundry Detergent Shelf Reset: One Product Per Job, Dose Line Marked

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the shelf every laundry room grows: a box of dye grabbing sheets, two spray bottles, a stain stick dried solid in its cap, and something a relative swore by. A hand reaches past all of them for the one bottle that actually gets used. Frame the real problem behind the crowding, that binning a mostly full bottle feels wasteful, so the bottles sit there being wasteful slowly while holding the one arm's reach of shelf next to the open washer lid.

Sort Every container comes down to the floor, and three named disqualifiers decide what earns a place back on the shelf.
Beats
  • Every bottle, stick, spray and pod tub lined up on the floor in a single row, so the true count is visible in one frame instead of estimated on a shelf.
  • The three disqualifiers applied on camera, one container at a time: crusted shut at the neck, label washed off so the dose cannot be read, bought for one stain that already came out.
  • Two open jugs of the same detergent resolved into one jug in use and one refill, rather than two half jugs each holding shelf space.
  • The hardest version of the call landed in frame: the one treatment whose work has actually been watched held beside a tub of oxygen powder, with every remaining spray and stick routed to the disposal pile in the same pass.
Shots
  • Overhead of the full floor row of containers, wide enough to count them

  • Every bottle on the floor
  • Crusted, unreadable, one stain
  • Keep what you have watched work
