Stands alone: Establish that this is the detergent and stain treatment shelf in a laundry room, name the three disqualifiers as containers are picked up, and state the keep rule, one treatment you have watched lift a stain plus a tub of oxygen powder.
Straighten Placement set by the open washer lid, with everyday detergent in the reaching spot and pods above the basket test.
Beats
  • The washer lid opened and the arm's reach arc from it traced on camera, then the everyday detergent and its dosing cap set inside that arc.
  • Bleach and the stain sprays moved onto a tray behind the detergent, second row, still visible but out of the one spot a hand goes to mid load.
  • The pod tub placed higher than a child reaches on tiptoe from an upturned laundry basket, with the basket in frame as the measuring stick.
  • The arc tested a second time with a wet hand holding a garment, so placement is settled by how the shelf is used with the drum open rather than by how the bottles look lined up.
Shots

  • Everyday within reach
  • Pods above the basket test

Stands alone: Explain that a toddler will climb on whatever is in the room, so pod height gets measured from an upturned basket, and that the tub needs a latched lid or a high shelf without exception.
Shine Detergent always drips, so the fix is a wipeable tray under everything rather than more wiping.
Beats
  • The tacky ring under a detergent jug and the dried trail down its spigot shown first, so the problem is visible before anything is cleaned.
  • The spigot and the shelf beneath it wiped, framed as the last time this shelf gets cleaned this way.
  • Every container stood on a shallow tray, so the next drip lands on plastic that rinses rather than a shelf that stays tacky for a year.
  • The tray lifted and rinsed once at the sink, which is now the entire maintenance job for this shelf.
Shots
  • Tripod close, macro framing on the sticky ring left under a jug
  • Close on a cloth wiping the spigot and the shelf beneath
  • Overhead of containers being lowered onto the shallow tray

On-screen text
  • It will always drip
  • Let it land on plastic
Short cut · 30–45s A detergent jug is lifted off a shelf and the camera holds on the tacky brown ring it has been sitting in.
Stands alone: Say that detergent drips no matter how carefully it is poured and that wiping is not the fix, then show the shallow tray going under every container and being rinsed in one lift.
Safety This is the 4th S. Two chemical hazards specific to this shelf, plus the blind high reach that drops a full jug.
Beats
  • The poison, choke or strangle question opened on a detergent pod, which looks exactly like a sweet to a toddler and bursts in the mouth, so the tub gets a latched lid or a high shelf without exception.
  • The separation rule enforced on camera with both containers capped throughout: bleach and any ammonia based cleaner moved onto different shelves, never sharing a shelf and never sharing a bucket, because a spill in a small room with the door shut can mix the two into a gas.
  • The fall, cut or crush question shown as the combination that causes it, a full jug stored above head height, a smooth handle, a wet hand, and a reach made with no line of sight into the shelf.
  • The same full jug relocated down to the low shelf in frame, so the correction is watched rather than recommended.

Sorting and Hamper Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Every bag is a load”

Laundry Sorting System: Hampers That Make a Full Load

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on five hampers, one of them a third full, with a hand lifting out the single garment someone has been waiting three weeks to wear, then setting it back where it was. Put the count on screen against the test that decides it, whether any of these bags has run as a full load, by itself, in the last month. Frame the problem as clothes taken out of circulation by a sorting scheme the household never actually honoured.

Sort Every hamper is emptied to see what a real week produces, and the streams that never fill get merged.
Beats
  • All five hampers tipped out into separate floor piles, whites, darks, towels, delicates and work clothes, so the real weekly volume is visible instead of assumed.
  • The test applied to each pile in turn on camera: a stream earns its own bag only if it has run as a full load, by itself, in the last month.
  • The failing streams merged into cold and gentle, with a mesh bag loaded and dropped into the drum so the merge is a real method rather than a compromise.
  • The spare hampers that served those streams carried out of the room, since an empty bag standing in the corner invites the stream straight back.
Shots
  • Overhead of five hampers tipped out into five distinct floor piles
  • Close on a hand lifting the pile too thin to have made a load in a month
  • Close on delicates going into a mesh bag and the mesh bag into the drum

On-screen text
  • What does a real week make
  • Full load in the last month
  • Merge, then remove the bag
Short cut · 45–60s Five laundry hampers are tipped into five floor piles and one of the piles is visibly too thin to ever fill a machine.
Stands alone: State the test in the opening beat, that a sorting stream earns its own bag only if it has run as a full load by itself in the last month, and show the mesh bag in the drum as where the merged items go.
Straighten Bags stand where clothes come off, and pocket contents get a dish so they stop reaching the drum.
Beats
  • One bag per surviving stream placed where clothes are actually taken off, cut against where those bags had drifted, which is wherever they happened to fit.
  • The walking line between the door and the washer shown as bare floor, with every bag standing clear of it.
  • A small dish added on the shelf for pocket contents, with coins, hair ties and a memory stick landing in it rather than in the drum.
  • Bag size treated as a placement decision, since a bag that empties before it passes half full is a bag the household keeps using.

  • Overhead of the floor with the walking line clear and bags set to the sides
  • Three-quarter of a bag moved from beside the machine to where clothes come off
  • Tripod close, macro framing on coins, hair ties and a memory stick dropping into the shelf dish
  • Wide of bare floor in front of the washer door
On-screen text
  • Where clothes come off
  • Clear the walking line
  • A dish for pockets
Short cut · 30–45s A hamper is dragged out of the path between the door and the washer, and the bare floor it leaves behind is held in frame.
Stands alone: Say that laundry bags belong where clothes are taken off rather than where they happen to fit, and show the pocket dish going onto the shelf as the second half of the fix.
Shine Hampers smell because of damp kit rather than dirt, so this pass is emptiness plus air.

  • Damp gym kit lifted from the bottom of a lined bag with the lid down, named as the cause of the smell rather than dirt.
  • The stained inside seams of that liner shown, which is what a bag that has been holding wet towels actually looks like when you inspect it.
  • Each bin wiped out while it is empty, which is the only point in the week it can be done properly.
  • The alternative shown in the same pass, damp kit laid out or hung until it can go straight into a load, and the bag left standing with its lid open.

  • Damp kit is the smell
  • Wipe it while it is empty
Short cut · 30–45s A wet towel is pulled from the bottom of a lined hamper and the camera drops straight to the stained seam underneath it.

  • The fall question staged at floor level: a hamper standing in the walking line between the door and the machines, then the same frame with the leading edge of a carried load blocking the floor where it stands.

  • Safety is the 4th S

  • Overhead of three bags, all labels legible in one frame

  • Hot towels. Cold darks. Gentle.

Stands alone: Explain that a colour tells nobody which setting the bag wants, and that labeling by the load it makes lets anyone in the house start a machine without asking.

  • The trigger shown exactly as it happens at the end of the day, hands turning a trouser pocket out over the shelf dish before the trousers drop into the bag.

Folding Surface

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Bare or one load”

Laundry Folding Counter Reset: Bare, or Holding One Load

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a folding counter carrying a growing bag of unmatched socks, kept because a partner does occasionally surface, which is exactly why the bag never gets thrown out. A dry load arrives with nowhere to land and goes back in for a second tumble. Frame the problem as a permanent tenant on the one surface in this room that has to stay clear, since the counter is where the whole room jams.

Sort Everything parked on this counter that was never laundry comes off, down to bare surface.
Beats
  • The counter cleared in one continuous pass, each object named as it comes off, the post, the toolbox, the parcel waiting to be returned, the vase from Christmas.
  • The connection made explicit, that whatever is parked here is why the dry load went back in for a second tumble.
  • The single sock call handled on camera: loose singles go into one shoebox and nothing larger, and everything already beyond that box goes today.

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Frame the problem as a running cost rather than a neutral care label, and name the resident garment as the thing holding the rack hostage.

  • The crevice tool that fits no vacuum still in the house test fitted to the hose, refused, and binned, since an attachment with no machine is not a spare part.
  • The rag rule applied: rags live in one bin and only one bin, nothing new becomes a rag until something old leaves as waste, and a bin that cannot be worked through in a year is cloth being stored rather than saved.
  • The second vacuum kept for the garage settled by the same test, since one that has not run in a year is a broken machine with an excuse rather than a spare.

broom storagemop storagecleaning supply storageshadow boardutility closetlaundry room organization6Shome reset

Room 14 of 20

Home Office

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteShoot on a bright overcast day with the desk turned so window light rakes across the surface from the side, which is what makes dust, toner film, and forearm grime read on camera. Everything in this room is either paper or electronics, so kill the overheads and bounce daylight off a white card rather than adding a lamp that reflects off screens and scanner glass. No lighting rig, no second operator, no crane, no drone: one person, one tripod, one clamped overhead arm, a beanbag for the positions a tripod leg will not fit. Headless throughout, meaning nothing above the wrists is ever in frame, no faces, no piece to camera, and no second body walking into shot. Two tripod positions cover most of the room: the overhead arm clamped to the desk edge for surface and drawer work, and a three-quarter tripod at seated eye height on the writing-hand side for shelf, printer, and cabinet work. Access is the constraint, not light, because a filing cabinet drawer or a printer back panel leaves no room for a tripod leg, so plan the beanbag for those and shoot them locked off rather than handheld where you can. For the floor spreads, raise the tripod and shoot high angle from the step stool rather than trying to get a true overhead. On-set safety: power everything down before any cleaning shot, spray cleaner onto the cloth off camera and never toward a screen, anchor the bookshelf and the filing cabinet to the wall before you load them for the anchoring shots, lift the fireproof box with two hands at floor level, and use the step stool in frame for every high-shelf reach, never the rolling chair.
MZ-076 · R14.01

Primary Desk

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Clear the desk first”

Home Office Desk Reset: The Full 6S Pass on the Desk Surface

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the one corner of the desk held by a half-finished project, papers fanned and untouched for weeks, while the rest of the surface gets swept clear around it in a few seconds of the same shot. Establish that this corner is the reason the desk never finishes, because putting it away feels like admitting it is over. Frame the real problem as a naming problem rather than a tidying one: nobody in this house can say out loud what the next physical action on that pile is, so it stays, and the desk grows around it.

Sort Everything comes off the surface and only what the task in front of you needs goes back, plus the inbox tray.
Beats
  • Lift the entire surface onto the floor in one continuous pass, monitor and keyboard aside, so the desk is bare wood before a single decision gets made.
  • Show why the floor is the holding ground rather than a drawer: a drawer lets an item skip the decision, the floor does not.
  • Work the return pile item by item against the task actually in front of you today. Dead pens, the second mug, and the fringe of sticky notes around the monitor bezel do not go back up.
  • Handle the half-finished project corner as the hard case. Say the next physical action in one sentence. If it can be named, that sentence goes on a card clipped to the papers and the whole thing goes into the inbox tray. If it cannot be named, box it, date the lid, shelf it, and set the rule that an unopened box on that date next year leaves unopened.
  • Set the finished state: the inbox tray holds fewer than a dozen sheets and nothing else claims the surface.
Shots
  • Overhead locked wide of the full desk, one continuous unbroken clearing move from cluttered to bare
  • Close on hands peeling sticky notes off the monitor bezel one at a time into an open palm
  • Macro on a pen scribbling a test line on scrap and being dropped into the discard tub
  • Three-quarter on hands writing one short sentence on a card and clipping it to a stack of papers
  • Overhead of the dated box lid being marked and the box sliding onto a shelf
On-screen text
  • Bare surface first
  • Name the next action
  • Cannot name it? Box and date it
Short cut · 60–90s A hand clips a single index card to a stalled pile of paper, and the card holds one short sentence. Hold on it before revealing what the sentence is for.
Stands alone: Re-establish in the first few seconds that this is a home office desk and that the pile has sat untouched for weeks, since the Short has no cold open to lean on. Also restate the box-and-date fallback in full, because it is the half of the rule that makes the test safe to apply.
Straighten Positions on this desk are chosen by how the keyboard, notebook, and mouse are actually reached for, not by symmetry.
Beats
  • Place the keyboard square in front of the monitor and mark the position, establishing that fixed means fixed rather than roughly central.
  • Put the notebook on the writing-hand side and the phone face down beyond it, following the reach you make most often.
  • Sweep an arm across the full arc the mouse travels and clear everything inside it, showing a stapler parked in that arc being steered around and then removed.
  • Compare the finished layout against the tape mark at the keyboard corner, so the viewer can see what fixed position means in practice.
Shots
  • Overhead of hands squaring the keyboard to the monitor, with a low-tack tape mark going down at the corner
  • Close on the notebook and face-down phone being set on the writing-hand side
  • Overhead of a hand tracing the full mouse arc across the bare desk and pushing a stapler out of it
  • Three-quarter locked at seated eye height, final layout, no hands in frame
On-screen text
  • Fixed positions
  • Clear the mouse arc
Short cut · 30–45s An overhead hand traces a wide arc across a bare desk, and every object caught inside the arc gets pushed out of frame.
Stands alone: Say plainly that the arc is the sweep the mouse travels, and name the three fixed positions again, because without the parent video the tracing move reads as decoration rather than a test.
Shine Cleaning around a live screen safely, and the underside lip where forearms rest.
Beats
  • Power everything down first and show the screen going dark, since the dark screen is what lets you see the film you are about to remove.
  • Spray cleaner onto the microfiber cloth, never onto the screen, and show why: liquid on glass runs down into the bezel and the electronics behind it.
  • Move to the desk edge, then to the underside lip where forearms rest, which is the grubbiest surface in the room precisely because it is the one nobody sees.
  • Show what the wipe turns up on this desk: the cable that has slipped out of its clip under the lip, the monitor arm bolt that has worked loose, the sticky ring where the mug has been parked.
Shots
  • Close on the power button and the screen dropping to black
  • Macro on cleaner being sprayed into a folded cloth held away from the desk
  • Raking side-light close on the cloth crossing the screen, film lifting on the pass
  • Low three-quarter under the desk edge, hand wiping the underside lip, grime visible on the cloth after
On-screen text
  • Power down first
  • Spray the cloth, not the screen
  • Clean to inspect
Short cut · 30–45s A cloth comes out from under the front lip of a desk visibly grey, from a surface the camera has not shown yet.
Stands alone: Establish where the underside lip is with one clear reveal shot before the wipe, and restate the spray-the-cloth rule, since a viewer arriving cold may copy the cleaning without the safety half.
Safety A mug sharing the surface with the power strip, and the trip hazard in the arc the chair rolls through.
Beats
  • Show the mug sitting behind the keyboard on the same surface as the power strip and the laptop charger, and name the hazard as water and electricity.
  • Move drinks to the far side of the mouse, away from cables and the machine, so the fix is a fixed location rather than a promise to be careful.
  • Lift the power strip off the floor onto a hook fitted to the desk leg, showing the fitting going on and the strip clipping up.
  • Roll the chair through its full arc and check that no charging cable crosses it. The standard is that your feet find nothing under there.
  • Test the fixes by using the desk normally: reach for the mug from the working position and confirm the reach no longer crosses the keyboard, the charger, or the strip.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the mug, power strip, and charger sharing one surface, then the mug being moved out past the mouse
  • Close on a hook being fitted to the desk leg and the power strip lifting off the carpet
  • Low floor-level wide of the chair rolling its full arc across bare carpet
  • Macro on a charging cable being run up the desk leg and clipped clear of the floor
On-screen text
  • Water and electricity
  • Nothing under the chair arc
Short cut · 45–60s A floor-level camera watches a desk chair roll its full arc and stop dead against a charger cable stretched across the carpet.
Stands alone: Name the two hazards explicitly as fall and as water and electricity, and show both fixes, the strip hooked off the floor and the mug moved past the mouse, because the Short loses the segment framing that identified them.
Standardize A photograph of this desk settles what clear means, so the word stops being a matter of opinion in this household.
Beats
  • Photograph the cleared desk from the seated three-quarter angle, framed as the ideal-state photo rather than a before-and-after.
  • Print it and tape it inside the top drawer, showing the tape going down, so the photo lives where the reset happens rather than on a wall.
  • Reload the desk lightly, then hold the print into frame beside it to show the gap the photo makes visible in one look.
  • Point to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, as where this comes from.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a phone framing the cleared desk, hands only
  • Close on the print being taped to the inside face of an open top drawer
  • Overhead split framing: the reloaded desk on one side of frame, the print held into the other
On-screen text
  • Photograph the finished state
  • Tape it inside the drawer
Short cut · 30–45s A printed photo of an empty desk is held up against the real desk behind it, and the two do not match.
Stands alone: Explain in one beat that the photo was taken at the end of a full reset of this same desk, otherwise the print reads as an aspirational picture pulled from somewhere else, and show where it gets taped.
Sustain The desk reset is tied to closing the laptop lid, because next morning is already too late.
Beats
  • Show the lid closing at the end of the working day and the reset starting before the person stands up.
  • Show why the trigger is the lid and not the morning: cut to the same pile at breakfast light, where it has been sitting overnight and now reads as normal.
  • Run the reset against the print taped inside the drawer, and finish with the surface matching it.
  • Restate the standard: the desk holds the tools of the current task plus one inbox tray, and nothing else stays overnight.
Shots
  • Close on the laptop lid closing, hands still on the desk
  • Overhead time-condensed pass of the surface returning to the photographed state
  • Three-quarter locked final of the desk in falling window light, bare, chair pushed in
On-screen text
  • Trigger: the lid closes
  • Nothing stays overnight
Short cut · 30–45s A laptop lid closes at the end of a working day, and instead of the hands leaving frame, they start putting the desk back.
Stands alone: State the standard in full, that the desk holds the current task plus one inbox tray, and say why the lid beats the morning, since the Short has no earlier segment to carry either point.
Close

Hold the final bare desk and put the standard on screen alongside the print taped in the drawer, then show the lid closing once more as the trigger that fires it. The point to land is that the photo and the trigger are the two halves of the same thing, one settles what right looks like and the other decides when you check.

Next: The surface is clear, which is exactly what you now need, because the next zone gets tipped out onto it.

Shot list
  • Overhead locked wide on the full desk, clamped arm, used for the clearing pass and the final reset
  • Three-quarter tripod at seated eye height on the writing-hand side, used for layout and the ideal-state photo
  • Macro on hands: pen tests, taping the card, clipping cables
  • Raking side-light close on the screen and desk edge for the cleaning pass
  • Low floor-level wide under the desk for the chair arc and the power strip lift
  • Close on the top drawer interior for the taped print
  • Same seated three-quarter in late-afternoon window light for the closing locked shot
Description hook

The desk is the first zone in the home office because every other zone in the room gets emptied onto it. Here is the full six pass reset, hands only, from bare surface to the standard that keeps it.

MZ-077 · R14.02

Desk Drawers and Pedestal

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Empty the cable bag”

Desk Drawers and the Cable Bag: A 6S Pass on the Drawer You Reach Into Blind

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the bag of cables, adapters, and wall bricks being lifted out of the pedestal, heavy and tangled, and set down on the cleared desk. Establish why it has survived every previous attempt: each individual cable is too cheap to think about and too specific to throw away, so the decision gets made one cable at a time and therefore never gets made at all. Frame the fix as emptying the whole lot at once so the decision is made in one sitting rather than a hundred.

Sort The top drawer gets tipped out and every pen gets tested, and the cable lot gets settled in one sitting.
Beats
  • Tip the whole top drawer onto the cleared desk, showing that the surface finished in the previous zone is what makes this possible.
  • Test every pen on scrap paper, since the test removes the argument: a pen either writes or it does not.
  • Clear dried highlighters, bent paperclips, loose staples, and dead batteries as a single sweep rather than as individual decisions.
  • Empty the entire cable lot at once. Pick up each cable, name the device it powers, and point at where that device physically is in this house. No device, no keep.
  • Keep exactly one spare of each connector type still used daily, coil and band it, and bag the rest for electronics recycling this week.
Shots
  • Overhead of the drawer inverting onto the cleared desk in one move
  • Macro on pen tips scribbling test lines on scrap, keepers and rejects landing in separate piles
  • Overhead wide of the full cable spread laid out flat across the desk at once
  • Close on a single cable being lifted, then a hand pointing off frame toward the device
  • Close on a kept cable being coiled and banded, then the recycling bag being tied
On-screen text
  • Test every pen
  • Name the device, point at it
  • One spare per connector
Short cut · 60–90s The entire contents of a cable bag hit a bare desk at once, and a hand starts picking cables up one at a time and pointing off camera.
Stands alone: Explain the point-at-the-device rule in the first line, and say why the whole bag has to come out in one go, because a viewer arriving cold will otherwise read this as a tidy-up rather than a rule with a pass and a fail.
Straighten Daily hand tools and hanging files each get their own drawer, and the two never mix.
Beats
  • Set the divided tray into the top drawer and load pens, stapler, and scissors into their slots.
  • Fill the deep pedestal drawer with hanging files and stand the tabs in one line.
  • Show the separation failing first: a stapler riding on the folders and a folder laid flat across the pens, then both put right, because the moment they mix, both drawers stop working.
  • Reach into the top drawer without looking and find the stapler first time, which is the test this layout has to pass.
Shots
  • Overhead of the divided tray dropping into the top drawer and being loaded slot by slot
  • Three-quarter of hanging file tabs being aligned into a single straight line
  • Overhead of both drawers open in one frame, the separation obvious
  • Close on a hand reaching in without looking and closing on the stapler first time
On-screen text
  • One purpose per drawer
  • Tabs in one line
Short cut · 30–45s Two drawers open at once in a single overhead frame, one all small tools in slots, one all file tabs in a straight line.
Stands alone: Name both drawers and their jobs up front, and state the never-mix rule as the takeaway, since the visual contrast alone does not carry the reason.
Shine The debris in a drawer bottom, and the runners that make a drawer need a shove.
Beats
  • Vacuum the drawer bottoms with a crevice tool and show what comes up: eraser crumbs, loose staples, paperclip fuzz.
  • Connect the loose staples to the blind reach, since a staple standing in a drawer bottom is what catches a finger going in without looking.
  • Wipe the runners and close the drawer with one finger, cutting that against the shove it needed before.
  • Treat the shove itself as the signal that was being ignored, which is what cleaning to inspect means in a drawer.
Shots
  • Macro into an empty drawer bottom, raking light picking out staples and crumbs
  • Close on the crevice tool running the drawer corners
  • Close on a cloth running along the runner rails
  • Side-on of the drawer closing with one finger, no shove
On-screen text
  • Vacuum the corners
  • Wipe the runners
  • The shove was the signal
Short cut · 30–45s Raking light across an empty desk drawer bottom reveals a scatter of loose staples standing point up.
Stands alone: Connect the staples to the blind reach in the same breath, because that link is what makes this more than a cleaning clip.
Safety Sharp points in a drawer you reach into blind, and a loaded pedestal that tips.
Beats
  • Show the blind reach in real conditions: a hand going into the open drawer while the monitor glows in the background, and name the hazard as fall, cut, or crush.
  • Give scissors and the letter opener their own slot with points facing the back of the drawer, showing the fitted slot rather than describing it.
  • Show the tipping risk with the loaded file drawer pulled fully out while the top drawer is open, weight visibly moving forward, then set the rule of one drawer at a time.
  • Land the point that the fix is a fixed slot and a rule, not carefulness, since a blind reach is exactly what removes carefulness.
Shots
  • Three-quarter at drawer height, hand entering the open drawer with the monitor glowing behind, nothing above the wrists in frame
  • Overhead close on scissors being set point-down and point-to-back into a fitted slot
  • Low three-quarter on the pedestal with the loaded file drawer extended, weight shifting forward
  • Close on the top drawer being closed before the file drawer opens
On-screen text
  • Points to the back
  • One drawer at a time
Short cut · 45–60s A hand goes into a desk drawer without looking, and the camera stays down in the drawer showing what is loose in there.
Stands alone: State the blind reach as the reason the slot exists, and restate the one-drawer-at-a-time rule with the tipping shot, since both halves are needed for the Short to be useful on its own.
Standardize Drawer fronts get labelled in the words this house actually uses.
Beats
  • Write what each drawer front holds using the household's own words, and show an office word being crossed out and replaced with the word people in this house actually say.
  • Run the test on camera: tape and stamps get found by reading the fronts, without pulling three drawers open.
  • Show the labels going on both fronts so the pair reads as one set rather than two odd labels.
Shots
  • Macro on a label being written by hand, an office word crossed out and rewritten
  • Close on the label going onto the drawer front, both drawers in frame
  • Three-quarter of a hand reading across the two fronts and opening exactly one drawer
On-screen text
  • Label in your own words
  • Found without hunting
Short cut · 30–45s Two labelled drawer fronts fill the frame, a hand reads across them, and only one drawer opens.
Stands alone: Show the label being written in plain household words with the office word crossed out, not only the finished front, because the wording choice is the whole point of the clip.
Sustain The drawers get put back when the household bills get paid.
Beats
  • Open on the bill-paying sitting already under way at the desk, which is the trigger that already exists in this house.
  • Gather everything that migrated out of the drawers onto the desk that week and put it back before the session ends.
  • Show why an existing sitting beats a reminder: you are already at this desk with the drawers at your knee and your hands free.
  • Close by restating the standard, one purpose per drawer, every pen writes, scissors point-down in a fixed slot.
Shots
  • Overhead of bills spread on the desk with drawer strays visible at the edges
  • Close on hands sweeping the strays back into their slots
  • Overhead of both drawers closing, desk clear
On-screen text
  • Trigger: bill day
  • Put back what migrated
Short cut · 30–45s A bill-paying session ends on a home office desk, and the hands do not stop, they start returning stray pens and clips to a drawer.
Stands alone: Name the trigger explicitly and say that it is an event this house already has, otherwise the clip reads as an extra chore rather than something riding on a sitting that was happening anyway.
Close

Open both drawers one last time against the labelled fronts and put the standard on screen, one purpose per drawer, every pen writes, scissors point-down in a fixed slot. Then cut to the bill-paying sitting to show the trigger firing, so the standard and the moment it gets checked land together.

Next: The hanging files now stand in one line, which raises the question this room has been avoiding, which of those papers you are actually required to keep.

Shot list
  • Overhead clamped arm on the desk surface for tip-outs, cable spread, and drawer loading
  • Overhead close directly into an open drawer for slots, staples, and labels
  • Macro rig for pen tests, label writing, and cable coiling
  • Three-quarter tripod at drawer height for the blind reach and the found-first-time shots
  • Low three-quarter on the pedestal for the tipping shot
  • Side-on close at drawer-runner height for the clean close
Description hook

The cable bag beats you because you keep trying to decide it one cable at a time. Empty the lot at once instead. A full six pass reset on the desk drawers and pedestal, hands only.

MZ-078 · R14.03

File Storage

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Keep, scan, or shred”

File Storage: Sorting Paper Into Keep, Scan, and Shred With a Retention Card

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a drawer of paper that is neither obviously permanent nor obviously rubbish, a bank statement, a utility bill, a receipt for something long gone, each held up and set back down undecided. Establish that this middle band is why the whole job stalls: the permanent originals are easy and the junk is easy, but most of the drawer sits between them and every sheet reopens the same unanswered question. Frame the video as supplying the rule that ends the question rather than the motivation to keep going.

Sort One drawer at a time into three piles, with the three-way rule that settles the middle band.
Beats
  • Set up three labelled piles on the cleared desk: keep as paper, scan then shred, shred now.
  • Work one drawer only, since this is hundreds of small calls in a row and a fresh start beats a long finish.
  • Split permanent originals out first, birth and marriage certificates, deeds, vehicle titles, wills, immigration papers. These leave the cabinet entirely and go to a closed fireproof box.
  • Give tax paper one folder per year, held for whatever the local retention period is, which gets looked up once and written down.
  • Apply the test to everything else: if the issuer will reprint it on request, or it already lives inside an online account, it is information rather than a record, and information does not get a folder. Warranties and manuals stay only for machines still in this house.
Shots
  • Overhead of three labelled piles being placed on a bare desk, drawer open at the edge of frame
  • Close on one drawer being pulled and a stack lifting out as a single block
  • Macro on a certificate being set into the fireproof box, lid closing
  • Overhead of tax paper being fanned into year folders
  • Close on a bank statement being dropped onto the shred pile
On-screen text
  • Three piles, one drawer
  • Originals leave the cabinet
  • Reprintable is information
Short cut · 60–90s Three labelled piles on a bare desk, and a single bank statement hovering between two of them before it lands.
Stands alone: State the reprint test in full in the opening line and name the three piles on screen, because the Short is carrying the one rule people came for and it has to stand alone.
Straighten Folders get named for the question you will ask when you go hunting, not for the type of document.
Beats
  • Write folder tabs as the questions people actually ask, so car, house, health, school.
  • Pull a tab reading Correspondence and replace it, since nobody has ever gone hunting for a folder with that name.
  • Set every tab in the same position so the eye runs one straight line down the drawer.
  • Ask a question out loud and land one hand on the right folder without a second look, which is the test the naming has to pass.
Shots
  • Macro on tabs being written, one word each
  • Overhead down the open drawer, tabs aligning into a single straight line
  • Close on a hand landing directly on one folder and lifting it clear
  • Three-quarter of the drawer closing on an even row of tabs
On-screen text
  • Name it as a question
  • Tabs in one line
Short cut · 30–45s A folder tab reading Correspondence is pulled out of a filing drawer and replaced with one reading Car.
Stands alone: State the naming rule as its own line, that folders get named for the question you will ask when hunting, since the swap on its own looks like a preference rather than a principle.
Shine Filing is the inspection pass, so the cleaning finds damp, silverfish, and fading print.
Beats
  • Empty a drawer fully and check the bottom for damp, showing what a stain and a wrinkled base look like.
  • Look for silverfish in the rear corners, because paper storage is exactly where they turn up.
  • Find a thermal receipt that has started to fade and photograph it flat before the print goes entirely.
  • Act on each find in the moment: the faded receipt's photo goes into its year folder, and the cabinet comes off the damp outside wall rather than getting noted for later.
Shots
  • Overhead into a fully emptied drawer with a torch raking the base
  • Macro into the rear corner of the drawer
  • Macro on a faded thermal receipt held to the window, print barely readable
  • Close on a phone photographing the receipt flat on the desk
On-screen text
  • Check for damp
  • Photograph fading receipts
  • Clean to inspect
Short cut · 30–45s A thermal receipt held up to a window is almost blank, and a phone photographs it before it goes entirely.
Stands alone: Say why an emptied filing drawer is the moment you catch this, and mention the damp and silverfish checks briefly, so the clip carries the whole inspection idea rather than one trick.
Safety Paper is the fuel load of this room, and a loaded cabinet tips.
Beats
  • Show the permanent originals coming out of a cardboard box on top of the cabinet and going into a closed fireproof box at floor level, lifted with two hands.
  • Name the hazard as burn or fire, and show the dense paper mass standing clear of the heater and of the power strip.
  • Show the tipping risk with a loaded top drawer pulled fully out, weight visibly forward, then anchor the cabinet to the wall on camera.
  • Set the working rule of one drawer open at a time and hold to it for the rest of the video.
Shots
  • Close on a cardboard box lifted off the cabinet top and its contents transferring into a fireproof box on the floor
  • Three-quarter wide showing the gap between cabinet, heater, and outlet
  • Low three-quarter on the loaded top drawer extended, weight forward
  • Beanbag close behind the cabinet on the anchor bracket and screw going into the wall
On-screen text
  • Originals to a fireproof box
  • Anchor the cabinet
  • One drawer at a time
Short cut · 45–60s A low camera watches a four drawer filing cabinet with the top drawer loaded and fully extended, and the whole unit starts to lean.
Stands alone: Name both hazards, tipping and fire, and show the anchor going in and the originals going into the fireproof box, so the clip ends on the fixes rather than on the scare.
Standardize The retention rule goes on a card taped inside the top drawer so it stops being re-decided.
Beats
  • Write the retention card: which categories are permanent, which run by tax year, which get scanned.
  • Tape it inside the top drawer where the decision actually happens, since a rule stored anywhere else gets re-argued every time.
  • Test the card by running a fresh sheet against it and letting the card make the call.
  • Land the frozen line, a standard is the best way you know today, written down, and point to Chapter 24, the checklist, the schedule, and the name.
Shots
  • Macro on the retention card being written, category by category
  • Close on the card being taped to the inside face of the open top drawer
  • Overhead of a new sheet held beside the card, then filed
On-screen text
  • Write the retention rule once
  • Tape it where you decide
Short cut · 45–60s A handwritten card is taped inside a filing drawer, and the next sheet of paper gets decided by reading the card rather than by thinking about it.
Stands alone: Read the three category bands the card names, permanent originals, tax by year, and scan then shred, since the card is the deliverable of the clip and a blurred prop will not do.
Sustain New tax paperwork arriving is the signal to pull and shred the oldest year that has passed retention.
Beats
  • Open on the new tax paperwork landing on the desk, which is the household event this hangs on.
  • Pull the oldest year folder that has passed the period written on the card and take it straight to the shred bag.
  • Drop the new year folder into the gap the old one left, so the one in, one out rhythm reads in a single frame.
  • Land why the drawer never overflows again: its size is now held by the swap rather than by a clear-out.
Shots
  • Close on new tax paperwork landing on the cleared desk
  • Overhead of the oldest year folder lifting out and the new one dropping into the same gap
  • Close on the shred bag by the door, filled and tied
On-screen text
  • Trigger: tax paperwork arrives
  • One in, one out
Short cut · 30–45s One year folder comes out of a filing drawer and another drops straight into the gap it left, in a single overhead take.
Stands alone: Name the trigger, tax paperwork arriving, and the retention card together, because the swap only works if the viewer knows what decided that the old folder was ready to go.
Close

End on the finished drawer, tabs in one line, the fireproof box closed at floor level, the shred bag by the door. Put the standard on screen, every folder named for the question you would ask, the retention card deciding what stays, then cut to the tax paperwork landing as the trigger that fires it once a year.

Next: Paper is settled, which leaves the shelf above it, and the books there are harder to release than any document in that drawer.

Shot list
  • Overhead clamped arm on the desk for the three pile sort and folder work
  • Overhead directly down into an open drawer for tabs and drawer base inspection
  • Macro rig with a torch for damp, silverfish, and faded thermal print
  • Low three-quarter on the cabinet for the tipping shot
  • Beanbag position behind the cabinet for the wall anchor, where a tripod leg will not fit
  • Three-quarter wide showing cabinet, heater, and outlet clearances
  • Close by the door on the shred bag for the closing frame
Description hook

Most of a filing drawer is neither obviously permanent nor obviously rubbish, and that middle band is why the job stalls. This is the three way rule and the retention card that end it.

MZ-079 · R14.04

Bookshelf and Reference Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Reference or display”

Home Office Bookshelf Reset: Reference at Eye Level, Weight Low, Unit Anchored

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the shelf holding textbooks from a degree, the professional library from a job that ended, and a reference set a website now answers faster, each pulled halfway out and pushed back. Establish that these are the hardest books in the house to release, because they stand for a version of you that has not been formally retired. Frame the coming decision as a question about when you last took one down rather than about whether you might one day.

Sort Every shelf empties in one go, and the display test settles the books that stand for who you used to be.
Beats
  • Take every book, binder, and manual off the shelves in one continuous pass rather than shelf by shelf, since partial emptying is what makes this job slow.
  • Clear the easy categories in one sweep: appliance manuals for machines that left the house, superseded editions with a year in the title, binders from finished projects.
  • Apply the call to the hard shelf. Ask when you last took it down since it arrived on this shelf, not whether you might one day.
  • If no specific occasion can be named and the book could be borrowed or reordered inside a week, it is no longer reference, it is display, and it goes into open competition for a display slot with everything else.
  • Handle manuals with the simpler blade: model still in the house, keep it, model gone, it goes today.
Shots
  • Locked wide from the tripod facing the unit, shelves emptying in one continuous sweep to bare boards
  • Macro on a copyright year on a title page and the book going to the out pile
  • Close on a hand lifting a textbook, holding it, and setting it into the display competition row
  • High angle from the step stool on the display competition row laid out on the floor, more books than slots
On-screen text
  • Empty every shelf first
  • When did you last take it down?
  • Reference or display
Short cut · 60–90s A row of books laid out on the floor beside a shelf that has visibly fewer slots than there are books.
Stands alone: Ask the when-did-you-last-take-it-down question out loud in the opening beat and name the borrow-or-reorder-in-a-week condition, because the display competition only makes sense once both halves of the test are on the table.
Straighten Height on this unit is set by the desk chair, mapped to how often you reach and how heavy the item is.
Beats
  • Mark seated eye level on the shelf upright with the tape held at the height of the desk chair, since that height is defined by where you actually sit rather than by the shelf spacing.
  • Load working reference at that mark, occasional reading at standing height, archive boxes highest, heavy binders lowest.
  • Show one rule doing two jobs at once, easy reach and low weight, which is why it survives contact with a real room.
  • Frame the finished unit from the chair position, the angle it was loaded for.
Shots
  • Three-quarter at seated chair height with a tape mark going onto the shelf upright
  • Locked wide facing the unit, books loading in bands, low to high
  • Close on heavy binders sliding onto the bottom two shelves
  • Locked three-quarter final from the chair position, no hands in frame
On-screen text
  • Eye level from the chair
  • Weight goes low
Short cut · 30–45s A strip of tape goes onto a shelf upright at the height of the desk chair rather than at standing height, and the shelf gets loaded around it.
Stands alone: Explain that the height is taken from the working chair, not while standing, since that is the entire difference between this and ordinary shelving advice.
Shine Dust from the top down, including the top edges of the books themselves.
Beats
  • Work top shelf downward with a dry cloth, since anything knocked loose lands on shelves not done yet.
  • Wipe the front edge of every shelf, which is the line the eye reads when it scans the unit.
  • Vacuum the top edges of the books with a brush head, because that is where the dust in this room actually settles rather than on the shelf boards.
  • Act on what the pass turns up, a shelf pin that has worked loose or a board that has bowed under the binders, before the shelf goes back on.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a dry cloth running the top shelf, dust visible in raking light
  • Locked close at shelf-front height, cloth travelling through a static frame, repositioned shelf by shelf
  • Macro on a brush vacuum head crossing the top edges of a row of books
  • Close on a shelf pin being checked and seated
On-screen text
  • Top down, always
  • Dust sits on the books
Short cut · 30–45s A brush vacuum head runs along the top edges of a row of books, and the dust line is visible where it has already passed.
Stands alone: State that book top edges, not shelf boards, are where the dust in an office settles, because that claim is the reason to watch, and say to work top shelf downward.
Safety An unanchored unit standing above the desk chair, with the weight loaded high.
Beats
  • Show the unit standing over the desk chair with binders and box files on the top shelf, and name the hazard as fall, cut, or crush.
  • Find the wall studs and screw the unit in on camera, showing the bracket and the fixing rather than describing them.
  • Move box files, binders, and any framed glass award off the high shelf that sits above head height at the working position.
  • Close on the finished sightline from the chair, so the proof is the shot rather than a claim.
Shots
  • Low three-quarter looking up at the loaded top shelf with the chair beneath it
  • Close on a stud finder crossing the wall and a pencil mark going down
  • Macro on the bracket and screw driving into the stud
  • Upward point of view from seated height, top shelf now light and clear
On-screen text
  • Anchor to the studs
  • Nothing heavy above your head
Short cut · 45–60s A camera at desk chair height looks straight up at a tall shelf unit loaded with box files, and the unit is fixed to nothing.
Stands alone: End on the anchor going into the stud and the top shelf cleared, and name the hazard plainly, so the clip resolves rather than only alarming.
Standardize A bookend and a hand's width of slack turn a full shelf into a visible signal.
Beats
  • Set a bookend closing every group and show the groups reading as separate blocks from across the room.
  • Leave a hand's width of empty shelf at the end of every row and measure it with an actual hand, so the standard needs no ruler.
  • Land the signal: when a shelf has no slack left, that is the visible sign a book has to leave, not that you need another shelf.
  • Point to Chapter 14, visual controls, where the shelf itself does the telling rather than a list.
Shots
  • Three-quarter wide of bookends closing each group across the unit
  • Close on a hand set flat in the gap at the end of a row as the measure
  • Locked close on two shelves in one frame, one packed solid, one with a hand's width at the end
On-screen text
  • A hand's width of slack
  • No slack means one leaves
Short cut · 30–45s A flat hand is placed in the gap at the end of a shelf row of books, and it just fits.
Stands alone: Say the rule that a shelf with no slack means a book leaves rather than that you buy another shelf, because that inversion is the whole idea, and show the hand as the only measure needed.
Sustain Finishing a book or closing a project binder is the moment the keep-or-go question gets asked.
Beats
  • Open on a book being finished and a project binder being closed out, the two moments that already happen in this room.
  • Stop the reflex return to the shelf and put the keep-or-go question right there, while the answer is still obvious.
  • Show both outcomes, one back on the shelf into its group, one into the outbound box.
  • Land why timing does the work: the same book asked about a year later is a much harder question.
Shots
  • Close on a book being closed on the last page
  • Close on project binder rings snapping shut
  • Overhead of the fork, one book to the shelf group, one to the outbound box
On-screen text
  • Trigger: you finish it
  • Ask before it goes back
Short cut · 30–45s A book is closed on its last page and the hand stops halfway back to the shelf.
Stands alone: Name the trigger as finishing a book or closing out a project binder, and say why asking at that moment is easier than asking a year later, since the pause on its own does not explain itself.
Close

Hold the finished unit from the desk chair position, bookends closing every group and a hand's width of slack at every row end, and put the standard on screen with the note that heavy binders and box files never live above head height. Then cut to a book closing on its last page as the trigger.

Next: The shelf is settled and anchored, which leaves the corner of this room that runs hot and gets ignored, the printer.

Shot list
  • Locked wide from the tripod facing the full shelf unit for emptying and loading
  • Three-quarter tripod at seated chair height for eye level marking and final frames
  • Low upward angle from the chair for the anchoring hazard and its resolution
  • Macro rig for copyright pages, shelf pins, bracket screws, and dust edges
  • Locked close at shelf-front height for the cleaning pass, repositioned shelf by shelf
  • High angle from the step stool for the display competition row and the outbound box
Description hook

The textbooks from a degree and the library from a job you left are the hardest books in the house to release. Here is the test that settles them, plus the anchoring and the slack rule that hold the shelf.

MZ-080 · R14.05

Printer and Scanning Station

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Plug it in today”

Printer Corner Reset: Clearance, a Paper Min Line, and the Backup Printer Test

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the old printer on the floor of the cupboard, dusty, cables still coiled on top of it, kept because it might be a backup. Establish that nobody has plugged it in for a long time and nobody knows whether it works, so it is not a backup, it is a large object with an undecided status sitting in a corner. Frame the video as settling that today with a test page rather than with a plan to test it sometime.

Sort Only ink, toner, and paper that matches the printer currently plugged in survives, and the backup gets tested now.
Beats
  • Read the model number off the printer that is actually plugged in and hold each cartridge box against it, one at a time.
  • Show the timing on unmatched cartridges: they sell this week for more than they will ever be worth again, because cartridge value only falls.
  • Clear the half reams of odd paper, the letterhead with the old address, and the envelopes from two houses ago.
  • Settle the backup printer on camera. Plug it in and print a test page now. If it prints and you will keep a spare cartridge in stock for it, it is a backup and it gets a home. If you will not plug it in today, it goes to electronics recycling this week.
Shots
  • Macro on the model number label on the printer body
  • Close on cartridge boxes being held one by one against that label, matches and misses landing in separate piles
  • Overhead of odd paper and old letterhead being fanned out and binned
  • Three-quarter of the old printer being plugged in and a test page feeding out
On-screen text
  • Match the model number
  • Print the test page today
  • Cartridge value only falls
Short cut · 45–60s An old printer that has not been switched on in years gets plugged in, and the camera holds on the output tray waiting to see whether anything comes out.
Stands alone: State the rule before the result, that a printer you will not plug in today is not a backup, so the clip works whichever way the test page goes, and name the spare cartridge condition.
Straighten Paper, spare cartridge, and scan tray each get a position in this corner that removes a hunt.
Beats
  • Put the paper bin directly beneath the printer so reloading is a reach rather than a walk.
  • Set the one spare cartridge in a labelled box beside it, since cartridge boxes all look alike on a shelf.
  • Build the scan tray with a to-do side and a done side, then show a sheet crossing from one side to the other after it goes through the glass.
  • Frame the finished corner in one shot so the three positions read together.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of the paper bin sliding into place under the printer
  • Close on the spare cartridge box being labelled and set beside it
  • Overhead of the scan tray with a sheet moving from the to-do side to the done side
  • Locked three-quarter of the finished corner, no hands
On-screen text
  • Paper under the printer
  • To do, then done
Short cut · 30–45s A single tray with two sides, and a sheet crossing from one side to the other the moment it comes off the scanner glass.
Stands alone: Explain what problem the two sides solve, that you otherwise cannot tell what has already been scanned, since the tray by itself looks like ordinary stacking.
Shine Scanner glass and toner dust each punish the obvious cleaning method.
Beats
  • Power the machine off and lift the lid, showing the glass in raking light so the smears read.
  • Spray cleaner onto the cloth, never onto the glass, since liquid on the platen runs down inside the machine at the edges.
  • Use a dry cloth for toner dust, because water turns loose toner into ink, which is the mistake that makes the mess permanent.
  • Vacuum the paper lint around the feed tray, which is what a lot of misfeeds on this machine actually are.
Shots
  • Close on the power switch, then the lid lifting
  • Raking side-light macro across the scanner glass, smears then clear
  • Macro of cleaner going into a folded cloth held off to the side
  • Close on a dry cloth lifting toner dust, then a vacuum nozzle at the feed tray
On-screen text
  • Spray the cloth, not the glass
  • Toner gets a dry cloth
Short cut · 30–45s A cloth is loaded with cleaner well away from the machine, then scanner glass goes from smeared to clear in one pass.
Stands alone: Say both halves of the rule, cleaner on the cloth for glass and dry cloth only for toner, because a viewer who takes only the first half will make the toner worse.
Safety The fuser runs hot and needs air, and nothing sits on the lid.
Beats
  • Show the machine pushed tight to the wall inside the cupboard, name the hazard as burn or fire, and pull it forward to leave clear air behind the fuser.
  • Trace the power lead and find the strip plugged into another strip, then plug the printer straight into a wall outlet instead.
  • Clear the top of the lid completely, including the plant and the drink, and name that second hazard as water and electricity sitting directly above the electronics and the paper path.
  • Point to Chapter 21, the hazard hunt, and treat everything found here the same way: find it, and fix it now.
Shots
  • Beanbag three-quarter behind the printer showing zero clearance, then the gap after it is pulled forward
  • Close following the lead from the printer to a strip and then to a second strip
  • Close on the plug going directly into a wall outlet
  • Overhead of the plant and glass being lifted off the printer lid, lid left bare
On-screen text
  • Clear air behind it
  • Straight to the wall outlet
  • Nothing on the lid
Short cut · 45–60s A hand follows a printer cable to a power strip, and then that strip's cable to a second power strip.
Stands alone: Name the fuser heat as the reason this particular machine wants its own wall outlet and clear air behind it, otherwise it reads as generic electrical advice.
Standardize A min line and a max line inside the paper bin make the reorder point visible.
Beats
  • Draw a min line and a max line inside the empty paper bin, then load the stack so it sits between them.
  • Set the rule: when the stack drops to the min line, the next ream goes on the shopping list that day, not the day it runs out mid-job.
  • Read the bin from standing height at the min line, so the signal works without bending down or counting sheets.
Shots
  • Overhead into the empty bin with a marker drawing two lines on the inside wall
  • Close on the paper stack sitting at the max line, then at the min line
  • Three-quarter from standing height showing the min line readable at a glance
On-screen text
  • Min line and max line
  • Min line means order today
Short cut · 30–45s Two marker lines get drawn inside an empty printer paper bin before a single sheet goes back in.
Stands alone: State what each line means and what the min line triggers, ordering the same day rather than the day it runs out, because two marker lines with no rule attached are just marks.
Sustain The refill happens when you take the last sheet, while you are already standing at the machine.
Beats
  • Open on the last sheet coming out of the bin and the bin bottom showing, which is the trigger.
  • Refill from the shelf before walking away from the machine, since the whole rule rests on you already being on your feet at the right spot.
  • Cut that against refilling later, when the trip has to be made specially and therefore does not get made.
  • Restate the standard, matched cartridges only, a min line in the bin, and a bare machine top.
Shots
  • Close on the last sheet lifting out and the bin bottom showing
  • Three-quarter of a turn to the shelf and a ream coming straight back
  • Overhead of the refilled bin sitting between its two lines
On-screen text
  • Trigger: the last sheet
  • Refill before you walk away
Short cut · 30–45s The last sheet of paper comes out of a printer bin, and the hands turn straight to the shelf instead of to the door.
Stands alone: Name the trigger and the reason it works, that you are already standing at the machine with your hands free, since the clip otherwise just shows someone loading paper.
Close

Finish on the corner with the bin between its lines, one labelled spare cartridge beside it, the scan tray split, clear air behind the machine, and a bare lid. Put the standard on screen, then show the last sheet coming out of the bin as the trigger that keeps it stocked.

Next: The spare cartridge has a home now, which raises the question of everything else this office has been stockpiling, and the cabinet where it lives.

Shot list
  • Three-quarter tripod on the printer corner, the main setup for placement and clearance
  • Beanbag position behind the machine where a tripod leg will not fit
  • Macro rig for model numbers, scanner glass in raking light, and toner dust
  • Overhead into the paper bin for the min and max lines and the refill
  • Handheld cable-follow tracking lead to strip to strip to wall outlet
  • Standing-height three-quarter for the at-a-glance min line check
Description hook

A printer you will not plug in today is not a backup, it is an undecided object taking up a corner. This reset settles it, then fixes the clearance, the glass, and the paper supply.

MZ-081 · R14.06

Supply Cabinet

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Count it out loud”

Supply Cabinet Reset: Counting the Bulk Buy and Writing Min and Max on the Shelf

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the bulk box of 500 envelopes, the multipack of sticky notes, and the case of paper bought because the price was good, all coming out of the cabinet and onto the floor. Establish the genuinely hard part, which is that you were not wrong about the price, so admitting the surplus was a mistake feels like throwing money away twice. Set up what the count will prove: the money left when you bought it, and the shelf space is being paid for now.

Sort Everything comes out and lines up in categories, because the counting is the part that does the work.
Beats
  • Bring the whole cabinet out onto the floor and line it up in categories, since a dozen packs of sticky notes look like nothing until they stand side by side in a row.
  • Count the true stock of each category and divide it by honest annual use, out loud. Six letters a year against 500 envelopes is a lifetime supply and then some.
  • Cap it: one open plus one spare of anything used monthly, and a single year of use for everything else.
  • Box the surplus for a school, a charity shop, or a neighbour this week, and show it leaving the room. Not to the top shelf, and not to a box in the garage.
  • Clear the dead stock in one sweep, dried glue sticks, dead markers, cracked folders, and adapters nobody can identify.
Shots
  • High angle from the step stool, tripod raised, entire cabinet contents laid out in category rows on the floor
  • Close on a hand counting envelope packs into a line, one by one
  • Macro on a dried glue stick and a dead marker going into the bin
  • Overhead of the surplus being boxed and labelled for the school or charity shop
  • Close on the box going out the door of the room
On-screen text
  • Line it up to see it
  • Count against a year
  • One open, one spare
Short cut · 60–90s Packs of sticky notes get counted out into a single line across an office floor, and the line runs past the edge of frame.
Stands alone: Do the divide-by-annual-use count on camera with one real category, and state the one open plus one spare cap, because the count without the cap gives the viewer a feeling instead of a rule.
Straighten Open pack at hand height with its backstock immediately behind it on the same shelf.
Beats
  • Put one open pack of each consumable at hand height and its backstock directly behind it on the same shelf.
  • Show the before condition first, a refill hunted out from behind three boxes of envelopes, then the same refill pulled in a single reach with nothing else moving.
  • Put reams of paper on the bottom shelf, which is doing double duty here since it is also the safety answer.
  • Read the finished cabinet from the doorway so the layout works without stepping in.
Shots
  • Three-quarter into the open cabinet, open pack going forward and backstock sliding in behind it
  • Close on a single reach pulling a refill without moving anything else
  • Close on reams of paper going onto the bottom shelf
  • Locked three-quarter from the doorway, cabinet open, no hands
On-screen text
  • Open pack in front
  • Backstock right behind it
Short cut · 30–45s One hand reaches into a supply cabinet, pulls a refill pack, and nothing else on the shelf has to move.
Stands alone: Show the before condition briefly, the hunt through boxes of envelopes, so the single reach has something to be measured against, and name the open-pack-in-front rule.
Shine Wiping the emptied shelves is when you find the leak, the split pouch, and the sticky ring.
Beats
  • Wipe the shelves with the cabinet emptied and look as you go rather than after.
  • Find a pen that has leaked and show the ink stain it left in the shelf board.
  • Check for a split toner pouch and handle it with a dry cloth rather than a wet one.
  • Lift a roll of tape that has gone soft and find the sticky ring under it, the sort of thing that only surfaces when the shelf is bare.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of a cloth running the length of an emptied shelf
  • Macro on an ink stain left by a leaked pen
  • Macro on a soft tape roll lifting to reveal a sticky ring on the board
  • Close on a dry cloth handling loose toner
On-screen text
  • Wipe with the shelf empty
  • Look while you wipe
Short cut · 30–45s A roll of tape lifts off a supply shelf and leaves a sticky ring behind it that nobody knew was there.
Stands alone: Tie the find back to the reason the shelf was bare in the first place, the whole cabinet being emptied, so the clip lands as inspection rather than as a satisfying reveal.
Safety Weight belongs low, and a rolling chair is not a step.
Beats
  • Show why the rolling chair fails as a step: a hand presses down on the seat and the castors turn under the load, with nobody standing on it.
  • Bring an actual step stool into the room and give it a standing place in the corner, so the fix is present rather than fetched, then do the top shelf reach from the stool.
  • Move reams of paper and boxes of envelopes down to the bottom shelf, and name the second hazard, a slipping box landing on your head and shoulders while your arms are up.
  • Finish with the top shelf holding only light, rarely needed items.
Shots
  • Low three-quarter of a hand pressing down on the empty rolling chair seat, castors turning under the load
  • Close on the step stool being carried in and set in the corner of the room
  • Three-quarter of heavy ream boxes coming down from the high shelf to the bottom shelf
  • Upward angle at the finished top shelf, light items only
On-screen text
  • The chair rolls under you
  • Heavy things live low
  • Keep the stool in this room
Short cut · 45–60s A hand presses down on an empty office chair seat and the castors turn under the weight, before anyone tries to stand on it.
Stands alone: Show the step stool arriving and staying in the room as the resolution, and name the falling box hazard too, since the clip should end with both fixes rather than one warning.
Standardize Min and max written on a card at the front edge of every shelf, readable from the doorway.
Beats
  • Write min and max on a card for each shelf and clip it to the front edge.
  • Read the cabinet from the doorway, where one shelf is visibly below its line without anyone stepping in or counting.
  • Show the cabinet being read and the last pack taken by a hand that never had to ask you, since the card removes you as the gatekeeper.
  • Point to Chapter 14, visual controls.
Shots
  • Macro on a min and max card being written
  • Close on the card clipping to the front edge of a shelf
  • Three-quarter from the doorway with one shelf visibly below its min
  • Close on a hand reading a shelf card and taking the last pack without counting
On-screen text
  • Min and max on the shelf edge
  • Readable from the doorway
Short cut · 30–45s A supply cabinet seen from a doorway, and one shelf is obviously below its line without anyone counting anything.
Stands alone: Show the card being written and clipped to the shelf edge before the doorway reveal, because the payoff shot only works once the viewer knows what the card says.
Sustain The shopping list gets written when you open the last pack, before you break the seal.
Beats
  • Open on a hand lifting the last pack of something off the shelf with the gap behind it, which is the trigger.
  • Carry it still sealed to the household shopping list on the fridge and write it on, since the seal is the deadline and the moment passes once it opens.
  • Cut that against adding it after it runs out, which is always the day you need it.
  • Restate the standard, one open plus one spare of anything used monthly, with min and max at the front of every shelf.
Shots
  • Close on a hand lifting the last pack from a shelf, gap behind it
  • Three-quarter of the sealed pack being carried out of the room
  • Macro on the item being added to the household list on the fridge door
  • Close on the seal finally being broken
On-screen text
  • Trigger: the last pack
  • List it before you open it
Short cut · 30–45s A still-sealed pack of office supplies is carried out of the office to the fridge door, and the shopping list gets written before the seal is broken.
Stands alone: State that the seal is the deadline and name the trigger as opening the last pack, because the walk to the fridge is meaningless without knowing the pack is deliberately still sealed.
Close

End on the cabinet read from the doorway, one open pack of each consumable at hand height with backstock behind it, reams low, min and max cards at every shelf edge, and the step stool standing in the corner. Put the standard on screen, then show the last pack being lifted and listed before the seal breaks.

Next: That is all six zones of the home office, so the room now runs on six standards and six triggers, and the next room in the series starts at the door you came in through.

Shot list
  • High angle from the step stool with the tripod raised, for the full category layout and counting
  • Three-quarter tripod at the open cabinet, the main working setup
  • Locked three-quarter from the doorway for the at-a-glance reads
  • Macro rig for cards, ink stains, sticky rings, and the shopping list
  • Low three-quarter on the rolling chair and the step stool for the safety pass
  • Upward angle at the top shelf for the weight check before and after
  • Handheld follow at hand height from the cabinet to the fridge for the sustain trigger
Description hook

You were not wrong about the price, and that is exactly why the surplus is still on the shelf. Count it against a year of honest use, cap it, and write min and max where you can read them from the doorway.
