MZ-088 · R15.07

Bulk and Overhead Storage

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Every Bin Down, Then Judged”

Overhead Garage Storage Reset: Every Bin Down, Judged, and Labelled

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open low, looking up at the overhead racks, then cut to the one box up there that moved in with you and has not been opened since. The problem is that opening it costs an afternoon and might cost more than that, so it has been renewing its own lease for years. Show a hand reaching up, touching the lid, and coming back down without it. Name what settles it, that the box comes down and gets opened on the floor with a rubbish sack, a donation box, and one empty container beside it, and that whatever you keep has to fit that one container and carry a living person's name.

Sort Nothing gets judged from a ladder, so every bin comes down to the floor first.
Beats
  • State the working rule before anything moves, that nobody sorts honestly from the third step of a ladder with one arm through a lid, then show the bins coming down and being set out on the slab.
  • Start with the two that always exist, the holiday bin that has not come down in three Decembers and the box marked misc.
  • Open the never opened box with the three things beside it, a rubbish sack, a donation box, and one empty container, and work it all the way through.
  • Show the wrong move refused, hands starting to tape the box shut to send it back up, then setting the tape down, with the reason given, that a box which goes back unopened has bought itself another five years and taught the rack that this is allowed.
Shots
  • Low wide looking up at the loaded rack, then the same frame empty.
  • Three quarter of bins being handed down and set out in rows on the slab.
  • Overhead of the never opened box being cut open, with sack, donation box, and empty container in frame.
  • Close on hands starting to tape a lid shut, then setting the tape down.
On-screen text
  • Judge it on the floor
  • One container, one named owner
  • Do not send it back sealed
Short cut · 45–60s A box that moved house with you and has never once been opened, cut open on a garage floor with a sack and a donation box already waiting beside it.
Stands alone: Establish that it came off an overhead rack and has never been opened, then give the one container and living owner rule so the Short hands over a usable method.
Straighten Weight goes low, bulk goes high, and bins are grouped by the time of year they come down.
Beats
  • Put the heavy bins on the lowest rack and the light bulky things, folding chairs and the artificial tree, highest, with the lift you are designing for made explicit.
  • Group by the time of year they come down rather than by category, so one December trip up the ladder brings the lights, the tree, and the wrapping bin down together.
  • Show the payoff as one trip, hands and bins only, with the December group coming down together instead of a separate climb for the lights, one for the tree, and one for the wrapping bin.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the rack loading sequence, heavy low and bulky high.
  • Close on the December group being set together on one bay.
  • Time condensed of the single trip retrieval, hands only on the bins.
On-screen text
  • Heavy low, bulky high
  • Grouped by when it comes down
Short cut · 30–45s One trip up a ladder that brings the lights, the tree, and the wrapping bin down together.
Stands alone: Explain that the bins were grouped by the time of year they come down rather than by category, otherwise the single trip reads as luck instead of design.
Shine Wiping the lids is inspection, and so is looking at the ceiling while you are up there.
Beats
  • Wipe the lids and read the dust, with the point made that the depth of dust on an overhead lid is a rough record of how long it has been since anything came out of that bin.
  • Turn the attention upward. While you are up there, check the rack underside and the ceiling above it for the brown stain that means the roof is letting water in.
  • Show what to do with a stain if you find one, outlined and dated so you can tell later whether it is growing.
Shots
  • Macro raking light shot of dust depth on a lid, then a wiped stripe through it.
  • Upward close on the ceiling above the rack, panning slowly.
  • Close on a brown stain being outlined in pencil with a date beside it.
On-screen text
  • Dust depth is a date
  • Look up while you are up there
Short cut · 30–45s A finger stripe drawn through the dust on an overhead storage lid, and what that depth actually tells you.
Stands alone: Say that this is an overhead garage bin and that nothing has come out of it, then add the ceiling stain check so the Short teaches the inspection idea rather than just the wipe.
Safety What goes overhead is limited by what you can get down safely, and the rack itself has to land in structure.
Beats
  • Fall. Set the two limits before anything goes back up, that nothing goes overhead you cannot bring down one handed on a stable ladder with the other hand on the stile, and nothing you might need in the dark or in a hurry.
  • Show the fall risk directly, a ladder rocking on a sloped slab, then the corrected version, ladder levelled and the bin handled so a hand stays free.
  • Check the rack bolts land in joists rather than only in plasterboard, shown with the fixing points found and marked.
  • Fall, cut, or crush. Check that loaded bins sit fully inside the rails rather than overhanging the parking bay, shot from below where a car door opens.
Shots
  • Low close on a ladder foot rocking on a sloped slab, then levelled.
  • Three quarter of a bin being brought down with a hand staying on the stile.
  • Macro on a fixing point being marked at a joist.
  • Low angle from the parking bay looking up at bins overhanging the rails, then fully inside them.
On-screen text
  • If you cannot get it down, it does not go up
  • Bolts into joists
  • Nothing overhanging the bay
Short cut · 30–45s Looking straight up from the spot where a car door opens, at storage bins hanging out over the edge of the rack.
Stands alone: Frame the shot from the parking position and say what is above it, then state the rule about bins sitting fully inside the rails and show the corrected rack.
Standardize Big labels, a last opened date, and a map by the light switch mean nobody climbs a ladder to find out.
Beats
  • Put a large label on every bin, sized to be read standing on the slab, and test it by shooting from floor level.
  • Add the month and year it was last opened to the end of each bin, and say what that date will be used for later.
  • Tape a small map beside the light switch saying which bay holds what, with the point stated plainly, that nobody climbs a ladder simply to find out.
  • Point to Chapter 24, the checklist, schedule, and name.
Shots
  • Close on a large label being written and applied to a bin end.
  • Floor level static reading the labels on the loaded rack, proving legibility.
  • Close on the map going up beside the light switch, hands smoothing the tape.
On-screen text
  • Readable from the slab
  • Last opened, month and year
  • See Chapter 24
Short cut · 30–45s The label test, stand on the garage floor and try to read your own overhead bins from there.
Stands alone: Show the failing small label first and the large one after, both shot from floor level, so the Short proves the point on camera instead of asserting it.
Sustain The date gets rewritten the moment a bin is open, and stale dates trigger the next clear out.
Beats
  • Run the trigger. The moment a bin is on the floor with its lid off, the new month and year goes on the end before it goes back up.
  • Show how the dates get used, a bin whose newest date is two Decembers old coming down and being opened at the next clear out rather than lifted straight back.
  • Close on the rack reading as a set of dates, with the point that the rack now tells you what to look at next without anyone remembering.
Shots
  • Close on a lid off on the floor and a marker updating the date on the end.
  • Floor level pan across the rack with the dates legible.
  • Close on one stale date being spotted and that bin being brought down.
On-screen text
  • Lid off, date on
  • “You do not finish 6S. You keep it.”
Short cut · 30–45s A storage bin lid coming off, and a marker going straight to the end of the bin before anything is taken out.
Stands alone: Explain that the date is what stops a bin renewing its own lease overhead, then show a stale dated bin being pulled down so the Short shows the date being used.
Close

Hold from floor level on the finished rack, every bin labelled in letters readable from the slab, a last opened month and year on each end, heaviest bins lowest, nothing overhanging the parking bay, and the map taped beside the light switch. State the standard, then replay the lid off date trigger in one cut.

Next: That closes the garage, seven zones from the bench to the rack, and the room that used to take everything the house evicted now gives every arrival a verdict the same day.

Shot list
  • Low floor level wide of the full rack, matched before and after, doubling as the label legibility test.
  • Tripod at full extension for bins coming down and going up, camera never on the ladder, hands only.
  • Slab lay out overhead for the bins set out in rows.
  • Macro focus rail for dust depth, dates, labels, and fixing marks.
  • Upward setup on the ceiling and rack underside with the clamped LED.
  • Parking bay low angle for the overhang check.
  • Light switch setup for the map.
  • Ladder foot close on the sloped section of slab.
Description hook

There is at least one box on your overhead rack that moved in with you and has never been opened, and it has renewed its own lease every year since. This is a hands only 6S reset of bulk and overhead storage, including the labelling that stops it happening again.

6Soverhead storagegarage rackbin labellingladder safetyseasonal storagegarage organization

Room 16 of 20

Workshop

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteShoot the whole room in one continuous daylight block, ideally an overcast morning through the shop window or open roller door, so the bench top does not blow out and blade steel does not flare. No lighting kit, no second pair of hands. Two core camera positions carry most of it: a tripod with a horizontal arm set over the bench centre for drawer dumps and tray sorts, and a three quarter position at shoulder height on the vise side for hands at work. Reposition that second tripod for the door board, the charger shelf, the rack, the sink, and the floor level angles rather than adding gear. Framing rule for the whole series: nothing above the wrists ever appears, so set the camera low or tight enough that forearms leave frame at the edge, and never stage a shot that needs one person to carry something while another operates the camera. If hands must travel, lock the camera off and let the hands pass through the frame. Practical safety on set: film every cutting and finishing sequence dry, tools unplugged and batteries out, and lay saw sound in afterwards. The finishing zone gets no hot lights, and the solvent cabinet stays open only as long as a shot needs, with the door opened for ventilation between takes. Oil finish rags used as props go into the lidded metal can the moment the shot ends, on camera when it serves the segment. Sawdust ruins both the lens and the audio, so vacuum before each setup rather than between takes, and put a wind sock on the mic because the extractor and the shop fan otherwise sit under every take.
MZ-089 · R16.01

Safety and PPE Station

5–7 min · thumbnail: “Gear at the door”

Workshop PPE Station: Glasses at the Door, Extinguisher Check, Visitor Set

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open tight on the doorway of the shop: one scratched pair of glasses hanging on a nail, an empty unmarked hook beside it, and beyond them the bench with an unplugged saw sitting on it. Establish that the awkward decision in this zone is not your own gear at all, it is what happens when a brother in law or a fourteen year old wanders in and wants to help. Show the current answer, which is no answer, an unlabeled hook and a spare pair nobody has claimed. Make the cost plain: that decision currently gets made in the moment, differently every time, by someone holding something sharp.

Sort Scratched and expired protective gear is worse than none here, because it is the reason people stop wearing gear at all.
Beats
  • Every piece of protective gear in the shop comes out onto a clean towel on the bench, glasses, muffs, dust masks, gloves, and the full contents of the first aid kit.
  • A hazed pair held into window light, with the chain that makes it dangerous spelled out: scratched lenses mean you lift them off to see the cut line, and that is the moment the chip flies. Verdict is the bin.
  • The same verdict applied down the towel, perished gloves, respirator cartridges past their printed date, and a first aid kit quietly raided for household plasters with no burn dressing left in it.
  • The distinction that governs this whole pass, that this gear gets replaced rather than rearranged, because rearranging expired protection only hides it better.
Shots
  • Overhead of the towel filling with gear, one item at a time entering frame from the side.
  • Macro on a scratched lens tilted into window light until the haze reads.
  • Close on a thumb finding the printed date on a respirator cartridge.
  • Close on the first aid kit lid opening to reveal three loose plasters and no burn dressing.
On-screen text
  • Scratched means gone
  • Replace, do not rearrange
Short cut · 30–45s A hand tilts a hazed safety lens into the window light until you cannot see through it, then drops it straight in the bin.
Stands alone: Name the room and the zone in the first few seconds and say these are workshop safety glasses off the door hook, or nobody knows whose lens this is or why it matters.
Straighten The gear hangs on the path you already walk, at the door you come in through, not on the far wall past the bench.
Beats
  • The current arrangement shown honestly in one frame, the gear rack on the far wall past the bench and the bare door frame in the foreground, with the walk between them being exactly the walk people skip.
  • Hooks going into the door frame stud, glasses and hearing protection paired on one hook so a set never gets split.
  • Sets sized and labeled to the actual people who work in this shop rather than one generic set for whoever shows up.
  • A silhouette traced behind each item, and what the silhouette buys, a missing pair reading at a glance instead of after a search.
Shots
  • Locked off wide down the entry path, far wall rack at the end of it, bare door frame in the foreground.
  • Close on a hand driving a hook screw into the door frame stud.
  • Overhead of a pencil tracing around a pair of muffs laid flat on the board.
  • Wide of the finished board with every silhouette filled but one.
On-screen text
  • On the path you walk
  • Silhouettes show the gap
Short cut · 30–45s A pencil traces the outline of a pair of ear muffs on a board, the muffs lift away, and the empty shape reads as missing.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a workshop door board with one labeled set per person, or the tracing looks decorative rather than functional.
Shine How you clean this gear is what keeps it wearable, and the shop rag is the thing destroying it.
Beats
  • The habitual wrong move shown first, a dusty shop rag dragged across a lens, identified as where the scratches actually come from.
  • Lenses washed in soap and water at the shop sink and left to air dry, with the clarity difference held against the window.
  • Sweat and sawdust wiped off the earmuff cushions, and what a stiff crusted cushion does, which is stop sealing while still sitting on your head, so the protection quietly stops working.
Shots
  • Macro on a dusty rag dragging across a lens with grit visible in the weave.
  • Close on hands lathering lenses under a running tap.
  • Macro on a cloth wiping a compressed earmuff cushion, dust lifting away.
  • Two lenses held side by side against the window, one washed and one not.
On-screen text
  • Soap and water, not the shop rag
  • A hard cushion stops sealing
Short cut · 30–45s Two safety lenses fill the frame against a bright window, one washed and one wiped on a shop rag, and the difference lands before a word is said.
Stands alone: Say plainly that this rag lives in a sawdust shop, so the viewer understands why it is loaded with grit rather than just dirty.
Safety Two physical checks this zone exists to guarantee, the extinguisher and the power cutoff.
Beats
  • The extinguisher lifted off its bracket, weight felt, gauge read on camera, with the needle needing to sit inside the green band.
  • The floor in front of the bracket shown as it actually is, a stack of timber leaning against the wall, then cleared, framed as the burn or fire question.
  • A hand flat on the shop power cutoff, then the real test run, the same reach repeated with eyes shut and hands only, because sawdust in your eyes and the lights off is the condition you will actually need it in.
  • A boundary taped on the floor in front of the bracket so the timber has a visible edge to stop at rather than creeping back over the next month.
Shots
  • Close on hands lifting the extinguisher clear of its bracket.
  • Macro on the pressure gauge needle sitting in the green band.
  • Three quarter of hands sliding leaning timber away from the wall below the bracket.
  • Close on a hand travelling the wall and landing on the cutoff switch, then the same travel repeated slower.
  • Overhead of tape being pressed onto the concrete to mark the clear floor boundary.
On-screen text
  • Gauge in the green
  • Clear floor in front
  • Reach it blind
Short cut · 30–45s A hand travels along a workshop wall in near darkness, searching, and lands flat on the power cutoff.
Stands alone: State that this is the shop power cutoff and that blind reach is the standard, since out of context the gesture just reads as fumbling.
Standardize Two dates written where you will actually read them, plus one placement trick that makes the glasses unskippable.
Beats
  • Masking tape torn, an inspection date written on it, and pressed onto the extinguisher bracket, then the same again on the first aid kit lid, because the date belongs on the thing rather than in a list somewhere else.
  • The safety glasses hung over the plug of the saw, with the consequence demonstrated, no powering up without handling the glasses first.
  • Both dates read from standing height without lifting or opening anything, which is the actual test of whether a date is written where it will be read. Point to Chapter 24, the checklist.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing a date onto masking tape.
  • Close on the tape being pressed onto the extinguisher bracket.
  • Three quarter of a hand reaching for the saw plug and having to lift the glasses off it first.
  • Wide of the finished board and extinguisher with both dates legible in frame.
On-screen text
  • Date on the thing itself
  • Glasses over the plug
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches for a saw plug and finds a pair of safety glasses hanging on it, blocking the grab.
Stands alone: Explain in the first beat that the glasses were deliberately hung on the plug of the saw, otherwise it reads as clutter rather than a designed obstacle.
Sustain The trigger that refills the board, tied to switching off the shop light, and the visitor rule made permanent.
Beats
  • The failure path first, glasses set down on the bench and slid into a jacket pocket, then the jacket lifted off its hook and out of frame with them still in it.
  • The trigger in its place, gear going back onto its silhouettes as the hand reaches the shop light switch, so whoever opens the door next finds a full board.
  • The visitor rule from the cold open closed out physically, the spare set hung on a hook marked for visitors and the rule written on a card pinned beside it, decided in advance rather than while holding a running grinder.
  • The reason this holds without willpower, that it is one rule on a wall, and the reminder that you do not finish 6S, you keep it.
Shots
  • Close on glasses going into a jacket pocket, then the jacket lifting off its hook and leaving frame.
  • Three quarter of hands hanging glasses onto their silhouette.
  • Close on a hand at the light switch with the full board visible behind it.
  • Macro on a marker writing the visitor rule onto a card pinned by the spare hook.
On-screen text
  • Board full before lights out
  • One spare set, marked
Short cut · 30–45s Safety glasses go into a jacket pocket, the jacket lifts off its hook and leaves, and the next hand through the door lands on an empty board.
Stands alone: Set up that this is a shared workshop door board meant to be full for whoever arrives next, which is the entire reason the pocket is a failure.
Close

Hold a slow wide of the finished board at the door, one labeled set per user plus the marked visitor set, silhouettes filled, dated extinguisher and dated first aid kit in the same frame, and state the standard as it now stands. Then show the trigger once in real motion, glasses coming off and going straight onto their hook rather than into a pocket or a drawer.

Next: With the glasses findable and the gauge in the green, the next zone is the surface everything else in this room happens on, the main workbench, and the half assembled project that has been sitting on it since spring.

Shot list
  • Overhead bench setup for the gear laid out on a towel.
  • Macro setup with window backlight for lenses, gauges, and printed dates.
  • Three quarter at the shop door covering the hook board and hook fitting.
  • Locked off wide down the entry path from the door toward the far wall rack.
  • Close on the extinguisher bracket and the floor space in front of it.
  • Wall travel shot ending on the power cutoff, shot twice at different speeds.
  • Macro marker and masking tape writing setup on the bench.
  • Close on the saw plug with glasses hanging over it.
  • Light switch shot with the finished board in the background.
Description hook

Start the workshop here, at its smallest zone, because everything else in the room involves a blade, a solvent, or a cloud of dust. Glasses at the door, muffs beside them, gauge in the green, and one visitor rule you decide before you need it.

MZ-090 · R16.02

Main Workbench

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Bare bench, one project”

Workshop Bench Reset: Clear the Top, Trace the Tools, Keep It Bare

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the half assembled something occupying the best surface in the shop, dust settled evenly across the top of it, its hardware waiting in a jar alongside. Establish how long it has sat there by running a finger through the dust on a joint. Name the real reason it has not moved, which is that the next step is one you are not sure how to do, so the bench pays for that hesitation every single session. Set the stakes in the room's own terms: this is the only surface where a project actually gets built, and while that thing sits there you do not have one.

Sort Every half finished project on this bench gets a verdict, and the test is a spoken next action plus a date.
Beats
  • The bench top and the shelf beneath it cleared completely onto a sheet on the floor, with the reason stated, that partial clearing is how the same pile survives every reset.
  • The call introduced as a test rather than a mood: name the next physical action and name a date this month, both in one breath, or the project is finished.
  • The failed verdict carried out in full on camera, the assembly coming apart, hardware back to the fastener drawers, stock back onto the rack, with the point made that keeping it assembled was never keeping the project alive, only keeping the surface unusable.
  • The fast throwaways run separately and quickly, snapped blades, glue bottles gone solid, brackets you cannot identify, all leaving now.
  • The holding decision for anything that genuinely earns its way back, which is a date written onto it in marker rather than a good intention.
Shots
  • Overhead of the bench top emptying, objects leaving frame in sequence.
  • Three quarter of hands lifting a dusty half built assembly clear of the bench.
  • Close on a screwdriver backing hardware out of the assembly into a tray.
  • Macro on a glue bottle being squeezed with no give at all.
  • Overhead of the bare bench top and the empty shelf beneath.
On-screen text
  • Next action plus a date
  • Cannot name both, it is finished
Short cut · 45–60s A dusty half built project gets lifted off a workbench and immediately taken apart on camera, screw by screw.
Stands alone: Give the one breath rule up front, next physical action and a date this month, or the disassembly reads as giving up rather than deciding.
Straighten Reach decides placement at this bench, and the tools your hand wants mid cut live inside the arc you can cover from the vise.
Beats
  • The arc marked in chalk from the standing position at the vise, covering only what a hand reaches without stepping, so the rule is drawn rather than argued.
  • The mid cut tools placed inside that arc, marking knife, combination square, and block plane, with the reason those three and nothing else.
  • Everything used once a project moved to the wall behind, sorted as two piles rather than a fine ranking.
  • Traced silhouettes introduced as the mechanism that makes a missing chisel show up before you finish vacuuming.
  • A run of bench in front of the vise cleared long enough to lay a board across, proved by laying a board across it.
Shots
  • Overhead of a hand sweeping an arc from the vise position with chalk marking the reach limit.
  • Close on the marking knife, square, and block plane landing inside the chalk arc.
  • Three quarter of tools going up onto the wall rack behind the bench.
  • Wide of a board laid across the cleared run in front of the vise.
On-screen text
  • Mid cut tools inside the arc
  • Once a project goes on the wall
Short cut · 30–45s A hand sweeps a chalk arc across a workbench from the vise, and everything left outside the line gets picked up and moved.
Stands alone: Establish that the arc is the reach you have while a workpiece is clamped in the vise, since the chalk line means nothing without that condition.
Shine Clean this bench to inspect it, not to impress, and the method matters more than the effort.
Beats
  • The bench top vacuumed in strips and the nozzle taken down into the dog holes, with the reason given plainly, that a broom launches the finest sawdust back into the air where it settles on wet finish and into your lungs.
  • Dried glue drips scraped off with a chisel laid flat, and why a proud glue bead matters, because it telegraphs straight into the next workpiece clamped over it.
  • The vise screw wiped clean and given a drop of oil, then the handle turned so the change is both audible and visible.
  • What the cleaning exposed named as the actual purpose of the pass, cracks, scoring, and wear along the front edge that dust was hiding.
Shots
  • Overhead of a vacuum nozzle travelling the bench top in strips.
  • Macro of the nozzle entering a dog hole and the dust disappearing.
  • Macro of a chisel laid flat lifting a glue drip in one curl.
  • Close on an oil drop landing on the vise screw, then the handle turning.
On-screen text
  • Vacuum, never sweep
  • Glue drips telegraph
Short cut · 30–45s A chisel laid flat pops a hardened glue drip off a bench top in one clean curl, macro and slow.
Stands alone: Say why the drip matters, that it prints itself into the next workpiece clamped over it, or this is a satisfying scrape with no lesson attached.
Safety Two failures this bench produces on its own, a vise that lets go and an edge lying up in an open tray.
Beats
  • A test piece clamped and then twisted by hand, with jaws worn smooth releasing a workpiece mid cut named as the fall, cut, or crush question here.
  • The verdict on worn jaws given as fresh faces or a rebuild, not a mental note to be careful with an unreliable vise.
  • The lamp cord moved off the run of bench a handsaw crosses, with the conflict made obvious by laying the saw along its cut path first.
  • The tray hazard taken head on, a hand reaching across the bench without looking and stopping above a chisel lying edge up, then the corrected storage with edges down or sheathed.
  • The damp concrete underfoot shown as the reason cord routing and standing position matter at this bench, framed as the water and electricity question.
Shots
  • Close on hands twisting a test piece in the vise jaws with movement visible.
  • Macro on jaw faces worn smooth and shiny.
  • Overhead of a lamp cord lying across the bench with a handsaw laid along its cut path.
  • Close on a hand reaching across an open tray and stopping a finger's width above an upturned chisel edge.
  • Low angle on a cord running off the bench down onto bare concrete.
On-screen text
  • Jaws that slip let go mid cut
  • Nothing edge up in a tray
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches across a workbench without looking and stops a finger's width above a chisel lying edge up in an open tray.
Stands alone: Frame it as the fall, cut, or crush question and show the corrected tray in the same clip, so the Short delivers a fix rather than just a scare.
Standardize Two visual controls make the right state obvious at this bench, traced outlines and one photo of the cleared top.
Beats
  • Every chisel and square traced onto the tool wall in permanent marker, so a gap reads as a missing tool rather than as empty space.
  • One photo taken of the fully cleared bench and taped at eye level where you actually stand, with the point stated directly, that the photo is what bare means here so bare stops being a matter of opinion.
  • The connection made to Chapter 25, the ideal state photo, and to the line that a standard is the best way you know today, written down.
  • The standard written in plain words on a card beside the photo, one project on the bench at a time, and the bench ending every session bare except the vise and the lamp.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker tracing the outline of a chisel on the tool wall.
  • Close on a chisel lifting away to leave a filled outline and an empty one side by side.
  • Overhead of a phone photographing the cleared bench, hands only on the phone.
  • Close on the printed photo being taped at eye level above the bench.
On-screen text
  • A gap reads as missing
  • This photo is what bare means
Short cut · 30–45s A printed photo of an empty workbench gets taped to the wall directly above the actual bench, and both end up in the same frame.
Stands alone: Explain that the photo settles what finished looks like at this bench, otherwise taping up a picture of your own bench looks strange.
Sustain The clear down is the last part of the session, and it is bolted to the task lamp switch.
Beats
  • The trigger in real motion, a hand rising to the task lamp switch over a bench that is already clear, because the clear down happens before the light goes out.
  • Why this trigger and not a time of day, which is that once the safety glasses come off you are finished and you know it, so the clear down has to land earlier than that.
  • The failure version for contrast, the same lamp going off over a loaded bench, and the state that leaves you to inherit next session.
  • The loop closed on the standard, one project on the bench at a time, held by a designed habit rather than by willpower.
Shots
  • Three quarter of a hand rising to the lamp switch with a bare bench beneath it.
  • Overhead of the last few items leaving the bench in one sweep into the project tray.
  • Close on the same lamp switch with a cluttered bench beneath, lit then dark.
  • Wide of the finished bench in low light, vise and lamp only.
On-screen text
  • Clear down before the light goes out
  • Glasses off means finished
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches for a task lamp switch above a cluttered workbench, stops, and pulls back to clear the last items off first.
Stands alone: State the trigger explicitly, that the bench must be clear before the lamp goes off, since the hesitation carries no meaning on its own.
Close

Hold a wide of the bench in its finished state, bare except the vise and the task lamp, one project tray holding the current job's parts, every chisel and square sitting on its traced outline, dog holes empty and nothing underneath. Restate the standard as one project on the bench at a time, then show the trigger once, the hand reaching for the lamp switch over an already clear bench.

Next: The tools that just went back on the wall are the hand tools. Next is the zone where the guards, the cords, and the batteries live, and the expensive tool inside it that has not cut anything in two years.

Shot list
  • Overhead bench setup for clearing, sorting, vacuuming, and tracing.
  • Three quarter at the vise side for clamping, reaching, and lamp switch work.
  • Macro setup for glue drips, jaw faces, vise screw oil, and marker tracing.
  • Low angle at floor level for cords running down onto concrete.
  • Chalk arc reach sequence framed directly overhead.
  • Board laid across the cleared bench run to prove the clearance.
  • Phone photographing the cleared bench, hands only on the phone.
  • Tool wall shot covering filled and empty outlines together.
  • Low light finish shot of the bare bench with lamp and vise.
Description hook

The workbench is the only surface in the shop where a project actually gets built, which is why the half finished one sitting on it costs you every session. Here is the test that settles it, plus the outlines and the one photo that keep the top bare.

MZ-091 · R16.03

Power Tool Storage

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Guarded, unplugged, complete”

Power Tool Storage: Guard Tests, Cord Tests, and the Tool You Never Use

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the case in this zone that cost real money and has not cut anything in two years, dust lying flat across the lid, latches stiff when a thumb works them. Open it and show the battery inside sitting at nothing. Name why it is still here, which is that selling it would mean admitting the purchase was wrong, so instead it quietly loses value on a shelf while the packs in it age out. Set the wider stakes of the zone in the same breath: every object on these shelves has a guard, a cord, or a battery, and each of those is a way this zone can hurt you.

Sort Duplicates and dead packs judged honestly, with the expensive tool call as the centrepiece.
Beats
  • The duplicates lined up in matched pairs on the bench, the second drill and the sander you replaced but kept, so the doubling is visible rather than theoretical.
  • Questionable battery packs put on a tester, with the standard set plainly, that a pack which will not hold a charge through one job is recycling, not a spare.
  • Every cord repaired with electrical tape cut out of the zone, with the tape unwound on camera to show the damage underneath.
  • The expensive tool call run on camera against its two questions, work done in the last twenty four months, and whether you would happily hire one for a day if the job came up tomorrow.
  • The reframe that makes the verdict stick, that a tool losing value on your shelf is a decision you are storing rather than an asset you are holding, and that selling now is what keeps its packs worth having.
Shots
  • Overhead of two drills and two sanders laid out in matched pairs on the bench.
  • Close on a battery pack clicking into a tester with the charge reading visible.
  • Macro on electrical tape being unwound from a cord to show the split sheath beneath.
  • Three quarter of the dusty tool case being lifted out of the zone and set down by the door.
On-screen text
  • Two years, no work
  • Taped cord is not a tool
Short cut · 45–60s Two nearly identical cordless drills get set side by side on a bench, and one of them is picked up and carried out of frame.
Stands alone: Give both questions in full, twenty four months of work and whether you would hire one instead, since the pickup means nothing without the test attached.
Straighten A tool is stored with the parts that make it usable, or it is not really stored at all.
Beats
  • One complete home built on camera, the circular saw with its rip fence and its blade wrench joined to the tool itself instead of floating in a drawer.
  • The same done for the router, collet spanners and the bits it actually takes, with the failure this prevents named, that hunting for a collet spanner is how a router ends up used without one.
  • The attachment method shown up close, a clip, a small pouch, or a magnet on the tool body, so the accessory travels with the tool rather than back to a drawer.
  • Hooks chosen and set for the weight they actually carry, one labeled home per tool, with the saw resting on its shoe rather than hanging by its cord.
Shots
  • Overhead of a circular saw with its rip fence and blade wrench laid beside it, then joined to it.
  • Macro on a blade wrench clipping into its holder on the saw body.
  • Close on router collet spanners going into a pouch that hangs with the router.
  • Three quarter of tools landing on labeled hooks along the wall, saw resting on its shoe.
On-screen text
  • Wrench lives on the tool
  • Complete or not stored
Short cut · 30–45s A blade wrench gets clipped onto the body of a circular saw instead of dropped into a drawer.
Stands alone: Name the consequence out loud, that a missing spanner is how a router gets used without one, so the clip reads as a safety move rather than tidiness.
Shine Cleaning here restores how the tool actually cuts, because packed dust and pitch change its behaviour.
Beats
  • Motor vents brushed and blown clear of packed sawdust, with what packed vents do to a motor trying to cool itself explained as it happens.
  • Pitch taken off saw blade teeth with resin remover, before and after held in the same frame, with pitch named as the reason cuts started burning.
  • Clogged sanding pads pulled and compared against a fresh one under raking light.
  • The parts nobody cleans in this zone done last, the saw shoe and router base scraped free of gum so they slide true, and dust wiped off battery terminals and charger contacts so a pack seats properly.
Shots
  • Macro on a brush clearing packed dust from motor vents, dust falling away.
  • Macro on saw blade teeth before and after resin remover.
  • Close on a loaded sanding pad peeling off under raking light beside a fresh one.
  • Macro on a cloth clearing dust from battery terminals and charger contacts.
On-screen text
  • Pitch burns the cut
  • Clean the shoe and the contacts
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on circular saw teeth going from black pitch to bare steel as resin remover does its work.
Stands alone: Explain that the pitch is why the saw started burning its cuts, or this is a cleaning shot with no reason behind it.
Safety The guard test, the cord test, and the storage rules that separate this zone from a shelf full of hazards.
Beats
  • The retracting guard on every saw worked with a thumb and confirmed to snap back on its own, with a sticky guard named as the injury waiting in this zone.
  • A guard that hesitates shown against one that does not, and the verdict given as service or retire, rather than a note to be careful with it.
  • Each cord flexed at the strain relief where the sheath cracks first, with cracked sheathing framed as the water and electricity question on bare damp concrete.
  • Loose blades stored flat in a drawer where your hand goes in first, then the corrected storage, sleeved or racked on edge.
  • The plugged in rule set and demonstrated, no corded tool ever stored plugged in, with the unplug happening as part of putting the tool away rather than as a separate task.
Shots
  • Macro on a thumb pushing a saw guard open and the guard snapping shut on its own.
  • Close on a guard that hangs open a beat too long before dropping, played back slowed.
  • Macro on fingers flexing a cord at the strain relief with the sheath cracking open.
  • Close on a hand entering a drawer of loose flat blades, then the same drawer with blades sleeved.
  • Close on a plug leaving the socket as the tool goes onto its hook.
On-screen text
  • Guard must snap back alone
  • Flex at the strain relief
  • Never stored plugged in
Short cut · 30–45s A thumb pushes a circular saw guard fully open and lets go, and the guard hangs there instead of snapping shut.
Stands alone: State that a guard must return on its own and that a sticky one is the injury waiting in a workshop, since the hesitation is subtle on a phone screen.
Standardize Labeled homes on the wall and one written charge rule at the chargers.
Beats
  • Each tool's home labeled on the wall or the shelf edge, so an empty space names what is missing instead of just sitting empty.
  • The charge rule written on a card at the charger shelf itself, partial charge, off the charger when the job ends, resting on a shelf that is not wood.
  • The reason behind the shelf material given in this zone's own terms, packs left on chargers indefinitely on a wooden shelf under a bench full of sawdust, framed as the burn or fire question.
  • The readable end state demonstrated, empty charger cradles and packs sitting on bare metal, so a glance at the shelf tells you whether the rule was followed.
Shots
  • Macro on a label being pressed onto a shelf edge beneath a hook.
  • Overhead of battery packs resting on a metal shelf with the charger cradles empty beside them.
  • Close on a marker writing the three part charge rule onto a card at the charger shelf.
  • Wide of the labeled wall with one empty labeled space clearly visible.
On-screen text
  • Off the charger at job end
  • Not on a wooden shelf
Short cut · 30–45s Battery packs come off their chargers one after another onto a bare metal shelf, and the charger lights go dark behind them.
Stands alone: Say why the shelf is metal and why the packs come off at job end, since the move looks arbitrary without the fire reason.
Sustain Battery onto the charger and tool onto its hook, travelling as one motion.
Beats
  • The paired motion filmed at the end of a job, the pack coming off and going onto the charger while the tool continues onto its hook, hands never stopping in between.
  • The rule that holds it stated, the two actions travel together or neither happens, with the failure version shown, a pack on charge and the bare tool abandoned on the bench.
  • The door check added, a hand pausing on the latch and turning back to confirm no charger is left running behind a locked shop door.
  • The state this produces held for a beat, every tool guarded, unplugged, and stored with the accessories it needs to work.
Shots
  • Continuous three quarter following hands from tool to charger to hook without a cut.
  • Close on a bare tool left on the bench with a charger light glowing behind it.
  • Close on a hand on the door latch, turning back toward the charger shelf.
  • Wide of the finished zone with every charger light dark.
On-screen text
  • Both moves or neither
  • No charger running behind the door
Short cut · 30–45s One unbroken shot follows a pair of hands pulling a battery, seating it on the charger, and hanging the tool, without a single pause between.
Stands alone: Name the rule that the two actions travel together or neither happens, otherwise this is just someone putting a tool away.
Close

Wide of the finished zone with every tool in a labeled home, guards closed, blade wrench and chuck key attached to their own tools, batteries resting on bare metal off the chargers, no loose blade in a drawer, and no taped cord anywhere on the shelves. State the standard as it now reads, every tool rests guarded, unplugged, and stored with the accessories it needs to work, then show the door check with all charger lights dark.

Next: The tools are complete, but a project still stops the moment you cannot find the right screw. Next is the fastener wall, and the inherited jar of mixed hardware that has followed you through two houses.

Shot list
  • Overhead bench setup for duplicate line ups and accessory pairing.
  • Macro setup for guard snap tests and cord flexing, shot at high frame rate on the phone.
  • Close setup on the charger shelf for battery, label, and card work.
  • Three quarter along the tool wall for hooks and labeled homes.
  • Raking light setup for sanding pads and blade pitch.
  • Continuous follow from tool to charger to hook with no cut.
  • Close on saw shoe and router base cleaning at the bench.
  • Door latch shot looking back into the zone with charger lights out.
Description hook

Every object in this zone has a guard, a cord, or a battery, and each one is a way it can hurt you. Guard tests, cord tests, a written charge rule, and the two questions that settle the expensive tool you never use.

MZ-092 · R16.04

Fastener and Hardware Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “One size per compartment”

Fastener Wall: One Size Per Compartment, Sample Screw on the Front

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the jar, a tin from a relative's garage holding a few kilograms of unsorted screws, nuts, and washers, tipping slowly onto a tray until it stops being a jar and starts being a heap. Establish the argument that has kept it alive through two houses, that there is obviously good hardware in there, and grant that the argument is true. Then name the trap this zone actually runs on, that tipping out a jar of screws feels like progress, which is exactly why this jar keeps getting relocated instead of decided.

Sort Keep only hardware you can name confidently, and give the inherited jar exactly one sitting.
Beats
  • The mixed jars emptied onto a tray in one motion and spread flat, so the actual content is visible rather than imagined.
  • The keep test set out loud, only what you can name confidently by size and type, with the failure case demonstrated, an unnameable fastener going straight to the scrap tin.
  • Rusted screws, bent nails, and the anchors that came free with a shelf you no longer own swept out, named as clutter rather than as a stock of hardware.
  • The inherited jar call run by pricing the alternative first, a full box of the screws you actually drive against the evening you would otherwise spend sorting, then one sitting only, picking out just the sizes that already have a compartment.
  • The ending that decides it, the remainder going to metal recycling that same day, and the warning attached, that tipping it into a smaller jar is exactly how it survived the last two moves.
Shots
  • Overhead of a jar tipping onto a tray with hardware spreading flat.
  • Macro on fingers isolating one screw and turning it to read the head and thread.
  • Close on rusted screws and bent nails being swept into a scrap tin.
  • Overhead of the tray at the end of the sitting, a small kept group and a large remainder.
  • Close on the remainder going into a recycling tub, lid on, tub lifted out of frame.
On-screen text
  • Name it or lose it
  • One sitting only
  • Do not refill a smaller jar
Short cut · 45–60s A heavy jar of mixed hardware tips onto a tray, and only a small handful of screws gets picked back out of the heap.
Stands alone: State the pricing test up front, that a box of the screws you actually drive costs less than an evening of sorting, or the small keep pile looks lazy rather than deliberate.
Straighten Type first, size second, with the sizes you drive weekly at hand height.
Beats
  • The kept hardware sorted by type first and then by size, with the two step logic laid out on the tray before anything enters a drawer.
  • Height bands walked by hand, the sizes you drive weekly at hand height, the specialty hinges and threaded rod up high.
  • The label that actually works built on camera, one sample screw glued to the outside of each drawer face so you match by eye rather than by reading, then tested with dusty hands.
  • The pairs that get confused deliberately separated, deck screws away from drywall screws, with what that particular mix up costs you in a joint. Point to Chapter 14, visual controls.
Shots
  • Overhead of the tray divided by type, then each type divided by size.
  • Close on a hand sliding a drawer at hand height, then reaching high for a second.
  • Macro on a dab of glue and a sample screw being set onto a drawer face.
  • Close on a dusty hand holding a loose screw against sample faces until it matches.
On-screen text
  • Type first, size second
  • Match by eye, not by reading
Short cut · 30–45s A dusty hand holds a loose screw against a row of drawer faces, sliding along until it finds the sample screw that matches it exactly.
Stands alone: Explain that a sample of the contents is glued to each drawer it lives on, since the trick is invisible if the viewer takes those for decoration.
Shine Cleaning these drawers is really an inspection, and the corners tell you where the cabinet is standing.
Beats
  • The drawers vacuumed of metal filings and grit, with the nozzle taken into the corners rather than wiped across the middle.
  • The bottom corners checked for rust bloom, and the bloom shown up close when it turns up.
  • The diagnosis that follows given immediately, that bloom means this cabinet is sitting against a cold outside wall and needs moving before it gets refilled.
  • The principle behind the whole pass restated in this zone's terms, that you clean to inspect, and corner bloom is exactly the kind of thing a layer of filings hides.
Shots
  • Macro on a vacuum nozzle working a drawer corner and lifting filings out.
  • Macro on orange rust bloom in the corner of an emptied drawer.
  • Three quarter of hands walking the empty cabinet away from the outside wall.
  • Close on a bare hand held flat against the cold outside wall.
On-screen text
  • Clean to inspect
  • Bloom means cold wall
Short cut · 30–45s Macro pushes into the corner of an emptied fastener drawer and finds orange rust bloom under the metal filings.
Stands alone: Deliver the diagnosis immediately, a cold outside wall behind the cabinet and move it before refilling, or the rust is just an unpleasant close up.
Safety A loaded fastener cabinet is far heavier than it looks, and spilled hardware is a floor hazard for more than you.
Beats
  • The weight shown honestly by lifting one loaded drawer and then the whole empty carcass, so the difference is felt rather than claimed.
  • The cabinet fixed into studs rather than plasterboard anchors, with the stud found and the fixing driven on camera, and the timing stated, before it gets loaded rather than after.
  • The tipping failure demonstrated safely, a lightly loaded unit tethered from behind out of shot, rocking forward as the highest drawer of bolts opens, then the fix, load low and secure the top.
  • The floor hazard split into its two real questions, spilled screws on concrete putting you on your back holding something sharp, and loose screws, washers, and wall anchors sitting at exactly the height where a toddler or a dog finds them first.
  • A deliberate spill swept and vacuumed on camera as the closing action of the pass.
Shots
  • Close on hands lifting one loaded drawer, then the empty carcass.
  • Macro on a stud finder, then a fixing driven into framing.
  • Three quarter of a tethered drawer unit rocking forward as the top drawer slides open.
  • Floor level shot of scattered screws on concrete at pet and toddler height.
  • Overhead of a vacuum clearing the spilled hardware.
On-screen text
  • Into studs, before you load
  • Floor level is toddler level
Short cut · 30–45s A top drawer full of bolts slides open and the whole small parts cabinet rocks forward off the wall before its tether stops it.
Stands alone: Say that a loaded fastener cabinet is far heavier than it looks and must be fixed into studs before loading, since the near miss needs its fix attached to it.
Standardize One compartment per size, no shared drawers, and a minimum line that announces a low bin.
Beats
  • The rule stated with no softening, one compartment per size, no exceptions and no shared drawers, then a shared drawer emptied and split into two on camera.
  • A minimum line marked inside the compartments you empty most, drawn on the inner wall so it is visible the moment the drawer slides open.
  • The effect demonstrated, a drawer opening with its contents sitting below the line, which is a reorder signal rather than a discovery made halfway through a project.
  • The purpose of the whole zone tied back to the mark, that a project never stops for a hardware run.
Shots
  • Overhead of a shared drawer emptied and split into two labeled compartments.
  • Macro on a marker drawing a minimum line on the inner wall of a bin.
  • Close on a drawer opening with the contents sitting visibly below the line.
  • Wide of the finished wall of drawers with sample screws catching the window light.
On-screen text
  • One size per compartment
  • Below the line means reorder
Short cut · 30–45s A small parts drawer slides open and the screws inside sit clearly below a marker line drawn on the inner wall.
Stands alone: Explain what the minimum line is and what crossing it triggers, otherwise the mark reads as a random scribble inside a drawer.
Sustain Pocket hardware goes home before the tools do.
Beats
  • The end of job pocket emptied onto the bench, which is where this zone quietly refills itself with mixed hardware.
  • The trigger given its motion, the handful of leftover fasteners returned to their compartments before a single tool goes back on the wall.
  • The unnameable leftovers handled on the spot, into the scrap metal tin rather than into a holding jar to be dealt with later.
  • The loop closed on the cold open, that a holding jar is precisely how the inherited jar was born in the first place.
Shots
  • Close on a pocket emptying onto the bench, hardware scattering across it.
  • Overhead of hands returning screws to labeled compartments one at a time.
  • Close on two unnameable fasteners dropping into the scrap tin.
  • Three quarter of tools going back on the wall after the last drawer closes.
On-screen text
  • Hardware home before tools
  • Cannot name it, scrap tin
Short cut · 30–45s A pocket empties onto a workbench and every screw goes back into a labeled compartment before a single tool gets hung up.
Stands alone: State the order explicitly, hardware first and tools second, since the sequence is the entire point of the clip.
Close

Slow pan across the finished wall, one fastener type and size per compartment, a sample screw glued to each drawer face, deck screws separate from drywall screws, no tin of mixed hardware anywhere on the shelf, and a marked minimum line inside the compartments you empty most. State the standard in those words, then show the trigger, pockets emptied into compartments before the tools go back up.

Next: Hardware sorted is the easy win, and it is the one you reach for to avoid the next zone. That is the material rack, and the offcut that is still perfectly good wood.

Shot list
  • Overhead bench setup for jar dumps, tray sorting, and drawer splitting.
  • Macro setup for sample screws, rust bloom, and minimum lines.
  • Three quarter at the cabinet for drawer height bands and stud fixing.
  • Floor level angle for spilled hardware at pet and toddler height.
  • Tethered cabinet tipping demonstration, camera locked off from the side.
  • Slow pan along the finished drawer wall in raking window light.
  • Pocket empty shot at the bench, close and overhead.
  • Scrap tin close up for unnameable fasteners.
Description hook

A project should never stop for a hardware run. One size per compartment, a sample screw glued to every drawer face, and a plain pricing test for the inherited jar of mixed hardware that has followed you through two houses.

MZ-093 · R16.05

Material Rack

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Size floor, fill line”

Material Rack: Store Wood Flat, and Set a Size Floor for Offcuts

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the offcut bin, overfull, with hands pulling out one short piece after another and standing them on the floor until the row runs out of frame. Grant the hard part immediately by turning a few of them over, clean grain, no nails, genuinely usable wood, every one. Then name the asymmetry that keeps the pile growing: the cost of keeping an offcut is invisible and the cost of tossing one feels sharp, so the decision goes the same way every single time and the bin only ever gets fuller.

Sort The offcut bin comes apart piece by piece against a written size floor, and some stock leaves for reasons other than size.
Beats
  • The size floor written on the bin face before anything is touched, shorter than your forearm or narrower than your palm, with the forearm and palm used on camera as the measure.
  • The bin taken apart piece by piece, each held against the floor, with the rule doing the deciding instead of the piece making its case.
  • The bin cap introduced as the second limit, one bin and no overflow, so when it is full the shortest piece in it leaves to make room for the newest.
  • The reframe that makes it workable, that you are judging whether a piece is better than the worst piece already in the bin, not whether it is good wood.
  • The stock that leaves for other reasons pulled separately, twisted or badly cupped boards, anything with hidden nails or an unknown coating, and pressure treated scrap, with the coated stock stated plainly as never going on the fire.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing the size floor onto the bin face.
  • Overhead of a forearm laid alongside an offcut as the measure.
  • Three quarter of the bin emptying piece by piece into two growing piles.
  • Close on a magnet finding a hidden nail in a board end.
  • Close on pressure treated scrap set aside with a marked tag, well away from the fire bucket.
On-screen text
  • Shorter than your forearm
  • Better than the worst piece
  • Coated stock, never burned
Short cut · 45–60s A forearm gets laid alongside a piece of offcut wood, and anything that comes up short goes straight into the leaving pile.
Stands alone: Give both limits, the size floor and the one bin cap, or the forearm measure looks like a gimmick rather than a decision rule you can copy.
Straighten Grouping and support decided by how you pull stock and by how it stays straight.
Beats
  • Boards grouped by length and thickness so one can be pulled without unstacking three others, proved with a single clean pull.
  • Pipe, trim, and dowel stood upright in a vertical bin, with the floor space that frees shown before and after.
  • Support intervals set close enough that nothing sags between brackets, demonstrated with a sagging board alongside a supported one.
  • Sheet goods walked up onto edge against the wall rather than leaning out into the room, named as a storage choice and a safety one at once.
  • The route from the bench to the door cleared along its full width and shown end to end from a locked off position at floor level.
Shots
  • Three quarter of a single board sliding cleanly out of a grouped bay.
  • Close on trim and dowel dropping into a vertical bin.
  • Wide side on of a sagging board beside a properly supported one.
  • Close on hands walking a sheet up onto its edge against the wall.
  • Locked off floor level shot straight down the cleared route from bench to door.
On-screen text
  • Pull one without moving three
  • Nothing sags between brackets
Short cut · 30–45s A single board slides out of a loaded material rack in one clean pull without disturbing anything stacked above it.
Stands alone: Explain the grouping by length and thickness that makes the clean pull possible, since the pull is the result and the grouping is the method.
Shine The cleaning that matters here happens behind the rack, in the gap you have not looked into in years.
Beats
  • The rack pulled forward and the gap behind it lit with a clamped torch, showing what collects out of sight, packed sawdust, webs, and mouse droppings.
  • What those droppings mean for the rest of the shop spelled out, and finding them named as the point of the pass rather than an unpleasant surprise.
  • The stored stock checked while it is out, board ends split and mouse damage along the bottom bay, so damaged stock does not go back in.
  • Surface rust wiped off steel stock and a light oil applied before it returns, before and after shown along one length.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the rack pulled forward with a clamped torch throwing light into the gap behind.
  • Macro of the vacuum nozzle lifting webs and droppings out of the gap.
  • Close on a split board end and gnawed edges in the bottom bay.
  • Close on an oiled rag travelling a rusted steel length, before and after in one pass.
On-screen text
  • Behind the rack is the real job
  • Check the stock while it is out
Short cut · 30–45s A material rack gets pulled forward and a torch beam finds years of packed sawdust, webs, and droppings in the gap behind it.
Stands alone: Say this is a workshop material rack and that the gap behind it never gets cleaned because the rack never moves, so the reveal has a reason.
Safety This zone stores the heaviest things in the shop, and the ways they move without warning.
Beats
  • The rack fixed into structural framing rather than just the wall skin, fixing driven on camera, then reloaded heaviest and longest at the bottom with lighter stock above.
  • The sheet goods failure shown without staging a fall, the scuff arc already on the floor where a sheet has slid before, the shallow lean angle that caused it, and a small panel released at that same angle from a locked off side position.
  • The corrected storage put in immediately, sheets on edge or leaned steep against the wall, so the Safety pass ends with the fix rather than the hazard.
  • The second fall, cut, or crush case, a board pulled from the middle of a stack and the stack shifting above it, and the grouping that stops it happening.
  • The burn or fire question handled directly, a dry offcut bin sitting near a heater, water heater, or extension lead, and the bin relocated on camera, with nothing left stored directly on the floor.
Shots
  • Macro on a fixing being driven into structural framing behind the wall skin.
  • Three quarter of the rack reloading with the heaviest boards going in low.
  • Close on the scuff arc on the floor where a sheet has slid, then a small panel released at a shallow lean, locked off from the side.
  • Close on a mid stack board being pulled and the boards above it shifting.
  • Three quarter of the offcut bin being moved away from a heater.
On-screen text
  • Into framing, not wall skin
  • Heaviest at the bottom
  • Steep lean or on edge
Short cut · 30–45s A torch picks out a long curved scuff on a shop floor, then a panel leaned at the same shallow angle lets go and slides flat across it.
Stands alone: Establish the shallow lean as the cause and show the corrected on edge storage in the same clip, so the Short teaches rather than just alarms.
Standardize Marks on the rack and on the bin that make the right state readable without thinking.
Beats
  • Lengths marked on the rack rails so stock returns to the right bay rather than the nearest bay.
  • The size floor written large and permanently on the front of the offcut bin, so the rule outlives the day you set it.
  • A fill line marked above which the bin counts as full, then the moment of crossing it demonstrated, with the shortest piece coming out as the newest goes in.
  • The pair explained working together, the size floor governing what comes in and the fill line governing what goes out, which is the whole reason the pile stops growing.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing lengths onto a rack rail.
  • Close on the size floor being written large across the bin front.
  • Macro on a fill line drawn inside and outside the bin.
  • Overhead of the bin at its fill line with one short piece being lifted out.
On-screen text
  • Lengths on the rails
  • Size floor in, fill line out
Short cut · 30–45s An offcut bin reaches the line marked on its inside wall, and a hand immediately pulls the shortest piece out of it.
Stands alone: Name both limits and which direction each one controls, into the bin and out of it, since the removal is baffling without the pair.
Sustain Offcuts get their verdict before the saw gets unplugged.
Beats
  • The end of a cutting session shown as it really looks, fresh offcuts scattered across the bench and around the saw on the floor.
  • The trigger given its motion, every offcut going into the bin or into the fire bucket before the saw is unplugged, and never onto the bench, the floor, or the top of the rack.
  • The rule applied live to fresh cuts against the size floor already written on the bin, so it works at speed rather than only during a reset.
  • The third destination handled for pieces that cannot burn, coated and treated stock going to its own marked tub rather than the fire bucket, then the plug leaving the socket over a clear floor.
Shots
  • Overhead of fresh offcuts on the bench after a cutting session.
  • Close on a hand measuring a fresh cut against the size floor written on the bin.
  • Three quarter of pieces dropping into the bin and into the fire bucket.
  • Close on treated scrap going into its separate marked tub.
  • Close on the saw plug leaving the socket with a clear floor behind it.
On-screen text
  • Verdict before unplug
  • Never on top of the rack
Short cut · 30–45s Fresh offcuts get held against a line written on the side of a bin and dropped into one of two containers, all before a saw plug leaves the wall.
Stands alone: State the trigger, that the saw does not get unplugged until every offcut has a verdict, or the sequence just looks like ordinary tidying up.
Close

Wide of the finished rack, boards lying flat and supported along their length with the longest and heaviest at the bottom, sheet goods standing on edge against the wall, the offcut bin with its size floor written on the front and its fill line marked, nothing stored directly on the floor, and the route from the bench to the door clear along its full width. State the standard, one offcut bin with a written size floor and a fill line, then show the trigger, the saw plug coming out after the last offcut lands.

Next: Everything so far has been solid and inert. The last zone in this room is the one that can start a fire with nothing touching it, the finishing and chemical cabinet, and the wall of half used paint inside it.

Shot list
  • Wide side on of the full rack for loading, sagging, and reload sequences.
  • Overhead bench setup for offcut sorting and forearm measuring.
  • Macro setup for marker lines on rails and bin faces.
  • Clamped torch and macro setup for the gap behind the rack.
  • Locked off side angle for the shallow lean panel demonstration and floor scuff.
  • Locked off floor level shot down the bench to door route.
  • Close on framing fixings going in behind the wall skin.
  • Saw plug and floor clearance shot for the closing trigger.
  • Separate marked tub shot for treated and coated scrap.
Description hook

The offcut pile never shrinks because every piece in it is genuinely good wood. Two written limits, a size floor and a fill line, make the decision for you, plus how to store boards and sheets so nothing slides or sags.

MZ-094 · R16.06

Finishing and Chemical Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Dated, separated, lidded”

Finishing Cabinet: Dated Lids, Separated Shelves, Rags in a Metal Can

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the row of part cans, lids crusted shut, masking tape labels naming rooms in a house you no longer live in. Work a lid off to show what is actually inside, a skin across the top and half an inch of solids under it. Name what you are really storing, which is the possibility of a touch up, and that almost none of this will still brush out matching in two years. Then name the second failure hiding in the same zone, the box of condemned paint that will sit by the door for a month, which is the same problem simply relocated.

Sort Open and judge every container, and take the failures to household hazardous waste the same day.
Beats
  • Every container opened on camera and judged by what it does rather than how full it is, with a thick skin or a sour smell being the end of that tin.
  • Wood glue run out onto a scrap to show it gone stringy or granular, which means it will not hold a joint, which means it is no longer glue.
  • A half bottle of polyurethane tipped fully and held, with nothing moving, cured solid.
  • The wall of paint call run properly, keeping only colours currently on a surface in this house, and keeping them well, one small sealed jar of each labeled with the room and the finish rather than the original half empty tin sitting open to the air.
  • The disposal rule given in full and acted on, all of it to household hazardous waste, never the bin and never the drain, on the same day it gets sorted.
Shots
  • Overhead of a lid coming off to reveal a thick skin across the paint surface.
  • Macro of stringy glue being drawn out on a stick until it breaks.
  • Close on a half bottle of cured finish tipped fully with nothing moving inside.
  • Close on paint being decanted into a small jar and labeled with room and finish.
  • Three quarter of condemned containers going into a crate and the crate leaving through the door.
On-screen text
  • Skin or sour, it is finished
  • Same day, hazardous waste
Short cut · 30–45s A lid comes off a tin of old paint to reveal a thick rubbery skin, and a stick lifts the whole sheet out in one piece.
Stands alone: Say this is workshop paint storage and give the keep rule, only colours currently on a surface in this house, so the reveal ends in a decision rather than a gross out.
Straighten Placement here is entirely about keeping apart the things that must never meet.
Beats
  • Shelves assigned physically, solvents and thinners on their own shelf, water based finishes on another, said out loud as each one lands.
  • Hardeners carried deliberately away from the resins they cure, with the reason stated as the move happens.
  • Stir sticks and brushes for each family stored with that family, so the wrong brush never travels between shelves.
  • The whole layout closed inside the metal cabinet, with a drip tray slid under the solvent shelf as part of the arrangement rather than an afterthought.
Shots
  • Three quarter of the open metal cabinet with shelves being loaded family by family.
  • Close on hardeners being carried to a separate shelf from their resins.
  • Close on stir sticks and brushes going into a holder on their matching shelf.
  • Overhead of a drip tray sliding under the solvent shelf.
On-screen text
  • Solvents on their own shelf
  • Hardeners away from resins
Short cut · 30–45s Two containers get deliberately set down on separate shelves of a metal cabinet, and the hand pauses in the gap between them.
Stands alone: Name exactly what is being kept apart and why, solvents from water based finishes and hardeners from the resins they cure, since the pause means nothing on its own.
Shine Cleaning here is what keeps the product usable, starting with the rim of the can.
Beats
  • The rim of a can wiped clear before the lid goes back on, with the mechanism given directly, that a rim packed with dried finish is why the can skinned over in the first place.
  • A lid seated flush on a clean rim shown against one riding high on a crusted rim, with the gap visible.
  • Brushes cleaned right through to the ferrule, showing the finish that hides up there and what it does to the bristles by the next job.
  • The spill tray wiped back to bare metal last, so a fresh drip reads immediately instead of disappearing into old ones.
Shots
  • Macro on a rag clearing the rim groove of a paint can.
  • Close on a lid seating flush, then a lid riding high on a crusted rim.
  • Macro on a brush being worked clean up into the ferrule with colour running out.
  • Close on the spill tray wiped back to bare metal.
On-screen text
  • A crusted rim skins the can
  • Clean to the ferrule
Short cut · 30–45s Macro on a rag clearing packed dried finish out of the rim groove of a can, then the lid seating flush for the first time in years.
Stands alone: Explain that the crusted rim is why the paint inside skinned over, or this is a cleaning shot with no payoff.
Safety The rag that heats itself, and the things that must never share space with a flame or a drink bottle.
Beats
  • The fact stated plainly and then respected on camera, that a rag soaked in oil finish generates its own heat as it cures and can ignite with nothing touching it.
  • Both acceptable endings for that rag shown, into a lidded metal can or spread flat outdoors to dry, alongside the wrong endings, balled in a bin liner or draped over the bench.
  • The gap between the flammable liquids and the water heater flame walked and measured by hand from a locked off wide, then anything within reach of the pilot relocated.
  • Ventilation opened as the first action of a finishing job rather than the last, the door and window going wide before a lid comes off.
  • The poison, choke, or strangle question handled head on, thinner in an unlabeled drink bottle emptied back into a labeled container and the bottle cut open and binned, framed by the line find it, and fix it now. Point to Chapter 22, prevent and prepare.
Shots
  • Close on an oil finish rag dropping into a self closing metal can and the lid falling shut.
  • Overhead of rags spread flat on a concrete slab outdoors.
  • Close on a rag balled up in a bin liner, then lifted straight back out.
  • Locked off wide showing the solvent shelf and the water heater flame in one frame with a hand measuring the gap.
  • Close on a drink bottle of thinner emptied into a labeled container, then cut open.
On-screen text
  • Oil rags heat themselves
  • Lidded metal can, lid down
  • Never a drink bottle
Short cut · 30–45s An oil finish rag drops into a metal can and the self closing lid falls shut behind it in one motion.
Stands alone: State that oil finish rags generate their own heat while curing and can ignite with nothing touching them, because the closing lid carries the whole message and needs the reason.
Standardize Dates on every container and the shelf layout written where you read it while putting things away.
Beats
  • Every container dated with a marker the day it arrives, with the date going onto the lid so it reads from above without anything being lifted.
  • The shelf layout written on the inside of the cabinet door, and why that spot specifically, because it faces you at the exact moment you are putting things away in a hurry.
  • A hurried put away run against the written layout, so the solvents and the water based finishes stay apart even when you are not thinking about it.
  • The standard restated in the zone's own words, original containers, dated lids, incompatibles on separate shelves, and rags in a lidded metal can.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing a date across a can lid.
  • Overhead of a shelf of lids, every date readable from above.
  • Close on the layout being written onto the inside face of the cabinet door.
  • Three quarter of a hurried put away with the door layout in frame.
On-screen text
  • Date the lid, not the side
  • Layout on the inside of the door
Short cut · 30–45s Overhead on a shelf of finish cans where every lid carries a date written large enough to read without lifting a thing.
Stands alone: Say the date goes on the day the container arrives and why it lives on the lid rather than the side, since the overhead only shows the result.
Sustain The brush under the tap is what cues the date check and the rag.
Beats
  • The natural end of a finishing job shown first, the brush going under the tap, which is the one thing you already do every single time.
  • The other two actions attached to it and run in sequence, the can lid date checked and the rag going into the metal can with the lid down.
  • Why this trigger works rather than a reminder, because washing the brush happens at the exact moment the rag and the can are both already in your hands.
  • The cabinet closed on the finished state with the layout card facing out, ending the room where it started, on things that cannot hurt you while you are not there.
Shots
  • Close on a brush going under a running tap.
  • Close on a wet hand checking the marker date on a can lid.
  • Close on the rag going into the metal can and the lid dropping shut.
  • Three quarter of the cabinet door closing on the dated, separated shelves.
On-screen text
  • Brush under the tap
  • Rag in the can, lid down
Short cut · 30–45s A brush goes under a running tap and, without a pause, the other hand drops an oil finish rag into a metal can and lets the lid fall.
Stands alone: Name the trigger relationship explicitly, that washing the brush is what cues the rag and the date check, or the two actions look unrelated.
Close

Open the cabinet slowly for the final state, every product in its original labeled container, each lid dated in marker, water based paint on one shelf and solvents and thinners on another, a drip tray under the solvent shelf, the layout written on the inside of the door, and the self closing metal can standing beside it with the lid down. State the standard, then show the trigger once, the brush under the tap with the rag going in the can and the lid dropping.

Next: That is all six zones in the workshop, from the glasses at the door to the cabinet that has to be safe while nobody is in the room. The next room in the series is the garage, starting with the bay you cannot park in.

Shot list
  • Three quarter at the open metal cabinet for shelf assignment and the final reveal.
  • Overhead bench setup for opening and judging containers.
  • Macro setup for skins, stringy glue, rim grooves, and marker dates.
  • Outdoor concrete slab setup for rags spread flat to dry.
  • Close setup on the self closing metal can and its lid.
  • Locked off wide covering the solvent shelf and the water heater flame together.
  • Sink setup for brush washing and the paired trigger actions.
  • Inside cabinet door shot for the written layout.
Description hook

This is the one zone in the house that can start a fire with nothing touching it, so it gets dated lids, separated shelves, and a lidded metal can. Plus a narrow keep rule for the wall of half used paint and a disposal trip on the same day.
