Room 17 of 20

Mudroom

6 videos · 36 Shorts
Production noteShoot the whole room in one daylight block, mid-morning, when light comes through the outside door and reads as weather rather than lamp light. No lights and no rig: the only two camera positions are a tripod with the centre column reversed or set high and angled straight down over the bench, tray and floor, and a three-quarter position backed into the adjoining hall doorway shooting along the wall run. Where a shot needs raking light, do not add a lamp, move the tripod so window light skims the surface and shoot that setup while the sun is in the right part of the sky. Wedge the outside door or take it off its catch, because a swinging door clips the frame on every wide shot. Wet floor is the real hazard on set: shoot the slip and wet sole sequences with the tray in place and dry the floor between takes rather than letting water sit under the tripod legs. Anything mains powered, the vacuum or a boot dryer, gets its flex run behind the tripod and out of the wet zone before the camera rolls. The failing hook demonstration is staged, not real: use a pre-started screw in an offcut clamped at the same height, never the live wall carrying the family's coats, and hang loaded coats only on fixings you have already found a stud or an anchor for. Keep hands the only human element in frame, sleeves pushed above the wrist, and where a shot calls for a child's reach, mark the height on the wall with tape and shoot a hand entering low rather than staging a second person. Record voiceover separately, since this room echoes off hard floor and bare wall.
MZ-095 · R17.01

Family Hook Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “One Column Per Person”

Mudroom Hook Wall: One Coat, One Bag, One Hat Per Person

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a hook rail carrying a stack four coats deep, then have hands dig out the good coat buried in the middle of it, the one not worn since March, cuff still dry. Set the real decision against that coat rather than the ugly one nobody would miss: it holds a hook because carrying it upstairs feels like admitting the season changed. State what the video settles, which coats have earned a hook this week and which are simply not entitled to one.

Sort Every coat, bag, hat and scarf comes off this wall into one pile, and each item goes to its owner to keep or release rather than being judged by whoever is running the session.
Beats
  • Strip the entire rail into one heap on the floor, then hold on the bare wall so the load the rail was carrying is visible before anything goes back.
  • Show hands passing single items out of the heap toward owners off frame, and give the reason handing beats sorting alone, only the person who wears the coat can say whether they still wear it.
  • Work the release test: anything nobody has worn since the last change of season leaves the door and goes up to a wardrobe, a move upstairs and not a bin bag.
  • Set out the week-long version for anyone who cannot decide today, hang everything, then take down whatever is still hanging exactly as you left it seven days later.
  • Give the tiebreaker for two coats that feel equal, keep the one that survives rain.
Shots
  • Overhead of the full heap on the floor with the emptied rail just in frame at the top
  • Static three-quarter from the hall doorway holding on the bare wall and empty hooks
  • Close on hands lifting one coat clear of the heap and extending it out of frame
  • Macro on a bone-dry sleeve cuff beside a still-damp one, showing which coat has actually been worn
On-screen text
  • Everything off the wall
  • Hand it to its owner
  • Untouched for a week means upstairs
Short cut · 45–60s Hands pull coats off one hook, one after another, and the count keeps going well past what the first frame led you to expect.
Stands alone: Open by naming this as a mudroom hook wall and stating the rule being tested, whether a coat has earned a hook at all, because the Short starts mid-strip with no room context.
Straighten The shared rail becomes a vertical column per person, hooks set at each person's own reach, bag low and coat high.
Beats
  • Reframe the wall from one horizontal rail everyone shares into vertical columns, one per person, and give the failure it fixes, a shared rail fills from whichever end the tallest person reaches first.
  • Set the lowest hooks at the height of the shortest person in the house, marked on the wall with tape before any hook goes in, so a child never has to ask an adult for their own coat.
  • Demonstrate the stacking order on one column, bag on the lower hook and coat on the upper, so a backpack is never lifted over a wet jacket.
  • Load two columns and hold the finished state, with bare floor running the whole length of wall beneath the hooks.
Shots
  • Static three-quarter along the wall run showing columns rather than a single continuous line
  • Close on the taped reach mark, then a hand entering low in frame and taking a coat off that hook without stretching
  • Close on a bag lifting off the low hook, clear of the coat hanging above it
  • Overhead of the empty floor strip directly beneath the loaded hooks
On-screen text
  • A column, not a rail
  • Set hooks to the shortest reach
  • Bag low, coat high
Short cut · 30–45s A hand reaches straight up at a height marked in tape on the wall and takes a coat down without a stretch, then the frame widens to show the hook was deliberately set that low.
Stands alone: Name the mudroom hook wall and state the column idea in the opening beat, since the Short shows the result of a layout choice the parent video spends longer building.
Shine The grey shoulder smear on the wall behind the rail and the grit strip directly under the hooks, both dealt with while the wall is bare.
Beats
  • Position the camera so window light skims the wall behind the empty rail, making the grey mark left by shoulders and sleeves readable on camera.
  • Wipe the rail top and the wall behind it, and give the reason this happens now, the wall is bare exactly once in this session.
  • Vacuum the narrow strip of floor directly under the hooks and show what comes up, hood fluff, dropped hair bands and door grit.
  • Turn cleaning into inspecting: with the rail wiped and bare, loose screws and cracked plaster around the fixings are visible, which is what the next segment acts on.
Shots
  • Static three-quarter with window light raking across the wall, smear visible before the cloth
  • Close on hands wiping the rail top and the plaster directly behind it
  • Overhead of the vacuum head running the narrow floor strip beneath the hooks
  • Macro on the collected hood fluff and door grit
On-screen text
  • Clean while the wall is empty
  • Clean to inspect
Short cut · 30–45s Window light rakes across a stretch of bare wall and a grey shoulder-height smear appears that nobody in the house had ever noticed.
Stands alone: Establish in the first frames that this is a coat hook wall stripped bare, and that the smear is coat shoulders, otherwise the shot reads as an ordinary wall wipe.
Safety Hook fixings that will not hold wet coats, dangling scarf ends at the height a small child plays, and dropped bags sitting in the walking line from the door.
Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as fall, cut, or crush: a hook carrying four wet coats and the screw that pulls straight out of plasterboard, bringing the rail down at head height. Stage this on a clamped offcut, not the live wall.
  • Check every fixing before the wall is reloaded, showing a stud detector finding the timber and a proper anchor going in where there is none.
  • Frame the second as poison, choke, or strangle: scarf ends, coat cords and drawstrings hanging at toddler height, and move them off the lowest hooks onto the upper ones.
  • Frame the third as a fall: bags dropped under a full wall land in the walking line from the door, which is where people go over in the dark. Clear the line and hold on it bare.
  • Close by driving the anchor and clearing the line on camera rather than listing them, and quote the rule line as the reason nothing here waits.
Shots
  • Macro on a screw pulling free of plasterboard with the crumbled hole edge visible, staged on a clamped offcut
  • Close on hands finding a stud and driving a proper anchor into the wall
  • Close on a scarf end swinging at low height, then the same hook cleared
  • Overhead of the walking line from the door, bags in it, then bare
On-screen text
  • Stud or anchor, every hook
  • Nothing hanging at toddler height
  • Find it, and fix it now
Short cut · 30–45s A loaded coat hook is pulled and the screw comes out of the plasterboard with the rail still hanging off it.
Stands alone: State up front that this is a family coat rail and that four wet coats weigh more than the plasterboard was built to hold, since the Short has no room for the reload and anchor sequence.
Standardize A name on every column at that person's own eye height, and the limit said out loud so the whole house hears the same three numbers.
Beats
  • Write each name onto its column at that person's own eye height and show the labels going on, low for a child and higher for an adult.
  • Give the reason the limit gets spoken as well as written, one coat, one bag, one hat, said out loud with everyone standing at the wall.
  • Quote the rule line as the reason the label exists at all, that a standard is the best way you know today, written down, which is why it can change when the weather does.
  • Hold on the finished wall so the named columns and the bare floor beneath them read as the reference picture for this room.
Shots
  • Close on a name label being written and fixed low on the wall at a child's eye height
  • Static three-quarter along the wall run showing every column named
  • Overhead of the finished run with the floor bare beneath it
On-screen text
  • One coat, one bag, one hat
  • Name at their eye height
Short cut · 30–45s A name label goes onto a coat wall at knee height, which looks like a mistake until the frame shows whose eye height that actually is.
Stands alone: State the one coat, one bag, one hat limit inside the Short, because a name on the wall means nothing without the number it is enforcing.
Sustain The check rides on hanging your own coat up at the end of the day, which already happens at this wall without anyone being asked.
Beats
  • Attach the check to something already happening, you hang your own coat at the end of the day, and while your hand is still on the hook you look along the run.
  • Show the correction it produces, moving a stray hat or bag from the wrong column back to its owner's, a few seconds of work that never becomes a chore.
  • Give the reason this trigger beats a reminder here, the coat comes off your shoulders whether or not anyone remembers the system.
  • Hold on the settled wall at the end of a day, columns named, floor bare.
Shots
  • Close on a hand hanging one coat, then a slow camera pan along the wall run at hook height
  • Close on a stray hat lifting off one column and going onto its owner's
  • Locked wide three-quarter of the settled wall at the end of a day
On-screen text
  • Trigger: hanging up your own coat
  • One move, then walk away
Short cut · 30–45s One coat goes onto a hook, one stray hat moves a single column along, and that is the entire daily upkeep of a family coat wall.
Stands alone: Show the named columns clearly in the opening frames so the correction reads correctly without the Standardize segment behind it.
Close

Land on the finished wall and state the standard as the house will live with it: one coat, one bag and one hat per named column, and the floor under the hooks stays empty. Show the trigger once in real use, a coat going up at the end of the day and a single stray moving back to its owner's column, then point to Chapter 14, visual controls, for readers who want the labelling worked through properly.

Next: Tilt down from the settled hooks to the bench directly beneath them, still carrying everything the wall would not hold, and name it as the next zone.

  • Static three-quarter tripod backed into the hall doorway shooting the whole wall run, used for bare wall, columns and the finished state

Description hook

A mudroom hook wall fails for one reason, it holds every coat the family owns instead of the coats this week's weather calls for. Full 6S pass on one wall, hands only, including the rule that settles the fourth coat.

MZ-096 · R17.02

Bench and Transition Surface

5–7 min · thumbnail: “A Seat, Not Storage”

Mudroom Bench: Keeping the Seat Clear and Sorting the Storage Lid

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a hinged bench lid with a full seat sitting on top of it, then have hands try to lift the lid and fail, because the whole surface would have to come off first. Name the dodged decision plainly: the box under that lid is full and nobody in the house can say what is in it. Set up what the video tests, that storage under a seat you use several times a day is storage you will never open.

Sort The bench clears to bare wood in one go, and the strays get carried to their real rooms now rather than slid down to the far end.
Beats
  • Clear the whole surface in one continuous sweep down to bare wood, with no sorting piles allowed on the seat itself.
  • Show the failure this replaces, things sliding to the far end of the bench, and give the reason it fails, anything moved sideways sits there another month.
  • Carry the strays out of frame toward the rooms they belong in, and note that this walking is where most of a bench session actually goes.
  • Set up the lid question for later by opening the now-clear seat and looking inside without emptying it yet.
Shots
  • Overhead of the loaded bench, then the identical frame bare
  • Close on hands lifting a stack off the bench and out of frame rather than along it
  • Static three-quarter of the open lid with the seat finally clear
On-screen text
  • Bare wood in one go
  • Sideways is not away
Short cut · 30–45s Hands clear a bench seat in one continuous sweep, and the only rule on screen is that nothing is allowed to move sideways.
Stands alone: Name the bench and its actual job in the first line, a seat for dealing with footwear, so the sweep reads as protecting a seat rather than tidying a shelf.
Straighten The empty seat is the thing being stored, and the strays get exactly one outbound basket for what is genuinely leaving the house.
Beats
  • Treat the bare seat as the item being stored, wide enough for two people to lace boots at once, and name that as the layout decision rather than a tidiness one.
  • Bring in one labelled basket at the end of the bench and load it only with outbound items, library books, the parcel to return, the form waiting for a signature.
  • Draw the boundary: the basket takes things leaving the house, and anything that lives here permanently does not get to sit on this bench at all.
  • Show the finished surface carrying no more than three objects.
Shots
  • Overhead of the clear seat with a pair of boots set at each end, showing the width the rule protects
  • Close on the labelled outbound basket taking a parcel and a library book
  • Static three-quarter of the finished bench, seat empty, basket at the far end
On-screen text
  • The empty seat is the point
  • Outbound only
  • Three things maximum
Short cut · 30–45s A basket at the end of a mudroom bench takes a parcel and a library book, then a hand tries to put a jumper in and takes it straight back out.
Stands alone: State the outbound-only rule in the opening beat, because the entire Short turns on what the basket refuses rather than what it holds.
Shine The scuffed front edge where boot heels land, and the drift behind the bench that only appears once it is pulled away from the wall.
Beats
  • Wipe the seat and the front edge where boot heels scuff it, and show why that edge is the dirtiest part of the whole bench.
  • Pull the bench away from the wall and hold on what has collected behind it, the drift of grit, receipts and single socks.
  • Give the reason this is a move-the-furniture job rather than a wipe job, which is why it belongs to the reset and not the weekly clean.
  • Send the single socks toward the laundry rather than back under the bench.

  • Macro on the scuffed front edge before and after the cloth
  • Static three-quarter of the bench pulled clear of the wall, drift revealed
  • Overhead of the brush pulling grit, receipts and odd socks out into the open
On-screen text
  • The front edge takes the heels
  • Pull it out, not just wipe it
Short cut · 30–45s A bench is pulled away from a wall and a season of grit, receipts and odd socks is sitting in a line behind it.
Stands alone: Establish that the bench has just been cleared as part of a reset, so the reveal reads as a step in a job rather than a neglect callout.
Safety Heavy things stored above a bent head, a hinged lid that drops on fingers, and a covered seat that forces boots off standing on one leg.
Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as fall, cut, or crush: a bike helmet or a paint tin on the shelf directly above where a head bends to a bootlace, and clear that shelf on camera.
  • Show the second version of the same hazard, a heavy hinged bench lid dropping onto small fingers, and lower it under hand control instead of letting it fall.
  • Frame the third as a fall: a seat covered in bags means boots come off standing on one leg on wet floor, and shoot the wobble and the recovery framed on feet and floor only.
  • Separate the two reasons the seat stays clear, the tidiness reason given in Straighten and the safety reason given here, so they are not confused for each other.
Shots
  • Static three-quarter of the shelf directly above the seat, loaded, then cleared
  • Close on a hand controlling the lid all the way down to closed
  • Low frame on feet and floor only, one boot heel levered off on a shifting wet floor, then the same removal with both feet planted
On-screen text
  • Nothing heavy above a bent head
  • Lower the lid by hand
  • A clear seat is a safety rule
Short cut · 30–45s Framed on feet and wet floor only, a boot comes off with one foot shifting and skidding, then comes off again in half the time with both feet planted.
Stands alone: Say in the first line that the bench behind the shot is covered in bags, since the Short shows the consequence before the cause and the bags are the cause.
Standardize Three objects maximum on the surface, an outbound basket that empties on the next trip out, and a photograph of the cleared bench as the reference.
Beats
  • Set the two numbers plainly, three objects maximum on the surface, and the outbound basket empties on the next trip out of the door.
  • Photograph the cleared bench and tape the picture inside the nearest cupboard door, with the reason a picture settles arguments a written line cannot.
  • Show the picture in use, held up against the live bench to read the state at a glance.
  • Land the lid decision as its own written standard, refilled only with things used while sitting, spare laces, a shoe horn, a rag for wiping soles.
Shots
  • Overhead of the cleared bench being photographed on a phone
  • Close on the printed picture being taped inside a cupboard door
  • Close on the picture held up beside the real bench for comparison
  • Overhead of the lid box holding only laces, a shoe horn and a rag
On-screen text
  • Photograph the finished state
  • Three things, and the basket leaves
Short cut · 30–45s A phone photo of an empty mudroom bench gets taped inside a cupboard door, and that photo turns out to be the entire written standard.
Stands alone: Keep the real bench in shot beside the photo so the picture reads as a comparison tool rather than decoration.
Sustain The check rides on sitting down to change shoes, which happens at this exact surface several times a day.
Beats
  • Attach the check to sitting down to change your shoes, the one thing this bench exists for.
  • Show the move, one thing lifted off the bench and carried into the house as you stand, a single item and never a tidy-up.
  • Give the reason it is one item and not all of them, a rule you can do while already on your feet survives a bad week.
  • Return to the lid and set the honest month test, if it is still empty in a month you leave it empty.

  • Close on hands finishing a lace, then one object being lifted off the bench and out of the top of frame
  • Overhead of the bench holding one fewer object than the shot before

  • Trigger: sitting down to change shoes
  • One thing, on your way up
Short cut · 30–45s A lace gets tied, then one single object is lifted off a mudroom bench and carried away, and that is the whole rule.
Stands alone: Re-establish that the bench sits by the outside door and the object is going deeper into the house, not onto another surface nearby.
Close

Show the standard as the finished room states it, the seat is always clear and the surface never carries more than three things. Play the trigger once in real time, sitting to change shoes and lifting one object away on the way up, then point to Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo, for the reference picture taped inside the cupboard door.

Next: Tilt down from the clear seat to the boots piled underneath it and name the rack and tray as the next zone.

Mudroom Boots: Two Pairs Per Person and Where the Wet Tray Goes

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the rack holding the proper wellies with dust on the toes, the hiking boots worn twice, and the smart shoes for the event nobody went to. Name the reason none of them have been decided on, they are expensive and undamaged, so every pair keeps getting a pass. Set up the split the video runs on, keeping a pair and giving it a slot at the door are two separate decisions, and only the second one is settled here.

Sort Every pair in the house comes down to this floor and gets matched, with out-of-season pairs going up to wardrobes rather than back onto the rack.
Beats
  • Bring every pair in the house down to this floor, including the ones under beds and in car boots, and match them into pairs across the floor.
  • Show the three categories that leave today, outgrown pairs, split soles and unmatched singles, physically separated from the rest.
  • Move anything for the opposite season up to its owner's wardrobe, with the reason, the rack is for the season you are actually in.
  • Give the door rule as the sorting test, a pair earns a slot only if it has been on someone's feet in the last four weeks.
  • Show a slip with today's date going into the toe of a pair nobody can decide about, so the calendar makes the call instead of an argument.

Straighten One row per person, heaviest at the bottom, and caked boots restricted to the tray so dried mud never drops onto the pair below.
Beats
  • Give each person their own row, with the reason, a shared rack fills from whichever end is nearest the door.
  • Put heaviest boots on the bottom row so nobody lifts them and lightest slippers on top, then show the lift each choice avoids.
  • Show the mud rule failure first, a caked walking boot on a shelf shedding dried mud onto the clean pair below, then move it down to the tray where it belongs.
  • Set the finished state, soles down and toes out, so a pair is identified without bending or turning it over.

Shine The tray gets tipped and washed rather than wiped, because dried mud in a tray turns to dust and walks back inside.
Beats
  • Tip the tray out onto the garden and wash it properly, with the reason, dried mud left in a tray turns to dust and gets walked straight back inside.
  • Wipe the rack rails, then vacuum the floor of the rack itself, where the grit the tray failed to catch lands and stays.
  • Show what comes out of the rack floor and connect it back to the tray's job, this is the same grit, one step further in.
  • Put the tray back and hold on it dry and empty, ready for the next wet pair.

Safety Wet soles on hard floor, a mains boot dryer sharing the wet zone, and studded cleats stored soles up at hand height.
Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as a fall: wet soles carried past the tray leave an invisible film on hard floor, right where everyone turns toward the kitchen.

  • Frame the second as water and electricity: a boot dryer or heated mat with its flex lying across the floor the wet boots drip onto, then lift the flex and the socket clear and dry.
  • Frame the third as fall, cut, or crush: studded cleats stored soles up on a low shelf, catching bare hands and feet at exactly the wrong height, then turn them soles down or move them to the tray.
  • Clear the line from the door to the bench completely, because a shoe left out in a dark hallway is what people fall over at night.

Mudroom Pet Station: Lead, Bags and Towel in One Grab, Treatments Above Reach

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a sack of dog food standing in the mudroom, then cut to the bowl sitting on the kitchen floor with a hand arriving carrying a scoop. Name the unasked question, the food is stored by this door only because that is the door the sack came in through, and every single meal costs somebody that walk. Set the boundary the video draws, this zone is for departures and arrivals, and feeding belongs wherever the bowl is.

Sort Every lead, collar, harness and chewed toy in this room comes out, and the walking kit narrows to the lead you genuinely use plus one spare.
Beats
  • Lay out every lead, collar, harness and chewed toy you can find in this room, including the ones hanging behind other things on the same hook.
  • Keep the lead you genuinely walk with plus one spare, and hold on how small that keep pile is next to the layout.
  • Release the outgrown collar, the harness that never fitted and the retired long line, and say plainly why a harness that never fitted will not start fitting.
  • Use the zone boundary as a sorting rule, anything to do with feeding, grooming or paperwork is not sorted here because it is leaving for the kitchen.

  • Overhead of every lead, collar and harness laid out in rows on the floor

Stands alone: Name the pet station by the door and state the one lead plus one spare rule inside the Short, since the layout shot alone reads as a general declutter.
Straighten The walking kit hangs as one connected unit so leaving is a single grab, and the towel and treats take positions decided by height.

  • Clip the lead to the collar and thread the bag roll on, then hang the whole assembly as one connected unit on a single hook.
  • Show the payoff directly, one hand taking the entire kit off the hook in a single movement instead of a search through three rooms.
  • Put the towel on top of the food bin within arm's reach of the door, so a filthy animal gets dealt with at the threshold rather than in the hall.
  • Put treats up high where a nose cannot reach, with the point that height is doing the work here and a lid would not.

Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as poison, choke, or strangle: spot-on flea treatment and worming tablets sitting in an open caddy at the same height as the waste bags a child is allowed to fetch.

  • Show the second version of the same question, a lead left hanging in a low loop, then coil it on its hook so no loop sits at a toddler's height.
  • Frame the third as a fall: a knocked water bowl on hard floor, right where people step in with wet soles, then move the bowl out of the entry line.

Land the standard as the house will keep it, lead, collar and a full bag roll hang together as one kit, and treatments stay behind a closed door above reach. Mudroom Gloves and Hats: One Bin Per Person, One Season in Reach

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the bag of unmatched single gloves being tipped out, one expensive ski glove landing on top with no partner. Name why that bag has survived three changeovers already, the other halves are in a coat pocket, a car door or the school lost property, and one of them cost real money. State what the video does about it, the bag stops getting another reprieve and gets a deadline instead.

Sort Every glove, mitten and hat goes onto the floor and gets matched, and the dates on the sun cream and insect repellent get read.
Beats
  • Tip every glove, mitten and hat onto the floor and match them into pairs, working the whole pile through before judging anything.
  • Put the singles into one bag and write today's date on it, then give the bag its rule, it lives through exactly one changeover.
  • Give the outcome the rule produces, whatever is still unmatched at the next pack goes, the good ski glove included, on the grounds that a right-hand glove on its own is not a glove.
  • Name the one exception worth making, a survivor that fits a child who will need a bigger pair by next winter anyway, and date that too.
  • Read the dates on the sun cream and the insect repellent, because a bottle opened two summers ago is no longer doing the job printed on the label.

  • Move umbrellas out of the bins and into a stand by the door, showing why, one wet umbrella soaks everything it lies against.

  • Frame the first hazard as poison, choke, or strangle: insect repellent and sun cream sitting in a low open bin a young child is actively encouraged to help themselves from.

MZ-100 · R17.06

Cleaning and Utility Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Everything Off The Floor”

Mudroom Cleaning Corner: Everything Hangs, Nothing Goes Back Wet

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on two vacuums sharing one corner, the older one parked in the good spot against the wall and the newer one standing in the walking line where everybody squeezes past it. Name why nobody has dealt with it, the old machine still works, roughly, and getting rid of something that works feels wasteful. Set the single question the video answers, whether that spare has ever actually covered for the machine you use every week.

Sort Every bottle comes out and gets read, four cleaners stay, and the last inch in the rest goes out by the disposal line printed on the label.
Beats
  • Line every bottle up on the floor and read them properly, including the ones with no label left on them.
  • Keep the four you actually reach for, the floor cleaner, the glass spray, the disinfectant and the pet stain remover, and stand them apart from the rest.
  • Send out the last inch in the six other bottles, following the disposal line printed on each label rather than pouring anything down a drain by guess.
  • Give the reason the time in this corner goes here, reading part-used bottles is slow, and skipping it is exactly what leaves unknowns in the caddy.
  • Set up the second vacuum question and give the test that decides it, whether the main machine ever broke down long enough that you went and got the old one out.
Shots
  • Overhead of every bottle lined up on the floor, labels turned toward camera
  • Close on hands turning a bottle to read the disposal line on the back
  • Macro on an unlabelled decanted bottle with cloudy contents
  • Static three-quarter of the four keepers standing apart from the outgoing group
On-screen text
  • Every bottle, read it
  • Four you actually use
  • Follow the label to dispose
Short cut · 30–45s Ten part-used cleaning bottles come out of a single mudroom corner and only four of them go back in.
Stands alone: State that all of these came out of one corner caddy, because the count against a single small container is the whole point of the shot.
Straighten Long-handled tools clip to the wall near their heads with bristles clear of the floor, and the vacuum parks flat against the wall.
Beats
  • Clip each long-handled tool near its head so the bristles hang clear of the floor and the handle points down.
  • Give the reason directly, a broom stood on its bristles bends them out of shape and holds on to whatever it swept last, and show a bent head beside a hanging one.
  • Park the vacuum flat against the wall instead of in the walking line, and show the difference in the width of path left through the corner.
  • Set the caddy with the four cleaners, each in its own labelled bottle, and hold on the finished corner with nothing standing on the floor.
Shots
  • Static three-quarter of the wall with broom, mop and dustpan clipped, heads hanging clear
  • Macro on a bent, splayed broom head held beside one that has been hanging
  • Overhead of the walking path through the corner, blocked, then clear
  • Close on the four labelled bottles going into the caddy
On-screen text
  • Clip near the head
  • Bristles never touch the floor
  • Nothing stands on the floor
Short cut · 30–45s A broom head that has spent a year standing on its bristles is held up next to one that has been hanging, and the splay is not subtle.
Stands alone: Name the wall clip as the fix and show the tool hanging from it, since the comparison alone tells you nothing about what to do instead.
Shine The mop dries fully before it goes back, the vacuum brush bar gets cut clear, and the dustpan is never stored loaded.
Beats
  • Rinse the mop head and show it hanging to dry fully before it goes back on its clip, with the rule, nothing goes back on a clip wet.
  • Cut the hair off the vacuum's brush bar with scissors, show what comes away, then show the bar turning freely by hand again.
  • Empty the dustpan rather than storing it loaded, with the point that a loaded pan means the last job was never actually finished.
  • Turn cleaning into inspecting, a stripped brush bar and a dry mop head are also the moment you notice a split ferrule, a cracked pan lip or a worn clip.
Shots
  • Close on the rinsed mop head hanging clear to dry
  • Macro on scissors running down the vacuum brush bar and hair coming away
  • Close on the freed brush bar being spun by hand
  • Overhead of the dustpan being emptied out, then hung
On-screen text
  • Nothing goes back wet
  • Cut the brush bar clear
  • Never store a loaded pan
Short cut · 30–45s Scissors run the length of a vacuum brush bar and a solid rope of hair comes away in one piece.
Stands alone: Say where this vacuum lives and that the cut happens during the reset, so the clip reads as a maintenance step inside a system rather than a satisfying one-off.
Safety Bleach never sharing a closed container with an ammonia-based cleaner, and a mains vacuum sharing this corner with wet boots and a damp mop.
Beats
  • Frame the first hazard as poison, choke, or strangle: bleach and an ammonia-based cleaner shut in one caddy, where a leaking cap mixes them into a gas you cannot get away from fast enough. Separate them and give bleach its own place.
  • Show the related version of the same question, decanted cleaners in unlabelled bottles at child height, then either label them properly or send them out.
  • Frame the second as water and electricity: this corner holds a mains vacuum beside wet boots and a damp mop, so socket and flex stay up off the floor and dry, shown being routed and clipped.
  • Frame the third as fall, cut, or crush: long-handled tools leaned against a wall instead of clipped slide sideways and come down across a doorway. Show the slide as a staged take, then the clip that ends it.
  • Close by getting bleach relocated and the flex clipped before the caddy is closed for the day, with the rule line over it.

  • Static three-quarter of a leaned broom sliding and landing across the doorway, staged take
On-screen text
  • Bleach stands alone
  • Flex and socket up and dry
  • Find it, and fix it now
Short cut · 30–45s Two ordinary cleaning bottles are lifted out of the same closed caddy, and the reason those two must never share a shut container is the whole clip.
Stands alone: Name both products by type and say the caddy was closed, since the hazard depends on a sealed box rather than an open shelf.
Standardize The vacuum parks inside a marked outline, every tool hangs, and the empty outline reads as a job in progress rather than a gap.
Beats
  • Paint or tape the vacuum's outline onto the floor, with the reason, a marked footprint tells you at a glance whether the machine is out or away.
  • State the corner rule in one line, nothing in this corner stands on the floor and nothing goes back on its clip wet.
  • Show the outline empty and read it correctly, a job in progress rather than a space waiting to be filled with something else.
  • Hold on the finished corner, tools clipped with heads clear, vacuum inside its outline, four labelled bottles in one caddy.
Shots
  • Close on tape or paint being laid down for the vacuum outline
  • Overhead of the empty outline with nothing standing in it
  • Static three-quarter of the finished corner from the hall doorway
On-screen text
  • Mark where the vacuum parks
  • Nothing on the floor, nothing back wet
Short cut · 30–45s Tape goes down on a floor in the outline of a vacuum, and the empty shape left behind turns out to be a status report.
Stands alone: Explain that the outline belongs to one specific machine, otherwise the empty shape reads as unused space rather than a machine currently in use.
Sustain The check rides on shaking out the door mats, which already happens and already sends you to this corner for the broom.
Beats
  • Attach the check to shaking the door mats out, a job that already sends you to this corner to fetch the broom.
  • Show the two-part move, the broom going back onto its clip and the mop head being felt for damp, both done with the tools already in hand.
  • Give the reason for feeling the mop rather than looking at it, a head that looks dry and is not is how the smell starts.
  • Hold on the corner in its settled state and quote the rule line, that you do not finish 6S, you keep it.
Shots
  • Static three-quarter of the mats being carried out to the door and shaken
  • Close on the broom going back onto its wall clip
  • Macro on a hand pressing into the mop head to test for damp
  • Locked wide three-quarter of the settled corner
On-screen text
  • Trigger: shaking out the door mats
  • Hang the broom, feel the mop
Short cut · 30–45s A mop head that looks completely dry gets pressed by hand and comes back damp, which is the one check this whole corner rests on.
Stands alone: Say the mop is being returned to its wall clip after the door mats were shaken, so the test has a moment in the day to belong to.
Close

Land the standard as written for this corner, every tool hangs with its head clear of the floor, nothing goes away wet, and bleach never shares a container with anything else. Show the trigger in real use, mats shaken, broom back on its clip, mop head pressed for damp, then point to Chapter 22, prevent and prepare, and close the room on the line that you do not finish 6S, you keep it.

Next: Pull back from the finished corner through the whole mudroom, hooks to bench to boots to pet station to gear shelf, and hand off to the next room in the series.

A mudroom cleaning corner fails in two ways, tools standing on the floor and bottles nobody has read in a year. Full 6S pass, hands only, including the single question that settles whether the second vacuum stays.

Room 18 of 20

Hall Closet

5 videos · 30 Shorts
Production noteThe hall closet is the hardest shoot in the house: deep, dark, and too narrow to stand a tripod inside. Shoot it as a hallway room rather than a closet. Pull the working shelf out onto a clean sheet on the hallway floor and film the sorting there in daylight from the nearest window or open front door, so the hands never need a light on them. Inside the closet, one small battery clip light bounced off the closet ceiling is enough, and it has to be bounced rather than aimed, because a light pointed at the boards throws the shelf lip as a hard shadow across everything stored under it. The tripod lives in the hallway at three-quarters to the open door for every wide setup, and a second tripod or a clamp arm carries the overhead for the floor sorting, repositioned by hand between setups rather than running at the same time. This is a one-person shoot with no assistant, so every slide, fall, and collapse is staged with the camera locked off and standing outside the fall line, then reset and repeated rather than caught once. Clear the hallway of shoes and cables before every take, because the same floor carries the walk-back trips and the shot. On-set safety: wedge the door open, since it swings into frame and into the lens; never stand a step stool in the doorway to reach the top shelf while the tripod blocks the way out; and film all battery and bleach material with every product capped and upright. Never have a bleach bottle and an ammonia cleaner open in the same frame, not even to demonstrate the hazard. No presenter appears anywhere in this room. Hands, objects, and shelf boards only.
MZ-101 · R18.01

Linen Shelf Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “Three sets. One grab.”

Hall Closet Linen Shelf: Three Sheet Sets Per Bed, Counted on the Label

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on hands sliding a crisp, clearly unused sheet set out from the very front of the shelf, checking the size on its band, setting it back in the same front position, then reaching behind it for a thinner, greyer set and carrying that one away to the bed. Establish the decision this whole zone turns on: a set too nice to use and too nice to give away is holding the easiest reach on the shelf while the beds get made from the worn ones behind it. Hold that unresolved.

Sort Every set is unfolded, because a folded bundle hides whether it is complete, whether the elastic still grips, and whether it fits a bed still in the house.
Beats
  • Strip the shelf onto a clean sheet on the hallway floor, showing that folded cotton stacked to the depth of an arm hides an entire back row, so nothing can be judged until the boards are bare.
  • Unfold one set fully and count the pieces against a bed size, working through the flat sheet whose fitted half never turned up and why it does not get to stay as a maybe.
  • Stretch and release the elastic at a fitted sheet corner, showing slack that has stopped gripping, and treat a sheet that lets go in the night as a fault rather than a spare.
  • Handle the towel that has been dry an hour and already smells sour, and explain why that is a leave decision rather than another wash.
  • Settle the good set from the cold open on camera: write a date on its band to put it on a bed this month, or move it to a memory box, on the reasoning that a keepsake does not get to hold a shelf you reach into every week.
Shots
  • Overhead of the floor sheet as stacks come off the shelf and spread into one flat layer
  • Three-quarter from the hallway of the emptied shelf, back wall visible, dust line along the lip
  • Close on hands unfolding one set and laying the pieces out to count them
  • Macro on slack elastic stretched and released at a fitted sheet corner
  • Close on a date being written on the band of the unused set as it leaves for the memory box
On-screen text
  • Unfold to know
  • Complete set or not
  • A date or a memory box
Short cut · 45–60s A folded bundle gets pulled apart on the hallway floor and turns out to be two pieces folded to look like a full set.
Stands alone: Open by naming the hall closet linen shelf and showing that every set came out onto the hallway floor first, because the reveal only lands if the viewer knows this was stored and counted as a complete set.
Straighten One folded footprint and each set nested inside its own pillowcase, so a bed change leaves the shelf as a single bundle.
Beats
  • Fold one set to a chosen footprint, then match every other set to it, showing how a shared footprint is what makes the stack stable and the shelf countable at a glance.
  • Nest the folded set inside one of its own pillowcases and square the bundle, so a bed change leaves the shelf as one object rather than four separate finds.
  • Load the shelf by height band, queen and king low, everyday towels at chest height, guest blankets on top, with the placement following how often a hand comes for it and how much it weighs.
Shots
  • Overhead timelapse of one full set folded down to a single flat footprint
  • Close on hands sliding the folded set into its own pillowcase and squaring the corners
  • Macro on two finished bundles side by side, footprints matching

  • One grab, not four
Short cut · 30–45s A whole sheet set gets folded down and posted inside its own pillowcase, then comes off the shelf later as one square bundle.
Stands alone: Say in the first beat that this is a hall closet linen shelf and that the bundle is a complete set for one bed, since the whole payoff is that a bed change becomes a single trip.
Shine Clean to inspect: the boards are wiped and fully dry before linen returns, and the grey line on the lip is read as information about the sheets stored under it.
Beats
  • Wipe the bare boards with a barely damp cloth, working through the fact that towels put away not quite dry have been leaving moisture in this closed board for months.
  • Hold on the drying board with the back of a hand testing it for coolness, and explain that folded cotton onto a cool board is where mustiness in the sheets you sleep on begins.
  • Point out the grey line along the shelf lip and follow where it has been falling, onto the top set of the stack that stood directly underneath it.

Stands alone: State that this is where the household sheets and towels are kept, so the dust line reads as something landing on clean linen rather than as a dirty shelf.
Safety The fall question here: a chest-high stack comes down as one mass, and the brackets are carrying more folded cotton than they look like they are.
Beats
  • Tug the bottom towel out of a chest-high stack and let the whole pile come down onto the floor sheet, which is the fall question this zone actually poses.
  • Set a strip of tape on the closet upright at forearm height and use it as the stack limit from then on, so the cap lives on the wall as a visual control rather than in someone's memory.
  • Bring the heavy blankets down from the top shelf to waist height, on the reasoning that a folded wool blanket carries more weight than its size suggests and height is what turns a drop into an injury.
  • Check the bracket screws while the boards are bare, showing the difference between a screw landing in a stud and one turning freely in plasterboard.

  • Close on tape being set on the closet upright as the stack height limit

  • Tape marks the limit

Short cut · 30–45s A hand pulls one towel from the bottom of a chest-high stack and the entire pile comes down in a single movement.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a linen shelf sitting above chest height in a hall closet, because the collapse only reads as a hazard once the height is clear.
Standardize The shelf label carries the count as well as the size, so a shortage shows up while you are looking at the shelf rather than at bedtime.
Beats
  • Write a label carrying the bed size and the number of sets together, and fix it to the shelf lip directly under its own bundles.
  • Show the mismatch doing its work: a label reading three sets with only two bundles standing above it and bare board beside them.

Sustain Stripping a bed already brings you to this shelf, so the count gets read inside a trip that already happens.
Beats
  • Follow the habit that already exists: a bed comes off on laundry day, the hand arrives at this shelf for a fresh bundle, and the label appears as the bundle lifts.
  • Amend the count on the label in the same movement as the lift, with the reading tied to the trip rather than to a reminder.

Cleaning Equipment Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Handles on the rail”

Hall Closet Cleaning Tools: Handles on a Rail, Vacuum in a Taped Outline

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on the closet door swinging in and catching a leaning broom, which slides down the wall and lands across the doorway. Track back to what put it there: an old vacuum with a split hose standing in the corner, kept because scrapping a machine that mostly runs feels wasteful, occupying the only patch of floor the working machine could stand on. Show every handle in that corner leaning against something because the floor they belong on is gone.

Sort Every tool is judged by its working end, and the broken vacuum gets a written repair date instead of another year of standing there.
Beats
  • Stand each handle up on the hallway floor and turn the working end to the window, since the handles are all sound and the verdict lives entirely in the head.
  • Sweep a short line of grit with the splayed broom and show it pushing rather than gathering, then repeat the same sweep with a straight-bristled head.
  • Try to twist the mop head off its plate and show it no longer releasing, which is what ends that tool.
  • Write a repair date on masking tape and press it onto the body of the broken vacuum, then set out the rule that follows: if the date passes with no part ordered, the repair was never going to happen and the machine goes for recycling.

  • Pushes, does not gather
  • A date on the tape

Straighten A rail, a taped footprint, and one attachment bag on the handle, so the corner empties and refills in one motion.
Beats

  • Lay tape around the vacuum's footprint on the closet floor and park the machine inside it, establishing the outline as the machine's home rather than decoration.
  • Gather every crevice tool and brush head into one bag, label it, and clip it to the vacuum handle, since attachments loose on a shelf are how a job gets done with the wrong nozzle.
  • Swing the door through its full arc at the end and show it touching nothing, which is the test of whether the layout worked.

Show the corner as the standard leaves it: handles hanging from the rail with heads clear of the floor, the vacuum parked inside its outline, attachments bagged on the handle, nothing in there wet. Then run the trigger once, the machine switched off after a clean and back inside the tape before anyone sits down.

Next: Next along, the shelf above this corner, where eleven part-used bottles are standing and two of them should never be stored side by side.

The cleaning tool corner of the hall closet, done the way the Micro Zone Manual sets it out: handles on a rail with the heads clear of the floor, the vacuum parked inside a taped outline, and its attachments bagged on the handle. Hands only, no presenter.

MZ-103 · R18.03

Cleaning Supply Zone

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Eleven bottles. One job.”

Hall Closet Cleaning Supplies: One Open Bottle Per Job

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open overhead as part-used bottles come out of one shelf and line up on the hallway floor: four glass cleaners, three floor sprays, and a scatter of others, not one of them full and not one of them empty. Establish the loop that built the line, that you buy a new one because you cannot see what is left in the old one, and the old one goes back onto a dark shelf where it disappears again. Land the real cost, that keeping all of them did not save money, it paid twice and then stored the evidence on the shelf you now need.

Sort Every bottle comes out to daylight, one open bottle per job gets applied to the survivors, and anything without a legible original label leaves.
Beats
  • Line every bottle up on the hallway floor in daylight with labels facing up, since a dark shelf at the depth of an arm is what hid four glass cleaners from each other.
  • Pour identical products together and stop there, with the limit stated plainly: only identical products are ever combined, and nothing else is mixed for any reason.
  • Apply one open bottle per job to what is left, keeping the fullest of each kind open and routing the rest out, and name the trade honestly, that a half bottle down the drain costs a little while keeping it costs the shelf.
  • Pick up the unmarked spray bottle nobody can identify and work through why it goes for disposal by its own instructions, which no longer exist, rather than down the nearest drain by guess.
  • Handle the specialty cleaner bought for one stain years ago and make the judgment on camera, that a product for a problem you no longer have is holding the easiest reach on the shelf.
Shots
  • Overhead of every bottle lined up on the hallway floor, labels facing up
  • Close on two identical bottles being poured into one
  • Close on hands turning an unmarked spray bottle, finding no identification anywhere on it
  • Three-quarter of the emptied shelf with its stained board showing
On-screen text
  • All of it, on the floor
  • Identical only
  • No label, no storage
Short cut · 30–45s Eleven part-used bottles come out of a single closet shelf and line up on a hallway floor, and four of them are the same glass cleaner.
Stands alone: Say at the top that these all came off one hall closet shelf, because the count and the duplicates are the entire content of the shot.
Straighten Caddies built by the room they serve, so the whole job leaves the closet in one hand instead of two trips.
Beats
  • Build the bathroom caddy and the kitchen caddy by room rather than by product type, so the grouping follows where the work happens instead of what the label says.
  • Load gloves and cloths in beside the sprays, since a glove kept in a drawer down the hall is why a job starts without one.
  • Lift a finished caddy in one hand and carry it out of frame, which is the test of whether the grouping is right, and note anything missing that would send you back.
  • Set the caddies down with their labeled ends squared to the door.
Shots
  • Overhead of two empty caddies filling, bottles going in by the room they serve
  • Close on gloves and cloths tucked in beside the sprays
  • Close framed tight on a caddy handle lifting and passing the camera, arm out of frame
  • Close on the labeled caddy ends squared up facing the door
On-screen text
  • Group by room
  • Gloves ride with the sprays
  • One hand, one trip
Short cut · 30–45s One caddy lifts off a closet shelf and the entire bathroom cleaning job leaves with it in a single trip.
Stands alone: Establish that the caddy is grouped by the room it serves and carries gloves and cloths as well as sprays, or the lift looks like ordinary tidying.
Shine The crusted ring comes off each bottle base, and a liner goes down so the next slow drip lands on plastic instead of the board.
Beats
  • Lift a bottle to reveal the crusted ring welded to the board underneath, then wipe the base before it goes back, since the ring forms on the bottle first.
  • Smooth a wipeable liner across the board, with its job being that the next slow drip lands on plastic instead of soaking into the wood.
  • Hold the lined section beside the bare stained patch and let the comparison make the argument for the liner.
Shots
  • Macro on a crusted ring at the base of a bottle, then the same base wiped clean
  • Close on a wipeable liner being smoothed across the shelf board
  • Three-quarter of the lined shelf beside the unlined stained section
On-screen text
  • Wipe the ring first
  • Drips land on plastic
Short cut · 30–45s A bottle lifts off a closet shelf and leaves a hard crusted ring welded to the board underneath it.
Stands alone: Say this bottle has been standing on a cleaning supply shelf for a long time, so the ring reads as built up over months rather than spilled that morning.
Safety Bleach and ammonia get separate shelves, everything stays in its original container, and the whole zone goes up out of reach or behind a latch.
Beats
  • Name the pairing and the reason, that chlorine bleach products and ammonia products can release a choking gas if they leak onto each other, then place the two types on clearly separate shelves, capped and upright, never open in the same frame.
  • Hold an original labeled container beside a decanted unmarked one and show what the label carries beyond the name, the disposal wording and the first aid wording, which is why the label is itself the safety control.
  • Raise the whole zone above a small child's reach or fit a latch, filmed from a low camera set at a child's eye height looking up from the hallway floor.
  • Move aerosol tins and solvent sprays off the closet wall that backs onto the boiler and onto the coolest shelf, framed as the burn or fire question in this zone.
Shots
  • Close on two capped products being placed on clearly separate shelves
  • Macro on an original label showing its instruction panel
  • Low camera at child eye height looking up at the raised shelf and its latch
  • Close on hands moving aerosol tins off a warm wall onto a cooler shelf
On-screen text
  • Bleach and ammonia apart
  • Original label only
  • Up high or behind a latch
Short cut · 45–60s Two capped bottles go onto two different shelves, and the reason is the one pair of household products that must never leak onto each other.
Stands alone: Name both product types and the gas risk in the opening seconds, because a Short about a hazard has to carry the hazard itself rather than point at a longer video.
Standardize Each caddy end reads its room, and one written line governs the shelf: a bottle without a legible original label is not stored.
Beats
  • Label each caddy end with the room it serves and check it reads from the open door without stepping in.
  • Write the one line rule and fix it where the bottles live, so the next incoming bottle is decided without anyone having to remember this video.
  • Run the rule once on a real case, the spray whose own drips have lifted the label off, following it out to disposal rather than back onto the board.
Shots
  • Macro on a marker writing a room name onto a caddy end
  • Close on the written rule card fixed at the shelf edge
  • Close on a bottle with a washed-away label being carried out rather than shelved
On-screen text
  • The room on the end
  • No legible label, not stored
Short cut · 30–45s A spray bottle whose own drips have dissolved its label gets carried out of the closet instead of put back on the shelf.
Stands alone: State that this shelf holds household cleaning products and that an unreadable label means nobody knows the disposal or first aid wording, which is what makes it unstorable.
Sustain Setting the caddy back is when the shortage gets noticed, and it goes on the list in the same movement.
Beats
  • Follow a caddy coming back to the shelf after a clean, with the hand registering the empty bottle standing in it as it lands.
  • Write the item on the list before the closet door shuts, with the trigger being the caddy landing rather than a later moment of remembering.
  • Close the door on a shelf where every caddy end faces out and nothing is left standing loose beside them.
Shots
  • Close on a caddy being set back on the shelf, empty bottle visible standing in it
  • Macro on the item being written onto the list at the closet
  • Three-quarter of the door closing on the finished shelf

  • Caddy lands, list gets written
  • Before the door shuts
Short cut · 30–45s A cleaning caddy comes back to the shelf with one empty bottle standing in it, and that bottle goes on the shopping list before the door shuts.
Stands alone: Establish that the caddy holds one room's whole cleaning job and has just come back from doing it, so the empty reads as a shortage rather than as rubbish.
Close

Show the standard holding: one caddy per room, one open bottle per job, original labels only, bleach and ammonia kept apart, and the whole zone up out of reach or behind a latch. Then run the trigger once, a caddy set back after a clean with whatever ran out written on the list in the same movement.

Next: Next along the closet, the reserve shelf of paper, bulbs, and batteries, and the two numbers that stop a warehouse pack blocking it again.

MZ-104 · R18.04

Paper and Household Backstock

7–9 min · thumbnail: “Min 6. Max 24.”

Hall Closet Backstock: Put a Minimum and a Maximum on the Shelf Edge

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on a shrink-wrapped warehouse pack being wrestled off the shelf in both hands, with everything behind it hidden until it is out and visible only once it is on the hallway floor. Establish the decision this zone turns on: the offer that made you buy twelve felt thrifty right up to the point where the pack blocked the shelf, and then you bought more anyway because you could not see past it. Land the test that settles it, that the maximum is whatever fits inside the bin without stacking above the rim, and a deal that will not fit the bin is not for you.

Sort The whole reserve comes out, and the batteries you cannot vouch for and the bulbs for fittings you replaced go now.
Beats
  • Take the lot out onto the hallway floor, on the reasoning that a reserve you cannot see the back of is not a reserve, it is a guess about what you own.
  • Separate the loose cells you cannot vouch for from the packaged ones, since an unknown battery is not stock, because you will never trust it in the one device that matters.
  • Hold a bulb up beside the fitting it was bought for and show it no longer matching anything in the house after the changeover to LED, which makes it stock for a house that no longer exists.
  • Take down the bulk paper towel pack that needs both hands and a step, and work through why size alone can disqualify stock you genuinely use.
Shots
  • Overhead of the whole reserve spread out across the hallway floor
  • Close on hands separating loose unlabelled cells from packaged ones
  • Macro on a bulb held beside the fitting it no longer matches
  • Three-quarter of the oversized pack coming down in both hands, the shelf behind it finally visible
On-screen text
  • All of it out
  • Cannot vouch for it, out
  • Too big to lift alone
Short cut · 30–45s A handful of loose batteries nobody in the house can vouch for gets pushed to one side, and not one of them counts as stock.
Stands alone: Say this is a hall closet reserve shelf holding paper, bulbs, and batteries, so the loose cells read as failed stock rather than as rubbish.
Straighten Store so the level is readable: rolls loose in a clear bin, bulbs boxed by fitting, cells standing by size, every label turned to the door.
Beats
  • Tip the toilet roll loose into a clear bin rather than leaving it in its wrapper, because the point is watching the level drop through the side.
  • Group the bulbs in their own boxes by fitting, with the box doing the labelling here, which is why it stays.
  • Stand the batteries upright in a shallow tray by size and read AAA from AA without lifting one out.
  • Place the heaviest packs at waist height and turn every label to the door, since a label facing the wall is not a label.

  • Overhead of bulb boxes grouped by fitting

  • Watch the level drop
  • Sizes readable without lifting
  • Labels to the door
Short cut · 30–45s Batteries stand upright in a shallow tray so AAA reads apart from AA without a single cell being picked up.
Stands alone: Establish that this is a household backstock shelf and that the cells stay in their original packs, since the packaging is doing safety work as well as labelling.
Shine Clean to inspect: the tray bottom and the underside of the paper packs report leaks and damp.
Beats
  • Wipe the shelf, then check the tray bottom for the white crust that means a cell has leaked, and follow what that crust tells you to do next.
  • Press the underside of a paper pack stored against a cold outside wall, feeling for damp before it goes back, since paper against cold masonry is where damp shows first.
  • Set a dry pack beside one that has been standing against the cold wall and let the touch test carry the difference.

  • White crust means a leak
  • Feel the underside

Stands alone: Say the tray lives on a hall closet backstock shelf and holds the household spare batteries, so the crust has a source the viewer can place.
Safety Loose cells short and heat, a button cell is exactly the size a small child swallows, and nothing is stored at floor level here.
Beats
  • Slide the loose cells back into their original packs rather than into a jar, working through what happens when terminals touch metal or each other and the cell heats up.
  • Place a button cell on the closet floor and film it from a low camera at a small child's eye height, letting the size of the cell against the floorboard carry the point about what gets swallowed.
  • Press tape across the terminals of a loose 9-volt, and explain why that shape in particular, with both terminals side by side, is the one that needs it.
  • Clear the floor level of the zone entirely, since emptying the bottom removes the reach as well as the roll.

  • Cells stay in their packs

Stands alone: State that this closet stores the household batteries and that loose cells roll off the shelf to the floor, since without that the shot is just an object on a floorboard.
Standardize The minimum and the maximum live on the shelf edge in front of each bin, not in anyone's head.
Beats
  • Write the minimum and the maximum on a card and fix it to the shelf edge in front of its bin, with the wording chosen so both numbers read at a glance.
  • Set out what each number does: below the minimum puts the item on the shopping list, and at the maximum you stop buying it regardless of the offer.
  • Derive the maximum from the bin itself, filling to the rim with nothing stacked above it, so the number comes from the space rather than out of the air.
  • Date a pack with a marker as it arrives, and follow the rule that comes with it, that the oldest gets pulled first.

Sustain Lifting the last item out of a bin is the moment you are below the minimum, and it goes on the list before you leave the hallway.
Beats
  • Follow the last roll lifting out of the bin, with the empty bin as the signal and the minimum on the card read in the same movement.
  • Write it on the list before leaving the hallway, since the trip to the closet is the only reliable moment to catch it.
  • Finish on the shelf with every label facing the door and both numbers readable from standing height.

Then run the trigger once, the last pack lifted out of a bin and the restock written on the shopping list on that same trip to the closet.

MZ-105 · R18.05

Seasonal and Guest Zone

9–12 min · thumbnail: “One bin per occasion”

Hall Closet Top Shelf: Seasonal and Guest Bins, One Bin Per Occasion

Cold open · beat 1 of 3 · the problem

Open on hands resting on a lidded bin on the top shelf, sliding it forward to the edge, then pushing it back without lifting the lid. Establish the decision: this bin has survived a house move and two closet reshuffles, and nobody in the house can say what is inside it. Land the point cleanly, that the avoidance is itself the answer, and that a sealed bin of unknowns is not storage but a decision that keeps being paid for in shelf space.

Sort Every lid comes off on the floor in daylight, and each item has to be matched to a named occasion in the next twelve months.
Beats
  • Bring every bin down to the hallway floor and take every lid off in daylight, since the lid has been the thing holding these decisions shut.
  • Work item by item, naming the specific occasion in the next twelve months when each one will be used, a birthday, a holiday, a trip already booked, and show a vague someday failing the test.
  • Take the obvious leaves on camera, decorations for a tree no longer put up and the guest pillow gone flat and yellow held beside a fresh one.
  • Open the bin marked misc and apply the test, that contents you cannot name without looking do not get the lid back on, then set that lid aside rather than reusing it.
Shots
  • Three-quarter of bins coming down onto the hallway floor, lids off in a row
  • Overhead of one bin's contents spread out in daylight
  • Close on a flattened yellowed guest pillow held up against a fresh one
  • Close on a lid marked misc being set aside rather than reused
On-screen text
  • Lids off, on the floor
  • Name the occasion
  • No occasion, no lid
Short cut · 45–60s A lid comes off a bin that has survived a house move and two closet reshuffles, and nobody in the house could say what was inside.
Stands alone: Establish that this is the top shelf of a hall closet holding seasonal and guest storage, so the unopened bin reads as a stored decision rather than as ordinary clutter.
Straighten One bin per occasion rather than one bin per overflow, with a shelf map taped inside the door.
Beats
  • Rebuild the bins one per occasion, drawing the distinction that matters, that a bin per overflow is exactly how a bin marked misc gets created in the first place.
  • Seal the guest pillows in a zip bag and place them with the guest bedding rather than beside the decorations they had ended up next to.
  • Draw the shelf map and tape it inside the door, with its real job being that you can send someone else for the guest bedding without the whole shelf coming down to find it.
  • Load the shelf so nothing sitting overhead is heavy enough to need both hands.
Shots
  • Overhead of contents being regrouped into occasion bins on the floor
  • Close on a guest pillow going into a zip bag and the seal closing
  • Macro on the shelf map being drawn, then taped to the inside of the door
  • Three-quarter of the upper shelf loaded with the map visible on the open door
On-screen text
  • One bin per occasion
  • Map inside the door
  • Nothing heavy overhead
Short cut · 30–45s A hand-drawn map goes up inside a closet door showing which lidded bin sits where on the shelf above.
Stands alone: Say this is the top shelf of a hall closet stacked with lidded seasonal bins, since the map means nothing without the stack it describes.
Shine Guest bedding is washed before it goes into the bin, and every bin gets checked at the base before anything goes back in.
Beats
  • Put washed guest bedding straight into the bin from the laundry basket, because the smell a guest notices comes from the year the bedding spent sealed in a box, not from the bed it was made with.
  • Take the dust off each open lid with a cloth, showing how much comes off one that has been sitting under other bins.
  • Tip each bin toward the light and check the base by nose as well as by eye, since mustiness at the bottom means something went in damp last season and the bin has been holding it since.

  • Wash before, not after
  • Check the bottom
  • Nothing goes in damp
Short cut · 30–45s Guest bedding goes into the storage bin clean, because what a guest smells is the year it spent sealed in a box.
Stands alone: Establish that this bedding sits in a lidded bin on a closet shelf for months between visits, or the washing looks like an ordinary laundry step.
Safety Overhead bins and a proper step stool, because the lid blocks the view of the step waiting underneath.
Beats
  • Lift a loaded lidded bin down from above head height with the camera set at the lifter's eye line, so the lid fills the frame and the floor below is simply not there, which is the fall question in this zone.
  • Slide the heaviest bins down to chest height, on the reasoning that weight should come down at the level where the step is still in view.
  • Set a proper step stool inside the closet and show the top shelf coming into reach from its height, with a hallway chair ruled out plainly.
  • Load a bin unevenly and let the contents shift audibly mid-lift, showing where that weight travels and why the doorway gets cleared before anything comes down.

  • The lid hides your step

  • A stool, never a chair
Short cut · 30–45s A lidded bin comes down from above head height and the lid completely covers the step waiting underneath it.
Stands alone: State that these bins live on the top shelf of a hall closet and that some are heavy, so the blocked view reads as the hazard rather than as a framing choice.
Standardize Every bin carries its contents and the date it was last closed, with a photo of it packed taped inside the lid.
Beats
  • Write the contents and the date last closed onto each bin label, with the date being what tells you next year how long it has gone untouched.
  • Photograph each bin packed from directly above and tape the picture inside its own lid, so repacking has a target instead of a guess.
  • Run a repack against the photo, matching the layout piece by piece, so the standard is shown working rather than described.

  • Contents and date closed

Short cut · 30–45s A photo of a storage bin packed gets taped inside its own lid, so next year the repack has a target instead of a guess.
Stands alone: Establish that these are seasonal bins opened only a few times a year, which is exactly why the packing gets forgotten between one use and the next.
Sustain Stripping the guest bed after a visit is the trigger, and the bedding goes back to its own bin, never onto the linen shelf.
Beats
  • Follow the guest bed coming apart after a visit and the bedding going straight to the wash, with the end of the visit being the trigger already built into the house.
  • Return the washed bedding to its own labeled bin, holding the line that it never lands on the linen shelf where it would quietly join the everyday rotation.
  • Close the lid, update the date on the label, and shut the door on a shelf that matches its map.

Show the standard in place: every bin lidded, labeled with its contents and the date it was last closed, photographed inside the lid, stored clean and dry, with the shelf map taped to the door. Then run the trigger once, a guest bed stripped after a visit and the bedding washed and returned to its own bin before the closet door shuts.
